noun. a self-adjustable balls-up

FULLARTON There are three words in the Middle East soldiers' vocabulary describing the normal maladministration of an Army. A Tabu, an acrostic word, is typical Army ball-up', a <i>Sabu</i> is 'self-adjustable ball-up', a <i>Nabu</i> is anon-adjustable ball-up' eg be on the receiving end of a tabu. (1944,Troop Target,38)

[NOTES: ca1940 Les Cleveland (Also used during WW2).]

Another sack-bashing party that arrived on Sunday gave up. But at 11 o'clock we judged it safe to start. (Jul 1959,Tararua Tramper,1)

sacrifice paddock¶

noun.

The farming technique known as the sacrifice' paddock, in which one paddock on a farm is heavily stocked during the winter to save pastures elsewhere on the farm for use by cattle after calving was criticised by the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals in the Palmerston North Magistrates' Court today. ... in Dalefield's case it had been the stock rather than the paddock which had beensacrificed' (Aug 14, 1958,Christchurch Star-Sun,13)

sacrifice paddock n. N.Z. a grassed field which is allowed to be grazed completely, so that it can be cultivated and resown later. (1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1015) [NOTES: [nf. 1986 NZPOD; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 428]]

His practice of putting his herd in a "sacrifice" paddock is common among dairy farmers. Rather than damage all his farm moving his herd around in the mud, he opts to sacrifice poorly performing paddocks and later cultivate and resow them with a crop followed by new grass when the weather improves. (Sep 9, 2004,Dominion Post,C7)

noun. [Rural] a fenced area on which a farmer will bring in silage, hay or other feed to stock in very wet weather , causing the sward to be pugged and trampled.

We fed 118 cows for a full month on this crop, supplemented by a 'sacrifice' paddock adjoining.. In wet weather we left the cows in the sacrifice paddock and fed hay out to them. (Jun 10, 1958,NZ Dairy Exporter,29)

MCMEEKAN The 'sacrifice paddock' system of wintering would be employed for the feeding-out of hay and silage during winter. (1960,Grass to Milk,187)

I used to think sacrifice paddocks were bound to be very fertile the next year and the heavier the stocking, the richer they'd be. (Sep 10, 1970,NZ Farmer,61)

Fortunately, the herd had to walk some distance from a 'sacrifice' paddock to the barn through a shingle bottomed stream, which is a first-class indicator of founder, or overheating of the feet. (Sep 1973,NZ Journal of Agriculture,61)

Sacrifice paddocks with feeding racks on platforms on the race-side border may be worth considering. (Sep 27, 1973,NZ Farmer,7)

I intend to throw away the backing wire, revert to the old 1950s practice of a 'sacrifice paddock' on the bad grub areas and really trample hell out of them. (Jul 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,69)

MAF is encouraging farmers to watch their image after complaints from townies and tourists over cattle being held in muddy sacrifice paddocks. (Aug 1, 1996,NZ Farmer,4)

SADD¶

abbreviation. Students Against Driving Drunk

SADD (Students Against Driving Drunk) is an organisation run by students for students, to eliminate drinking and driving through education and positive peer influence.... I was surprised at how much SADD affected me. (Sep 2003,AA Directions,No. 57/11)

When I was at school, I worked for SADD (Students Against Drunk Driving). (Apr 2004,AA Directions,No. 59/31)

The future of anti-drink group Sadd is uncertain despite last-minute funding which has thrown the student lobby group a six-month lifeline. Students Against Driving Drunk, which has operated in New Zealand schools for 17 years, received $75,000 from the Road Safety Trust on Thursday.... Sadd operates in more than 80% of Kiwi high schools and is run mostly by students. It aims to raise awareness about the dangers of drinking and driving. (Nov 30, 2003,Sunday Star Times,A15)

noun.

noun. [Rural] a hunting rifle.

LEVY First came the tent and then the whare - the forerunner of so many homes of the hills - with its single room containing bunks of sacking - on a stay at the far end would be the saddle rifle. (1970,Grasslands of NZ,240)

noun. [Rural] a discomfort in a rider through movement in a saddle [especially when riding on steep country or when stirrups are too long, or girth is loosened slightly.]

FOSTER & WRIGHT The mincing comes from slight saddle slide. (1983,Stockman Country,12)

noun. a track across the saddle of a hill

Our first week's prospecting was north of the Government saddle track, without obtaining a single color for our trouble. (Sep 22, 1868,Evening Post,2)

The report of the Committee on the Hurunui saddle track was adopted. (Aug 17, 1872,West Coast Times,2)

Mr A. Thomson moved, and Mr Beuke seconded, that the Mines Department be applied to for GBP40 for each of the following - Chandler's to Wangapeka saddle track, Table Land track, Dove river to Baton saddle track. (Nov 24, 1892,Colonist (Nelson),3)

He must have crossed there by means of a saddle track from Seacliffe, a distance of 40 miles, in a southerly direction. (Nov 25, 1907,Poverty Bay Herald,5)

MARSHALL Letty has for days now been ... sneaking off. She's been getting rides on gravel trucks, ...'The Golightlys happened to see her today on the saddle track, and brought her home. ...' (1982,Master of Big Jingles,35)

verb. to join by or across a hill-saddle

... showing that the southern branch saddles with the Karangama [?], at a point to the Mount westward of Sefton. (1877,TrNZI,9/579) [NOTES: (S.H.Cox)]

HARDIE ... the pass at its head actually saddled with what appeared to be a tributary of the Hongu to the west. ... [?p] ... I wanted to examine the Hongu tributaries to confirm the suggestion that the Iswa saddled with the Hongu. (1957,In Highest Nepal,57)

(1958,Tararua,13/47) [NOTES: [get quot]]

saddleback¶

noun. a bird, the tieke

Oliver recorded the saddleback as having a peculiar association with whitehead; how two or more saddlebacks followed a flock of whiteheads and acted as guardians to it. (Jan 2002,NZ Geographic,No. 55/16)

A pair of those rare birds, the Saddleback (Creadion cinereus), were seen at work, busily seeking for grubs in the cracks and openings in the bark of the tree. (Jul 15, 1871,Otago Witness,17)

In those days the flitty and fragile North Island saddleback was confined to a single habitat. (Feb 1999,North & South,68)

Sad́.dle-bacḱ. (s&abreve.d́.d'l-b&abreve.k), n. .us:2. (Zoo.l.) [Add.] (d) A passerine bird of New Zealand (Creadion carunculatus), resembling the starling; - so called from the chestnut-coloured band of feathers on its back and wings. (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2030)

The birds and animals to be protected are as follow .. saddleback (tieke - Creadion carunculatus) ... (Aug 30, 1905,Otago Witness,13)

He there made his first acquaintance with a saddleback (Apr 27, 1922,Auckland Weekly News,15)

Fourteen pairs of saddlebacks, ground feeders, were released in February and at last report were thriving. (May 12, 1984,Listener (New Zealand Listener),23)

This makes them the first North Island saddleback to be hatched and successfully fledged in the wild, on the mainland, in over 100 years. (Jan 2, 2003,Capital Times,5)

adjective. [Rural] [of trousers] made of strong woollen twill fabric [teamed with tartan shirt and hobnailed boots as a high-country worker's 'uniform'].

NEWTON Even their working attire - the best of sports coats and saddle tweed trousers, which were in complete contrast to what I had been accustomed - set them apart. (1947,Wayleggo,34)

DAVIS In spite of the cold, the drizzle, and the clammy wetness of the grass which was starting to penetrate my thick saddle-tweed trousers... (1962,Mutton on the Menu,115)

OGONOWSKA-COATES .. some of the older shearers prefer saddle-tweed pants and a pair of braces. (1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,41)

SINCLAIR & TROTTER I was lucky I was well shod, O'Brien mustering boots on, my saddletweed trousers tied down, so I was dry as could be. (1994,From Caithness to Southland,17)

The bar for those who enter the stand and saddling paddock will be entirely distinct and separate from the one outside. The saddling paddock is close boarded six feet high as it should be. (Mar 19, 1883,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

noun.

Sa-eeda Ahmed, Akers, arrak,/ Bints, Bomonti. backsheech, barrak;/ Centipedes and Cleopatra,/ Dust and desert, djinns and Fatima;/ Eggs-cook, ana miskeen,'/ Fever, flies, and felaheen;/ Gehenam, Galabeyah, gods,/ Harems, hooshters, heat and hods;/Igri wallah, imshi Y'allah.'/ Jackos, jackals, gala gala';/ Khamseen, kan kan, tala hena,/ Lice and locusts, love and Lena;/ Mirage, Mahomet, mosquistoe,/ Niggers, T.A.B. and C2;/ Olives oranges, askarie./ Peanuts, pyramids, and gharry;/Queens' and Quacks' andk'weis kateer,'/ Ruins, rum, and Gyppo beer;/ Scorpion, sand, sun, sin, and Scarab,/ Tibbin, taube, and tricky Arab;/ Whizz-bangs, wadis, yin-al-deenak,'/ Yids, and yesterday, yeh meenak;/ Kestrels, kingfishers, and kites,/ Torrid days and sleepless nights;/ Mosques and minarets--maleesh;/O'ariglak,' `feluce--mafeesh'--/ Bookra, badein, ack-ack-emma,/ The soldier's farewell--ma-es salemma; (Jul 10, 1919,Quick March,33)

noun. [Environment]

The town is playing host for the winter to four of the world's remaining kakapo, the world's heaviest parrot. The chicks are being reared in a Department of Conservation "safe house". (Jun 18, 2005,Listener (New Zealand Listener),23)

noun. [Rural] a field close to a woolshed, cowshed, stable or homestead where stock can receive ready attention.

As calving approaches sort through the herd each week and bring the close-up cows into the safe paddock near the shed. (Mar 1967,NZ Journal of Agriculture,37)

noun. [Rural] a paddock that is low-fertility, free of disease or of conditions that create disease.

safen¶

verb. to make safe

David Gregorie of Waikanae quotes a letter in his local paper from Niki Trotter, of Raumati Beach: "I find it hard to see why anyone would be against safening a very dangerous piece of road with an extremely bad accident history." Now that's a truly marvellous word. "Safen". to "make safe", follows all the best precedents, using that Germanic -en ending to make a verb out of an adjective. It mimics fasten, worsen, harden, sweeten, sharpen, shorten, stiffen etc. (Apr 28, 2004,Dominion Post,B5)

safety-proof¶

verb. make something safe (the intended meaning at least)

At the foot of the Pukerua Bay hill is a large sign proclaiming that some authority (I presume the LTSA (I didn't have enough time to read the sign safely) is "safety-proofing" the road. My dictionary is very clear that proofing in that sense is to render impervious to something, with waterproofing being a good example, and rabbit proof another. (Aug 24, 2004,Dominion Post,B4)

Therefore, the pressure is truly on Transit NZ to safety-proof, as far as it can, the highway people travelling to and from the capital from the west are forced to use. (Oct 7, 2004,Dominion Post,B4)

...Transit New Zealand workers have erected signs at each end of the notoriously dangerous Centennial Highway between Pukerua Bay and Paekakariki saying they are "safety-proofing" the killer stretch. He suggests this means the road is being made resistant to safety. (Oct 20, 2004,Dominion Post,B5)

Coast Road Safety Proofing. Yeah, right. (Sep 29, 2004,Independent Herald (Wellington)) [NOTES: Graffitied caption in photograph of sign erected by Transit NZ]

salading¶

noun.

salami syndrome¶

phrase.

We see this proposal as part of the 'salami syndrome' with a little taken here and a little taken there, until little or nothing is left and access and recreational values are severely compromised. (Mar 10, 2004,Otago Daily Times,19)

sale¶

noun. spew(usually from a surfeit of liquor) and in various constructions, from ca1940 at least (Les Cleveland) and in various expressions

[NOTES: ca1945 I slipped in a mess of sale outside the pub.]

verb. to vomit (cf. sell out)

[NOTES: ca1945 I saled on my twentieth beer.]

McGILL sale to vomit; often make a sale . (1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,96)

sale crutch¶

noun. [Rural] a removal of dirty wool from rear ends of lambs or sheep prior to sale.

The job may be small, such as ring crutching, but those heavy sheep have to be handled. Ideal for full crutch, ringing and wigging, dagging or sale crutch of prime lambs. (Jun 1982,NZ Journal of Agriculture,49)

sale day¶

noun. [Rural] a regular day of the week on which a stock sale is held at a particular venue.

[NOTES: also saleday]

Batistich The casuals came and went as usual, the Sale Day visitants flooded us briefly. (1987,Sing Vila in the Mountain,156)

SILK For the last few years, the farmers in general found that sale-days were by no means 'Red Letter Days', but days of gloom and disappointment. (1923,History of Puhoi,85)

MCNAUGHTON Next morning was sale day, and Stewart went to the saleyards with his hack and his dogs. (1970,Tat,104)

MACINTOSH The busiest day was on 'saleday' when farmers and agents gathered for the fortnightly stock sale. (1974,Never a Dull Moment,18)

MACINTOSH Saledays often brought added diversions ... (1974,Never a Dull Moment,35)

WATERS Stock sale days from the mid-1920s were quite a cockies' gathering. (1976,Mostly a Farmer,105)

RICHARDS If the weather was suitable, sale days turned into a 'picnic day' or a get-together for all the families. [saleday] (1991,Off the Sheep's Back,54)

noun. in country towns, the day on which a farm livestock sale is held

[NOTES: also saleday]

ROBT. SCOTT, DENTIST, TAY STREET, INVERCARGILL. VISITS Otautau every fortnight, and may be consulted at Mrs Jaquiery's Buildings on Sale Day and second and fourth Fridays. (Dec 10, 1929,Otautau Standard & Wallace County Chronicle,4)

Why, Sale day was Otautau's Gala day! (Mar 29, 1932,Otautau Standard & Wallace County Chronicle,4)

Stratfordites are beginning to recognise the necessity of having a more substantial bridge over the Patea river, and teamsters are a bit frightened about crossing over with a load of medium weight. And no wonder. It is surprising to many it has not collapsed before this. At all events to a town like Stratford it is an unsightly structure, whether fit to carry the traffic or not, and it is a menace to pedestrians when there is much traffic in the streets, especially on sale days, when cattle are being driven across. (Apr 4, 1896,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

The supply of medium horses has been good, but vendors looked for an advance; whereas prices ruled, upon the whole, lower. Consequently, a smaller number than is usual on a regular sale-day, was disposed of. (Jan 13, 1875,Taranaki Herald,2)

The required quorum of 10 ratepayers not being present at the annual meeting called for Tuesday, the chairman (Mr. E. Constable) adjourned the meeting to Wednesday, the 14th instant, the cattle sale day. (Oct 9, 1868,Daily Southern Cross,3)

TURNER (1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,150)

An owner is wanted for a Hereford calf, left in the yards last sale day. (Mar 12, 1918,Otautau Standard & Wallace County Chronicle,3)

September 2: first cattle sale day. (1988,From Bush-Burn to Butter,52) [NOTES: 1881 John Hurndall's Diary in 1988 Warr From Bush-burn to Butter 52]

Sale day, Christmas week, and not a beast to be got for love or money. (Dec 1904,NZ Illustrated Magazine,251)

SCANLAN The little market town, with its handful of shops, its public house, its saleyards, was only two miles away. Thursday was Sale Day, when the farmers came in to buy and sell sheep or calves, heifers and pigs, and the farmer's wife to trade her butter and eggs at the grocer's for stores, and to buy towels and sheets and shoes. Market day, they would call it in England, but there was no market in these small New Zealand towns. There were no stalls in the street or square, where the farmer and his wife sold poultry and apples, eggs and butter, fruit and cream. The cows and sheep and horses and other farm stock were gathered into pens at the saleyard, and sold by auction. (1949,Rusty Road,10)

Tell him I'll be wanting another pup and I'll look him up next saleday. (1978,Listener Short Stories,2/40) [NOTES: 1956 Middleton in 1978 Listener Short Stories Vol 2 40]

TURNER [In winter] a farmer does not have to be mindful of cow-time or milking time on town day(or sale day, equivalent to English `market day'). (1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,161)

McNAUGHTON Next morning was sale day, and Stewart went to the saleyards with his hack and his dogs. (1970,Tat,104)

KEENE Sale Day was always exciting in Kaitaia - especially in those early times when wild frightened cattle from the most northerly stations - cattle that had seen few human beings - were driven down the main road to the saleyards, then into the A. & P. grounds. (1982,Myrtle and Sophia,45)

Sale Day causes a hive of activity in our village. (Dec 1, 1945,NZ Dairy Exporter,63)

Sale Day was the big day for business in town. The farmers drove in with their families and the four roads that met at Aorangi House resounded to the ring of sulky wheels along the macadam. (1987,Sing Vila in the Mountain,43)

HENDERSON I came to appreciate the farmers' saleday when I was running a small country town bakery and tearooms. (1967,Return of Joe,172)

KENNEALLY Fences, gardens and residents suffered just prior to saleday. (1981,Johnsonville Yesterday,35)

sale draft¶

noun. [Rural] a group of livestock for sale that are separated from a larger group.

noun. [Rural] the gathering of stock in preparation for drafting or a clearing sale.

noun. [Rural] an evening following a stock sale day [usually a social occasion in a rural area.]

noun.

salmon¶

noun.

THOMSON The lower portion of the Hunter Valley and the northern end of the lake [Hawea] are a sportman's paradise, with brown and rainbow trout in plentiful supply, as well as a type of salmon which is often referred to as landlocked salmon, their size or weight being from three to four lbs. (1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,34)

noun. chinook salmon, found spawning in South Island rivers

When rivers are low, chinook salmon, known locally as quinnat, linger at sea, waiting for higher flows before running upstream to spawn.Ibid. 26 Between 1901 and 1907, Ayson made five importations and releases of fry, fingerlings and juveniles, and by 1907 the chinooks (which would became known here as quinnat, another native American name for salmon) were already coming back to spawn... By 1911-1912, quinnat had colonised the Waitaki River system and were spawning as far inland as the Ohau, Pukaki and Tekapo Rivers. (May 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 63/19)

noun.

OVERTON On another occasion we were at Te Anau together fishing for Atlantic salmon in 1929. (1949,Fifty Years Sheep Farming,76)

With both brown and rainbow trout firmly established in New Zealand, Ayson set out to Europe and North America to research the Atlantic salmon and its habitat and to source the best breedsing stock... [25] Whatever the reason, the Atlantic salmon failed to establish a sea-going - or at least returning - population. (May 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 63/25)

AYLING KAHAWAI (Australian salmon) Arripis trutta (1982,Collins Guide,222,1984)

noun. New Zealand salmon, see KAHAWAI. (obsolesc) usu. with descriptive epithet MAORI, NATIVE, NEW ZEALAND salar, =KAHAWAI [cf AND Arripis trutta 1790 Collins (1798); salmon trout young of A trutta or A esper 1848 Tasmania]

BIDWILL Other shell-fish are also abundant, particularly Cockles - of these I have seen more than a man could carry collected by one woman during the space of a tide; Scallops are also tolerably abundant, and are most delicious eating. There are no Lobsters nor Crabs, but a great abundance of fish of all kinds; one, the Salmon of the English, or Carwai (Carwhy), is a most excellent fish, the best I have tasted in the Southern Hemisphere; ... (1841,Rambles in NZ,115,1952)

POLACK Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called para[as-acute] paraua [a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, mungu nui (black physeter); right whale, tohora (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, mango (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. (1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202 fn)

MORRIS Salmon, n . The English Salmon is being acclimatised with difficulty in Tasmania and New Zealand; the Trout more successfully. But in all Australian, New Zealand, and Tasmanian waters there is a marine fish which is called Salmon; it is not the true Salmon of the Old World, but Arripis salar , Gunth., and called in New Zealand by the Maori name Kahawai . The fish is often called also Salmon-Trout. The young is called Samson-fish (q.v.). (1898,Austral English,400)

SARAH MATHEW ... very fine fish they are [off Whangarei] - schnappers, gurnet and what is called salmon in these seas. (Apr 20, 1840,Journal) [NOTES: 1840 Apr 20 Sarah Mathew Journal in 1940 Founding of NZ 121]

MORELAND KAHAWAI [ Arripis trutta ] ... In Australia it is known as salmon, sea salmon, and Australian salmon. Small examples are known as kopapa in northern New Zealand. (1967,Marine Fishes,50)

MORELAND salmon 1 n. (pl. usu. same) large fish with orange-pink flesh highly valued for food and sport; the colour of its flesh; similar unrelated NZ and Australian fish. (1967,Marine Fishes,50)

salube¶

verb.

[NOTES: ca1938 (R. Mason)]

MACLEAN [John Pascoe] appreciated fitness, though not speed, and above all he appreciated relaxation, especially sunbathing. To promote this concept he coined the term 'to salube', which soon became synonymous with his name and has become part of Tararua folklore. (1994,Tararua : the Story of a Mountain Range,174)

adjective.

To offset these rather gloomy expressions there are those that derive from salubrious. They are J.D. Pascoe terms and were brought by him from Canterbury to Wellington. They obviously arose from the habit of describing sunny, pleasant weather or places as salubrious'. First is the <i> salubrium</i> , a rest or sunbake in salubrious conditions. This first appeared in <i> The Tramper</i> in 1937. About 1939 people were <i> salubriating</i> , or taking a <i> salube</i> in the sun. The previous year Te Matawai was described as asalube hut'. By 1943 trampers were sunbathing and salubing . So far as Tararuas are concerned, salube as a noun and a verb is the word that has survived. (Sep 1958,Tararua,28) [NOTES: 1958 Sep Ruth Mason `Track and Trail' in Tararua 28]

noun. a period of relaxation (in the sun)

[NOTES: (Ruth Mason: from salubrious)]

MASON SALUBE n and v: a tramping term c1938: Wellington only I think. Not as common as it once was. (Jun 7, 1952,Personal Communication) [NOTES: a1938 p.c. R. Mason June 7 1952 (Wellington)]

To offset these rather gloomy expressions there are those that derive from salubrious. They are J.D. Pascoe terms and were brought by him from Canterbury to Wellington. They obviously arose from the habit of describing sunny, pleasant weather or places as salubrious'. First is the <i> salubrium</i> , a rest or sunbake in salubrious conditions. This first appeared in <i> The Tramper</i> in 1937. About 1939 people were <i> salubriating</i> , or taking a <i> salube</i> in the sun. The previous year Te Matawai was described as asalube hut'. By 1943 trampers were sunbathing and salubing . So far as Tararuas are concerned, salube as a noun and a verb is the word that has survived. (Sep 1958,Tararua,28) [NOTES: 1958 Sep Ruth Mason `Track and Trail' in Tararua 28]

KILIKITI: Samoan cricket bears about as much resemblance to the ... territory of Lords as the sound of the word does to English. ... For one thing the bat - fashioned in triangular shape from the springy fau tree, decorated in gaudy splashes of colour and bound with coconut fibre - has nothing to do with the sissy wider blade of the willow. It's an out-and-out war club of such bold length ... The ball, spun by hand from liquid rubber tapped from a living tree and compressed to rock-hard consistency, bounds down the pitch with a dangerously unpredictable velocity. ... [T]eams are of indefinite size - 15 a side is considered a minimum for serious competitions... When the batting team reaches 35 runs, to keep the action alive, the teams swop over. Taipo is a foreign word, its native place and etymology I cannot trace, but as it appears to mean the Devil and is of universal use I shall not disturb it. Save Manapouri¶

noun. [Environment] a term used from 1959 for a nationwide protest against the raising of Lake Manapouri to high levels for hydroelectricity generation.

[NOTES: also Save Manapouri campaign]

MANAPOURI stickers seem to come in a number of different forms. There is the common "Save Manapouri," a simple plea from the heart. "Help Save Manapouri," a call not to be just sympathetic but do something about it. Then there is "I Want to Save Manapouri," a pitiful cry by someone who feels impotent to do anything. But my favourite is the cynic's sticker indicating that he is tired of the whole business: "Drain Manapouri." (Mar 2, 1970,Evening Post,32)

The 1970 Save Manapouri petition was the third to be drawn up with the object of preserving the lake and was the largest petititon ever to be presented to Parliament. (Aug 1970,Forest & Bird,8)

Within the past 12 months we have received powerful support from "Save Manapouri" committees, which have been organised throughout the country. (May 1970,Forest & Bird,10)

Neville PEAT Save Manapouri is a cry deeply embedded in the collective consciousness of New Zealanders and is still capable of being dusted off. (1994,Manapouri Saved,10)

PLEA MADE FOR PRESERVATION. 'Swift Action Needed to Save Manapouri' [hdg]. (Oct 21, 1959,Evening Post,22)

Exploratory Talks Here on How to Save Manapouri [hdg] Substantial interest had been shown in the activities of the Save Manapouri Committee ... (Jan 20, 1970,Evening Post,15)

Roger WILSON The turning point of the opposition to the raising of the lake came when a crowded and lively public meeting was held in Invercargill on 30 October [1969]. As a result of that meeting, the first "Save Manapouri" committee was set up. Similar groups were quickly established in other centres around the country. (1982,From Manapouri to Aramoana,15)

The movement to "Save Manapouri" is a case book example of how trends are adopted in a democratic society. (Apr 1970,Comment,4)

Save Manapouri campaign¶

noun. [Environment] an extensive nationwide campaign to prevent high level raising of Lake Manapouri for hydroelectricity generation.

The Save Manapouri campaign has been lauded as "the birth of the modern conservation movement" in New Zealand. The Save Manapouri campaign began in the late 1950s with the proposal to build a power station to supply power to an aluminium smelter in the far south of New Zealand and gained momentum in the 1960s when it was proposed that the level of Lake Manapouri would be raised 8.2 metres to harness its hydro-electric potential for the project. (May 7, 2008,Internet - see Notes,1) [NOTES: www.forestandbird.org.nz/what-we-do/publications/forest-bird-magazine/article]

Among other things he was - with his wife - a driver of the Save Manapouri campaign, which succeeded in preventing the Crown from raising the level of the lake by some eight metres to generate electricity for the Bluff smelter. (Feb 26, 2009,Dominion Post,B3) [NOTES: from obituary of Dr Ian Prior - refer dawn raid and overstayer]

Neville PEAT The Save Manapouri Campaign lifted the lid. New Zealand had seen nothing of its kind before. It was a phenomenon in public awareness, concern and agitation. (1994,Manapouri Saved,3)

In an effort to discern basic attitudes to the issue of the southern lakes' exploitation for power, members of Parliament are to be sent questionnaires by the Save Manapouri Campaign. (Aug 21, 1972,Evening Post,3)

And he [Mr R J McLean] said he thought that out of the Save Manapouri Campaign would evolve a permanent organisation to fight for the people of New Zealand when their natural environment was threatened by foreign or local industrialists, local bodies, or by their own Government. (Feb 21, 1970,Evening Post,7)

Roger WILSON The Save Manapouri Campaign was well funded and had a professional approach to publicity. (1982,From Manapouri to Aramoana,11)

noun. [Rural] a highly-infectious disease of sheep, caused by a mite Dematodecles ovis [rife among NZ flocks between 1845 and 1892.]

[NOTES: note from previous hdwd: the sheep disease of early NZ (1845-46) has been general English since 14 cent. (OED) see discards @n and @v get quote: Scab Act 1848]

PAUL In New Zealand a well-bred merino flock, on a good run, will fully average 4 lbs. With the exception of scab, sheep appear to be exempt from all the ailments. (1857,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,40)

RICKARD Scab was not finally eliminated from New Zealand until 1892 when D'Urville Island, where it had lingered longest, was prounced clean. (1967,Strangers in the Wilderness,102)

SCAB. - Let emigrants in the cabin who are likely to possess sheep, carry out with them the little volume of Cunningham, "Hints to Emigrants" - the best receipts are there for curing the scab. (Feb 3, 1844,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3)

The scab boiler sheds produced a hell-brew based on tobacco leaves, into which the sheep were slung to rid them of the dreaded mange mite. (Mar 21, 1992,Dominion,4)

McRAE Edgar Jones to destroy all his sheep, numbering 5,000, some or all said to be infected with scab. (1963,By the Braes of Balquether,57)

McCASKILL He [sc. Fowler] has scab at Tophouse and has neither the capital nor the skill to keep country like the Rainbow clean.IBid. 70 Scab is caused by a mite (not an insect, but a relation of spiders). The eggs are laid on the skin at the base of the wool fibres. The young mites puncture the epidermis and suck lymph. Small pustules develop from which a liquid exudes, coagulating to form a hard, pale-yellow crust, the scab. ... Infected sheep rub against rocks, posts ... and will bite at the skin, causing serious damage to the wool. ...Some flocks were affected as early as 1848, the Nelson area having serious trouble for many years after that. (1969,Molesworth,56) [NOTES: Quote from ACTON-ADAMS 1885]

The station owners were.. Mr Anderson (called the "father of the scab").. (May 8, 1890,Otago Witness,36)

THE success of Mr. Costello's specific for the cure of scab is said by the judges appointed by the Board of Agriculture to be complete. (Sep 13, 1864,Southland Times,3)

Scab is now eradicated, and foot-rot, to a great extent, can be avoided ... (1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,98)

The scab in sheep is the pest of all the settlements of Australia and New Zealand: it has materially retarded their adnvancement, from the great havoc that the disease makes among the large flocks in an open undivided country. (Jun 14, 1851,Lyttelton Times,6)

WELD Isolated cases of foot-rot and staggers do occasionally occur, but never to any extent. I wish I could say as much for scab. Ibid. 9 Every sheep should be thoroughly examined before he is passed to the dippers, and if any symptoms of scab should be discovered, the spots must be scarified ... (1851,Hints to Intending Sheep-Farmers in New Zealand,3)

SAM STEPHENS ... that horrid disease, the scab (1853,Journal,699)

(1853,Adventures of a Surveyor,27)

ACLAND Scab is very prevalent in some parts of the colony. (1858,Notes on Sheepfarming in NZ,11)

The disease of "scab".. is now come to be regarded with more complacency, and really, when proper treatment is used, the disease ceases to be a very serious matter. (Nov 22, 1855,Nelson Examiner,2)

They could not prevent scab running rampant through the district. (Sep 20, 1879,Auckland Weekly News,13)

verb. [Rural] to inspect and treat sheep for scab disease.

WARD Uncle at my place scabbing sheep. (Jun 18, 1845,Diary)

scab committee¶

noun. [Rural] a local or regional committee set up to control scab in the 1800s.

(1976,Wairarapa : An Historical Excursion,451)

noun.

adjective.

[NOTES: aka scab-infected]

Price, scab inspector saw them ... (Mar 31, 1884,Hawera & Normanby Star,3)

There appeared a letter in your paper a few weeks since, complaining of the disgraceful state of the sheep in the Waimea, and inquiring after the Scab Inspector, whose business the writer presumes it to be to see that the sheep running on the wild lands are not diseased. noun. a viral disease of sheep and goats producing ulceration around the mouth.

scabweed¶

noun. [Rural] a member of the Raoulia spp, Raoulia lutescens, that grows mainly in stony high country areas.

The most notable plant to appear is one of the mountain-sheep (Raoulia lutescens) which forms large, rounded, cushion-like masses, and is commonly known as "scabweed." (Jun 15, 1910,NZ Journal of Agriculture,14)

Growth of scab-weed is prolific on bare flats and hill slopes and does much to hold the soil against erosion, but it is useless as fodder. (May 31, 1945,NZ Farmer,11)

MCCASKILL Where no depletion has taken place the scabweed is confined to river bed or other stony ground ... (1969,Molesworth,154)

LEVY The scabweed and cushion-like pimeleas are of great ecological interest because they can claim to represent the first colonisation stage in vegetation and the last stage in retrogressive succession. (1970,Grasslands of NZ,35)

ASPINALL The flats and hillsides were nothing but scabweed and rabbits. [scab-weed] (1993,Farming Under Aspiring,226)

noun. any of the cushion plants, most of which are native to New Zealand. Raoulia lutescens

[On Molesworth there is] the great circular, silvery or green, dense, low cushions of the scabweed (Raoulia lutescens), between which, especially where exposed to the wind there may be no other plants. (1919,NZ Journal of Agriculture) [NOTES: c1919 Cockayne Journal of Agriculture in 1969 McCaskill Molesworth 154]

This [Central Otago] country in its natural state carries a very poor type of vegetation, consisting of Poa and Festuca tussock, reduced over large areas by burning and rabbit infestation, to depleted country, where scabweed (Raoulia lutescens and R. australis), together with sorrel (Rumex acetosella), storksbill (E. rodium cicutarium), Poa maniototo, hairgrass, may form the dominant cover. (1936,Agricultural Organization in NZ,365)

A [caption] Windward slope, scabweed and Poa maniototo. (1939,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,20/230)

A [caption] Windward slope, scabweed and Poa maniototo. (1939,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,20/230)

COWAN No wonder scabweed - a most fitting name -covers many hill slopes. (1948,Down the Years in the Maniototo,3)

LEVY ... shrubs common in the tussock zone: matagouri, native brooms, dwarf koromikos, monoao, sarmentose tutu, the grasslike spiky-leaved Spaniard, the harsh patotara, golden cottonwood, cushion-like pimeleas, and the low, matted, carpet-like growth of the scabweeds are characteristic of the low tussock country, ... Ibid. 273 Montane tussock, on the other hand, has, ... given place to bare earth or to low mat-like plants such as scab-weeds (Raoulia). (1951,Grasslands of NZ,35,1970)

McLINTOCK [Rabbits'] depredations accelerated vegetation changes which included spectacular increase of scab weed (Raoulia australis), a composite mat plant. (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/487)

McCASKILL (1969,Molesworth,[facing 144 - photo caption])

scabweed [=] scleranthus [s] ... scabweed [s] Raoulia australis Hook.f Raoulia hookeri Allan (1969,Standard Common Names for Weeds,67)

(1978,Manawatu Tramping Club Jubilee,89)

MOORE & IRWIN RAOULIA AUSTRALIS, scabweed. (1978,Oxford Book of NZ Plants,136)

DAWSON The tussocks were largely replaced by grey patches of Raoulia australis, unflatteringly termed `scabwed'. (1988,Forest Vines to Snow Tussocks,150)

noun. Raoulia lutescens

Now in many parts even the hardy tussock (Poa caespitosa) has disappeared, leaving the earth bare, or perhaps occupied by the native scabweed (Raoulia lutescens) or the introduced so-called star-thistle (Centaurea Calcitrapa). Since then, the culture has been immortalised in the moved Scarfies, and sensationalised, annually, in documentary and news footage of orientation week. SUTTON-SMITH It is important to distinguish these `Action-Terms' of marbles from the innumerable merely descriptive marble terms which have no effect on the course of the action - terms such as Ringer, In, Smug, Dead Stick, Skun, Skinned, Sported off, Scat, Cannons, Dubs, Kills, Funs, Keeps, Pink. (1953,Unorganized Games,2/770)

SUTTON-SMITH Some of the typical terms used in marbles referred to the act of shooting and the movement of the marbles. Those related to ways of shooting marbles were cribbing, firsts, fudging, funks, funnicks, funnigans, flunks, forces, knee-high, knuckle-down-stiff, knuckles, and lasts. Terms connected with the movement of the marbles were: cannons, clears, dead-stick, double-hits, fires, funs, gees, haystacks, in smug, keeps, kills, kisses, lay-ups, manyes, ones, pink, ringer, rolls, scat, screws, skinned, skun, spiders, sported-off, stays, stops, tracks, throughs. (marbles) Ibid. 176 [Waitara, Taranaki, 1899: reference, game of Little Ring] Many heated arguments arose as to who said everythings' ornothings' first. If a player's taw' touched a marble and lay alongside it, the others would shoutknuckle down' just before his turn. ... Knuckle down' meant that the player had to hold his taw close to the marble attacked and fire it in that very inconvenient position. ... When a boy lost all his marbles at play he wasscat' [?related to skint ?HWO] . ... A ringer' was a taw which, when fired at the commencement of the game, lodged in the track of the ring itself; that, and knocking a marble out when hefired' were the perfect shots. ... To fire a shot while holding the hand nearer to the ring than where the taw had lain, was to `funk', an unforgiveable crime. (1972,Folkgames of Children,175)

schnapper¶

noun. variant of snapper q.v.

WILSON SNAPPER ... The common name snapper' was given to the fish by Captain Cook in 1770. He mistook it for a member of the true snapper family <i>Lutjanidae </i>, a group of fish with which he had become familar in American waters. Although he did mistake the fish Captain Cook spelt the name correctly, whereas many subsequent writers have usedschnapper' - an erroneous spelling of unknown origin. Perhaps some of the early snapper fishermen took bottles of schnapps along on their outings, hence going `schnapping'! (1981,Fisherman's Bible,226)

DEVANNY Sometimes as many as twenty schnapper would be caught. (1928,Dawn Beloved,102)

His sorrow at the struggles of the dying schnapper was pitiful to behold. (Mar 5, 1904,NZ Observer,7)

The barns were stored with glorious schnapper. (Jun 28, 1913,NZ Observer,17)

Poor Hansard, known as the "Dying Schnapper", was there. (Oct 1, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,7)

Instead, I got some freshly cooked pipi and raw schnapper. (Oct 6, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),93)

Bellamy's menu has qualified as the most snobbish of all State papers. Whenever the well-known New Zealand fish called snapper is an item of Parliamentary diet it is invariable [sic] spelled schnapper.' The gourmets of the Food and Wine Society could be forgiven for such literary heresy, but the old prosaic spelling should be good enough for the dining-room in Parliament House. Incidentally, the legend is that the fish was given the namesnapper' by Captain Cook when he was here on his voyage of exploration in 1770. As he and the members of his crew leaned over the side of their galleon two centuries ago and threw their fishing lines into the waters off the New Zealand coast the fish used to snap at the bait. Hence the name snapper. (Mar 5, 1956,Dominion,8)

My reference in last week's column to the snobbishness of Bellamy's in using the spelling schnapper' when that fish was on its menu has broughtbites' galore - from fish merchants to schoolmasters. Most of them, it is fair to say, have taken up the cudgels on behalf of Bellamy's, but none of them has disproved my argument that the correct spelling is snapper.' ... Some historians support my Captain Cook theory, though there are others who place the first use of the namesnapper' at a later date, certainly not earlier. They think the name may have been given the fish by Captain W. L. Edwardson, the commander of a New South Wales Government cutter called the Snapper which was in New Zealand waters in 1822 and 1823 investigating sealing prospects. He gave the name Port Snapper to an inlet on Ruapuke Island in Foveaux Strait. Whatever the origin of the word, the fish served at Bellamy's is indigenous to New Zealand and is spelt `snapper.' (Mar 12, 1956,Dominion,8)

The fishing off the island is very good, there being abundance of hapuku, kohikohi, maumau, schnapper, kahawai, tarakihi, in addition to plenty of shell-fish such as koura or cray-fish, crabs, paua,etc. (1885,TrNZI,17/419) [NOTES: (Goldsmith)]

SHERRIN SCHNAPPER (Pagrus unicolor ). ... Dr. Hector says: `There are few fishes better known in the northern parts of the Colony than the schnapper. This name, by which it is known, is adopted from Australia, its Maori name, tamure, being seldom used by Europeans. It represents in these seas the braize of the European markets, ...' (1886,Handbook Fishes of NZ,85)

SARA MATHEW ... very fine fish they are [off Whangarei] - schnappers, gurnet and what is called salmon in these seas. (Apr 20, 1840,Journal) [NOTES: 1840 Apr 20 Sarah Mathew Journal in 1940 Founding of NZ 121]

HAY We have, indeed, a wealth of fish in all the tidal waters. Sharks, schnapper, rock-cod, mackerel, mullet, herring, sole, halibut, albacore, barracouta, king-fish, and others. (1882,Brighter Britain,2/230)

MORRIS Schnapper or Snapper ... a fish abundant in all Australasian waters, Pagrus unicolor , Cuv. and Val. The latter spelling was the original form of the word (one that snaps). It was gradually changed by the fishermen, perhaps of Dutch origin, to Schnapper , the form now general. The name Snapper is older than the settlement of Australia, but it is not used for the same fish. `O.E.D.,' s.v. Cavally , quotes: ... In New Zealand, the Tamure (q.v.) is also called Schnapper , and the name Red-Schnapper i s given to Anthias richardsoni , Gunth., or Scorpis hectori , Hutton. (1898,Austral English,404)

The name Greymouth Schooner' is not the name of a ship but the designation given to a drinking vessel which is supposed to have a capacity of an imperial pint, or 20 ounces- double the size of the ordinary glass. West Coasters are inordinately proud of their reputation of being able to consume more beer in any given time than those in less favoured parts of the Dominion and support for their contention was forthcoming in the glass that was famed in many a story of the early Coast days as theGreymouth Schooner' These have almost disappeared from the West Coast hostelries but one has been secured through the generosity of Mr. H.E. Wedde of Oamaru, for the Otago museum. The Museum boasts a particularly fine collection of glassware going back to the days of the early Egyptians and the Director, Dr H.E. Skinner seemed overjoyed that such a famed drinking measure as the `Greymouth Schooner' should find a place in such select company. The claim that the glass provided a full 20 ounces is disputed by Dr Skinner however, who finds that it is only [?] 17.5 ounces. (Nov 22, 1950,Wayleggo) [NOTES: 1950 (? 51 ? 52) Evening Star (Dunedin) ca Nov 22; or Feb 23-25; or Feb 15 (R.Mason)]

scotia¶

noun. a (usually concave) moulding between a wall and a ceiling.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes: NSOD, Collins and Chambers define scotia as a concave/hollow moulding, esp. at the base of an (ionic) column. The OED definition is "a hollow moulding = casement". The latest citation (1878) reads "another kind of base is frequent in which a bead is subsituted for the scotia". Casement in turn is defined in the relevant sense as "a hollow moulding, a cavetto, not exceding one quarter round". Cavettos, it appears, are "principally used in cornices". All this is a bit obscure, but the definitions in NSOD etc would suggest a fairly uncommon word. The ordinary NZ use is specialised though common, and familar to most homeowners - a (usually concave) moulding between a wall and a ceiling. In NZ, it is standard and as well-known as skirting board.]

Scottish alley¶

noun.

SUTTON-SMITH Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as taw' orshooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; dubs',dates', stakes',dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. (1972,Folkgames of Children,174)

KEITH & M,AIN Marbles were the currency of childhood and there were an astonishing number of names for them, some referring to the material or colour, others to value or function in the game. There were agates, aggies, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cats-eye, [sic] chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, mollies, peelies, peewees, pisswees, pretties, Scotties, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers and whities. The march of technology added ball bearings - ballies or steelies - which were unbeatable when it came to smashing an opponent's miserable glassie. World War II[roman] brought `clayeys' often imperfectly spherical they were pathetic terracotta substitutes for real marbles. (1984,NZ Yesterdays,288)

SUTHERLAND Do you play Bull Rush at your school?' John asked.Bull Rush?' said Ewan. ... You get out on the field and draw a line at the ends. You pick someone to be He to stand in the middle. He calls out someone's name, and he has to get across to the other end. The guard has to try to tackle the runner and hit him three times. But if the runner gets across he calls out Bull Rush and everyone runs ...[sic]'That's King-a-Sene!' said Ewan. But we're only allowed to tag the player, we're not allowed to tackle him ...'[sic] ...Do you play with the girls at all?' Sometimes we play Drop the Hnadkerchief. The girls can join in. But most of the time they play Eely Ily Oh, or Queenie, or some cissy game like that...'[sic]Do you play shinty or football?' `Yeah. Football. And we play scrag in the winter and tippeny runs in the summer...'[sic] (1978,Elver, The,61)

noun. an inferior whale deficient in blubber

[NOTES: OED lean person or animal 1542. 5. scrag-whale (Nth ?) =scrag-tail whale 1701: EDD. various dial. meanings all connoting residue, useless remainder, rejects. eg wood, offal of meat, small, inferior apples.]

McNAB The cow whales ... had been the scarcest, their places being taken by young bulls and `scrags' [perhaps McNab's writing-if so delete] (1838,Old Whaling Days)

He (Mr. Morris) reports the capture of a right whale (a scrag) by Mr. Barkett's party, yesterday, the 12th inst. (Aug 19, 1862,Hawke's Bay Herald,3)

noun.

Into these the blubber cut into lumps two feet square - cut from the carcase on the beach - was thrown and boiled until the oil was extracted. The residue, called scrag, then served to feed the fires. (1940,Marlborough,43)

noun. [used elsewhere to describe all animals] [sp. use in NZ] a poor, unthrifty ewe or a broken-down horse.

GUTHRIE-SMITH They were Merino ewes - skin and bone, scrags, their wool peeling off - anxious to escape .. If the sight of those scrags at the Waikoau ford had thrilled us with pride of possession, our hearts exulted at the sight of these lambs ... (1921,Tutira,150)

a very old ewe: a scrag. (2001,Questionnaire Respondents (DB))

The `spear' is simply a spike of iron, about a foot long, on the end of a pole ... (1873,Wonderland of the Antipodes,54)

verb. sc. flax

Iu [sic] the leader, it should have been stated that a native could scrape ten pounds of flax a day, with a pipi-shell, - not that he could make by scraping flax ten shillings a day. (Oct 4, 1859,Daily Southern Cross,2)

The best kind of flax was the Tihore. The native plan of preparing it was very simple. They tore out the fibres, rubbed them together in their hands to open the bundles, and removed the small tissue that remained by scraping it with their nails. The inferior kind they prepared somewhat differently. They scraped it with a shell, having sometimes previously steeped it in water to soften the skin; they then soaked it in water for from two to four days, heated it with stones while it was wet, and scraped it again, then soaked it again, and then bleached it and dried it on poles ... (Jul 13, 1870,Daily Southern Cross,3)

It is considered necessary to scrape the flax before beating it, in consequence of the coating being chiefly composed of silex, attempting to remove which merely by the process of bruizing [sic] is attended with the destruction of the fibre. (Mar 3, 1841,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2)

HOWARD ... inside were many bed places built of wicker work, ... upon which lay their shells &c. for dressing and scraping flax. (1940,Rakiura,345) [NOTES: 1823 June 1 Capt.J.R.Kent Mermaid log in 1940 Howard Rakiura 345]

Three species of giant weta and an undescribed species of ground weta live in the Kaikoura ranges: the Kaikoura giant weta is restricted to South Marlborough; the bluff weta is found only in South Marlborough and at Mt Somers in mid-Canterbury; and the scree weta reaches its northeastern limit in the area. Having depleted our daily scroggin allowance that day and taken five hours, not the rcommended four, the next, longest leg to Portage seems ominous: an eight or nine-hour tramp of more than 20km. ... We coax the boys regularly - a barley sugar at half past each hour, a scroggin stop on the hour. (Nov 1, 2005,NZ Herald,E8)

If any word originating in the mountain clubs deserves to be incorporated in the language it is perhaps scroggin. That mixture of raisins, sultanas, chocolate, nuts, boiled lollies, a mixture of bits and pieces of whatever one fancies, was evolved to fill the need for a sustaining, palatable, easily-carried food, one as readily available for a bite snatched in a cold, wet, momentary halt as for a welcome spell in the warmth and sun. The word seems to come from Otago but its derivation is not clear. There is a Scotch and North of England dialect word scrog which refers to stunted bushes, and if some Otago Scot had this in mind it prompts dark thoughts as to what the original comestible may have been like. Perhaps it is one of those words that have no known ancestry, that come out of the blue, such as children sometimes so happily coin. (Sep 1958,Tararua,26) [NOTES: 1958 Sep Ruth Mason `Track and Trail' in Tararua 26]

SCROGEN 1 cup peanuts 3/4 cup dried apricots 1 + 135 gram block energy chocolate 1/2 cup mixed dried fruit 1/4 cup sunflower seeds 1/2 cup coconut 2 tablespoons powdered glucose. Roast the peanuts at 180 degrees C for 10-15 minutes, or until lightly golden. Cool. Chop the apricots and chocolate coarsely. In a strong plastic bag, put the penuts, apricots, chocolate, mixed fruit, sunflower seeds, coconut and glucose. Shake to combine. Secure closed. Use as a high energy snack food. Makes about 4 cups. verb. to treat or regard a thing or idea as worthless; cancel irrevocably, write off; wipe; wash out, in racing (of a horse) to scratch; write off' esp. exclamation: scrub itforget (all about) it; wipe it; `it doesn't matter'.

[NOTES: [The NZ senses, if not variants of imported Austr (cf P. above) would seem to be orig. associated with, if not originated in, the racing slang: (phs cleaning the bookmaker's slate): scrubbed or scrub (a horse) to have lost; be scratched: or scratch. But the senses also parallel those of words with similar meanings: to wipe (off) (a person or thing), get wiped; wash out (sthg), a wash-out; to write off (sbdy or sthg), a write-off. The word seems noticeable after WW2, so perhaps it was popularised by NZ servicemen who may have picked it up from British Servicemen (or Australians): cf P.4. The connotation of contempt may have derived in part by association with SCRUB n and aj `poor, mean' etc, scrubby etc; and the particular uses of this in Australasia: scrub-bull; scrubber, scrub along.]]

MORRIS Scrub, n. country overgrown with thick bushes. Henry Kingsley's explanation (1859), that the word means shrubbery, is singularly misleading, the English word conveying an idea of smallness and order compared with the size and confusion of the Australian use. Yet he is etymologically correct, for Scrobb is Old English (Anglo-Saxon) for shrub; but the use had disappeared in England. (1898,Austral English,405)

Scrub, n. Thicket of shrubs or bushes of too low a growth to be called bush (q.v.). On the plains it usually grew in belts or patches. The best known components in Canterbury are Manuka, Wild Irishman, Miki-miki (of which the shepherds make walking sticks), and Moutain pine (Totara nivalis). A single plant of scrub is called a bush, while of course a single specimen in the bush is a tree. Perhaps (if the question couldn't be settled by species) ten feet would be the dividing height between s. and b. (Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: 1933 Acland Glossary Press 25 Nov 15]

The pigs had eaten nearly all the flesh off the limbs, and to look at the bodies would have given one a "scunner" at pork, if there had been anything else to eat. (Apr 18, 1867,Daily Southern Cross,5)

He has evidently taken a "scunner" at the Templars. They have not backed up his political prospects as he expected. (Oct 5, 1878,Otago Witness,14)

A 'scunner' is (in the vocabulary of the Scot) a feeling of sickening, loathing disgust - worse than sea-sickness or nausea of any kind - therefore is most applicable to the epidemic revolt against Parliamentary Government which prevails as universally as la grippe did a few months ago. (Oct 11, 1890,Observer (Auckland),3)

Every horse has his own way of galloping, and though English trainers have a scunner upon any colt which keeps his head up, Craganour must be taken as an exception from their rule. (Jun 12, 1913,Poverty Bay Herald,5)

Sex is one of the great facts of life, and the public never will cease to be interested in sex, but to blame the public for the orgies of riotous sex portrayed in the movies is too much. The fact is the public is fed on this stuff until it is a marvel a "scunner" has not set in. (Sep 3, 1921,NZ Truth,1)

sea ear¶

noun. a former name for paua

POLACK Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called para [as-acute] paraua [a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, mungu nui (black physeter); right whale, tohora (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, mango (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. (1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202 fn)

ANDERSON Of other shellfish there are ten or twelve sorts such as periwinkles, wilks, limpets, and some very beautiful sea Ears and another sort that sticks to the weeds , with some other things as sea eggs, starfish ... ed. fn Periwinkles, Melarhapa spp. (2), and probably Zediloma and Melagraphia spp. Whelks, Cominella sp. Limpets, Cellana spp. The `very beautiful sea Ears' were certainly the Paua, Haliotis iris; ... GRAHAM SEAPERCH (POHUIAKAROA) JOCK STUART, HIGHLANDER, FIVEFINGER, SOLDIERFISH or SCRODDIE Helicolenus papillosus (Bloch and Schneider) The seaperch is a fish well known to all fishermen both sports and commercial fishermen alike, who give it quite a number of vernacular names, a few of which are as follows: Jock Stuart, Highlander, Fivefinger and Soldierfish. These names have a bearing on some distinguishing characteristic of the fish. For instance the first two names are supposed to be given on account of the colouring of the fish resembling, in some ways, the tartan of a Scot; while Fivefingers is given on account of the so-called five (really more) fingers (rays) of the pectoral fins, on which the fish has a habit of resting on the floor of the aquarium tank. The name Soldierfish is derived from the similarities of this fish to the activities of a soldier or picket on sentinel duty. I have often seen Seaperch stand or, rather, rest at attention on its pectoral fins for lengthy periods. When it did move, it moved to the right or to the left with the precision of a well-trained soldier. The name Scroddie, commonly used at the northern end of the South Island, is derived from the word Scrod which means a young Dogfish. It appears from my researches that when the early colonists first saw a small Seaperch they at once named it Scrod and later the `ie' was tacked on to make Scroddie. (1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,344)

seal's ballast¶

noun.

Anyone who had ever been about old whaling and sealing stations must have seen collections of round smooth stones of various sizes but mostly about the size of cannon-balls, lying on the beach. On asking any of the old hands' what these are, you will at once be told that they areseal's ballast' ... You will probably be gravely told that the seal is a migratory animal, and that when it is about to take a long journey it will trim itself to exactly the proper weight for long and easy locomotion through the water. It picks up one of these stones and swallows it and goes into the water to try the effect. If it finds it requires more ballast it comes ashore again and repeats the dose. If it has too much weight .... it vomits one or two of the stones out on the beach. Hence the stones are always termed `seals' ballast' (1871,TrNZI,4/417) [NOTES: (Otago)]

BISLEY The shed overseer's chief object should be to prevent 'second cuts' being made ... (1897,Practical Treatise on Wool and Sheep Breeding,35)

BOWEN The loss to our annual wool clip by second cuts is very large. (1955,Wool Away!,3)

second cut: a blow made to remove wool that has been left too long in shearing. (Feb 21, 1968,Straight Furrow,20)

OGONOWSKA-COATES In competition shearing a blade shearer is penalised for a second cut. (1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,28)

MCMILLAN They [sheep] were horny, thorny, sandy - we were making 'second cuts' ... (2000,Country Bloke and Other Verse, The,14)

An efficient shearer will not make many `second cuts', but the presence of them among the fleeces in a bale will antagonise the wool buyer. (Oct 16, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,311)

FERNANDEZ ... he was past his best [as a shearer] and could only maintain his number by some very rough work, making second cuts to clean up the job and nicking the sheep badly. (1973,Tussock Fever,13)

second cut NZ & Austral. second blow made to remove badly cut fleece, inferior piece of wool resulting from this. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,688) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

second cut NZ & Austral. second blow made to remove badly cut fleece, inferior piece of wool resulting from this. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,688) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

second cut: This results when the shears are allowed to move off the sheep's skin and so into the fleece, making another blow necessary. Second cuts spoil the fleece and are said to cost the wool industry millions of dollars a year. This is because the second cut of prime wool is downgraded to the price of locks, and the main fleece brings a lower price because of its uneven staple length. (1989,NZ English Newsletter,3/27) [NOTES: (Wallace Shearing Glossary)]

noun. [Rural] a lock of wool missed by a shearer and subsequently shorn.

It is impossible to make a good "second cut" to the wool as with the shears, therefore the clip is longer and more valuable. (Sep 9, 1899,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

MCKEE WRIGHT Mighty lot of wool you've lost! Second cuts? (1897,Station Ballads,34)

second cut: short wool that has been cut in "second cut". (Feb 21, 1968,Straight Furrow,20)

MAF Second cut: Wool which is cut twice during shearing when the first cut is above the base of the staple. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58)

McKEE WRIGHT Mighty lot of wool you've lost! Second cuts? Well, that ain't my fault, you've his wrinkled hide thanks; (1897,Station Ballads,34) [NOTES: (`The Bloke that Ran across a Snag')]

`Locks' consist mainly of short pieces of wool such as second cuts, sweepings and short wool that falls on to the table during handling. (1936,Agricultural Organization in NZ,710)

BOWEN Figures taken out in this country have shown that the loss to our annual wool clip by second cuts is very large, costing many hundreds of pounds (money). (1955,Wool Away!,3)

Second cut: (i) A blow made to remove wool which has not been cut close enough to the skin; (ii) Short wool which has been produced by second cutting. (Feb 26, 1965,Listener (New Zealand Listener),15) [NOTES: (H.A.L.Laing)]

SECOND CUT: (i) A blow made to remove wool that has been left too long in shearing. (ii) Short wool that had been cut in a `second cut'. (Feb 21, 1968,Straight Furrow,20)

Second cut (1) A blow made to remove wool that has been left too long in shearing. (2) Short wool that was cut in a `second cut' (Feb 24, 1977,Dominion,11)

Second cut: Wool which is cut twice during shearing when the first cut is above the base of the staple. These short pieces of wool are of little value. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58)

noun. [Rural] a group of stock left after the faster-moving leaders or first cut has been separated off. (It is possible to have a third cut.).

NELSON second cut - the group of stock left once a cut or draft has been taken. (1999,Eugene Nelson Glossary,7)

second cutting¶

noun. [Rural] a second attempt at removing wool from the same skin site of a sheep.

The shearer who can take off a fleece with a minimum of second-cutting, even if his sheep look a little 'ridgy' when finished, is a far better investment than the 'chaff-cutter' who may 'shave' his sheep and chop the fleece to pieces. [second-cutting] (Sep 3, 1940,Manawatu Daily Times,2)

All sheep to be well and carefully shorn, to the satisfaction of the person in charge of the shed, the wool on all parts of the sheep to be taken off evenly and closely without second cutting or breaking the fleece. (Sep 24, 1887,Marlborough Express,3)

noun. [Sport]

Of course, anything like a real restoration of the original bush is out of the question, but the `second growth' has a beauty of its own which is by no means to be despised. (1897,TrNZI,29/496) [NOTES: (Walsh)]

(Jul 1950,NZ Timber Journal,49/2) [NOTES: could be 1957; database gives both dates]

SHADBOLT (1959,New Zealanders, The,12, 19)

noun. [Rural] self-sown vegetation growing naturally where land has been cleared of bush or scrub.

noun. [Rural] [mustering] a team member second from top or under the top beat man.

noun.

noun.

second pieces¶

noun.

second shearing¶

noun. [Rural] the shearing of sheep within twelve months of wool growth.

See: double shearing

Different names are given to the sheep, according to its age or sex; for instance, in England, the male is called a tup (we call it here a ram); after weaning he is called a tup hog or a teg, and if castrated, a wether hog; after shearing, when he is a year or a year and a-half old, he is called a shear hog or shearling; and a shearing wether if castrated, after second shearing, he is a two shear tup, or wether, and so on. (Oct 11, 1873,Taranaki Herald,2)

These sheep cut an average of 6lb of wool at the second shearing, and the time of growth was five months. (May 22, 1880,Otago Witness,7)

He declined to commit himself in regard to the other three men, as he was doubtful if he would require 15 men for the second shearing. (Jan 31, 1895,Otago Witness,23)

Now he plans to stick to second shearing. (Aug 9, 1984,NZ Farmer,37)

Second shearing, 66lb at 11d. (Feb 15, 1911,Poverty Bay Herald,8)

secondary growth¶

noun. a school for children from about 13 years old (cf. UK from about 11)

noun. [Rural] land cleared of original ground cover and bush, but subsequently growing scrub and fern.

noun.

seconds¶

noun. goods with a slight defect in their manufacture.

[NOTES: Jim writes: Sometimes in the form manufacturers' seconds. This sense is recorded in Macquarie 1981 and AMO and has been long familiar to me. [me also - DEH]. The relevant NSOD definition is less specific - "goods of a quality second and inferior to the best." Collins is similar. NZPOD following POD defines seconds as "inferior goods". If British usage accords with these definitions, this sense of the word may be distinctly NZ and AusE.]

noun.

The officers made sure of Leong and gathered up the paraphenalia which comprised three opium bowls, the lamp, and in all about 12 ounces of opium, consisting of liquid opium and seconds,' which is the ashes of opium, and which the economic Cantonese re-smoke in an eager desire to get to ...Elysium.' verb. [Rural] to shear sheep twice within twelve months.

Crossbred farmers shearing lambs or second shearing hoggets this autumn ought to test first to see if lice treatments are necessary ... [second-shear] (2002,Wool Grower,Autumn 7)

They second shear [x] sheep a day. (May 3, 1987,TV1) [NOTES: Country Calendar TV1 (Shearing at Tautane Station)]

For the second shear crossbred wool which made up 35.8 per cent of the North Island catalogue, prices were generally down 2.5 per cent, though second-shear oddments were up to 3 per cent dearer. Bulky skirtings, second-shear bellies and pieces and first crutching were unchanged on Nov 8. (Nov 24, 2001,Manawatu Evening Standard,9)

adjective. [Rural] [of sheep] shorn twice within twelve months.

Woolly ewes $80 second shear ewes $74. [second shear] (Oct 31, 2001,Dominion,12)

noun. [Rural] a small land-holding [esp. in North Island bush land.]

Mr Isaac Wilson's 100 acre section at Kaponga, adjoining Mr Hayes, has been sold to a resident of Kaiapoi at a satisfactory figure. (Jun 30, 1888,Egmont Star,8)

[For Sale] Good sheep and cattle sections, Waitara River, Whangamomona, Pokohura and Omona. Prices low. (Dec 31, 1904,Hawera Star,3)

C. Haggitt (Feb 26, 1880,Otago Daily Times,3c)

TOWNSHIP OF ROTORUA. HOT LAKES DISTRICT. Block IX, Sections 5 and 6, 2r, upset price per annum GBP10. (Aug 22, 1885,Te Aroha News,7)

noun.

noun. a land boundary marker

sectionist¶

noun.

See: cf. section

[NOTES: 1867 Richard Taylor Wanganui 7 of the [N.Z.] The holders company's land orders were called, in the infancy of the colony, `sectionists', and were thought to be great men, as they were the only possessors of the land [ca1839-40]]

It is perhaps not known to your readers ... that the natives here will not permit any sectionist to take possession of his land without payment for it. They allege that Mr Jerningham Wakefield either did not buy the land or did not give sufficient payment for it .... Four sectionists only have been able to settle on their land; others have attempted, but after some trouble and expense have been driven back to town .... If the Company had appointed a proper officer here to purchase the land from the natives, and see possession given to the sectionists, they might by all this time have been settled. In the meantime the settlers are condemned to inactivity. (1843,Twelve Months in Wellington,26) [NOTES: 1843 Wood Twelve Months in Wellington, Port Nicholson 26-27 in 1958 Miller Early Victorian NZ 57]

A public meeting of the inhabitants of Wanganui, was held at the Rob Roy M'Gregor Hotel, on Saturday, the 17th July, to take into consideration the circumstances of their situation as sectionists of the New Zealand Company, and unprotected subjects of Great Britain. (Aug 21, 1841,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3)

WOOD Colonel Wakefield, at the last selection of land in November, promised that the New Zealand Company would return to the sectionists any amount of [27] property (under 10 l.) they might give to the natives as payment for the land. ... Seddonian¶

adjective.

The ordinary track of ordinary mortals is not to be pressed by Seddonian boots. (Mar 12, 1880,West Coast Times,2)

The Secretary of the Auckland branch of the Seddonian Library and Labour Federation has (according to a contemporary) been appointed Auckland manager for the Tourist Department. (Feb 26, 1902,Evening Post,4)

Lord Plunket's arrival in New Zealand was signalised by a remarkable piece of stage-management on the part of the late King Dick Seddon. Had there been any interval between the departure of Lord Ranfurly and the arrival of Lord Plunket, Chief Justice Sir Robert Stout would have been sworn in as Acting-Governor. Mr. Seddon and Sir Robert were old political rivals. "King Dick" was determined that Sir Robert should not be his "boss" even for twenty-four hours. He therefore so aranged matters that when Lord Ranfurly was steaming out of the harbour of Wellington Lord Plunket was steaming in. The episode was unique, but quite Seddonian. (Feb 4, 1910,Evening Post,3)

THE WEEKLY LEADER OF THIS WEEK, PUBLISHED TODAY, CONTAINS: Original Articles on .. Seddonian Taxation ... (Apr 8, 1875,West Coast Times,3)

The Exhibition at Christchurch represented about the best that New Zealand could do at the close of the constructive Seddonian period. (Nov 21, 1925,NZ Truth,6)

In speaking of the evil effect of partygovernment worked on the Seddonianprinciple, Mr. Monkhouse got in a thrustat the sitting member. (Sep 7, 1899,North & South,3)

There is a Seddonian and Massey touch of masterfulness in the reply by Premier Forbes to a statement current in Wellington. (Apr 3, 1934,Feilding Star,4)

Seddonism¶

noun.

The actual strength and constitution of parties will not be known till Parliament meets, but enough is known to warrant the conclusion that Seddonism will no longer be the auto[c]ratic domineering thing it has been in the last year or so. (Dec 2, 1893,North Otago Times,2)

Electors will recognise, however, that consistency can scarcely be expected of one who is prepared to swallow the whole creed of Seddonism with its falsities, its injustices, and its masses of corruption without so much as a wince ... (May 14, 1898,Mataura Ensign) [NOTES: 1898 May 14 The Ensign (Gore) in 1985 Bromby Eye Witness History 74]

A further "Slap at Seddonism," and "New Zealand's Socialistic Policy," is given today by the Financial News. (Sep 15, 1899,Auckland Weekly News,8)

A further "Slap at Seddonism," and "New Zealand's Socialistic Policy," is given today by the Financial News. (Sep 15, 1899,Auckland Weekly News,Suppl. 8)

seed¶

noun. a grade of kauri chip

... it is no doubt also responsible for the dark coloured varnishes produced from the chip grades. [fn] The terms dust, seeds, chips, nubs, &c., are the names given to certain of the lower kauri gum grades according to the relative sizes of the pieces. From dust' the size of the fragments increases in the order given, as does also the purity of the grade. Chalk, orchalky gum,' is a particular grade recovered from swampy country and is characterized by its white or chalky appearance and large water content. (1936,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,17/371)

select¶

verb. to select or be allotted land

From the extreme value of allotments with water frontages for commercial people, the [Auckland] waterside was subdivided into very small allotments ... but two of the best of these [allotments], bordering on a fresh-water creek, which runs down through the valley, have been selected by Government officers. (1842,GBPP,1842 (No.569) 134) [NOTES: 1841 July 19 D.Sinclair to Lord John Russell in GBPP 1842 (No.569) 134]

He was to have selected the town sections for me during my absence in the country ... I purpose selecting in Christchurch for the following reasons: ... (Feb 12, 1851,Torlesse Papers,195,1958)

HOCKEN The 21st of April [1848] was fixed for the formal selection of their own town sections by the land purchasers, ... Mr.David Garrick ... was the first private individual to select in Dunedin, and ... he chose what is now probably the most valuable site - that quarter acre upon which now stands the Bank of New Zealand ... Upon this he erected his frame house brought out on the John Wicliffe, ... Brown, Ewing's corner [in Dunedin] was selected [in 1848] by James Williamson. (1898,Contributions to the Early History of New Zealand,99)

verb. to select (?by ballot often) Crown rural land

The directors feel assured that they need not impress on you the necessity of being careful to select, in such cases, the best land then open to choice. (Aug 21, 1839,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3)

WAKEFIELD [Terms of Purchase of Land in the Settlement of Otago' agreed on by theOtago Association' and the Company] 16 In exchange for each sum of 120l. 10s. ... each Purchaser to receive ... three separate Land-Orders, namely, for the Town quarter-acre, the ten acres of Suburban Land, and the fifty acres of Rural Land, respectively. These lands to be severally selected according to priority of choice, to be determined by Ballot. (1848,Handbook for New Zealand, The,317)

Under a system where the price at which the land is offered is fixed, and where the choice of selection is by ballot, the poor settler has the same chance as the rich one ... The limit that a selector may hold is fixed as to encourage the class of small farmers, and up to that limit the amount he selects is left entirely to himself. (1894,NZ Official Yearbook,202)

The total area opened up for selection ... [17] A Number of selectors on the books ... Lands selected under sections 114, 115 and 117 of the Act. (1895,AJHR,C-1/16)

It is quite possible within this district to select land early in the winter, fell and burn off by the ensuing summer, sow in grass in the autumn, and put on stock within twelve months from selection. (1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,4)

SINCLAIR Where leaseholders were not permitted to select' land, or where conditions of residence were enforced,dummyism' was rife-that is, a leaseholder would pay some `swaggie' to act as the ostensible selector and fufil the requirements for him. (1959,History of New Zealand,156)

noun. prob felt to be Aust. in this sense, and only occasionally used in recent times in NZ (cf as dry as a cocky's selection).

noun. the operation or act of selecting Crown land for occupation or settlement

A total area of 76,208 acres of Crown land will be opened for selection in various parts of New Zealand during the present month. (Feb 6, 1914,Evening Post,2)

Thus a great opportunity for investment will be opened in a few months when the Hua Block and the Waiwakaiho Block will be proclaimed as open for selection ... (Mar 13, 1854,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,1/145,1960) [NOTES: (C.W.Richmond)]

G.M. WILSON The land up here is far too hilly for anything but grazing purposes and unless they allow the selector the right of running over so much ground besides his selection as they do in New South Wales it will be a long time before it is taken up. (Feb 2, 1873,Diary) [NOTES: 1873 Feb 2 G.M.Wilson Diary in 1973 Wierzbicka Wilson Family 164]

HOMESTEAD SYSTEM. Under this system the settler makes no payment for the land, the only cost to him being the expenses of survey. On the fulfilment of conditions, which are five years' residence, the erection of a house, and the cultivation of one-third of the selection if open land, and one-fifth if bush-land, the Crown grant is issued. Ibid. 287 SUMMARY OF LANDS OPEN FOR SELECTION. (1892,NZ Official Handbook,284)

Under a system where the price at which the land is offered is fixed, and where the choice of selection is by ballot, the poor settler has the same chance as the rich one ... The limit that a selector may hold is fixed as to encourage the class of small farmers, and up to that limit the amount he selects is left entirely to himself. (1894,NZ Official Yearbook,202)

The total area opened up for selection ... [17] A Number of selectors on the books ... Lands selected under sections 114, 115 and 117 of the Act. (1895,AJHR,C-1/16)

HOCKEN The 21st of April [1848] was fixed for the formal selection of their own town sections by the land purchasers, ... Mr.David Garrick ... was the first private individual to select in Dunedin, and ... he chose what is now probably the most valuable site - that quarter acre upon which now stands the Bank of New Zealand ... Upon this he erected his frame house brought out on the John Wicliffe, ... The Government Insurance section was not worth selection, as it was in a hollow; ... (1898,Contributions to the Early History of New Zealand,99)

It is quite possible within this district to select land early in the winter, fell and burn off by the ensuing summer, sow in grass in the autumn, and put on stock within twelve months from selection. (1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,4)
