selling a horse¶

phrase. a bar game to determine who in a group is to pay for drinks

[NOTES: ca1920s p.c. W.H.B. Orsman (Marlborough): similar to Hokitika Swindle.]

A riot occurred at an hotel about 5 p.m. yesterday, when a young man from the country entered into a game called "selling a horse," but then withdrew. (Jan 7, 1909,Wanganui Herald,5)

Another form of gambling ... is that known as `selling a horse' ... A member of the party thinks of, or writes down a number and another member starts counting, beginning at any number below ten, and the party takes it in turn to count, much as in the Army a platoon is numbered off. The member saying the number thought of or written down collects the pool. (1948,Auckland Capping Book,16)

BELTON The procedure is sometimes referred to as `selling a horse' Each person pools so much money and a number is written down and hidden from view. The person who writes a number down requests one of the others to start counting, commencing at any number desired, provided that it is lower than the winning number. The counting is then carried on in rotation and stops when the written number is reached. The winner then takes the pool and pays for whatever has been purchased .... (1939,Outside the Law,139)

HYDE That doesn't buy our drinks,' said Sam. Another man said:We'll sell a horse, and find out who pays.' They were selling the horse, when a big black car slid up against the kerb. A voice called: `What's the trouble, you men?' (1938,Nor the Years Condemn,85)

Another form of gambling which I view much less harshly is that known as selling a horse.' The process is as follows. A member of the party thinks of, or writes down a number and another member starts counting, beginning at any number below ten, and the party takes it in turn to count, much as in the Army a platoon is numbered off. The member saying the number thought of or written down collects the pool. This game, though coming under the heading Games of Chance is probably the one really honest game in that category. I myself usually win it, especially in parties where there is no one with a pencil and I think of the number. <i>(1928,Auckland University Carnival Book,16</i>) [NOTES: 1928 Auckland U.C. Students' Association Souvenir Programme RevueTilly in the City' 16-17]

servantgalism¶

noun.

Amazing, the words people find buried in unlikely websites. Geoff Sommerville was browsing through Papers Past last 19th-century section of the National Library's site, and chanced on servantgalism. He reports the context told him it was a term for servants who got too big for their boots. Servantgalism, and its male equivalent flunkeiana, were slang words in use in colonial Australia when servants were hard to come by. Melbourne Punch in 1861, for instance, ran a cartoon of a prospective employer offering to drown a few of his children to accommodate a maid who found looking after seven would be too much. (May 25, 2002,Dominion,14)

He told me of an odd New Zealand phenomenon, the service car. A cross between a taxi, bus and freight truck, these big cars plied their trade on country roads gathering together the various threads of rural society. verb. [Rural] to graze stock in the same location all season.

(1958,Sheep. Part 1, Sheep husbandry,61)

The games were known as Fives, Tens, Sevens, and Walls and have been recorded more often since under the names O'Leary or Sevens. shagroon¶

noun. an immigrant esp. from Australia, but also from other settlements) to the early Canterbury settlement, often applied to one settled there before the main influx of PILGRIMS (contrast PILGRIM, PRE-ADAMITE, PROPHET)

[NOTES: History: an early non-Canterbury Association settler in Canterbury. (hist) [OED2 (following Morris) Phs f. Irish seachra'n wandering.: searchan transliterates shaughraun =?/sh |r n/: I have not been able to find Walls's shabberoon, etc., but if these forms exist they are more likely to be alterations of shagroon towards a play on shab, a common English dialect variant of scab, the dread sheep disease of early NZ, which would fit in with the usu.derogatory or dismissive connotations of the word.b But shab, shabbaroon are not yet otherwise attested in NZ contexts and must be ruled out; as must Sinclair's suggestion of shagreen (rough exterior) spg also shagaroon, shagrun; ?erron. spg or misprint shaproon; cf Walls's shabberoon etc. occas. cap. Morris 1898]

In a letter dated 8th March 1850, in mentioning a visit to the Taieri Plain, the writer says: "We visited the warri or hut of a Shaproon - ie., one of the retired whalers 'who have married Maori wives.' Can you tell me the meaning and derivation of the word Shaproon, and why the retired whalers were so called?" Ibid 22 September. 24 Shaproon is from the French chaperon, and originally meant "little captain." ..There is no doubt that the term was used by French sailors and those in contact with them with the same meaning as English sailors use the word mate. Mispronounced and misspelt by its adoption into the English of rough-and-ready sea-faring men, shaproon would have this signification, and even under certain circumstances might reassume its original acceptation of little leader, and be addressed to the captain of a small band, and become equivalent in a new country, as this was 50 years ago, to the word pioneer. (Sep 15, 1892,Otago Witness,24)

PARTRIDGE Shagroons. Australian settlers that went en masse, to Canterbury, New Zealand, in 1851-2: Australian and New Zealand: ca. 1851-70. B., 1942. With a pun on shagreen, the rough skin of sharks. (1949,Dictionary of Slang Addenda,1165)

Apr 19 Lyttelton Times Government might have founded a colony composed of stragglers from other settlements, of whale-fishers and stock-drivers, but would they have persuaded a body of English gentlemen to transfer their homes to these shores?' The following was written in reply:]Dream of Shagroon' [title] I saw men of another aspect arrive at the pilgrim-land. ... The Pilgrims looked with contemptuous eye on this people of strange aspect and impure blood, and did despise them. ... I awoke - and lo! the land which was to have been sacred to the orthodox foot only of a body of English gentlemen', was in possession of thestragglers, the whalers, and the stock-drivers from other settlements'. Alas! for the goodly land, - the land of the Canterbury Pilgrims. (May 7, 1851,NZ Spectator) [NOTES: 1851 May 7 NZ Spectator and Cook's Strait Guardian (Wellington) in 1947 Reed Story of Canterbury 111 [1851]

[note on Dream of a Shagroon from the Wellington Spectator: (May 24, 1851,Lyttelton Times) [NOTES: check]

The Eudora and Raven have arrived with a good stock of Shagroons who will soon infuse a new vitality into the drooping pilgrims. It is true the Shagroons don't know what to think at the great change between the arid plains of Australia, and the moist green sward of New Zealand, nor will they be able to draw any comparison if they should stay until mid-summer and behold the verdant plains, .... [Autograph marginal note `beachcombers'] (Jul 4, 1851,Australian & NZ Gazette,30/483) [NOTES: (Letter from Christchurch)]

... we need only to point to the numbers of careless, free-and-easy, undisciplined shagroons, which infest every colonial port town; men who live from hand to mouth, whose employment is generally precarious, and whose earnings have an evident tendency towards the pocket of the publican, or of the tobacco merchant. (Nov 1, 1851,Lyttelton Times,6)

The Shagroon's Lament. [ Title ] The following Stanzas are, we believe, the production of a gentleman who arrived in this settlement from Victoria the early part of last year. (May 8, 1852,Lyttelton Times) [NOTES: 1852 May 8 Lyttelton Times, in 1866 Canterbury Rhymes 8, and 1950 Woodhouse Farm and Station jVerse 5 (M.P. Stoddart)]

... the whole distance (between Nelson and Canterbury) may be traversed in 12 days easily ... I think that many of the Canterbury pilgrims and many also of the Nelson Shagroons may be expected to exchange visits next year. (May 29, 1852,Lyttelton Times) [NOTES: 1852 E.J. Lee to Elliot (? in Nelson Examiner May 29; or in Paul Letters from Canterbury) in 1940 McIntosh Marborough 126]

The term Shagroon' was used to describe pastoralists and stock-drivers who came to Canterbury direct from Australia and without the blessing of the Cby. Association. The Cby Assoc. settlers werePilgrims', while those established in Canterbury before their arrival were `pre-Adamites'. (1951,Journal of Edward Ward,132[fn])

A term formally used for a settler in Canterbury, New Zealand, who came from Australia or anywhere but Britain. (1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),362)

SINCLAIR Even the Canterbury Association, almost as soon as its sattlement was founded, had to let in the `shagroons', as the Australian stock-men were called. Ibid. 303 Shagroon Term used in Canterbury for Australian stockdrovers, 1851. (Derived from Irish Shaughraun, Saxon [hence foreigner]?) (1959,History of New Zealand,92)

McLINTOCK A term peculiar to early Canterbury is shagroon, for Australian squatters invading that province. (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,2/680) [NOTES: Wall NZ Speech]

WALL Who first called these immigrants by this opprobrious name is not stated, but it seems to me most probable that the Pilgrims used it as a term of contempt, and [110] that the immigrants took it to themselves much as the Old Contemptibles' ... adopted their enemies' names in a spirit of defiance. ... There arises the further question as to the origin of the word which ... has been explained as an Irishshaughraun'. Now why should an Irish word have been used at that time by the English settlers in Canterbury? ... My belief is that the word was not originally Shagroon' butShabroon', shabberoon',shabbaroon' (all spellings occur) which is on record from the 18th century onwards, meaning a mean, shabby fellow',a disreputable or mean-spirited fellow', and this, which would be probably familiar to the English Pilgrims, is just the sort of term which would naturally be used to describe their rivals. This shabroon' derives from the slangshab', a low fellow, recorded as early as 1637, and no doubt closely alied to the standard shabby', and ultimately fromshab' and scab', two forms of the old English word. ... I conjecture that theshabroon' [?does Wall mean shagroon] of the English Pilgrims was by some pronounced with theb' and by others with the g', nobody ever having seen the word written or printed. [EDD records onlyshaggareen' from east Yorkshire `an untidy, slovenly person'; possibly f. shabrag] (Nov 25, 1948,Letter) [NOTES: 1948 Nov 25 Arnold Wall letter in 1947 Reed Story of Canterbury 109-110]

REED It appears to have been the Australian squatters [let in to Canterbury by Godley to provide capital and flocks for unsold land] who jocularly termed the pioneer English settlers the Canterbury Pilgrims', ... The Australian squatters were dubbedShagroons', a term the origin of which appears to be somewhat elusive. [Quotes Webster and Funk and Wagnall: both definitions erroneous] (1947,Story of Canterbury, The,109)

Shagroon.- The Australian squatters who invaded Canterbury in 1851-(2) We probably owe most of the Australian sheep farming terms and practice we have here to them. They always spoke of coming down (not over) from Australia. They were also called prophets(q.v.). (C.R., p. 8; [1898 Morris Austral-English], which derives ss. from Irish Shaughraun.) (Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

THOMSON ...An old Australian squatter, who visited the Canterbury settlement in 1851, divided the inhabitants into pilgrims, shagruns, and prophets; the first were the original colonists, the second were people from other parts of New Zealand, and the last were settlers from Australia. (1859,Story of New Zealand, The,186)

The pilgrim toiled for his crop. ... Shortly the pilgrim and prophet agreed The plough and the crook couldn't live far apart. (1866,Canterbury Rhymes) [NOTES: [1851] 1866 Canterbury Rhymes 5, 9, 125 Pilgrims and Prophets'. [title of Poem] 9.[NOTE 1866] 125. During the first year of the Settlement, Canterbury was invaded by a body of sheep-farmers from Port Philip (Victoria) who were regarded by the settlers partly with admiration as successful Colonists, and partly with horror as disbelievers in the art of colonisation and theCanterbury System'. The visitors found the country admirably adapted for sheep-farming, and they treated with some contempt the raw emigrants from England who looked to agriculture as the foundation of their fortunes. One of the vistiors, who seem to have delighted in the soubriquet of Shagroon', ventured to prophesy, in a letter, which found its way into print, that theCanterbury Pilgrims' would soon be ruined and their country left for occupation by his more enlightened comrades. The pilgrims' sought no harsher revenge than to nickname their Port Philip visitorsprophets' and to take example from their experience in pastoral pursuits. The Canterbury pasturage system was quickly adapted to the requirements of sheepfarming on a large scale, and pilgrims' andprophets' were soon merged into one class of Canterbury runholders.]

PRATT In the Dream of a Shagroon' which bore the date Ko Motinau, April 1851, and which first appeared in theWellington Spectator' of May 7th, the term Pilgrim was first applied to the settlers; it was also predicted in it that the Pilgrims', would besmashed' and the `Shagroons' left in undisputed possession of the country for their flocks and herds. This was carried out principally by stock owners from Australia, who, to distinguish them from the Pilgrims or those who came from England direct to Canterbury, were called Shagroons. What this title is derived from is not quite clear. An amusing piece ... respecting the climate of New Zealand, and particularly Canterbury, was published about this time, and as it shews what opinion our Australian visitors held of our vaunted New Zealand climate, perhaps to reproduce it would be interesting. ... our Australian bard, under the title ofThe Shagroon's Lament,' discourses as follows:- (1886,Stray Leaves,10)

shaker¶

noun.

CARR When the flax arrives at the mill it is weighed and credited to the cutter. The bench loader' then takes two or three bundles and puts them in a barrel (heavy end down). He then takes the longest leaves and places them on a bench convenient to thefeeder'. ...[44] The feeder' takes each blade separately and places the butt end into thestripper' which takes the green outer covering off. ... The fibre as it leaves the stripper is caught by the fly boy', who collects enough to make into a hank, which he places convenient for theshaker'. The latter, with a motion like cracking a whip, gets rid of as much rubbish as possible, after which he places the hank handy for the `washer'. This man places the fibre in a vat, through which ... clean water is running. (1913,Country Work,43)

Shakers¶

noun. (usu. as the Shakers) a Wellington-based netball franchise competing in the National Bank Cup.

Well, you have had a fair go behind the line ... I think the whole lot of us are getting due for a shake-up. (1935,Slang Today,19287) [NOTES: 1935 A.E. Strong WW1 scene in Partridge Slang Today 287]

noun. New Zealand

Three expression found in Australian dictionaries.. testify to New Zealand's susceptibility to earthquakes. AND has Shaky Isles (also Shakey isles) and Shivery isles, both of these again being associated with the Bulletin, and both dating from 1933 (just after Napier, that is). (Oct 2000,NZWords,4 : 2)

I suppose it's to be expected in the Shaky Isles, but the clear division of red votes to the west and blue votes to the east of the Southern Alps, and likewise about the fault line through the Hutt Valley did surprise. (Nov 30, 2011,Dominion Post,B4)

Rolls any cask, beats any carpet, flies any kite, uses any bows and arrows, or catapult, or shanghai, or plays at any game to the annoyance of any person in any public place.' <i>(1884,NZ Statutes</i>) [NOTES:Police Offences Act, New Zealand,' sec. 4, subsec. 23:]

MORRIS Shanty, n. (1) a hastily erected wooden house; (2) a public-house, especially unlicensed: a sly-grog shop. The word is by origin Keltic (Irish). In the first sense, its use is Canadian or American; in the last, Australian. In Barrere and Leland it is said that circus and showmen always call a public-house a shanty. (1898,Austral English,411)

Shań.ty (sh&abreve.ń.t&ybreve.), n. [Add.] 2. A small inn in the Australian bush; - public house in a bush township. (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031)

HAY There are shanties and shanties. It is necessary to explain. Primarily, in its Canadian and original sense, the term means a log-house - a hut made of rough squared logs, built up upon each other. Such log-huts are not common in this country, though they may be seen here and there. ... The native whare[e-grave] of thatch is quickly and easily raised, serves all requirements, and lasts for years ... A shanty here, is a name applied to almost any kind of nondescript erection, which would not come under the designation of [117] whare[e-grave], or be honoured by the ambitious title of house. Rough edifices of planking are the common form. a hut (cf built a warre Jan 6) (1882,Brighter Britain,1/116)

He may call it various names according to its materials, but three names would not enter his head - i.e., crib, bach, or shack. He may call it a cabin, a shanty, a cottage, a warrie [whare], but probably he would use the commonest term of all - hut. (1947,Early Runholding in Otago,38)

Take the sharemilker who is milking his 100 cows. He rises at half-past two a.m., and musters his cows, has to get them miked by seven o'clock, take his milk to the factory; and after that has to feed over 90 calves, and about thirty pigs. He has to provide root crops for his pigs, and see that he has a sufficient supply of hay, etc., for his cows in the winter, keep his fences in repair, and stump what ground he requires to grow his crops. There is no eight hours for that sharemilker. (Mar 9, 1905,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

When you're playin' these Sons of the Sharemilkers, yous have to make real sure that if anythin' niffs even slightly of dried milk powder, yous knock it over, stamp on it until it stops squeakin', and then jump on it again just to make sure. (Oct 18, 1998,Sunday Star Times,B3)

As for the last verse.. it's so much thefarmhand and the sharemilker and everyoneexcept the boss that it just isn't true. (1955,She'll Be Right Record Sleeve,00)

BACON sharemilker-One who contracts to milk a herd of cows for a share of profits. In general, sharemilkers fall into three categories: first, the 29 per cent sharemilker, second, the 39 per cent man, third, the 50 per cent man. The 29 per cent man contracts to milk the farmer's herd and attend to their wants only; he helps at haymaking, etc. as part of the herd's `wants', but in general, once the cows have been attended to for the two daily milkings, his time is his own. The 39 per cent man contracts to milk the herd owned by the farmer and to do all the other general farm work. For this he receives 39 per cent of the herd profits. The 50 per cent sharemilker runs his own herd of cows on another man's land. He does all the farm work, and receives 50 per cent of the profits. Many farmers who today have their own farms in New Zealand started off as 39 per cent share milkers, saved enough to buy their own herds and so became 50 per cent milkers, then saved again to purchase land themselves (or on which they put sharemilkers!) (1963,In the Sticks,183)

A feature of dairy-farming in New Zealand has been the development of share-milking, akin to the old French system of me[acute]tayage or the sharefarming common with annual crops such as cotton in the United states of America. Under this system the owner usually provides the land, plant, and herd, while the share-milker provides labour and receives in return one-third to one-half of the gross returns. In other cases the sharemilker also provides the dairy herd and receives two-thirds of the gross receipts. (1943,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,24/231a)

POWDRELL The share-milker's remuneration consists of 1/3 of all milk moneys, 2/5 of calves sold, and 1/2 of the profits from the pigs sold. (1920,Dairy Farming in NZ,9)

Shavaughn¶

noun.

The widespread use of the name Shavaughn (who appears on What Now?) stems from its introduction on Havoc to mean someone particularly attractive. This can be confusing in, for example, "She's Shavaughn", when she may actually be a good-looking Doris. Thanks to Havoc and Newsboy, Shavaughn (that's how she spells it) has achieved the special fame of becoming part of the language (Jan 8, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),61)

she¶

pronoun. Used colloquially; (informal) used more generally of objects instead of it':How's the tractor?' `She's fine'; or in some phrases such as: she's right, (informal) that's all right. instead of "it" for IT, for inanimate objects, espec. undefined references well-known to the speaker' very common in NZ, as elsewhere. (see P: under RIGHT)

"She's all go," he said, adding it had the potential to bring $200 million a year into Upper Hutt's economy. (Dec 19, 2001,Evening Post,3)

"She's a whopper when she rolls"... "She" was the New Zealand Division and when "she" rolls, she is undoubtedly a "whopper". (Apr 26, 1943,NZEF Times,II/96 : 3)

After that I used to strip her down [sc. a watch] and build her up half a dozen times a day. (Jan 10, 1944,NZEF Times,III/133 : 10)

Celebrated shift boss Nic Botica, in charge of a concrete mixing crew, once barked down the phone to tell Macky his crew had just set an eight-hour record: "Boss, she won't do more." (Jun 27, 2002,Evening Post,7)

We went to go up the stairs and she was full on. It was all flames and we had to pull back. (Jan 4, 1999,Evening Post,2)

It was a bad year for Harty, myself, for everyone last year. But she's water under the bridge. (Jan 15, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),11)

BAINES Suppose a piece of timber - a flitch nine inches by twenty-four and sixteen feet long - is on the carriage, and that we intend cutting nine by three-quarter boards. After taking off a face' cut, setting the gauger rollers, and placing the flitch in position, the man at the head starts the machinery.Kreash,' says the saw. and in twelve seconds she is out at the other end. The man at the `tail' at that instant reverses the motion of the table, which gigs back. (1874,Edward Crewe,180)

BATHGATE I shall not care to venture on that rapid river in a tub like that [Maori canoe]', said Gilbert [a new chum] ... [75]Oh! She will be getting more colonised py and py [sic], and not caring so much', was Dougal's [the Highland shepherd's] patronising remark ... (1881,Waitaruna,74)

She's a young country, I grant you, but she's got the biggest future of all Australasia. (1987,Happy Endings,101) [NOTES: 1902 Lancaster Our Lady of the Plains in 1987 Happy Endings 101]

WILSON Along the [Kaituna] road we met various pedestrians, who asked our driver the rather obscure question: How is she?' They meant of course, the river .....Oh she's a bit thick,' was his laconic reply. (1904,In the Land of the Tui,206)

`Six-29!... We'll just catch her [sc. a sunset] by the time we get to the beach.' (1919,Quick March,21) [NOTES: of a threshing engine]

ANTHONY You haven't got your skeith set properly. Give her more land, and just notice the different work she makes. (1924,Follow the Call,18,1975)

Rush Ho! Rush Ho! Rush Ho!' ... It passed with greater speed than a telegram. ...Where away, mate? Where is she?' - (1928,Grey River Argus) [NOTES: 1928 Grey River Argus in 1974 Heinz Bright Fine Gold 30]

Brand gives the mill full power,/ On the last lap she's running/ Full sixty bags an hour./ (1928,Centennial Treasury of Otago Verse,50) [NOTES: 1928 David Ross Stars in the Mist (`Down South') in Centennial Treasury of Otago Verse 50]

HYDE Yes,' nodded a fellow blue coat,I could do with a popgun like that myself. How does she work, Starkie?' [132] At the earliest possible moment as many of the Bluecoats as could walk departed for Alexandria. (1936,Passport to Hell,131) [NOTES: of a gun]

HYDE `Jakeloo, Starkie; she's a little beauty, clean through my arm!' (1936,Passport to Hell,174) [NOTES: [of a wound]]

MARSH We tried her out till we was sick and tired of her and she worked corker every time. She worked good-oh, didn't she. [i.e. a specially- prepared gadget] (1937,Vintage Murder,49)

HYDE One night they had Chinese brandy in the back-room. `She's sweet and easy to take, but what a kick,' said Starkie ... (1938,Nor the Years Condemn,70)

FINLAY She'll do,' says Uncle Ted finally.We'll let the fire burn out. Come and get a cup of tea.' (1948,Tidal Creek,96,1979)

[defined in section 3 The electoral Laws Amendment Act, 1893] (1894,NZ Official Yearbook,252)

Shearer.- One who shears (and while so employed does nothing else). Ss., who always work in company and generally stick to the work for years, meet a great many people and see a great many stations; so they have a great store of expressions connected with their work. Some of them have already been noted (rosella, cobbler, etc.) If two ss. are working out of sight of each other, they can tell one another where they are' (what part of the sheep they are on) to an inch. A shearer first shears the belly (<i>on the b</i>.), then<i> opens up</i> or goes <i>up the neck</i>, then successively does his <i>first leg, first side, up the back,</i> and so on; finally the last blows trim the <i>last leg</i>, and he is <i>off</i>. But they also use a rhyming slang sometimes among themselves; say,<i>found a nail' for round the tail',hutch' for `crutch', and so on. I have always meant to collect these terms but never have. (C.) shearing blast¶

noun. Shearing-blast may be of two kinds. True shearing-blast is caused by the comb of the shearing-machine actually damaging the surface of the skin. This defect is seen as numerous lines parallel to each other running in various directions on the skin. The other defect [in pelts] often described as shearing-blast is really due to sunburn.

TAYLOR there is a large building containing about 6 large coppers with furnaces beneath which the blubber is boiled or technically speaking tryed out. ... there are three large poles erected in the sea forming a triangle which are called shears on which a platform is made and to this the whales are towed, and here cut up ... (Apr 1843,Journal,15)

DIEFFENBACH The tongue was of a white or ash colour, blackish towards the root. This organ gave several barrels of oil, and is a monopoly of the tonguer,' orcutter-in.' The latter operation is performed in Te-awa-iti near the shores, where by means of a windlass the whale is raised to the surface of the water under a scaffold called the `shears.' (1843,Travels in NZ,1/51)

SHORTLAND A pair of sheers, such as are used for taking out or putting in the masts of ships, must be erected [at whaling stations], in order to raise the immense carcases above water, that they may be cut up more [conveniently]. (1851,Southern Districts of NZ,108)

shearwater¶

noun. rain-bird, wet-bird, laughing jackass, hakoakoa

PARKINSON We saw several albatrosses, pintados, and shear-waters. Latitude 33[degree sign]35'. (Aug 27, 1769,Journal)

FORSTER About the Evening [in the Indian Ocean] I saw vast numbers of small Petrels, the black Puffin or Shearwater, Cape Pidgeons or Pintadas, & two kinds of Albatrosses viz the great white Diomedeaa exulans; & a large brown-reddish one, which I had seen before ... (Nov 24, 1772,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/183)

FORSTER We saw immense flocks of blackbanded Petrels, common & black Shearwaters, ...[ed. fn] White-chinned petrel. Forster calls this species `black petrels or shearwaters'. (Feb 11, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/225)

FORSTER [Mid Atlantic] ... we knew it to be the common shear-water (procellaria puffinus.) (1777,Voyage Round the World,1/50)

MONRO The cottages in Stewart's Island are all well garnished with a luxury of the southward - the mutton bird. This I take to be the bird which is sometimes called the sheerwater, or the sooty petrel - a black bird about the size of a duck, with long wings, which all of us have seen on our voyage out skimming over the waves. In the month of December these birds resort to the rocky islands about Foveaux's Straits in great numbers, for the purpose of breeding. (1844,Notes of a Journey) [NOTES: 1844 Monro Notes of a Journey (Nelson Examiner July 20 et seq.) in 1898 Hocken Contributions 254]

HUTTON 125. PUFFINUS GAVIUS. Forst. Rain-bird or Wet-bird. Shearwater. Laughing Jackass(?). Hakoakoa. P. opisthomelas. COUES. P. assimilis. HUTTON (1871,Birds of New Zealand,45)

It answers somewhat that description of a hagdon, or shearwater, but is much larger, nearly the size of a goose. (Jul 8, 1899,Poverty Bay Herald,2)

shebang¶

noun. a low grog shop (confused with shebeen?)

noun. a disturbance; a fight

shed¶

noun. a wool shed

They got another shed at better wages and better conditions. (Mar 20, 1911,Maoriland Worker,5)

verb. [Rural] to separate or draft stock in the open paddock.

It was what was called 'shedding' - ie separating different flocks that had got mixed without taking them down to the pens. When a wether came your best dogs had to dash in and separate or 'shed.' (Aug 1884,Northern New Zealand Settler,241)

shed: (ii) (v) to draft off sheep or cattle in the open paddock. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,71)

verb. [Rural] to place sheep in a woolshed prior to shearing or crutching, particularly if adverse weather is expected.

LOUGHNAN shed: (iii) (v) to put sheep in the shed (i.e. the woolshed). (1981,Loughnan Glossary,71)

noun. a shearing contract

He won't stay at home and endeavour to cultivate, but gets a hold of about 100 old ewes, and depends on the sale of the wool and of their lambs for a part of his living, and seeks employment - a day's chaff-cutting here and there, a little harvesting and threshing in the season, and if he can get a shed at shearing he tries to make a few pounds at that. (Oct 17, 1895,Otago Witness,11)

When a shearer applies for a shed, and his application is granted, he shall forward his union ticket (if a unionist) to the employer. (Mar 30, 1909,Ashburton Guardian,2)

noun. a wharf storage shed.

At the same time a portion of the mechanics should be engaged in erecting, in the immediate vicinity of the wharf, an extensive range of sheds for the reception of goods, and a spacious building, comprising a large dormitory, for the immediate reception of the first body of colonists on their landing. (Feb 17, 1843,New Zealand Colonist & Port Nicholson Advertiser,3)

Shortly after 2 o'clock this morning a fire broke out in the wharf office of the railway, and which speedily communicated with the large export shed on the breastwork. (Jun 18, 1877,Thames Star,2)

The Board decided not to engage labour for their sheds through the recently formed Stevedoring Association, but to adhere to the present system of the foreman hiring any men he wished. (Nov 27, 1890,Timaru Herald,3)

Before resuming this afternoon the Board members visited the No. 4 shed, and the discussion was resumed at 2.15 p.m. (Oct 25, 1920,Poverty Bay Herald,6)

noun.

shed boss¶

noun. [Rural] a person in charge of a particular shearing [often the farm owner or manager, or a 'gang boss'].

STUDHOLME Shearing was all done by hand; there were twenty-two shearers on the board, their average daily tally being about 110 sheep, which meant that the shed boss had to arrange for over 2,400 sheep to be brought in and taken out each day. (1940,Te Waimate,127)

STUDHOLME One day, a new shed boss, exasperated by Simpson's slowness gave him the sack.. (1940,Te Waimate,129)

THORNTON .. 8 shepherds and the shed boss - in the early days this was the manager but as agricultural work increased a special shed boss was engaged. (1986,NZ Heritage,235)

MARTIN Everyone in the shed was commanded by the 'shed boss,' usually the manager or wool classer ... (1990,Forgotten Worker, The,79)

However, the shearers were quick to observe that instead of taking charge of the shed with the somewhat arrogant masterfulness of most shed bosses, this youthful-looking super. was inclined to slip past them in what seemed a nervous, apologetic manner, as though not wishing to notice their delinquencies. (Nov 23, 1912,Evening Post,10)

STUDHOLME In the early days the manager acted as shed-boss. Later, when the agricultural work increased, a special shed-boss was engaged Ibid. 127At Waimate there were about 50 men and boys employed for the shearing - 22 shearers, 1 sheep-oh, 4 fleece-pickers, 4 wool-rollers, 1 brander, 1 wool-classer, 1 classer's boy, 3 pressers, 1 waggoner, 1 cook, 1 cook's mate, generally known as the offsider or `slushy' 8 shepherds; and last, but not least the shed boss, ... [fn] In the early days the manager acted as shed boss. Later, when the agricultural work increased, a special shed boss was engaged. (1940,Te Waimate,110,1954)

LANCASTER A shed-boss must know all that breathes under the roof. (1905,Sons o' Men,81)

SWANTON Then there is the `shed boss' who looks after everything, sees the sheep are shorn properly, takes the tally, looks after pressing etc. (1892,Notes on NZ,97)

shed broom¶

noun. a broom used in a woolshed to sweep up dags, etc., differing in construction from an ordinary broom.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes: the term is not in DNZE, and it is not personally known to me, but an informat tells me shed brooms were standard in Otago woolsheds in the 1970s. DEH notes large brooms known as shed brooms were also used in cowsheds to sweep down the shed after milking as far back as the 1930s.]

shed cow¶

noun. [Rural] a milking cow that produces well.

Build up your herd from those cows which have a series of records, cows which calve normally year by year, and in most cases, these cows are also your best 'shed' cows. (Dec 9, 1932,Northern Advocate,13)

If you want ... a wonderful shed cow, you just can't go past pedigree Jerseys. (Jun 1970,NZ Dairy Exporter,80)

noun. [Rural] a milker working in a cowshed.

[NOTES: aka shedhand, shed-hand]

noun.

When shearing wet ewes, the shed-managermay alter the smokes and extend thehours. (1906,Awards etc.,VII/625)

(Nov 15, 1883,Hawke's Bay Herald,4)

verb. [Rural] to separate stock into sub-groups [e.g. to separate unlambed ewes from those that have lambed.]

Other types of fleece which may be dealt with in the course of a rouseabout's day are: Dags (dirt-clogged wool) if the farmer hasn't bothered to dag before shearing; shed stain, which is good body wool spoilt when one sheep empties bowels on another while penned up closely (avoided by keeping sheep off grass for at least six hours prior); . (Mar 1988,More Magazine,31)

verb.

Sheep brought in for shearing should be spelled before shedding up, other wise the pens in the shed get very dirty ... (Oct 16, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,310)

verb. [Rural] to place sheep in a woolshed [in preparation for shearing or crutching and/or protection from weather].

The simplest and least expensive installation, where the contour of the country allows, consists of a distributor into which all the shed washings gravitate ...The second type of installation consists of a sump in which the shed washings for several days or even weeks can be collected. noun.

noun.

[NOTES: source:http://www.theregister.co.uk/2003/11/14/click_here_if_you_love/quote:Click here if you love sheds The wonderful world of sheddie net porn By Lester Haines Published Friday 14th November 2003 12:34 GMT]

shedding¶

noun. [Rural] the separating of a flock or mob into smaller sections or groups in a paddock.

LILICO [The dog] was no use in forcing, but at shedding and control of a small lot, he was perfect. (1934,Sheep Dog Memoirs,5)

It was what was called 'shedding' - ie separating different flocks that got mixed without taking them down to the pens. (Aug 1884,Northern New Zealand Settler,241)

Before penning, two sheep have to be separated - 'shedding' the sheep men call this operation - and confined to a circle apart from the others destined to be driven into the pen. (Oct 27, 1938,NZ Farmer,9)

set on 12 ha with preferred varieties and good shedding...this property comes with large shedding, on a busy road. (May 25, 2001,Hawke's Bay Today,19)

Excellent shedding and good location .. Shedding, coolstorage and covered loading on site. (May 25, 2001,Hawke's Bay Today,34)

SHEARING will COMMENCE at LINBURN STATION on 7th DECEMBER. Shearers and other Shed Hands will be expected on FRIDAY, the 4th. (Nov 5, 1891,Otago Witness,23) [NOTES: Advert]

ATTENTION SHEARERS, SHEDHANDS AND PRESSERS (Jun 29, 2005,Hawke's Bay Today,28)

noun. a sheep farmer

sheep district¶

noun.

noun. [Rural] one of six divisions of New Zealand farmland formed in the late 1880s [each looked after by a sheep inspector.]

The Committee recommend that New Zealand can be divided up into six sheep districts, with an Inspector over each. The six districts should be as follows: (1.) Otago and Southland (2.) Canterbury, Amuri and Kaikoura. (3.) Marlborough, Nelson and Westland. (4.) Wellington and Taranaki (5.) Hawkes Bay and Cook Country (6.) Auckland. (Aug 11, 1888,Egmont Star,09)

noun. [Rural] an area that is predominantly farmed for sheep meat or wool.

[NOTES: aka sheep-feed, includes some crops fed as grain]

BEATTIE There is a danger of all writers about the old days using modern terms which were not used in the period they are writing about. .... But some older writers make some surprising slips, and a really noticeable instance is in the inscription in the porch of the Memorial Church at Cave, South Canterbury, which reads: This porch is erected to the glory of God in memory of the sheep-men, shepherds, bullock-drivers, shearers, and station-hands who pioneered the back-country of this province between the years 1855 and 1895' When I first read this inscription, the wordsheep-men' made me involuntarily flinch. Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term for runholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., flock-owners, flock masters, pastoralists, run holders, run owners, sheep owners, sheep holders, sheep masters, squatters, station holders, station owners, stock holders and stock owners. The wordsheepmen' is a modern Americanism and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial ..... Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `run holder' was the most used. (1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11)

sheepdog¶

Sheep dog.- Dog to work sheep; collie (q.v.). S.ds. run naturally either to bring sheep towards you or to drive them away; and when a puppy shows his preference he is broken in for that work. The dogs that bring sheep are called heading ds. (q.v.) and most of these can be taught to lead (q.v.) if desired. Dogs which take to driving sheep away are broken in to huntaway and are called htwys (q.v.). Some dogs will both hd. and htwy and are called handy ds. They are not generally high-class heading dogs but very useful about hand and sometimes very useful mustering dogs. Some men have a special slewing d., but a well-trained, hdg. dog or htwy. will usually slew (q.v.). (C.) (Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

BEATTIE When I first read this inscription [in the Memorial Church, Cave], the word sheep-men' made me involuntarily flinch. Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term forrunholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., flock owners,'flock masters,' pastoralists,'run holders,' run owners,'sheep owners,' sheep holders,'sheep masters,' squatters,'station holders,' station owners,'stock holders,[sic] and stock owners.' The wordsheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... [12] Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `runholder' was the most used, and it is the word that I think should be substituted. (1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11)

shellfish¶

noun.

[NOTES: An Australian lexicographer points out there is a difference between most dictionary definitions and what the public see as a shellfish; likewise in NZ the fishery regulations define for their convenience shellfish as including, from memory, crayfish, sponges and possibly even sea-grass. The sensible thing would be to redefine using as the basic definition the scientific one. The present OED definition is: Any animal living in water whose outer covering is a shell, whether testaceous, as an oyster, or crustaceous, as a crab. This wording is followed by Random House and Macquarie whereas the general public and scientists tend to think of a shellfish as a member of the class Mollusca, i.e. mostly animals with a hard calcareous shell or shells.]

BEATTIE The custom in the old days was to call the buildings on a run the station,' and the land that went with it wasthe run.' On a big property you could find several stations,' and the principal one was calledthe home station,' while the others were out-stations.' This was the old Australian usage which was carried over to New Zealand at first, but gradually the signification was altered by loosely calling the whole run a station, and then the real station became a homestead and the out-stations became shepherds' huts. In this present book it will be noticed that generally the writer has preserved the olden custom of calling the main buildings the station and the land the run. The runs over in Australia being, as a rule, much larger than those in New Zealand, thestation' and out-station' phraseology was preserved much longer than over here, where even in advertisements in the late 'fifties we see the English wordhomestead' ousting the colonial word station.' <i>Ibid.</i> 12 . provisions becamerations' ... when served out to the man at the `shepherds' huts' (or out-stations). (1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,11)

phrase. as a catchphrase in increasingly common use from ca1942 on, becoming noted almost as a NZ trick of speech indicating a trait of national character); expressing a happy acceptance of, or happy anticipation of something, a state of affairs etc in which the speaker is personally concerned. =good, ok, oke, jake, sweet, righto

(Jul 18, 1958,Listener (New Zealand Listener),6/2)

Sir, - I read The Dominion's' second editorial of Jauary 25,Our She'll-Be-Right' Attitude,' with interest, but as a Grim Dig I feel that it is my duty to point out to the younger generation the origin and meaning of the expressionshe's right' She's right' orShe'll-Be- Right' originated in the Army and was only used when the person using the saying was satisfied that he had done his particular job to the best of his ability and took pride in it. If, on the other hand, he had done the job to the best of his ability but he was not satisfied with the job, he used the phrase She's not too good' orShe's pretty poor' Never was the phrase She's right' used in the sense that politicians and various other people not in the know use it to refer to a job badly done or done with acouldn't-care-less' attitude. This was never necessary because in the Army we had other phrases to cover such contingencies when things did not go according to plan, such as NAFU and SAFU, the first being a non-adjusting fiasco, and the second being a self-adjusting fiasco. To say the least of it, I feel strongly that it is disrespectful to the originators of the saying She's right' to use it in the present accepted sense, and I feel also that all Grim Digs should rise up in righteous wrath, butdon't do your scone boys.' Belmont. INFANTEER. (Jan 30, 1963,Dominion,8)

she's right: popular term to say that everything will be alright in the end; e.g., `She'll be right mate, don't worry about it.' (1981,NZ Police National Headquarters) [NOTES: (Goldie Brown Collection)]

McGILL right secure state philosophically important to traditional Kiwi person; I'll see you right reassurance that hospitality or a loan will be extended; she's right/she'll be right/she's jake/she's apples/she's sweet/too right all emphasising that all is secure and settled. NZA. (1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,92)

'Get y'a beer?' 'Nah she's right thanks,' I say, giving my new full jug a nudge. (2005,Huia 6: Contemp. Maori Fiction,29)

The words he might have used, but didn't need to, are honoured shorthand on both sides of the Tasman: "She's right, mate."... So let's say to Bichel and to every Australian: "Good on ya, mate!" (Mar 18, 2003,Dominion Post,B4)

phrase. constr. with a complement (with she'll be most often jake, right, sweet; with she's most often apples, jake, right, sweet, but also jakeloo, o.k., set) indicating that the speaker is hopeful or happy with the circumstances, or considers everything is under control: possibly a concretisation in catchphrase form of attitudes earlier expressed by e.g. she'll do

Yiddish) Shikkur is undoubtedly the source of the term (and cf variant spellings) there was probably some associative reinforcement from Eng. or Sc dialect shig, shiggry (see shickery). LOCKWOOD Yiddish became a main source of Rotwelsch [the cant language of thieves, etc.] In the course of time a number of originally cant words of Hebrew provenance passed into general use in German, though tending to remain at a more or less substandard level. Modern examples are colloquialisms like acheln eat, Chuzpe f. insolence, ... mies ugly, Moos n. money, schicker drunk, schofel trashy. These examples also occur in Standard Yiddish: akhlen (slang), khutspe, ... mies, moes (slang), shiker, shofl. (1987,Informal History of the German Language, An,263)

ROSTEN shikker Pronounced SHICK-er, to rhyme with stick her'. Hebrew: <i>shikor</i>:drunk1. A drunk. He's a shikker.' 2. (Adjective) Drunk.She got a wee bit shikker.' ... Polystichum cystostegium snow shield fern ... Polystichum Richardi black shield-fern ... Polystichum cystostegium alpine shield fern (1882,Out in the Open,98)

COCKAYNE (And). Polystichum Richardi black shield-fern (1915,AJHR,C-6) [NOTES: Plant Covering Kennedy's Bush (Canterbury)]

COCKAYNE (And) Polystichum Richardi hard shield fern (1919,NZ Plants & Their Story)

DOBBIE (And) Polystichum cystostegia alpine shield-fern (Nov 21, 1921,Letters)

DOBBIE (And) Polystichum shield fern (1921,NZ Ferns)

MARK & ADAMS Polystichum cystotegia (Hook.) Cheesem. MOUNTAIN SHIELDFERN (1973,NZ Alpine Plants,28,1979)

More palatable are the young fiddleheads of many species, especially the hen and chickens fern, kiokio (Blechnum novae-zealandiae), gully fern (Pneumatopteris pennigera, shining spleenwort (Asplenium oblongifolium) and the shield ferns (Polystichum richardii and P/vestitum). (2001,NZ Geographic,No. 49/77)

shift¶

verb. to move house

My father was camped at Breakfast Creek, and I helped him to shift along the beach to the mouth of the Waiau River, and when coming along the beach with the horse and dray we got stuck in a quicksand, but we got out after a lot of trouble. (Dec 23, 1897,Otago Witness,57)

MARJORIE E. ALCOCK I list below the words I can think of [as having different meanings in Britian and NZ.]: N.Z. shift: English Move house, or Remove. Shift' is used colloquially for moving small objects, or oneself, i.e.shift up.' (Dec 3, 1957,Letter)

GILDERDALE shift Move house. Noted in I.M. Peacocke's When I Was Seven (1927) page 175: Wemoved', the children nex door called it shifting', ut we were instructed that while it was permissible to saymoving' only the vulgar said `shifting' (1982,Sea Change,241)

shift ... NZ & Austral. move house. ... 2 n. NZ & Austral. change of residence. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,705) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

shift along¶

verb. to move speedily; to travel at a fast pace.

[NOTES: ca1951 He shifted through the invoices and had them all done by five o'clock.]

shilling¶

noun. to express a degree of intellectual or mental handicap, or eccentricity, on the part of the addressee on a rough scale based on 20 shillings = 1 pound; and graded from say 1/6 IN THE POUND, TWO SHILLINGS IN THE POUND (of low intelligence, highly eccentric) to say NINETEEN SHILLINGS (slightly abnormal or missing): PAY variant from horseracing betting the metaphor resembles those implying that the person is NOT ALL THERE, is MISSING see also BOB, QUID, SHILLING; small entry only at POUND (check)

McGILL shilling-a-month man a remittance man, paid a shilling a month working his way on the ship out. The remittance man was often the black sheep of an English family, perhaps aristocratic, banished to a colony like New Zealand to live on a modest remittance from home. (1888,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,100)

HOWE [MR. A. said] I don't believe he is the full shilling' meaning,I don't believe he has good sense' (1913,Travel Letters,112) [NOTES: AC 1942]

DAVIN He wasn't a bad bloke even if he was only fifteen bob in the pound. (1947,For the Rest of Our Lives,118)

PARTRIDGE Shillings in the pound. eighteen or, say, twelve and six, to indicate slight mental dullness or mild insanity; `He's only twelve and six in the pound': New Zealand: since ca. 1925. Niall Alexander, Oct. 22, 1939. (1949,Dictionary of Slang Addenda,1166)

SLATTER Every small town has its characters: ... Possum who only came out at night, Joey who was eighteen shillings, ... the local pervert, the local anarchist. (1968,Pagan Game, The,153)

HUNT He used to tell the story of one old bloke who wasn't quite twenty bob in the pound, a sort of village idiot. (1981,Speaking a Silence,95)

McGILL shillings in the pound dull or somewhat insane; a specified figure is given, eg `He's only 12 shillings/bob in the pound.' C.1925. (1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,100)

noun. a semi-circular notch in an axe-blade

LYON To use such [a well-ground] axe on rimu stone veins, as they were termed, on maire, or on certain hard timbers, meant many hours' grinding, and to `knock a shilling' out of the face of an axe brought one to the soft core. ... (1952,Faring South,182)

shiner ... 4. N.Z. old-fashioned sl. a tramp. (1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1064) [NOTES: [nf. 1986 NZPOD; ccom 448]]

shingle¶

noun. coarse gravel

Shingle for tar-sealing has been startedout for the road fronting Powdrell'sproperty. (Oct 9, 1917,Wanganui Herald,8)

Waimate Road Board. Committee met (Chairman and Mr Stewart) on Wednesday, 20th April, when following tenders were opened and dealt with:- .. 190 Eltham Road, R. Warner, broken stone, 5s 6d (accepted); shingle, 3s 9d; Brough and Whittington, stone, 6s 3d; shingle, 3s 3d; Dillon and Humphries, 6s 9d; shingle, 5s; B. Sheerin, shingle, 4s 9d. (Apr 21, 1898,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

The height of the Tararua was computed to be three thousand feet above the level of the sea. It was covered with shingle and a heavy growth of black birch. (Aug 22, 1840,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2)

Tenders are invited by the Government architect for the supply of shingle and sand, and delivery of the same, at Mount View, Wellington. (Jun 4, 1909,Evening Post,7) [NOTES: Advert]

Owen Marshall (2009,Living As A Moon,28) [NOTES: Faster and faster, but when we got to scree slope, where it's better to cross on the trot when the shingle and rocks start to move, I left him lagging behind.]

TURNER Bush-line or sometimes [161] forest-line (for American timber-line, English tree-line and Australian tree-line or forest-line), bush-clad, bush burns (areas where the bush has recently been burnt off) are tramping as well as general terms, as is the use of shingle for angular as well as rounded stones in shingle slide, or (earlier) shingle slip, also recently called scree as in Scotland and northern England. eg. 1890-1910 Ac. Loose, rather sharp, shale or similar rock. Much more widely used in NZ than C.O.D. `small rounded pebbles on sea-shore', esp. in loose combinations, or attributively eg shingle tops, basins, facings etc (Ac) (1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,160)

HAAST In examining these angular fragments (usually called shingle in New Zealand, whence the expression `shingle slips' for these huge taluses of debris covering the mountain sides), we find that they have a polyhedrical shape, their planes being sharply defined, and cutting, as seen in the conglomerates, clean through even the hardest pebbles of which the latter are composed. (1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,174)

Light loam, shingle and gravel subsoil. (Mar 1849,Torlesse Papers,64,1958)

... the water flows in several streams through a wide bed of shingle, and between flooded islands which bear a luxuriant vegetation. (Jun 21, 1851,Lyttelton Times,6)

GOLDIE ... Titaroi, whose singularly looking shingle upon its top brings it the appellation of `Whitehead' (1863,Diary) [NOTES: 1863 Goldie's Diary in 1947 Beattie The Pioneers Explore Otago 141]

Shingle.- Loose, rather sharp shale or similar rock. Hence S.tops, shingle basins, sy. facings, etc. (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

THOMSON I went towards the head of the valley, carefully picking my way through a large rock slide, when up above me I heard the sound of moving shingle. (1982,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,74)

(1959,Tararua,13/46)

Jim began to work up the side of the dry river bed, testing the piles of shingle thrown up by the floods. (Feb 12, 1924,Otago Witness,73)

WANTED, 2 Men to carry 2 yards of Shingle from road to house. (Nov 2, 1945,Evening Post,3)

William, after you have carted a load or two of shingle, set to work and hoe those mangels. (Aug 28, 1926,NZ Dairy Produce Exporter,29)

WALL Helichrysum depressum. "Sticks." L.S., Moraine, Riverbed, Shingle. (1925,Flora Mt Cook,55)

As the poor car skidded around with shingle flying, it turned almost broadside on. (Nov 20, 1935,NZ Free Lance,43)

Self-fed clamps without a base are quite satisfactory on sand, shingle and pumice soils. (Feb 1960,NZ Dairy Exporter,21)

The county bought shingle from Granny to metal the roads. (1987,Alfredton,237)

We have already the aristocratic carpenter idle because of the shortage of shingle. (Sep 1, 1911,Maoriland Worker,5)

verb.

Users of the road were pleased with the prompt action of the council in immediately shingling the road, thereby effecting a temporary improvement. (Aug 6, 1937,Evening Post,8)

I consider they have been very patient in not asking for the lower part of it being shingled before, seeing that the Board has shingled many cross roads, some of which are only used by three or four settlers. (Sep 13, 1913,Ashburton Guardian,7)

A petition was received for shingling Fountaine's Road and another for shingling Perrin's Road from School Road to Bennett's Corner. (Aug 2, 1916,Ashburton Guardian,7)

He is an excellent groom; ... he is a very fair carpenter, has shingled houses, made gates and troughs for pigs for me. He is also a very good fencer, and an excellent helper in the garden. (Apr 13, 1850,Report of Auckland Agricultural Society) [NOTES: 1850 Apr 13 Report of the Auckland Agricultural Society in 1853 Swainson Auckland 140]

NAILS - Spikes, Weatherboard, Flooring, Shingling, &c. (Sep 20, 1851,Lyttelton Times,4)

noun. [Rural] [high country pastoral land] sharp angular shale shattered from basic rock.

MCLEOD .. we call a dog which doesn't like running on shingle a "carpet grass so-and-so." (1951,NZ High Country,43)

NZ Farmer April 11. 45 The 'Lake' country is mainly open shingle and it's mostly 'topside' work - slewing sheep downhill. (Apr 11, 1968,NZ Farmer,45)

LOUGHNAN shingle: shale shattered from the basic rock by the frost action of ages. It lies feet-deep, loose, and pretty sharp-edged too. From it come the many terms such as shingle tops, shingle basin etc. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,72)

noun. [Rural] a dag of encrusted faeces on a sheep's rear end.

dags: shingle. (2001,Questionnaire Respondents (DB))

adjective.

Driving fast on shingle roads, / fishtailing and spinning loose. (May 27, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),93)

There are a few small creeks not deep but mostly shingle bottoms. (Jan 15, 1885,Wairarapa Daily,2)

They [sc. musterers] can stand days of shingle sidling.. and be quizzical through it all. (Apr 1945,NZ Geographer,I : 27)

Away up the Rakaia, there's a glimpse of the bare shingle tops of the Double Hill country.Ibid. From there we were to muster Shingle Hill, a block which lay in behind Main Range. (1966,Boss's Story, The,11)

noun. a piece of split (now also sawn) wood, usually rectangular used for roofing is general English (OED from 1200) but OED quotations (esp. in combinations) seem to have a provincial, and later a `colonial' flavour, although the sense does not occur in EDD. Certainly in early NZ, shingles were perhaps the commonest roofing material. British observers in the 19th century often feel obliged to explain the term. e.g.

FORSTER The latter [sc. argillaceous slate] is commonly found in great quantity, and broken pieces, on the sea beaches, and is what our seamen call shingle, by which name it is distinguished in the account of captain Cook's former voyage. (1777,Voyage Round the World,1/204)

WILLIAMS Mr Fairburn tried the Tanakaha to split for shingles ... (Jul 23, 1828,Early Journals of Henry Williams, The,139,1961)

WILLIAMS ?collective Mr. Davis ... and a party of natives went up the river in quest of timber for the purpose of making shingle. (Sep 17, 1828,Early Journals of Henry Williams, The,144,1961)

... houses built mostly of wood ... but generally painted white outside, and roofed with `shingles' (flat squares of wood), which from exposure to the weather looks like slate. (Dec 17, 1848,Letters from Otago,23,1978)

WAKEFIELD ... shingles, N.Z. [per] 1000, 6s. to 8s. ... whalebone [per] ton, 135l. to 140l. - finners, 40l. (1848,Handbook for New Zealand, The,180)

Some [houses] are merely covered with grass, others built with clay, others weather boarded, ... and for slates we have shingles, or a sort of lath one foot long, 4 inches broad, 1/4-inch thick; ... (Apr 16, 1849,Letters from Otago,31,1978)

EMIGRATION BARRACKS will be commenced both here and at Christchurch as soon as ... timber, 300,000 shingles and 16 carpenters, which have been ordered from Hobart Town, arrive. (Aug 23, 1849,Torlesse Papers,98/5,1958)

A material feature in these shingles is their economy: ... They are as durable as ordinary English slates, and cover the same surface at half the expense. (May 31, 1851,Lyttelton Times,7)

HIGGINS The roof is covered with shingles, which is wood made into pieces about 12 inches long and 6 inches wide and of course thin. These are nailed one over the other like tiles. (Dec 27, 1858,Letters) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection)]

The bed [of the Racia] is two miles across, the water a mile but split up into many branches. The water is melted snow; ... and roars along ... over large boulders, quicksands, shingle and stumps of trees. (Mar 16, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,28,1950)

I got here [Mount Brown Station] ... fortunately there were carts going up to the run with shingles (wooden tiles) so I got my swag up free and trudged myself. (Nov 10, 1862,Journal and Letters (Walker)) [NOTES: (Mt Brown, Canterbury)]

AYLMER It was a cottage roofed with cob' orshingle' as it is often called; namely little pieces of wood in the shape of slates. (1862,Distant Homes,60)

COLLINSON Houses are generally built throughout the colony of a frame-work of timber, weather-boarded outside, and roofed with shingles (1853,Military Operations in NZ,29)

BARKER [He] found the roof, tore off some shingles, and returned with a few aged hens ... (1867,Station Life in NZ,163,1870)

Blenheim Timber Yard. ... Straining and Fencing Posts and Rails ... Shingles and Piles. (Jan 4, 1868,Marlborough Express,8)

KENNAWAY ... not having been initiated into the art of putting on shingles for a roof, ... we secured a professional shingler from the port town. (1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,22)

A LADY Habitations with wooden walls and `wooden tiles', locally called shingles. (1882,Facts Relating to NZ,8)

BARLOW Instead of slates or tiles, thin strips of wood, called shingles, split off small blocks of Kauri, are most commonly used for the roofing ... (1888,Kaipara and Waitemata Echo,177)

REEVES Shingles [FN], pieces of split wood 10' x 3 [and a half]' x [a quarter]' used for roofing. (1892,Homeward Bound,63)

SALMOND Shingle. a machine sawn shake. (1986,Glossary of Building Terminology,233)

SCOTT Shingles Thin, oblong, tapered pieces of wood produced by sawing and used in covering roofs and outer walls. Western red ceder shingles are commonly imported into New Zealand. (1987,Imported Timbers,73)

NEWTON .. the sheep were just quietly sidling out through a shingle basin. (1964,Straggle Muster,12)

LOUGHNAN From it [shingle] come the many terms such as shingle tops, shingle basin etc. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,72)

STACEY The shingle basin I was in came to a chute which shot over a lip of rock to land on the shingle below. (1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,71)

shingle bed¶

noun. [Rural] land or soil previously a river bed or shingle slide.

Sometimes.. Alice and I would head to where the shingle beds of bush-clad streams led us to dappled pools, seldom more than knee deep, where with gentle hands we would catch the brown trout nesting unsuspecting under the banks. (Sep 2000,North & South,138)

Walked half a mile E., when we took to a river, which is here wide and shallow, with large shingle beds. (Jan 27, 1844,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,393)

KAKAHI RAPID; the channel on right bank; swift run; the shingle bed on left bank keeps water over into channel; good water. (Jul 4, 1900,Wanganui Herald,1)

SEWELL I have heard it [the soil] described as a dry shingle bed, but in fact it is a good soil covered accidentally with pebbly shingle ... (Jan 1856,Journal,217) [NOTES: in McIntyre (1980) Sewell Journal 1853-1856 217]

Was the House to commit itself to the payment of 15s. an acre to the New Zealand Company for the shingle beds and mountains of the Province? lands not worth 5s. an acre, which would be the case if we fixed the arbitrary price at GBP3? (May 9, 1855,Lyttelton Times,2)

The party made a detour and at the base of the cliff on a shingle bed discovered L. J. Potham, aged 20, Hastings, seriously injured. (Mar 27, 1939,Evening Post,15)

A wide shingle-bed. (1862,AJHR,E/9/24) [NOTES: (C. Hunter Brown).]

... these rivers, are torrents which at one time come tearing down to the lakes in heavy streams and at another leave the most part of their shingle beds dry. ... The [Clutha Valley] soil consists of rich alluvial flats and shingle terraces. (Aug 23, 1862,Otago Witness,6)

HOOKER Shingle beds on Mt.Torlesse and the Ribbonwood Range (1864,Handbook NZ Flora,6)

The Dart flows along a wide shingle-bed (1881,Report on Geol. Exploration of NZ,123)

The river had moved to one side cutting right into the side of the range, making cliffs on one side.. and leaving flat shingle beds on the other. (Feb 12, 1924,Otago Witness,73)

New Zealand rivers are peculiar; they cover immense shingle-beds, at all times difficult to ford, in flood impassable. (Sep 24, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,29)

Then it was out of the water into the bush, out of the bush into the water; here it was simply shingle bed and rapids. (Feb 23, 1922,Auckland Weekly News,57)

shingle chute¶

noun. [Rural] [high country] a long narrow gut of sharp moving stones.

MCMILLAN He knows those far out shingle chutes and lonely places well. (2000,Country Bloke and Other Verse, The,249)

shingle country¶

noun. [Rural] steep, barren high-altitude land of the South Island, often with faces of sharp and angular running shingle.

The great point in planting bare districts is, of course, to choose the proper descriptions of trees - trees that will have a commercial value - and the experience of Canterbury will be useful to other places in determining the selection best adapted for shingle country. (Sep 2, 1896,Tuapeka Times,5)

He urged the importance of appointing some responsible officer from the Public Works Department to get together all necessary information for Mr Hancock, such as the volume of water in the principal streams, the carrying capacity of races in shingle country, etc. (Aug 5, 1903,Otago Witness,30)

In bad shingle country, like that in the Rakaia gorge, the men's faces and hands are cut by flying shingle. (Aug 1, 1936,NZ Dairy Exporter,69)

NEWTON - the Triangle is as steep as a hen's face, and hard, broken shingle country. (1964,Straggle Muster,16)

.. when they were mustering the Craigieburn range - four days on hard shingle country - sheep stringing away ahead of the musterers could cross over on to Big Ida, an adjoining block. (Apr 11, 1968,NZ Farmer,45)

You simply want to know the area of the shingle country, and you can estimate pretty closely how much can be brought to bear on the work; and I say from my knowledge, with full confidence, that not one-thousandth part of the shingle brought down and deposited at Timaru can be deposited at Napier. (Jan 13, 1885,Hawke's Bay Herald,2)

The soil is typical of river deposit and varies from good quality river loam to poor sandy shingle country of very recent origin. (Nov 6, 1935,Evening Post,21)

It could be used with advantage in any country where timbering was required, such as shingle country, but not in hard rock. (Jul 20, 1944,Evening Post,4)

NEWTON shingle country: Typical South Island high country is characterised by bare shingle tops and face - the latter often `running' shingle. According the high country is commonly referred to as shingled country. (1966,Boss's Story, The,189)

shingle creep¶

noun. [Rural] [high country] the movement of eroded stony material downslope.

CUMBERLAND In the extreme south of the region acclerated shingle creep is reported from the greywacke mountains west of Lake Wakatipu. Once initiated shingle creep is itself often responsible for the destruction of steppe vegetation. (1944,Soil Erosion in New Zealand,70)

shingle deposit¶

noun.

HAAST In course of time, the shingle deposits of the main river ... filled the whole with their enormous masses ... (1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,150)

shingle dog¶

noun. [Rural] a high country mustering dog, adapted to running on sharp angular stones.

NEWTON Normally the musterers walked out to camp - mainly on account of the dogs. Forty or more of them, all hard-going 'shingle' dogs, they used to go clean mad when following the dray. (1949,High Country Days,23)

NEWTON Hard-going 'shingle' dogs, they earned something of a reputation in that locality. (1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,34)

shingle face¶

noun. [Rural] a steep slide of angular rock pieces on the side of a hill or mountain.

I saw the black gorges, the grey shingle faces, the river with death in its blue foamy track, / And I said: "I'll be with you - we'll face it tomorrow, though it's odds on it, Allan, we never come back." (Oct 22, 1896,Otago Witness,41)

The dredge was almost half its length ahead of the shingle face, so it may have to fall back on the shingle lead again after this week. (Sep 28, 1904,Otago Witness,25)

MCKEE WRIGHT I saw the black gorges, the grey shingle faces ... (1898,Station Ballads,47)

NEWTON .. the old hind, joined by two others, was sidling through a shingle face downwind. (1949,High Country Days,142)

MCLEOD The same dog on a hot shingle face in mid-summer is likely to go and lie under a bush instead of climbing a thousand feet to hunt a dozen woollies through a bluff. (1951,NZ High Country,45)

The country above me was a great open shingle face ... (Mar 23, 1967,NZ Farmer,35)

It [the property] also includes large areas of unproductive flats leading into rolling valleys and some steep shingle faces. (Apr 12, 2001,NZ Farmer,38)

While using a pick at the foot of a shingle face 12ft in height in a pit at Leeston this afternoon, John Grey was caught in a fall of material. (Jun 3, 1931,Evening Post,8)

Five chains of shingle face gave way near Aicken's, a few miles on the Grey side of Otira, and while steps were being taken to meet this trouble a further series of slips occurred. (Jan 19, 1944,Evening Post,6)

Work here will not be completed for some time, and passengers will have to walk over a distance of about two hundred yards to-morrow, skirting a shingle face. (May 16, 1923,Evening Post,12)

... Messrs Crosby Smith and Cuthbert again collected it on the shingle-faces of Mount Burns, Fiord County ... (1915,TrNZI,47/59) [NOTES: (D. Petrie)]

shingle fan¶

noun. [Rural] a broad slope of loose angular stones that have been washed down by water action between hillsides.

See: fan

At 9 o'clock, after drying the things left on the shingle fan, we began to ascend the Tasman spur, and reached the Bivouac at 12.30 p.m., where we boiled the billy with some scrub that we had carried up, and had dinner. (Jan 17, 1895,Otago Witness,50)

TEMPLE .. snow covered the shingle fans of creeks. (1971,Mantle of the Skies,76)

When Mrs Scott declared a cook unnecessary, the hut was carted through the Tekapo township and Lilybank Station and across the Godley River to a new site on a high wide shingle fan. (May 1994,NZ Historic Places,36)

We pass shingle fans of all dimensions, landslides from the treacherous hills, gaily bubbling brooks showing green tracks down the tawny hillsides, and cosy hidden gullies where lurk the few trees, if one can call them trees, that grow up here. (Jan 8, 1921,Ashburton Guardian,5)

Fan Creek, flowing west from Tauherenikau into the Tauherenikau River. Name suggested by the Tararua Tramping Club because of the shingle-fan at the mouth of the creek. (Dec 18, 1936,Evening Post,7)

HAAST For two miles more we kept along the eastern side of the valley, travelling mostly on the slopes of huge shingle-fans, ... (1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,131)

A number of introduced plants ... have made their appearance on the shingle-fan and in the river-beds ... (1915,TrNZI,47/334)

I have shown how in post-pliocene times from the material brought down by the enormous glacier torrents, forming huge shingle fans at the foot of the glaciers, two bars were thrown across the sea ... (Sep 18, 1874,Star, The,2)

Across the Canterbury Plains, the Selwyn flows "along the depression between the two huge shingle fans formed by the Rakaia and Waimakariri, emptying itself into Lake Ellesmere, into which it has already advanced its delta considerably." (Jul 12, 1881,Star, The,3)

Mr H. McLean wrote, re shingle fan in the dam paddock. (Apr 9, 1903,Ashburton Guardian,2)

shingle flat¶

noun.

The "half acre of ground" is the only level space in the neighbourhood - a little shingle flat above the beach where the party must have landed. (Oct 23, 1905,Taranaki Herald,3)

The land is principally rolling downs and shingle flats, all subject to wind. (May 10, 1879,Otago Witness,15) [NOTES: Advert]

The valley of Jackson's river is cut up into extensive shingle flats, which, as a rule, instead of supporting a stunted vegetation, like those to the coast, are covered by fine open forests of splendid timber. (Mar 19, 1863,Otago Daily Times,5)

It was wide and shallow here, spreading out over a little shingle flat before entering the sea. (Apr 14, 1923,Evening Post,16)

(1937,NZ Alpine Journal,7/24/57) [NOTES: [see quot. bush-hiking]]

With William and James, as with all otherresidents of Shingle Flat, to think is toact (Aug 2, 1918,Chronicles NZEF,V/49 : 14)

GREEN Then came a shingle flat, across which weran to restore circulation to ourextremities. (1883,High Alps of NZ,145) [NOTES: From 1976 edition]

shingle gut¶

noun. [Rural] a narrow vertical stony pass in steep grazing country.

NEWTON There is only one way by which it can be reached and that is by way of a narrow shingle gut running down through the rocks. (1964,Straggle Muster,104)

NEWTON .. the Esk facings are a series of great shingle guts and bluffs, steep as a hen's face and interspersed with tracts of heavy tangle matagouri. (1966,Boss's Story, The,76)

shingle heap¶

noun. shingle slip

What were a few years ago rich level fields, on which cattle and sheep browsed knee deep in succulent clover and grasses, are now, Mr Mackenzie said, waste desserts of great barren shingle heaps. (Nov 14, 1906,Otago Witness,26)

HOOKER Shingle heaps on the alps (1864,Handbook NZ Flora,142) [NOTES: R.Mason's note: `Sinclair, Travers, Haast ...? or Hooker's term?]]

The roads are not shingle heaps now as they were when I first visited the place some years ago, and yet there are miles more of them. (Sep 3, 1912,Grey River Argus,8)

Are people suffering from shingle heaps on public highways entitled to claim upon the local body at fault? is the question raised by a correspondent ... (Mar 25, 1930,Evening Post,8)

From Reginald Orton, calling attention to the habit of contractors leaving shingle heaps unprotected. (Apr 14, 1880,Timaru Herald,3)

The considerable advance of the shingle heap alongside the breakwater has apparently been made at the expense of the beach further south. (Jun 29, 1895,Timaru Herald,2)

noun. store-heaps of road metal stockpiled by local bodies

[NOTES: ca1940 at least]

The wind carried over the whole town large flakes of fire, which fell on old roofs, shingle heaps, old building materials, &c. (Oct 24, 1872,Tuapeka Times,5)

shingle nail¶

noun.

[Emigrants should bring] also some shingle nails, which are small nails about 1-1/2 inch long, with broad points. (Sep 13, 1849,Letters from Otago,38,1978)

shingle pit¶

noun. [Rural] a quarry from where sharp stone fragments are taken for use in building tracks or roads.

Edward Green was killed to-day by an immense fall of earth and shingle while working in a shingle pit in the Cust district. (Jan 10, 1878,Grey River Argus,2)

While working in a shingle pit at Wakanui to-day James Dwyer was killed through the sides of the pit caving in, and the fall of debris burying him. (Jul 25, 1906,Grey River Argus,3)

.. and in the principal streets where no asphalt has yet been laid the City Council have caused a quantity of the metal screenings obtained from the Lincoln road shingle pits to be spread. (May 8, 1874,Star, The,2)

From Mr Gladstone, accepting the Board's offer of GBP12 per acre for land for a shingle pit. (Jul 9, 1881,Timaru Herald,3)

Cockburn later boarded a lorry, which passed the shingle pit and stopped about fifty yards further along the road. (Nov 5, 1930,Evening Post,12)

It dealt only with stone quarries and shingle pits where men were frequently killed through accident due to neglect or bad management. (Sep 28, 1944,Evening Post,4)
