It was resolved to procure hurdles and gates for some shingle pits. (Mar 7, 1913,Ashburton Guardian,7)

The Clerk was authorised to arrange for the extra shingle pit on Barnswood road, and some repairs were ordered to be done on Railway Road. (Jul 28, 1920,Ashburton Guardian,5)

shingle plain¶

noun.

The shingle terraces by which these rivers are enclosed on both sides are high and abrupt towards the south, where they ascend to an altitude of about 120 feet, rising gently on the northern side and forming a shingle plain with a great deal of swampy ground, cut through by numerous smaller rivulets and creeks. (May 11, 1870,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,3)

Large masses of gravel overlie the limestone, and if the shingle plains were not of themselves sufficient to the construction and macademising the road, might be advantageously used for that purpose. (Feb 9, 1863,Otago Daily Times,5)

And there's nothing can be said / Of shingle plain or river bed / That I don't know, from A to Z. (Sep 9, 1887,Star, The,3)

This trap, I am told, is admirably adapted for river flats and shingle plains, as it is absolutely impossible to choke it, and it takes a very light covering. (Feb 20, 1896,Mataura Ensign,4)

One saw fine mobs of robust, strong-boned sheep coming from these pastures, but they had a different style of wool from those grazed on the clay and shingle plains. (Jul 29, 1914,Evening Post,6)

shingle plant¶

noun. a crushing plant for extracting natural shingle from riverbeds etc. for crushing into shingle

[NOTES: ca1920 at least]

The new shingle plant was now dredging the spit below Melling. (Aug 13, 1936,Evening Post,11)

noun. a plant which grows on shingle slips

Then it was karts, which still race on a track just over the fence from the vineyard Alan and his wife, Glenice, established in the early 1980s on a very stony, free-draining piece of land across the way from a shingle plant in Mere Rd. (Feb 21, 2004,Dominion Post,E7)

This [Veronica spathulata] is a true shingle-plant, (1908,TrNZI,40/281) [NOTES: (Cheeseman)]

Only specially adapted shingle-plants, such as Muehlenbeckia, could, therefore' hope to survive in such a station. (1912,TrNZI,44/209) [NOTES: (Aston)]

... shingle-plant ... (1914,TrNZI,46/42) [NOTES: (Aston)]

SPEIGHT shingle plants', e.g. form a perfectly distinctive group and hardly one of them is ever found in any other locality than a truescree' or `shingle-slip' (1927,Natural History of Canterbury,151) [NOTES: 1927 A. Wall Alpine and Sub-Alpine Flora in Natural History of Canterbury 151 ...]

VON HAAST The names of the friends are associated in the `Shingle Plant', Haastia Sinclairi. (1948,Julius Von Haast,181)

(1959,Tararua,46)

Shingle plant for the type of plant which grows on shingle or shingle slides may be noted in passing. (Sep 1959,Tararua,13 : 46)

shingle range¶

noun. [Rural] a ridge or range of steep hills that are on at least one side, made up of broken shingle faces.

NEWTON This great shingle range is on the station of which I am writing. (1973,Big Country of the South Island,210)

shingle roof¶

noun.

... but the best houses have shingle roofs, which are split pieces of wood about 16 inches long and three-eighths of an inch thick, and from 3 to 6 inches broad, put on like slates, either on close boarding on battens. (Sep 13, 1849,Letters from Otago,34,1978)

shingle saddle¶

noun. [Rural] a depression in a high country ridge or between two hills, covered in sharp angular stones.

HENDERSON They mobbed up during the night, and when dawn came the musterers saw Merino wethers stringing out through the shingle saddle onto what was known as no-man's -land ... (1969,Open Country Calling,35)

MCGREGOR But if you see a dog with four sore feet, and the sheep getting through a shingle saddle half a mile ahead ... (1980,Dog's Life, A,10)

shingle scree¶

noun. [Rural] [ S. I. high country] angular stones weathered from pieces of rock.

CLARK .. the [eighteen] fifties saw the expansion of the 'squatocracy' set in the northern reaches of the tussock grasslands in the forties, repeat in Canterbury and Otago (including Southland) and extended to the borders of the alpine shingle screes of the former ... (1949,Invasion of New Zealand, The,189)

I'm going to sit and look out across the vast emptiness of the land, look at the rivers running down the gorges, look at the shingle screes and the bush.. (Oct 10, 1974,NZ Farmer,104)

MORRIS In the roughest bluff, deepest creek, the hottest shingle scree she'd give her all. (1997,Different Worlds,21)

shingle shooting¶

noun. [Rural] the killing of several ducks or geese at once, by firing a bullet into shingle.

FARMER A bit of 'shingle shooting' was called for. The theory behind that was fairly simple. Firing a shot into the shingle the geese were standing on created a small burst of shrapnel which would usually account for a number of birds. (1994,Best Job Ever, The,167)

shingle short, a¶

phrase. .

See: take a shingle off

[NOTES: aka a shingle off, a shingle loose. 1953 16 M A33 Thames DHS 2 SHINGLE SHORT (with variations) `a screw loose' perhaps deriving from have a tile loose, with shingle a metaphor for head or hair (cf thatch); or from be a bit short, missing on top; to be not all there (on top)]

A man would have been thought a shingle short if he had said 15 or 20 years ago that the present reapers and binders would be invented ... (Jun 13, 1889,Otago Witness,34)

The same member of the Board, later on, speaking of another tenant, said that after a conversation of half an hour's duration with the tenant the conviction came to him that "the tenant should have been a shingle-splitter instead of a selector - for he was a shingle short!" (Dec 2, 1901,Wanganui Herald,2)

Fool, idiot, lunatic, daft, "shingle short,' are easily said. (Jul 3, 1876,North Otago Times,2)

Is the man sane who wrote it, or has he a shingle off, or does he suffer from some severe hallucination of the brain? (May 17, 1876,Grey River Argus,2)

John Smith Harris, known to the foolish as the "Whiffler," hereby gives public notice that, if anyone who is worth powder and shot states in the presence of witnesses - and he (J.S.H.) has plenty on the look out - that Mr Harris has a "screw lose [sic]," "a tile short," "a shingle off the roof," "a bee in his bonnet," or that "he is not in his right mind," by the powers he'll go for them, straight from the shoulder. (Jan 7, 1885,Manawatu Standard,2)

.. in short it was his firm opinion that Maitai himself could not be held responsible for his actions; and he should very soon begin to think that those who advanced him money were, in vulgar parlance 'a shingle short.' (Oct 15, 1861,Colonist, The,2)

No, Melisande, Sancho Panza is not the patron saint of the German talk divisions. He rode an ass and his master, Don Quixote, a sorry steed, but although the Don was a shingle short and tilted at windmills, he was a kind-hearted, chivalrous gentleman, which is more than can be said of the Nazi panzer commanders. (Nov 29, 1941,Evening Post,8)

As a matter of fact half the people in the world have a shingle loose somewhere, and if an evil gust happens to strike them just there the whole brain may be unroofed. (Apr 5, 1892,Bruce Herald,2)

Screws loose in the head are rivetted. Shingles off are fixed. (1865,Punch in Canterbury,73)

We think there are more shingles loose than he speaks of (1865,Punch in Canterbury,7/24)

THATCHER (Christchurch Signboards) And here you have a Thatcher/ If you're a shingle short! (1862,Canterbury Songster,2)

LYTTELTON Mr. Acland used an odd colonial phrase for a half-witted person: `shingle-short'. Wooden shingles being used, like the wooden church-spires in Kent and Sussex, for house-roofs, it means, weak in the head. (1868,Two Lectures,34)

GRACE I smiled, and ranked him [an eccentric major] a shingle short. (1899,Sketch of the NZ War,22)

18 shingle short, to be a v.not completely balanced mentally. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins))

McGILL shingle, short, a mentally deficient. NZA. (1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,101)

LYTTELTON Mr. Acland used an odd colonial phrase for a half-witted person: `shingle-short' Wooden shingles being used, like wooden church-spires in Kent and Sussex, for house-roofs, it means, weak in the head. (1868,Two Lectures,34)

COTTLE He was a `shingle short' without doubt (1891,Frank Melton's Luck,6)

BAUGHAN Shingle-short: Australasian for `a tile loose.' Anglice: Wanting in intellect. Aj. (1908,Shingle-Short,11)

His Worship: Was the accused sober?' Witness:Well, he looked muzzy.' His Worship: What do you mean by that?' Witness:He looked either drunk or a shingle short.' His Worship: A what?' Witness:A screw loose.' His Worship: I don't understand you.' Witness:He seemed to have a rat in his garret.' His Worship: Oh, speak English!' Witness:Off his dot - balmy [sic] - dilly.' Sergeant: He says the man was mad, your Worship.' Witness:No, I didn't. I said he was either drunk or ratty.' (Apr 16, 1910,NZ Truth,251/1/6)

ANTHONY He was a shingle short, in some ways, and farmed on original lines. (1927,Gus Tomlins,106) [NOTES: 1977 ed. Sturm]

Shingle short.- Silly fellow; foolish. -- used an odd Colonial phrase for a half-witted person: `Shingle short' Wooden shingles being used, like the wood church spires in Kent and Sussex, for house roofs, it means weak in the head.' (Lord Lyttelton: Two Lectures on Canterbury. . . ., 1868). (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

PAR TRIDGE Shingle short, be a. The New Zealand shape (1862+) of `have a shingle short' (p. 757). B., 1941. (1949,Dictionary of Slang Addenda,1167)

FRAME Toby Withers, the shingle-short with the dirty fingernails and the brown greasy hair ... . (1957,Owls Do Cry,77,1958)

DAVIN Her mouth was always open: the lower lip very thick and always wet. She wasn't bad really, but a shingle short somewhere. (1970,Not Here, Not Now,8)

have (or be) a shingle short NZ & Austral. colloq. be somewhat crazy. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,705) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

shingle slide¶

noun. [Rural] a slip on a steep hill or mountain face covered with running angular pieces of rock.

The country between the Griffiths and Clifford Creeks is very rough - a combination of high cliff, shingle slides and big boulders - and we made slow progress as far as the hut of the roadmen. (Jul 23, 1887,Te Aroha News,4)

Above me, before, slopes up for 1500ft the snow-bright shingle slide, the whiteness of the snow contrasting with the blackness of the stunted scrub on either hand. (Oct 1, 1902,Otago Witness,32)

Back on that first day mustering down to the hut, he got lost and tried to come down a shingle slide. (Sep 1985,NZ Journal of Agriculture,43)

The adoption of the grade mentioned necessitated the line being constructed high up on the sides of the mountains from the tunnel entrance in the Otira Gorge to below Aicken's Station, and fears for the stability of the line in such a position from shingle slides and avalanches induced the company to consider other schemes ... (Aug 21, 1918,Ashburton Guardian,3)

The result is that the sides of the stream are merely shingle slides, and the former series of deep holes and strong ripples is merely a chain of shingle bars. (Apr 21, 1928,Evening Post,17)

shingle slip¶

noun. [Rural] a steep slide of running scree or loose stones [usually on high mountain or hill country. ]

Turning a little along the ridge to the left, we descended a steep shingle slip of some 300 or 400 feet, and following down a gully with loose stones, alpine plants, and finally black birch, found ourselves, by about four, p.m., on the S.E side of the range, and to our joy, once more upon the banks of the East Wairau, which here pierces right through the mountains, and leads directly to our camp of the morning. (Jun 2, 1855,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

The runs on [t]he east side of Lake Tekapo are [s]till practically wholly white, the only contrasts being shingle slips, new slips and wind-swept rocks. (Aug 26, 1895,North Otago Times,1)

BARKER .. a deep drift of snow still lingered, filling up a furrow made in former years by a shingle-slip. (1873,Station Amusements in NZ,82)

.. the sub-alpine shingle-slips have increased in size. (Jan 20, 1919,NZ Journal of Agriculture,6)

MCCASKILL Do not burn on greywacke mountains in the vicinity of shingle-slips or where the soil is hallow and slips are already made. (1920,Hold This Land,151,(1973)) [NOTES: Report App. House Reps]

MCCASKILL On open plains and sunny hill faces this [soil diminishing] has led to accelerated wind and frost erosion and on higher mountain slopes to increased down-hill creep of shingle slips and mantles of waste. [shingle-slip] (1973,Hold This Land,4)

With the possible exception of certain littoral and alpine shingle slip plants, Otari presents a wealth of conditions suitable for our native plants from rainforest, alpine, swamp, and sub-tropical areas. (Aug 17, 1939,Evening Post,27)

TURNER Bush-line or sometimes [161] forest-line (for American timber-line, English tree-line and Australian tree-line or forest-line), bush-clad, bush burns (areas where the bush has recently been burnt off) are tramping as well as general terms, as is the use of shingle for angular as well as rounded stones in shingle slide, or (earlier) shingle slip, also recently called scree as in Scotland and northern England. (1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,160)

COCKAYNE Shingle-slip, in its unstable typical form, is confined to those mountains of South Island with a tussock-grassland climate and is most strongly in evidence in the North-eastern and Eastern districts. (1928,Vegetation of New Zealand, The,289)

HOOKER Shingle slips, Wairau Gorge, alt. 4500 ft. [Travers.] (1864,Handbook NZ Flora,11)

HAAST The shingle-slips ... are also not without an interesting vegetation .Ibid. .. 174 In examining these angular fragments (usually called shingle in New Zealand, whence the expression `shingle slips' for these huge taluses of debris covering the mountain sides), we find that they have a polyhedrical shape, their planes being sharply defined, and cutting, as seen in the conglomerates, clean through even the hardest pebbles of which the latter are composed. (1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,36)

At times we were scrambling through the thick bush or over steep shingle slips. (1885,TrNZI,17/352) [NOTES: (Park)]

One of the most characteristic features of our Canterbury Alps is afforded by the numerous `shingle-slips' formed by the weathering of the rocks, and often covering almost entire hill-sides. (1900,Canterbury Old & New,190)

The old and mature shingle-slips are far larger than those now existing. (1908,TrNZI,40/38) [NOTES: (Speight)]

The great screes called locally `shingle-slips', which are such a characteristic feature of mountain scenery in much of the South Island ... (1912,TrNZI,44/34) [NOTES: (Cockayne)]

On these mountain are numerous `shingle-slips,' with their characteristic vegetation. (1915,TrNZI,47/334)

... a few moderate sized shingle-slips on the slopes of Middle Peel ... (1927,TrNZI,57/82) [NOTES: (Allan)]

(1959,Tararua,46)

shinplaster¶

noun.

See: see also Southland shinplasters

(Aug 5, 1908,Otago Witness,14)

Depend upon it, fellow colonists, if they could not keep their mercurial fingers off the sacred fund of the widows and orphans, they will have small respect for those provisions of the Colonial Ordinance which professedly provide a security for the payment of the shin plasters. (Jun 29, 1850,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,69)

He hurled denunciations at the head of Sir John in particular, and the Stock Exchange in general, and in heroic language declared that New Zealand was a self-reliant, non-borrowing colony, and that Sir John and the Stock Exchange could depart for Sheol forthwith, and that he and Seddon and M'Kenzie could run the show by the aid of Consols, Postal notes, and shin plasters of a variety of patterns till further orders, and be d--d to him. (Apr 19, 1895,Evening Post,4)

A feature of the exhibit is a number of debentures or "shin plasters" as they were irreverently termed, which were put into circulation during the term of the governorship of Captain Fitzroy... The Government debentures were for 5s, but the private ones were for sums ranging down as low as 3d. (Feb 20, 1890,Otago Daily Times,17)

But these war advances we got from J.B. were, perhaps, part of the shin plaster J.B. borrowed from Uncle Sam, and Downie Stewart may have learned from U.S.'s pawnbrokers exactly how England funded her huge war debt with them. (Jun 27, 1925,NZ Truth,5)

And Sir Samuel/Hoare - he goes / With shin plaster / On his nose ... (Dec 18, 1935,Evening Post,8)

JOSEPH MASTERS Many tradesmen [in the early 1840s] had to make their own money on strips of paper called by the settlers `shin plaisters'. Governor Grey [sic] established a bank issue and issued one pound promisery [sic] notes, to get change for one of these, you would get a hat full of shin plaisters. (1871,Autobiography,26)

MACDONALD I do not know exactly how wholesale mercantile business was carried on, but the retail business in the town [?Wellington] was carried on [c1840s] mostly by means of little bits of printed paper, issued by shopkeepers, for from one penny to two or three shillings. This currency went by the general name of shin plaster'. <i>Ibid.</i> 117 When eggs fell from six silver shillings per dozen to one shilling ofshin plasters', the Hutt, Porirua Road and Karori settlers looked anxious. (1910,Reminiscences,109) [NOTES: c1840s in c1910 Macdonald Reminiscences (TS:VUW) 109]

SUTHERLAND Shinplasters.- The fact that private traders found it necessary themselves, to issue paper notes in denominations below five shillings suggests that at the outset ... the Fitzroy notes were not issued for values below five shillings. The private paper notes were issued for small change, redeemable mostly in Five Shillings, in Government debentures.' Both the debentures and the private notes were issued on poor paper, and soon became known asGovernment Rags' and Shinplasters' respectively. The termShinplaster' for paper money appears to have come to New Zealand from America, via New South Wales. *[fn] In the latter Colony the issue of paper money of a denomination lower than twenty shillings was prohibited in 1826 to promote the circulation of sterling instead of a colonial currency, and the prohibition was welcomed by the people as preventing the Colony being inundated with beggarly rags' and dollar and half-dollar notesused often as a paltry contrivance to evade payment of debt,' vide "The Australian," 19 July 1826. [fn] Various reasons have been given for the origin of this curious term for paper money issued in the forties. The most likely explanation comes from America (p. 650 The Numismatist, 1938), where it is stated that in the good old days post-boys and out-riders, wearing high boots, were required, at times, to pay toll-fees at toll-gates, and in order to facilitate progress they placed paper money or coins in bags in their boot-tops, against their shins - hence the term `shin-plaster.' (1941,Numismatic History of NZ,158)

HARGREAVES The [Governor Fitzroy's (1844)] Debentures, popularly known as government rags', were given various nicknames such as<i> assignats,</i>shinplasters', and flash notes'. All these terms had reference to worthless paper money, some of which had been issued in the past. <i>Assignats</i> was the name given to large amounts of paper money issued in France during the French Revolution, but which depreciated to such as extent to be almost worthless.Shinplasters' - sometimes written skinplasters' - had its origin in North America, and again referred to depreciated paper money, whileflash notes' was a popular term in use for any counterfeit money or worthless forged paper money. (1972,From Beads to Banknotes,40)

shooter¶

noun. a marble

SUTTON-SMITH Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as taw' orshooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; dubs',dates', stakes',dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. (1972,Folkgames of Children,174)

short tussock¶

noun.

Less grand and altogether less fortunate are the short tussocks. Growing up to half a metre in height, they include such hardy species as blue tussock (Poa colensoi), silver tussock (P. cita) and hard, or fescue, tussock (Festuca novaezelandiae. With a penchant for lower country, short tussocks have had to compete over the last 200 years with the runholder's arsenal of fire, exotic grases and grazing stock, and also wih the runholder's enemies - weeds and rabbits. [29] While the grass family is most likely to have originated in South America, our short tussocks appear to have arisen from ancestors that moved to, and diversified in, the northern hemisphere and then trickled back south. ... Short tussocks migrated up-slope from dry valley bottoms to meet them. (Nov 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 66/28)

shortjaw kokopu¶

noun.

[NOTES: also shortjawed kokopu.]

The shortjaw kokopu is one of five native fish species commonly referred to as whitebait when they are juveniles migrating back to fresh water. Two of these species are classified as endangered, with a similar threat classification as eastern falcon, kereru and great spotted kiwi ... (Aug 28, 2008,Dominion Post,B5)

McDOWALL The fifth species is the rarest of all. It is the shortjawed kokopu (Galaxias postvectis), a species that is also rare as an adult. Ibid. 50 Shortjawed kokopu behave similarly to banded kokopu. They also climb falls and move well inland... Most shortjawed kokopu are found in small streams in unmodified native forest, usually in pools with thick cover,especially where there are piles of logs or boulders among which the fish can hide. (1984,NZ Whitebait Book, The,14)

PAUL Shortjawed kokopu Galaxias postvectis Widely distributed but localised, secretive and seldom seen. (1986,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,48)

Several shortjaw kokopu, a nationally threatened species, were found in the lower reaches of the stream. (Jan 25, 2005,Independent Herald (Wellington),9)

On the West Coast, the season runs from September 1 till November 14 to improve the minor late-running species' chance of reaching coastal wetlands for giant kokopu, or forest-covered streams for short-jawed and banded kokopu, and koaro. (Nov 11, 2003,Dominion Post,A18)

The short-jaw kokopu usually grows to about 20 centimetres and lives in streams with native forest cover. (Aug 26, 2006,Dominion Post,E7)

Inanga are the most common species, but whitebaiters may also capture the young of giant kokopu, koaro and banded kokopu. "Shortjaw and giant kokopu are described as threatened species. ..." (Aug 17, 2005,Whakatane Beacon,4)

DENNIS The juveniles of five species of galaxias make up the whitebait catch: inanga (Galaxias maculatus), koaro (G. brevipinnis), banded kokopu (G. fasciatus), giant kokopu (G. argenteus) and short-jawed kokopu (G. postvectis>/i>). -- (1981,Paparoas Guide,187)

Shout, n. to stand treat. (1) Of drink. (2) By transference, of other things. The successful digger used to call passers-by to drink at his expense. The origin may also be from noisy bar-rooms, or crowded bar-parlours, where the man who was to pay for the liquor or refreshment called or shouted for the waiter or barman. When many men drink together the waiter of course looks for payment for the man who first calls or shouts out for him to give him the order. Or is pay the shout' a variant ofpay the shot,' or tavern reckoning? In its first sense the word has reached the United States, and is freely employed there. [1859] (1898,Austral English,416)

sick¶

adjective.

Various chemical modes of cleansing have been tried with only partial success, but recently it was accidentally discovered that a current of electricity would almost immediately expel the troublesome impurities, no matter how abundant or how "sick" the mercury had been rendered. ..With the current flowing, the mercury could not be made sick. (Nov 5, 1883,Evening Post,2)

This sick mercury also powders away, or as it is termed "flours," so that the floured fluid metal is carried away and lost, leaving fresh surfaces to be attacked by the injurious ingredients in the ore. (Mar 20, 1890,Otago Witness,12)

MAY The mercury plates were seldom perfect: the finest gold was lost by flotation while with cemented gold a thin coating of iron oxide (rusty gold') often prevented amalgamation. The mercury itself becamesick' or floured'; both sodium and nitric acid were employed to improve its amalgamating qualities. <i>Ibid.</i> 527 FLOURED MERCURY: mercury that has lost its amalgamating properties because of impurities in the ore or the wash. The mercury is thensick'. (1967,West Coast Gold Rushes,238)

adjective.

... those in the bush sick' area were inspected and a dozen found to have died ... the herbage grown on the so-called sick country.' <i>Ibid.</i> 40 ... periodical changing of the stock fromsick' to what is known to be `healthy' country every few months. (1928,TrNZI,58/39) [NOTES: (Aston)]

[caption] Second crop of lambs from ewes confined to sick paddock, Sherry River. (1938,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,20/195A)

adjective. NZ colloquial usage follows US and earlier British usage in assigning a main sense of ill, unwell, ailing' to this word, esp. in the phrase <i>be sick </i>; contrast modern British usage with main sensevomit'. That is, NZ usage follows OED a. I 1. Suffering from illness of any kind; ill, unwell, ailing. Now chiefly literary and U.S. [9-19c]. rather than 2. Having an inclination to vomit, or being actually in the condition of vomiting [18-20c]. An ambiguous statement, e.g., I was sick on Thursday' would usually be interpreted in NZ asI was ill' etc; in Britain probably as I vomited etc' (Dr. R. Savage); and this can lead to some immediately horrifying images for Englishmen in N.Z., needing quick reshuffling to extract the correct sense: e.g., I was sick in bed last Thursday. Unambiguous statements naturally assign themselves appropriate senses, mainly on aspectual grounds: I was sick twice before breakfast; I have been sick for months.Ill' is often used in NZ by, e.g. mothers and nurses, as a euphemism for the vomit' sense: Little Tommy has just been ill all over his shoes. (When used as a verb, sick is alwaysvomit': N.Coghill and C. Tolkien have an interesting note to l.71 of their edition of Chaucer's The Nun's Priest's Tale (Harrap pp 94-5). l. 71 Repleccioun [overeating] re made hire nevere sick sick':ill', not sick'. The withering away of the old sense of sick is relatively recent, and has not taken place in America; cf also <i>sickbay, sickroom, a sick man,</i> etc. Chaucer knew the word <i>ill, but for him it was a word characteristic of the North and East of England (it was of Scandinavian origin), and he only used it to give an impression of dialect in the talk of John and Aleyn, the Two Cambridge students from the North of England in the Reeve's Tale; for them, in any case, it meantbad, evil'. Chaucer's word for being sick (in our sense) was spew.'

MARSH ... and I must say he did look a bit sick. (1937,Vintage Murder,96)

sickle-fibre¶

noun. [Rural] an unusual wool-fibre in the birthcoat of Romney lambs, similar to halo-hairs.

Shedding is common among hairy sickle-fibres; sometimes all are shed, while occasionally, at the other extreme, all persist, every intermediate condition being found. Many of these fibres are much shorter than any shed hairy sickle-fibres. (Jan 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,13)

When a name for these intermediates is needed, the term "super-sickle" is used. (Mar 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,141)

Fibres of this kind that do not grow after birth are called "baby sickle-fibres." (Mar 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,144)

Other somewhat longer sickle-fibres, it would appear from their length, are shed after growing for just a short time after birth. These are termed "infant sickle-fibres" (Fig 4). Infant sickle-fibres are much less abundant than baby ones. Most sickle-fibres with coarse medulla in the post-natal region sustain this up to some eight weeks after birth. For these it is convenient to use the term "chalky sickle-fibres," from their dull white appearance. Super-sickle-fibres, some with a good deal of medulla in the neck, occasionally remain fine after birth ... (Mar 20, 1933,NZ Journal of Agriculture,145)

The stoutest of birthcoat fibres, halo-hairs, are almost all shed and the super-sickle-fibres with necks coarser than those of sickle-fibres, shed the more readily. (Jun 20, 1934,NZ Journal of Agriculture,342)

noun.

OWEN & PERKINS Another important part of the swaggy's equipment was his bedroll. Generally it was called a `wagga'. Now the old wagga was popular in the wintertime - a bit heavy to carry, but it came into its own in the winter. The wagga rug was made out of the old one-striper sacks, ... The old one-striper was the fair-dinkum chaff sack ... Later came the three-striper bag. It was a much shorter, smaller bag with a very much lighter weave, but the old heavy one-striper made a wonderful wagga. The wagga originated over on the Aussie side, and generally to improve it you opened up two sacks, and this made a wonderful rug. (1986,Speaking for Ourselves,72) [NOTES: (Bob Edwards, bushman)]

sidle¶

noun. an act of sidling; a track that runs at an angle across a slope.

[NOTES: ca1953 R. Mason e.g. make a high sidle to avoid the bluffs, or a broken ridge.]

PASCOE When the Whitcombe River is in flood there are many such whirlpools which the usual route avoids by a high steep sidle in the thick bush. (1960,Over the Whitcombe Pass,33fn) [NOTES: 1863 Lauper in 1960 Pascoe (ed) Over the Whitcombe Pass 33 fn]

LAUPER [Note]. There are many such whirlpools which the usual route avoids by a high steep sidle in the thick bush. (1863,Over the Whitcombe Pass) [NOTES: The footnote is a 1960 one by Pascoe.]

Near the head of the creek, the track climbs over a saddle of regenerating forest to begin a sidle towards Kaitoke... (2008,NZ Geographic,94/30)

verb. [Rural] [mustering] to traverse a steep slope [ in a horizontal team formation.]

STRONACH Most of the Clarence block is sidled. That is to say, the spurs are so big that it is necessary to have several men sidling on the 'face' or side of each spur. I have seen as many as ten men on a face sidling along about half a mile apart. (1953,Musterer on Molesworth,23)

verb. to negotiable a steep slope of a hill by going round the side of it rather than straight up to the crest. (probably a back form from SIDELING.)

To sidle , to go around the side or across the face of a hill, is a characteristic New Zealand expression, strange to the Englishman or Australian. The example of 1821 in O.E.D.: Ye know the footpath sidles down the hill', suggests that something of the New Zealand meaning was not unknown in England, but it cannot have been well known, or mountaineers would not have started to use <i>traverse </i>, both as a noun and as a verb, towards the end of last century. <i>Sidle </i> is well known among high-country musterers. As it is a word most likely to be used in open hilly or mountainous country, one may guess that musterers and up-country people gave it currency, whence it was adopted by mountain club people. If ski-ing had not brought its more or less international vocabulary with it we should no doubt be sidling slopes, on skis, that we now traverse... From 1936 to 1938 in <i>The Tramper </i> there are a number of references tosidling tracks' and sidling routes'. Towards the end of 1938 comesafter sidling round the head of the said stream', and, a year later, we sidle the top of Three Johns', and from then on the verb flourishes. In 1940 comeson a long sidle', and from then on the noun is as common as the verb. Ibid. 41 From the top basin we sidled up tiresome scree, ... and at last emerged on the top of the divide. (Sep 1958,Tararua,29) [NOTES: Ruth Mason `Track and Trail']

Often, with back bent low, he must thread [sic] the dirty overgrown bed of a steep little watercourse, or, still with back bent, sidle along the muddy slope of a steep hill, through a tunnel in the koromiko copse; or, straightening his back with a sigh of relief as he emerges on the open shingle-bed, find that he has to ford and ford again and again the cold rapid stream, slipping ahd splashing over weed-covered stones. (Aug 18, 1862,Daily Southern Cross,3)

A few blows with the tomahawk, a fire-stick judiciously employed, and, should the brook be high, a little sidling over a low bank or two, is the most that can be needed, though the gorge being very narrow, its aspect may at first appear discouraging for a mile or two. (Jun 2, 1855,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

We sidled along the spurs, slipping and stumbling over the steep, wet, frozen, stony ground, for three of four miles, which seemed interminable, there the river Mataura approaches the hills, and made our course more westerly; a little further on we crossed the Otamita, a mountain stream, that came rushing out from between the hills, with a clear stony bottom. (Oct 3, 1894,North Otago Times,1)

Come and let us sidle up thes bonnie brae and ha'e a look roond. (Sep 6, 1905,Otago Witness,86)

Come and let us sidle up this bonnie brae and ha'e a look roond. (Sep 6, 1905,Otago Witness,86)

BLAIR There was heavy snow as we sidled along above Bealey gully. ... and carelessly sticking to the ridge I carelessly continued sidling. (1956,Life & Work at Canterbury Agricultural College,83) [NOTES: (1926 Hilgendorf in) 1956 Blair Life and Work at Canterbury Agricultural College 83]

To work one's way round, up or down a facing by an easy grade. Usually sidle out, sidle round etc. (1933,Press, The) [NOTES: Acland]

JONES .... sheer precipice for thousands of feet. One could not sidle round in mustering, but had to go under or over the top. (1933,Autobiography,82)

Sidle .-To work one's way round, up, or down a facing by an easy grade. Usually s. out, s. round, etc (Jan 27, 1934,Press, The,15)

NEWTON Sidling to a handy shoulder, he scanned the basin ahead. (1949,High Alps of NZ,30)

(Oct 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,295/1)

THOMPSON We then sidled for a few miles on a slight uphill grade until we reached a long sloping spur. 1952 Ibid. 55 ... Errol and I ... then sidled round the cliffs until we reached the basin at the head of the stream. (1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,42)

R. MASON `To go around the side of; to go along a hill-side. (tramping.) To sidle a hill; to sidle along a valley (not on the ridge, not on the valley floor, but along the hillside.) In common use among trampers. The term was not understood by Dr. I.V. Newman, lecturer in Botany, V.U.C., an Australian.' (1953,Personal Communication)

STRONACH Most of the Clarence block is sidled'. That is to say, the spurs are so big that it is necessary to have several men sidling on theface' or side of each spur. I have seen as many as ten men on a face sidling along about half a mile apart. The man on the top beat, in all but exceptional circumstances, keeps a little in front, and each man down the face is a little behind the man above. (1953,Musterer on Molesworth,23)

(1958,Tararua,12/29)

SHORTLAND While passing in front of a hut [at the whaling station], I was invited to visit a sailor who lived within, and who had had a bad leg for many years, which rendered him unfit for any other work than that of signal man. While the rest of his companions were actively engaged in the boats, he was carried every day during the season to the summit of the most projecting point of the cliff, where he sat under a shed, glass in hand, to look out for whales. By means of a mast and yard, and some signals, he was able to give notice to the boats in whatever direction he discovered a whale; and so earned a small share in the fortunes of the fishery. LAING & BLACKWELL [115] The New Zealand species are not so curious in this respect as those of most countries, though the little Silverback ( Corysanthes macrantha), with its lurid purple flowers, and long antennae, has somewhat the appearance of a purple spider or cockroach. (1907,Plants of NZ,110)

silverbellied¶

adjective.

[NOTES: eels]

EDWARDS Tuna are better cooked on a wire rackover embers, very nice this way,especially the whakaheke, the silver-bellied ones. (1992,Mihipeka,39)

silverbelly¶

noun. a native freshwater eel; tuna

[NOTES: ca1910 Marlborough W.H.B. Orsman; aka silver-belly, silver belly, silver bellied eel, silver-bellied eel, silver-belly eel, silverbelly eel]

MORRIS name given (I) in New South Wales, to the fish Silver-Bream (q.v.); (2) in Tasmania, to various species of Atherinidae. (1898,Austral English,418)

BEATTIE I suppose I am the only person living who has seen a hinaki (eel-pot) put there. ... I ... saw him put a hinaki in the river, and next morning it was full of silver bellies. (1945,Maori Place-Names of Canterbury,34)

HENDERSON ... the eels were so plentiful ... that we often hauled the line up with two fat silver-bellies clinging to one bob. (1961,Friends in Chains,67)

FULLER Silver-bellies and small eels. (1978,Maori Food and Cookery,69)

WILSON She said they tasted muddy, though they were beautiful silver-bellies. (1984,South Pacific Street,7)

silver belly NZ a freshwater eel. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,713) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 452]]

(1979,Heinemann Dictionary of NZ Quotations,1015)

LOCKLEY The big silver-belly eels don't come here. We [Maoris] used to take them in river dams in the hinaki, the eel-basket - where the freshwater runs fast. (1980,House Above the Sea,13)

HULME Then one night I added [to the soup stock] two silverbelly eels. After that, more water, a pigeon, cresses, puwha, more potato, o the soup grew. (1983,Bone People, The,366)

There can be no doubt that the so-called broad-nosed eel is the female (local fishermen call it the "glott") and that the sharp-nosed eel is the male, and more popularly known as the "silver-bellied." Snigs, glotts, brotts, and other distinctive names given by eel-catchers are merely varieties, distinguished by colour and other very slight differences, due, a great deal, to environment; all mean one and the same - Anguilla vulgaris. (May 9, 1906,Otago Witness,68)

A large silver-bellied eel, measuring 45in. in length and 13 1/2in. in girth, was caught in the fluming of the turbine engine at the Tuarangi Old Men's Home a night or two ago. (Apr 18, 1914,Ashburton Guardian,4)

The first stage called Hao or Tuna heke is a small silver-bellied eel, which migrates downstream whenever the water increases in volume, and returns upstream after the flood abates. (Aug 1, 1925,Evening Post,13)

silverbird¶

noun.

See: also silvery petrel

FORSTER We shot the grey Eggbirds, which they called Silverbirds on board the Adventure, & found them to be of the Petrelkind ... (Dec 23, 1772,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/204)

silvereye¶

noun. a small bird widespread throughout New Zealand, recognizable by the silver ring around its eye; also called waxeye, white-eye, blight-bird or blighty, tahou; Zosterops halmaturina (silvereye is perhaps the commonest or most widely used modern name for this bird)

[NOTES: Falla et al. in Collins Guide use SILVEREYES: Zosteropidae' as the Family and chapter heading. Appeared at Waikanae, Wellington in June 1856. ca1935 1984 Heard Marlborough, Wellington, Auckland, Otago.]

A notable exception is the silver-eye,white-eye or blight-bird (zosterops)which was blown across the Tasman Sea bya storm some fifty or sixty years ago. (Jun 18, 1904,Press, The,8)

Silvereye is one species which seems to do well in suburban gardens being both insectivorous and fruit eating. (May 2002,Forest & Bird,25)

We named it silver-eye, on account of the ring of white silky feathers around each of its eyes, and blight-bird because of its useful habit of eating the woolly aphis on apple trees. The Maoris named it tau-hou, which means stranger... There was a paternal veto against killing the white-eye. (Feb 9, 1922,Auckland Weekly News,15)

[Caption] Silver-eyes feeding from the apples, bananas, suet and other food attached to an elderberry tree. (Jul 24, 1935,NZ Dairy Produce Exporter,34)

We have a flock of lively tauhou, the white-eye or silver-eye..... pegging away at the scraps in tins hung on a tree for them. (Jul 1937,NZ Railways Magazine,25)

Isolated in their own areas of the painting are three cells containing a silvereye, a man aiming a gun at the sky, and the dancing couple again. (Jul 21, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),55)

They are impaling halved apples on fencetop nails for silvereyes. (Jun 24, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),28)

I have got a great many birds since you have been away, which I shot with your gun or a catapult (excuse spelling), and which I stuff and hang up by the beak. ... One of them is a New Zealand bittern ... I have also the mako-mako, silver-eye, riro-riro, miro-miro, fanny etc... (Aug 16, 1875,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,2/399,1960) [NOTES: (?Bill Atkinson, Nelson, 15 years]

Siĺ.ver-eyé. (-&imacr.́.), n. (Zoo.l.) An Australian name for the white-eye; - called also wax-eye, and, in New Zealand, blightbird. See WHITE-EYE, in the Dictionary. (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031)

(1870,TrNZI,3/21) [NOTES: Buller [see Blight-bird.]]

PARK But she hasn't the sense of a silvereye! (1992,Fence Around the Cuckoo,226)

BULLER ZOSTEROPS LATERALIS {CAERULESCENS}. (THE SILVER-EYE.) ... Native names. Tau-hou, {Whiorangi, Hiraka, Motingitingi,} Kanohi-mowhiti, Karu-patene, {Karu-ringi,} Karu-hiriwha, Poporohe, and Iringatau. (1873,Birds of New Zealand)

BULLER By the settlers it [sc Zosterops] has been variously designated as Ring-eye, Wax-eye, White-eye, or Silver-eye, in allusion to the beautiful circlet of satiny-white feathers which surrounds the eyes; and quite as commonly as the Blight-bird', orWinter Migrant'. (1888,Birds of New Zealand,1/82)

To-day my son was dissecting a common bittern ( Botaurus poecilopilus) ... We found the `bill of fare' for that day to have been a silver-eye ( Zosterops caerulescens), ... It is well known that the bittern varies its feeding ... adding still another enemy to our useful little migrant blight-bird. (1897,TrNZI,29/285) [NOTES: (Drew)]

MORRIS Silver-eye, n. a bird-name. Same as Wax-eye, White-eye, or Blight-bird (q.v.). (1898,Austral English,418)

WHITE The little Silver Eye' orBlight Bird,' so called from its very useful propensity of eating various blights, has a silvery circle round its eyes, composed of tiny white feathers which are sweetly becoming. (1905,My NZ Garden,71)

STUDHOLME Wherein the silver-eyes their fragile nests did make (1940,Te Waimate,201,1954) [NOTES: 1917 Effie Studholme in 1940 Studholme Te Waimate (1954) 201]

silvereye: forest bird (1947,Reeds' School Dictionary: NZ Suppl.,175)

WILLIAMS this is the first (?only) use of this term in any Williams. Kanohi-mowhiti, zZosterops lateralis, silver-eye or blight-bird (mod.). (1957,Dictionary of the Maori Language,94)

silvereye n [silver + eye] : any of several small Old World singing birds of Zosterops or related genera (as Z. palpebroso of India or Z. lateralis of Australia and New Zealand) having the eyes encircled by a ring of white feathers - called also white-eye (1961,Merriam-Webster Third International,2119)

FALLA et al. SILVEREYE Zosterops lateralis Other names: Tauhou, Waxeye, White-eye, Blightbird, Blightie. (1966,Birds of New Zealand,223)

McLINTOCK Silvereye.. .. tauhou .. .. Zosterops lateralis (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/705-712)

silvereye n. one of several varieties of small birds with pale circles round the eyes. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. (Aust.-NZ Suppl.),624)

NATUSCH Family ZOSTEROPIDAE (silvereyes). Zosterops lateralis ... , called ring-eye in the south, wax-eye, white-eye, silvereye, blightie, etc., elsewhere, is probably in actual fact a blown-away Australian. Not seen here before 1886, it is certainly plentiful . . (1967,Animals of NZ, The,282)

silver-eye n. one of several varieties of small birds with pale circles round the eyes. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

263. Zosterops lateralis lateralis (Latham, 1801) Silvereye (Tauhou) Originally Tasmania and Bass Strait islands; the species colonised the South Island ... (before 1856), North Island (1856) ... (1970,Annotated Checklist of Birds of NZ,69,1980)

silver-eye n. Austral. & N.Z. another name for waxeye or white-eye. (1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1076) [NOTES: [1986 NZPOD 713; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 452]]

Silvereye Zosterops lateralis lateralis (LATHAM, 1801) ... OTHER NAMES: White-eye, waxeye, blightbird, tauhou. (1985,Reader's Digest Book of NZ Birds,288)

Inside are more patients - two more tui, another kereru and two tiny silvereye fledgelings in a modifies cornflakes carton ... (2005,Branch Out,Vol16 p6)

[The birds above spoken of have been known in Nelson for several years by the name of the "Silver Eye," and are now so numerous that they destroy friut to a serious extent...] (Jul 20, 1867,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,3)

I wonder if people are aware that most of our birds do migrate. For instance, we have in the winter time such birds with us as the yellow hammer, the little black fantail, and the silver eye, and, as far as my judgement goes, they are not to be found in the colony in the summer time. (Sep 3, 1912,Evening Post,3)

In Mr Buller's papaer there is some very interesting information with regard to the little bird which now abounds in our shubberies, which is known to the colonist as teh "blight bird" or "silver eye," by the scientific termed "Zosterops lateralis." (Jul 22, 1871,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,7)

In Mr Buller's paper there is some very interesting information with regard to the little bird which now abounds in our shubberies, which is known to the colonist as the "blight bird" or "silver eye," by the scientific termed "Zosterops lateralis." (Jul 22, 1871,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,7)

[Caption] Silver-eyes are also known as "Blight Birds", being particularly valuable in removing aphids from orchards and rose bushes. (Dec 18, 1935,NZ Free Lance,36)

silverfish¶

noun. Seriolella amplus

Griffin, described and figured a new species of fish, very closely related to the Warehou (Seriolella brama) and Silverfish (Seriolella punctata), from specimens caught by hand lines in a rocky locality near Mayor Island, Bay of Plenty. This species probably replaces the Silverfish in our Northern waters. (1957,Sea Anglers' Fishes of NZ,60)

noun. smelt (cf silvery)

There are only three fish in the River Avon, sufficiently common to justify the supposition that either of them may be the adult form of the Whitebait; these are the Bull-head, the Silver-fish, and the Smelt. The name of Smelt is applied indiscriminately to the two latter fish, we will ... retain the trivial name of Silver-fish as a distinction. We may first dismiss the Bull-head ... It is an Acanthopterygious fish ... Head, large, one third of the length of the body ... [86] The Silver-fish again belongs to the Malacopterygii abdominales, or fishes having soft fin rays, with the ventral fins placed below the abdomen. ... We now come to the ... fish ...called, by boys, the Smelt; but why a Smelt, I know not. ... the Smelt is a Galaxia ... (1870,TrNZI,2/85) [NOTES: (Powell)]

This fish is called Silverfish by Mr Powell, but Smelt (Retropinna richardsoni) by Dr Hector. (1879,TrNZI,11/275)

verb. =dissolve in quicksilver amalgam

KITTO Save all the cleanings [gained by washing the gold, etc] until there is a dishful, which you may silverise. Work the quicksilver in in an iron dish and when all of the gold is taken up pan off the sand. (1900,Practical Dredgeman's Manual,46)

noun. in N.Z. always (or chiefly) refers to a better class of corned beef (distinct from brisket).

noun.

noun.

silvery¶

adjective. ?holding

If they are silvery' they will walk out again; ifstiff' they will work a week or two to get a few shillings to take them on the road again, ... (Sep 15, 1906,NZ Truth,65/3/6)

adjective. as a descriptive epithet in the names of plants and animals see cotton plant; grass, hair; oarfish; grass, sand; tauhinu,

noun. cucumber smelt

See: cf. whitebait

PHILLIPPS NEW ZEALAND SMELT Retropinna retropinna Richardson. ... The smelt is the cucumber fish of some localities and the silvery of others. Ibid. 54 In some other localities these young [smelt, Retropinna] are called tuarenga. The half-grown fish is termed tikihemi and the adult paraki. Certain races of fish have a broad silvery band running along the side; hence the term `silvery.' It is to be regretted that in Canterbury the term smelt is still used to apply to the minnow, Galaxias attenuatus. (1940,Fishes NZ,53)

STUDHOLME When the silveries (cucumber smelts) were running up the [Canterbury] rivers in the spring of the year, Maoris would catch huge quantities of them in nets. Ibid. 236 Enunga[sic] Smelts (mature whitebait) and silveries (Cucumber smelts). (1940,Te Waimate,22)

PAUL Common smelt Retropinna retropinna Also called silvery, estuarine smelt, or cucumber (from the smell of freshly caught fish). Silvery, particularly along the sides. (1986,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,49)

"A novel sight was witnessed in the north branch of the Waimakariri, near the railway bridge, last week, when for a chain in length and width a shoal of silveries were [sic] seen making their escape from a shoal of trout. .." (Feb 15, 1905,Otago Witness,59)

The silveries were little fish about 6in long, but the herrings were of a good size, some weighing 1/2lb, and they had very silvery scales which flashed in the morning sunlight like polished metal. (Jan 16, 1890,Otago Witness,30)

The fact demonstrates that the New Zealand waters are peculiarly adopted [sic] for the production of fine fish; and no doubt one reason for this is the superabundance of silveries in some of the streams. (Mar 3, 1882,Grey River Argus,2)

Vernacular Name.- Powell [TrNZI 2/84] was the first to point out that two fish were referred to as smelt' in north Canterbury. These were <i>Galaxias attenuatus </i> and <i> Retropinna retropinna</i>. At present Canterbury residents refer to </> R. retropinna</i> assilvery,' on account of the silver line running along the side of the half-grown fish. [NOTES: [AND see SWILL: six o'clock swill 1955]]

Sir, - Like the great majority of New Zealanders who finish work at 5 or 5.30 p.m. I like two or three beers and a chat to my friends before I go home for dinner. That is when I feel like a drink, and when I enjoy it. They call it the `six o'clock swill,' but we enjoy it. After all, when service is required by so many at the same time, there must be a crush. New Zealander's liquor hours, notably the `five to six swill' produced gusty debate and plenty of laughs at the National Party Conference yesterday. (Jul 23, 1963,Dominion,1)

Wellington New Zealanders will choose in a referendum later this year between their notorious 6 o'clock swill and a more civilized style of drinking liquor. .. (Jun 29, 1967,San Francisco Chronicle,4) [NOTES: 1967 July 29 Ian Templeton in San Francisco Chronicle 4]

Though the six o'clock swill ceased in 1967 .. there was still a powerful linkage between drinking beer and masculinity. (Mar 13, 1988,Dominion Sunday Times,16)

They have become booze barns run by a private company which is still in the six o 'clock swill mode . (Jan 20, 1993,Independent Herald (Wellington),1)

Maybe one day we'll look back on Sunday closure with the same amazement with which we now view the six o'clock swill, but surely never with the same horror. (Aug 13, 1990,Listener (New Zealand Listener),15)

(2003,Penguin History of New Zealand,389)

The teen-age binge-drinking so evident at the New Year is part of a New Zealand tradition that goes right back to the six o'clock swill, known affectionately as the six o'clock spill. (Feb 10, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),32)

For husbands, release from their emotional repression came only with the "six o'clock swill" at the pub or Saturdays at the footy. (Sep 19, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),31)

In the dim glow of yellow lights, you can smell again the perpetually beer-soaked carpets of the six o'clock swill and consider that you are just another battery hen queueing for a fix. (Apr 8, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),52)

When licensing laws were relaxed in 1989, and again in 1999, to allow the sale of alcohol in supermarkets and, it turns out, dairies, the changes were supposed to reflect a new, more mature, attitude to drinking. Unfortunately, the attitude of some is unchanged from the days of the 6 o'clock swill; they just don't have to travel as far to buy alcohol. (May 4, 2009,Dominion Post,B4) [NOTES: Editorial]

This hurried hour of drinking between 5 and 6 was known as 'the 6 o'clock swill' and the decibels spilling out of the public bar onto the streets got louder and louder as six o'clock approached. (Jun 2004,NZ Memories,No. 48/6)

Those were the days of six o'clock swill, when alcohol could not be sold after 6pm and only hotels could operate bottle stores. (Apr 23, 1983,Listener (New Zealand Listener),14)

OGONOWSKA-COATES Ages of sheep. Although there are many variations, the following names are usually used: A sheep is a lamb until weaned. After weaning a lamb is called a hogget until shorn. A male lamb is a ram lamb until castrated, then a wether. A female lamb is a ewe lamb. After shearing, a ewe or ram lamb is usually called a shorn hogget until cutting the first two teeth. It is then called a two-tooth. Some use the term two-tooth as soon as the lamb is shorn. Next year the sheep is a four-tooth, then a six-tooth and then an eight-tooth or full-mouthed sheep. It is full-mouthed as long as the teeth remain perfect but then becomes broken-mouthed and gummy. (1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,94)

POLACK Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called para[as-acute] paraua[a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, mungu nui (black physeter); right whale, tohora (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, mango (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. It was, of course, these cross pieces or skids, that gave the road its name ... . (1953,Story of the Kauri, The,180)

He looked into his woolshed and said, 'Oh yes, there's plenty of room in the skillions.' [skilion] (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The (Acland Glossary),15)

noun. [obsolete] (in pl.)

See: -

BUTLER The wool-shed .... has a large central space, and an aisle-like partition on each side. These last will be for holding the sheep at night. ... In a wool-shed, the aisles would be called skilions (whence the name is derived, I know not, nor whether it has two `l's' in it or one). All the sheep go into the skillions Ibid. x/158 In a wool-shed the aisles would be called skilions (whence the word is derived I know not, nor whether it has two l's in it or one). All the sheep go into the skilions. The shearers shear in the centre ... [and] pull the sheep out of the skilions as they want them. (1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,139)

BARKER ... a constant succession of woolly sheep being brought up to fill the skillions' (from whence the shearers take them when they want them), and the newly-shorn ones ... being turned out after they have passed through a narrow passage, called arace,' where each sheep is branded ... (1865,Station Life in NZ,34,1870)

Skillion.- [Variant of 'skillin' and skilling', recorded from the fourteenth century, all late examples being provincial English; origin unknown. --A.W.] In old Australian and New Zealand books (up to about 1880) it is common and means the sheep-holding part of a woolshed. I can remenber an old hand mentioning the word in the 'nineties. I have tried it on several elderly shepherds since the war I and none of them understood it. I imagined the word had gone completely out of use until last month (May 1933), when I bought five tons of chaff from a man and asked him to store it for a few weeks. He looked into his woolshed and said, Oh yes, there's plenty of room in the skillions.' I felt as if I had met a notornis. ' . . called skillions (whence the name is derived I know not, nor whether it has two l's in it or one). All the sheep go into the skilions.' (Butler A First Year in Canterbury Settlement], p. 139).A constant succession of woolly sheep being brought up to fill the skillions.' ([1874 Lady Barker Station Life], p. 34). (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

TEMPLE ... he saw the clearest satisfaction in the sunlight falling through the skillion door over the heaving backs of the sheep and on to the board, slick with wool grease ... (1979,Stations,99)

noun. a lean-to; a built-on room, shed, etc.

[NOTES: also in combinations (skillion roof, kitchen, cottage, etc.)]

BEATTIE (Mr Busbridge drew me a plan of the place, and its five compartments. One of these, a long room known as the `Skillion' had rows of bunks along each wall. (1947,Pioneer Recollections,21,1956) [NOTES: (sc. on an Otago station)]

In a similar way the baled straw can be built to form the walls of a shelter-shed, with a skillion roof made of saplings overlaid with thatch and supported, where necessary, by forked uprights. (Jun 7, 1919,Evening Post,11)

All these terms had reference to worthless paper money, some of which had been issued in the past. <i>Assignats</i> was the name given to large amounts of paper money issued in France during the French Revolution, but which depreciated to such as extent to be almost worthless.Shinplasters'--sometimes written skinplasters'--had its origin in North America, and again referred to depreciated paper money, whileflash notes' was a popular term in use for any counterfeit money or worthless forged paper money. NATUSCH Family ELATERIDAE. The well known click beetles or skipjacks of many species ... Wireworms are the larvae of some kinds. many live in the bush. (1967,Animals of NZ, The,150)

noun.

Saw some fish like skip Jacks and a small sort that appear'd very transparent. 5 [fn5] Any sort of fish that had a habit of leaping out of the water tended in the eighteenth century to be called a skipjack. In the twentieth century the name is sometimes given in Australia and New Zealand both to the Striped Tuna (Katsuwonis pelamis) and to more than one sort of Trevally (Usacaranx spp.). Early whalers gave the name to the Trevally. But that does not cast much light on the fish Cook saw, for which other candidates have been suggested, and which must be left unidentifiable. (Oct 3, 1769,Cook's Journals,1/166,1955)

noun. trevally (Caranx georgianus)

noun.

noun. ?striped bonito; tuna

(b) Suggested commercial name[s]: (i) Skipjack Tuna (ii) Southern Bluefin Tuna (iii) Yellowfin Tuna. (c) Other common names: (i) Skipjack; Striped Bonito (ii) Bluefin Tuna; Southern Bluefin; Southern Tuna (iii) Yellowfin All sometimes referred to as Tunny. (d) Principal localities where taken: (i) A summewr visitor to New Zealand ... (ii) Southern Bluefin Tuna is a large species of temperate Australasian seas and migrates south to Foveaux Strait in summer months. (iii) A widely distributed tropical species which ranges into northern waters ... in summer months. (1970,Nomenclature of NZ Fish,49)

WILSON TUNAS ... Tuna were generally known as tunny' until the discovery of a potentially big export market to America, where tuna is rated a luxury fish. The name as then changed to conform with that used in America. Since then Southern Bluefin tuna, Yellowfin tuna and Striped, or Skipjack, tuna have been developed into important export fishes. In New Zealand the Albacore has become an important commercial fish. <i>Ibid.</i> 267 BONITO Offshore anglers use bonito fillets for snapper bait and deep-sea anglers claim its dark-red flesh attracts almost every sporting fish up to shark and marlin. The Classer, by feel, sight, and general knowledge, decides what class it belongs to. (1913,Country Work,15)

A considerable saving in time and wages is effected in not having to pick over and chip the pieces from the dags after the wool is skirted. (Nov 30, 1938,Auckland Weekly News,86)

skirt heavy¶

phrase. [Rural] to take a wide amount of wool from a fleece when skirting.

Almost 15 years ago the phrase that filtered down from stock agent to farmer and thence to the battler in the woolshed was 'skirt heavy.' In other words, when a fleece was thrown on the table, you were expected to tear off large strips of any wool which might conceivably be a little inferior to the best part of the fleece. (Feb 13, 1963,Weekly News,39)

Terms connected with the movement of the marbles were: cannons, clears, dead-stick, double-hits, fires, funs, gees, haystacks, in smug, keeps, kills, kisses, lay-ups, manyes, ones, pink, ringer, rolls, scat, screws, skinned, skun, spiders, sported-off, stays, stops, tracks, throughs. We were fazed for a minute as the handle "lovely gent" didn't seem to fit anyone we know [sic], but we fought back gamely by claiming that "this bloody Skypoo was planning to shoot through at sparrow fart tomorrow without paying you his tariff," and a fascinating screaming match developed between the descendant of the old Phonecians and her with the gasper and pom-pommed slippers. (Nov 1986,Geological Society of NZ Newsletter,74/78)

Then there was the evening with the little hawker of Lebanese extraction whom we cheerfully referred to in those spacious racist days as a Skypoo. (Nov 1986,Geological Society of NZ Newsletter,74/78)

skyshaft¶

noun.

McARA Overwind: Failure by the engine-driver to stop his machine before the safety detaching-hook on the winding-rope came into contact with the detaching ring mounted in the headframe, thus suspending the cage in the skyshaft and allowing the rope to go over the head-sheave pulley. Overwinds had to be reported to the Inspector of Mines. To prevent overwind there were generally two warning bells which rang in the engine-room as the cage was approaching the surface. (1978,Gold Mining at Waihi (Glossary),328)

slab¶

noun. a fish in poor condition (?)

Another important [trout] food was a small mollusc ... of which no less than 140 were counted in the stomach of a slab' taken at Rotorua. ... A considerable number of the trout examined were definitelyslabs'. The slabby condition appeared to be due not only to the usual poor health of the fish for some months after spawning had taken place, but more definitely to both semi-starvation and indigestion. (1921,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,3/272) [NOTES: (Tillyard)]

HINTZ Anglers complain about the presence of slabs'; the marine biologists sustain their complaints by proving that the lake holdsan undue proportion of matured trout'. Ibid. 171 And if you land your fish you are well rewarded. The kelts and slabs seem to have little chance of competing with vigorous, well-conditioned trout during a green beetle rise. (1964,Trout at Taupo,67)

ANDERSON It was a rainbow and it was a `slab'. I don't know what was wrong with it but its body was just bones and not very much longer than its big head. (1957,Men of the Milford Road,197) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection)]

Another important [trout] food was a small mollusc ... of which no less than 140 were counted in the stomach of a slab' taken at Rotorua. ... A considerable number of the trout examined were definitelyslabs'. The slabby condition appeared to be due not only to the usual poor health of the fish for some months after spawning had taken place, but more definitely to both semi-starvation and indigestion. (1921,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,3/272) [NOTES: (Tillyard)]

But of course lots of the fish are "slabs" that should be returned because they are not the best eating. (Dec 2, 2005,NZ Herald,Super Sport D15)

noun. a pack of (12 or 24) beer cans

In a dark corner.. about 10 youths two patched Black Power members in their twenties are drinking a slab of beer, whisky and on assortment of other spirits. (Jun 4, 1999,Dominion,11)

Does this mean he is one of "them" or can I proceed with my plans for next Friday night's seduction - a slab of beer (on me) and the latest Oasis CD at full volume? (Sep 29, 1997,Dominion,12)

I couldn't drink a slab without falling over. (Jul 29, 1999,Listener (New Zealand Listener),64) [NOTES: if not 64, try 43]

HUGHES Only the driver had drunk less than a slab of Stein-grenades in the course of the eleven-hour journey. (1999,Shooting from the Lip,158)

A couple of country jokers take their Auckland cuz fishing, then send him off to the nearest pub for a slab. (May 14, 1994,Listener (New Zealand Listener),33)

An average fishing day for him is a "six-pack day" with a really bad day being "a slab". (Nov 8, 2000,Independent Business Weekly,21)

Throw a sheila in the front and the dogs in the back, there's only really room in the boot for a box of .308 shells and a slab of Speights. (Dec 12, 2001,Evening Post Drive,3)

verb. to support (sides of a shaft, well, etc) with slabs [AND mining 1854]; (also vbl n slabbing

The road from Kapanga to Ring's diggings is nearly impassable. It is slabbed two-thirds of the way by Messrs Ring, and the government might easily have the remaining portion slabbed and made fit for bullock drays. (Jul 8, 1862,Daily Southern Cross,3)

This shaft is sunk to a depth of 30 feet, the whole distance being slabbed through blue sediment. (Oct 6, 1893,West Coast Times,2)

Before stating anything farther, it may be necessary to say that there were three branches of gold-digging we did not try, viz. - turning the water in creeks or streams of any size, to try the beds of them, because we were not strong enough, and on account of the time it would take; sinking in flats, where the holes might go deep and require to be slabbed ... (Jun 20, 1857,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

No 2. shaft is sunk to a depth of 41 feet as follows:- 21 feet slabbed at 4s per ft., - GBP4 4s; 20 feet not slabbed at 3s per ft., - GBP3; 3 feet additional, No 1. shaft, at 3s, 9s. total GBP7 13s. (Oct 6, 1893,West Coast Times,2)

Sinking on the head lead of the south-west extension 30ft or 40ft, all slabbed, and a quarter of a mile wide, but the washdirt is in patches. (Oct 11, 1876,Tuapeka Times,2)

... the slabbing in a mine (1865,Evening Post,1/245/2)

LADY BARKER Wood was wanted for building a stockyard, or slabbing a well (1873,Station Amusements in NZ,3)

MORRIS mining term: to keep up the sides of a shaft with timber slabs. [1871] (1898,Austral English,420)

slab n. coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. slab v. to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs. slab n. a horse in poor condition. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

slab n. coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. slab v. to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs. slab n. a horse in poor condition. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

MAY Drives, too scantily lathed, collapsed; shafts, too hastily slabbed, caved-in; (1967,West Coast Gold Rushes,280,1962)

noun. a rough plank split from a log (perhaps still holding the general sense of slab ); often split slab of wood; outside cuts, or rough offcuts, of logs (in early days, often used for rough constructions, hence slab-house, slab-hut).

CHAPMAN Sometimes the whare is built of large "Slabs"; sometimes of toi-toi (a sort of bulrush), sometimes of wattled clay; and sometimes of brushwood. (1847,Letters to His Father, 1843-1851,00) [NOTES: Quoted in Miller; Early Victorian NZ, p. 140]

The old-time navvies' camps on the Main Trunk Railway were rough ephemeral affairs of slab and canvas. (May 2, 1928,NZ Free Lance,7)

McRAE The house itself was large - fourteen rooms - and made of plastered slab. (1963,By the Braes of Balquether,31)

Also, the house adjoining the brickyard, being a two-roomed slab building, with brick chimney, wooden partition, floored, and having two casements and two doors; ... (Apr 29, 1843,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,237)

The new tenants of the land have made improvements in clearing, fencing and erecting houses, most of them being composed of nikau and slabs. (Dec 17, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,8)

BRIGHT The walls were formed of broad upright slabs of timber. (1841,Handbook for Emigrants,22)

The partitions which are very rough (made of slabs, the outside board in sawing up a tree, bark on one side) do not reach up to the roof. (Apr 20, 1851,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,1/94) [NOTES: (H.R. Richmond)]

John & Seal cutting firewood Jem & Georgie splitting slabs for pig-stye (May 1, 1856,Journal Kept at Rockwood and the Point) [NOTES: 1856 May 1 Phillips Rockwood Journal [ATB FS TS 31/Cant.Pub. Lib. 37]]

PAUL You are fairly entitled to something better than a warre[e-acute], say a two-roomed hut for yourself ... and a large, strong wata, or store raised on posts to keep your provisions safe from rats. ... slabs plastered with clay are also used for walls ... One of these huts must serve you for your first year's wool-shed, with the help of a few hurdles in front, ... (1857,Letters from Canterbury, NZ,90)

HODDER ... slabs of which the tenement was made. (1862,Memories of NZ Life,155)

We are now busy putting up a sheep yard we are making of upright slabs with a cross rail and rammed in the ground. (1861,McLean Papers,20/70) [NOTES: (Condie, Hawkesburn Station Canterbury)]

WHITWORTH The hut was made of slabs ... [rough cut trunks] (1875,Cobb's Box,6)

BULLER At nearly every bend, a rude and lonely hut was standing. This was made of slabs, and thatched with grass. (1878,Forty Years in NZ,27)

FEATON To strengthen their defences two detachments ... were detailed to cut slabs in the bush. (1879,Waikato War,52)

PRINCE The Beech Hut is built of slabs with a tree-fern roof, and contains eight sleeping berths ... (1889,Diary of a Trip,10)

ARTHUR ... Covered at the bottom with wire-netting or `slabs' (split pieces of wood) (1894,Kangaroo and Kauri,98)

MORRIS slab n. coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. slab v. to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs. slab n. a horse in poor condition. Slab, n. In English, the word slab , as applied to timber, means an outside piece taken from a log in sawing it into boards, planks, etc.' (Webster.') In Australia, the word is very common, and denotes a piece of timber, two or three inches thick: a coarse plank, axe-hewn, not sawn. Used for the walls of rough houses. (1898,Austral English,420)

BAUCKE It is a low whare of split slabs, adzed over, and sunk into the earth as closely as the inequalities of adze-joining will permit. (1905,Where the White Man Treads,259)

MACDONALD ... then I split slabs and made all the furniture I considered necessary. (1910,Reminiscences,33)

Our new home of two rooms with timber hewn out of trees and split into lengths called `slabs' and put up in the rough state. (1916,Letter) [NOTES: 1916 Letter in 1939 Winter The King Country 13]

MILLER Sometimes the whare is built of large `Slabs';[sic cap] sometimes of toi-toi (a sort of bulrush), sometimes of wattled clay; and sometimes of brushwood. (1958,Early Victorian NZ,140)

A flat thick piece of material; it may be stone or even cake. In Australia and New Zealand a slab is a thick plank; a `slab-hut' is a shanty built of such planks. (1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),370)

slab n. coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. slab v. to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs. slab n. a horse in poor condition. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

slab n. coarse axe-hewn plank, used for rough dwellings called slab-huts. slab v. to reinforce sides of a shaft with timber slabs. slab n. a horse in poor condition. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

MURRAY He will make his house .... of slabs split in the bush from Totara. (1866,Southland,28)

Your chimney must be built of slabs. (Jul 1863,Southern Monthly Magazine,1(5) : 21)

STOLEN, from a saw-pit at the back of Col. Wakefield's residence, a number of strong wide slabs. (Nov 28, 1840,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2)

The kauta or cooking houses, are proportionably large; in that part of the pah belonging especially to Heuheu, there is a row of cooking houses 40 feet long by fifteen broad, and 10 feet high in the walls; which are constructed of enormous slabs, well fitted together; round windows, with sliding shutters, admit the light, and let out the smoke. (Mar 19, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3)

The hut is of split slabs with a good roof of thatch to defy the weather. (Mar 6, 1890,Otago Witness,40)

McARA Slabs: See timber slabs. (1978,Gold Mining at Waihi (Glossary),332)

It was a simple building of three rooms, built of split slabs, lined with cob, and thatched roof and earthen floor (kept from becoming dusty by sprinkling it with skim-milk). (Apr 8, 1920,Ashburton Guardian,2)

noun. often with bark still adhering, trimmed by saw from a log or baulk of timber

[NOTES: this group tending to scrap wood or off-cut reading]

GUTHRIE How you worked at felling that tree and splitting it into slabs . (1935,Little Country, The,352,1937)

Slab (sl&abreve.b), n. [Add.] 5. A very thick undressed board, obtained by splitting, not sawing. (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031)

WEEKES Edwards knew a saw-mill down the harbour and was sent off ... to tow up some slabs which he said would make an excellent chimney ... (1846,My Island) [NOTES: c1846 Weekes My Island in 1940 Establishment of New Plymouth 118]

RICHMOND [The house was] made of slabs, the outside board in sawing up a tree, bark on one side. (1851,Letters,1/255)

MUELLER ... an old chief whose whare ... was composed of slabs I had found useful for making benches and tables ... (Oct 10, 1865,My Dear Bannie,61,1958)

BAUCKE (1905,Where the White Man Treads,259)

HENDERSON It was cross-cut into three lengths and then sawn up into boards and scantlings. With the outside slabs Tod built a workshop ... (1948,Taina,26)

JEWELL Slabs: Pieces cut from the outer portions of a log, and unsuitable for converting to sawn timber. (1948,Accounting in the Timber Industry,128)

GROVER He was a slabby, loading slabs of useless wood onto a trolley and carting them away. Eighteen months later he graduated to the goose saw. About two feet across, it is used for docking the ends of sawn timber, and is fixed to the end of a beam that swings like a pendulum from a rafter. (1967,Another Man's Role,34)

SANSOM He became a slabby on the wharf and also ran a small shop for a time. ... Perhaps the term Slabby needs needs explanation. A slab was the outside cut with its bark attached, sawn from the log at the mill. ... A slabby was a mill-hand who sorted the timber on the wharf before loading it on to the cutters and ... steamers. (1970,Stewart Islanders,142)

MASSEY Slab The outer portion of a log which is cut off so as to make the log square. (1987,Woodturning in New Zealand,94)

verb. to ?face cut

slab ... 4. Austral. & N.Z. a. a rough-hewn wooden plank. b. (as modifier): a slab hut. ... vb. slabbing, slabbed. tr. 6. to cut or make into a slab or slabs. 7. to saw slabs from (a log). (1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1084) [NOTES: [1986 NZPOD 719; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 455]]

slab bunk¶

noun.

BAUCKE (1905,Where the White Man Treads,304)

slab chimney¶

noun.

slab door¶

noun.

MANDER ... he had won through a gale with food and medecine for a camp where two men were ill. He had had to ... row up a creek, and then walk over a mile on a vague bush track ... The slab door of the camp was unbarred by a man who expected some suppliant for shelter, but when he saw Allen he stared as at a ghost. (1925,Allen Adair,15,1971)

slab drain¶

noun. [Rural] a ditch lined with slabs of native timber, especially white pine.

TAIT ... has been extensively drained by hand-dug slab drains. (1961,Farms & Stations of NZ Vol III,47)

slab fence¶

noun.

The slab fence is seldom put up now because it is extravagant of timbe; ... The whole fence is composed of posts, or rather slabs, say 3in. x 8in., which are set in the ground likeposts with 3in. or 4in. spaces between them. Sometimes a wire or capping rail is run along the top ... (Jul 15, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,10)

The dog ran up and turned once, then Phillis got in and showed some clean work, wrenching twice, and at last turning under a bullock dray, which saved pussy's life, and darting through a slab fence, she got away. (May 28, 1880,Wanganui Herald,2)

3 The greater portion of the land is enclosed with a furze and slab fence, divided into three paddocks, and laid down in English grasses. (Jan 22, 1876,Evening Post)

W. Pinches, who had made a drawing of the locality of the scene of the shooting, said that the fence was an old slab fence. (Apr 14, 1896,Wanganui Herald,3)

370 ACRES, Kimbolton road, all in grass .. 12 paddocks wire and slab fences. (Oct 2, 1907,Feilding Star,4)

In Western Canada, slab fences have made their appearance, nailed or wired to supports. (Apr 4, 1933,Evening Post,13)

slab heap¶

noun.

We lowered the truck down as far as the slab heap. (1983,Port Craig,9)
