slab house¶

noun.

When he was through that portion of the electorate 12 months ago some of the places he spoke at were scarcely inhabited; now there are numbe[r]s of settlers on their sections, with slab houses erected and stock grazing about. (Apr 19, 1905,Taranaki Herald,7)

He and Mr Rowan had just built a large split slab house at the edge of a fine bush. (Oct 31, 1894,North Otago Times,1)

What with the various discomforts of shipboard, bush travelling, New Zealand hotels and slab houses I find it most uphill work to write. (May 19, 1851,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,I-96) [NOTES: (J.C. Richmond)]

Arthur is going to make a clearing on our land this year, and ...[sic] after the burn would put up a slab house of two rooms which might serve afterwards for cowshed or kitchen or workshop ... `Bird's heart is in the bushland, his heart is not here.' (Aug 8, 1855,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,1/172,1960) [NOTES: (Jane M. Atkinson)]

What with the various discomforts of shipboard, bush travelling, New Zealand hotels and slab houses I find it most uphill work to write. (May 9, 1851,Richmond-Atkinson Papers) [NOTES: (J.C. Richmond)]

RIDGWAY `A split-slab house' in the Bush. (1860,Voices from Auckland,54)

MRS GRACE A rough slab house, in which we were able to have a fire, was placed at our disposal. (Feb 1878,Journal) [NOTES: 1878 Feb Mrs Grace Journal in Grace Pioneer Missionary (1928) 289]

slab hut¶

noun.

The only building was a slab hut under construction, probably the local store. (Mar 14, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),26)

At the bottom of this precipitous ravine, they had to ford the river, then toil up a narrow track on the other side before finally reaching shangi-la! A 20 ft x 12 ft totara slab hut with a mud floor. (Dec 2001,NZ Memories,No. 27/39)

In one of the gullies they are erecting slab huts with a view to the winter. (Apr 25, 1857,Taranaki Herald,2)

In May, 1866, witness erected a slab hut on the piece marked Panapa's section. (Apr 30, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,19)

They have erected a comfortable and commodious slab hut. (Nov 19, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,8)

FERGUSON When Harry's song came to a pause/ The old slab hut rang with applause. (1883,Castle Gay,187)

But a rough slab hut with shingled roof, was quickly put up and Mr Robert Allan ... afterwards built a house of sawn timber for Mr Filleul. (1914,History of North Otago,21,1978) [NOTES: 1906 W.H.S.Roberts in 1914 History of North Otago (1978) 21]

A flat thick piece of material; it may be stone or even cake. In Australia and New Zealand a slab is a thick plank; a `slab-hut' is a shanty built of such planks. (1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),370)

MASTERS While on that job Sam got married, and went to live with his young bride in a slab and bark hut he had built on a lonely part of the Holden's property called Evertree. [1860's] (1959,Tales of the Mails,115)

MASTERS He built himself a slab hut on the bank of a creek near the bush edge, ... [in 1890] (1960,Back-Country Tales,150)

SHADBOLT One of those slab huts with corrugated iron chimneys in the bush, and eleven ragged kids, six boys and five girls, standing outside; ... (1965,Among the Cinders,92)

SARGESON One of those slab huts with corrugated iron chimneys in the bush, and eleven ragged kids, six boys and five girls, standing outside; ... (1989,Joy of the Worm,7)

HILL ... Jack had roughed it in tents or slab huts. (1988,More from Moaville,31)

BUTLER A person would understand the almost oppressive feeling of newness about everything [43] were he to enter into a colonial slab hut and see an old carved oak chest in a corner ... (1860,Forest Creek MS,42)

MONEY It [the run manager's residence] consisted at this time of only one small slab hut, with four bunks and a chimney; a couple of hundred yards away was an old wool shed, ... (1871,Knocking About in NZ,84)

BELL A large clearing opened out on the right, and a little way back from the road-line stood a slab hut - or whare [e-acute], as it is generally called in New Zealand - of a rather better appearance than ordinary, from the iron chimney of which issued the smoke which the travellers had seen. Farther back from the road were yards and a larger building evidently used as a wool-shed. (1889,In the Shadow of the Bush,8)

BROOKES The dwelling-places consisted of slab-huts and whares, belonging to fire-wood-splitters, bullock-punchers, and a pig-hunter and a bacon-curer. (1892,Frontier Life,110)

I have a smudgy sketch made in 1859 ... A wretched little slab hut in the foreground and burnt bush. (Mar 18, 1894,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,2/597,1960) [NOTES: (C.W. Richmond)]

The settlement of canvas and slab huts has quickly soared to good buildings, and the latest index of advancement is an illuminated address. (Jan 26, 1911,Evening Post,6)

Once on the track, better time was made, and an old slab hut, on the walls of which were many names of prospectors of last century, was reached before nightfall. (Jan 7, 1931,Evening Post,5)

This magnificent watercolour by John Barr Clark Hoyte depicts miners' slab huts in the Coromandel district between 1864-1867. (Oct 2003,NZ Memories,No. 44/1)

slab over¶

verb. to smooth over, trim the rough edges off (something)

A small footbridge lately crossed the Ho Ho Creek, close to the Blue Spur township. It has been used by packers and horsemen as well as foot passengers, and was constructed on primaeval principals, two or more longitudinal sleepers being laid across, and these roughly slabbed over, with a couple of braces on each side. (May 19, 1874,West Coast Times,2)

CRAWFORD The country is either a mountain or a morass; it wants slabbing over, sir. (1880,Travels,232)

slab table¶

noun.

slab up¶

verb.

[NOTES: There is little doubt they have a very good claim, as on eac]

slagged¶

adjective. [Rural] [of land or feed] topdressed with slag.

The most notable feature of these tests, which extended over nine grazing seasons, including that of 1906, was the remarkable live weight increase furnished by the slagged portions of the field. (May 27, 1908,Otago Witness,7)

The carrying-capacity of the untreated Cockle Park land for the twenty weeks' grazing season was 2 sheep to the acre, which was increased to 4 sheep on the slagged and 2.7 on the superphosphate-dressed plots. Mr G L Marshall .. estimated the carrying-capacity of the slagged paddock as 5.23 sheep. (Jan 20, 1919,NZ Journal of Agriculture,16)

The relative merits of superphosphate and basic slag for pasture top-dressing are much discussed in certain districts, particularly North Taranaki and North Auckland. Many experienced farmers are firmly of the opinion that slagged pastures have better milk production and fattening capacities than ones treated with superphosphate. How much this may be due to a greater effect from slag, how much to some effect on the mineral content of the herbage, and how much due to management it is impossible to say. (1936,Agricultural Organization in NZ,389)

This season the slagged plot was so much improved that it has carried twelve sheep for four months, whereas the untreated plot is much barer with only six sheep. (Jan 28, 1899,Southland Times,6)

In some trials made at Cockle Park Agricultural Station the "slagged" soil, which had been longest under treatment, produced - as compared with "unslagged" soil - about 140 per cent. more oats, 30 per cent. more mustard (first crop), 70 per cent. more mustard (second crop), and about 40 per cent. more wheat, the average increase at Cockle Park being 62 per cent. (Mar 17, 1917,Evening Post,10)

Every agriculturist knows that it is not customary to place stock on land immediately it has been slagged, but it may be done when the dew has carried the phosphate into the land or immediately after a fall of rain. (Nov 5, 1921,Evening Post,16)

Today I found a slater. (Apr 1979,Islands,7(3) No. 25 : 236)

...amusingly, Lex has a pet slater called Dubcek... (Dec 18, 2002,Listener (New Zealand Listener),104)

slather¶

verb. box, fight, do battle

See: slather n.

On the 28th of this month, Gisborne stoush lovers will have another bonzer night, when the Gisborne Association will bring Bert Lowe and Bill Bartlett together. These two are scheduled to slather for fifteen rounds, but this is not going to be nearly all the fun. Viv Lowe and Poesy will try to deal out oblivion to each other during six rounds, while Mellow and Heany and also Harrison and Frurie will put up their 'dukes'. (May 23, 1914,NZ Truth,6)

ANTHONY They [sc. hungry cows] slathered at the mouth, with hunger and eagerness .. (1927,Gus Tomlins,91,1977 ed. Sturm) [NOTES: (?is this an authorial error)]

noun. vigorous 'unscientific' fighting; unrestrained toe-to-toe boxing action

[NOTES: from the idea of slathering or plastering blows on one's opponent (often in the collocation 'slather and whack'); see OED slather sense 3 to thrash, defeat thoroughly; see also open slather; compare slather-up n.]

[In the last round they both tired visibly, and casting caution to the winds slathered each other.] ... A wild slather ended when Finnie missed with a left and came in with his head low, owing to the impetus. ... Early in the round, Bennetts emerged from a slather, shaking his head and seemed to forget all about his opponent. (Aug 1, 1914,NZ Truth,12)

Then both warriors made a speech, which was lost amid the roar. It was a great slather and whack fight. There is no gainsaying Grim's pluck and ability to take punishment. But there is a big chunk of his reputation gone now that Griffin dropped him. (Dec 12, 1908,NZ Truth,3)

Chris. Rusterholz (8.5) versus Cliff Pearce (7.12). This was the tit-bit of the evening and provided five rounds of ding dong slather of a high order. Both are quick two-handed fighters and they went at it hammer and tacks without a dull moment intervening. (Mar 4, 1922,NZ Truth,8)

The feathers, J. Whittome (8.7) and C. McCarthy (8.5), followed, and they gave a clean, clever exhibition, more like a professional bout than that of amateurs. There was none of that wild slather, but good, scientific punching throughout. (Dec 24, 1921,NZ Truth,8)

Seldom indeed has a crowd voiced its approval of an out-and-out boxing match as it did at Wellington last week. Scientific stuff nine times out of ten leaves the audience cold - it is the slather and whack artists that get 'em on their feet, yelling encouragement. But the exception was bumped into last week when Jack Carroll gained a points decision over Charlie Purdy. Carroll came to us with a reputation of a bit of a killer, but his first fight in Wellington showed he was more of a stylist. He showed up as a nice mover, possessing plenty of speed at both ends, but totally lacking as a purveyor of hefty wallops. (Aug 16, 1928,NZ Truth,10)

BOXING AT GREYMOUTH. ...Now, when the time is ripe, it might be mentioned that Cook's exhibition throughout the mill, his genuine smile of good fellowship when picking up his opponent on a couple of occasions when he slipped, and his palpable desire to box instead of indulging in 'slather and whack', bears the impression that when his recent mill with Billy Hannan at Gisborne was declared 'no fight' and he lost his share of the purse, there was some truth in his words, 'I don't profess to be a fighter; I'm a boxer, pure and simple, and I tried my hardest to beat Hannan.' (Mar 28, 1914,NZ Truth,6)

slather up¶

verb. thrash, hammer; castigate; get the better of, defeat (in fighting or words)

[NOTES: variant of OED slather v. sense 3]

NORTH AUCKLAND FARMERS CO-OPERATIVE LIMITED. ... Looking at the paid up capital, viz., GBP120,376, and taking a glance at the reserve for income tax (GBP9468) the astounding position is discovered that the preference shareholders are practically receiving fifteen per cent., and for that reason the ordinaries are only able to get a seven per cent. dividend, and they, too, are "slathered up" for eight per cent. of taxation. (Nov 23, 1918,NZ Truth,4)

I read a lot of chucks off [sic] about our Member in your paper, but I reckon our Member slathered up the capitalistic class to some tune in his speech the other night. (Dec 15, 1915,Grey River Argus,3)

THE CARTERTON SHOOTING TRAGEDY ...Then Spicer came on the scene and drew them aside, and they started to talk about 'slathering up somebody'. ... Describing what lead [sic] up to the shooting, accused said Rzoska said at the hotel, 'I hear you want to slather me up. I hear you want to have a smack at me!' (Feb 12, 1921,NZ Truth,5)

These officers and men, commented upon at the time of their departure as 'the flower of New Zealand's manhood' etc., went to Samoa expecting to slather up the Germans. When they got there they found that the Teuton preferred to leave out the slather, and the eager lads had to enter upon the dull dreary round of garrison life. (Mar 27, 1915,NZ Truth,7) [NOTES: also slather n. here (q.v.)]

"That I slathered up a Federationist last night," William Newton Railway Guard sworn said ... (Feb 7, 1913,Ohinemuri Gazette,2)

After the correspondence had been read, Colonel McDonald said that his object was that the board and public should know that what he had been "slathered up" for in his absence at the May meeting of the board was completely justified. (Jul 16, 1936,Evening Post,20)

slathering¶

noun. ca1940 a beating

slathering-up¶

noun. a (verbal) beating

[NOTES: compare slather-up]

OUR WONDERFUL WILLIAM (BY AN AMATEUR ARTIST.) Concerning the cartoon, the artist writes: 'I confess I am an amateur at the biz., so therefore I do not seek a slathering up if I have ill-designed the old dear.' (Oct 20, 1917,NZ Truth,5) [NOTES: below a cartoon of William Massey]

When you read in the capitalist press, how this member or that member, gave the Labour Party Leader a severe slathering up, publishing verbatim reports of their speeches and finishing up, that Mr Holland "made a spirited reply["] it is easy to realise there is a conspiracy of silence and the general reader will not get the Labour Members' views unless the Labour people make it their business to place them before them. (Aug 14, 1920,Grey River Argus,5)

slather-up¶

noun. a fight or brawl

See: slather up v.

Writing to his mother, Mrs D. Gordon, from Egypt on January 23 last, Lance Corporal W. Heany said he was still in good health. They expected another big 'slather up', and he was sure they would shatter the Turks and Germans because they had plenty of confidence in themselves. (Mar 27, 1916,Poverty Bay Herald,5)

'Anzac' Before we got shut of it, the battle [a street fight] had developed into a first class slather-up. (1916,On the Anzac Trail,100)

adjective. dirty, muddy; wet, rainy

noun. a slater

slats¶

noun.

Kicking him fair in the slats. (Sep 11, 1944,NZEF Times,IV/168 : 4)

noun.

Naturally by the time he'd lowered a cold pie or two on the way home he was feeling as healthy as a vegetarian on a ... slaughter chain. (1976,Loosehead Len's Bumper Thump Book,31)

This [achievement of target weights] will determine drafting dates of slaughter lambs ... (Sep 2001,In the Paddock,1)

noun. .

...staff would have nothing to do with the ... meatworkers' union, two officials of which were on the slaughterboard. (Feb 16, 1982,Dominion,1/1)

Miss Robin ... spent the last two Christmas holidays working on the slaughterboard at Whakatu [freezin works] to earn money for her education. (Jan 7, 1987,Dominion,3)

No learner to be employed on the slaughtering-board unless he can do six sheep per hour; and the apprentices to be limited to one to every six slaughtermen, and to receive the minimum wages. (Sep 21, 1903,Poverty Bay Herald,2)

The slaughtermen employed at the Canterbury Frozen Meat Company's works at Pareora went out on strike yesterday morning, in consequence of one of their number having been discharged for smoking while at the slaughter-board, a practice which is prohibited by the company, on account of the especial risk of fire. To decide course of action re certain individuals who have worked on Slaughtering-board. (Mar 22, 1913,Poverty Bay Herald,1)

sledge¶

verb.

[NOTES: re farm vehicle]

The stones [are] required to be quarried and sledged in any case, whether broken by hand or machine. (Nov 5, 1867,Daily Southern Cross,4)

A pair of horses, belonging to Mr. Griffiths, were employed in sledging stone from the City of Dunedin Claim to Russell's battery, along the road that has been formed from that mine. (Apr 11, 1870,Daily Southern Cross,3)

One energetic settler on the plain has timber already sledged up for the purpose of erecting a store, and another old identity is fitting up a bakery at the foot of the eastern slopes in readiness for sledging to the summit. (Jul 18, 1885,Otago Witness,12)

The body was wrapped in canvas and sledged down the mountain to the hut, where the party rested for the night. (Feb 12, 1892,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

This case came out of a dispute between the settlers in the North Harbor West as to the right to sledge wood over a certain road. (Apr 27, 1865,Otago Daily Times,5)

The Mountain Maid stone is being sledged to the paddock preparatory to crushing. (Apr 26, 1884,Otago Witness,12)

Then it so happened that district decided to make a rough golf course, and the old whare was right in a fairway, so it was pulled down and sledged back to the new little golf house - and the old carvings boiled the billy during the whole of last winter! (Jan 4, 1939,Evening Post,5)

Hitherto all machinery had to be sledged down the hill from the tableland. (Nov 28, 1891,Northern Advocate,2)

This season has seen the increasing use of small threshing plants driven by oil-engines, the whole outfit having to be small and compact to enable it to be sledged on the hills from one thrashing floor to another. (Mar 3, 1914,Ashburton Guardian,4)

It is stated that the body was wrapped up in a blanket and sledged out on a six-feet track for about two miles to the road, where the police, doctor and parson held an inquiry and the corpse was buried on the side of the road at Blake Point. (Mar 27, 1920,NZ Truth,1)

verb.

[NOTES: Aust. origin (see below)]

In the New Zealand team, current coach David Trist and his predecessors during the 1990s...have all been in charge of various teams that have sledged... One provincial coach I spoke to says he likes he players to ger worked up and he certainly doesn't mind sledging... I don't take any pride in the news that New Zealand out-sledged England in 1999. (Feb 5, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),58)

[Former Aussie test spinner,Kerry O'Keefe] said the term traced back to a barbecue after a day's play in a Sheffield Shield match between South Australia and NSW in the early 1970s... one of the NSW players made inappropriate comments to a woman and was pulled into line by former state captain John Benaud. "Benaud added that the transgressor's outburst was 'as subtle as a sledgeghammer'. He momentarily became known as 'Percy Sledgehammer' a reference to soul singer Percy Sledge. The 'Percy' soon disappeared and for the remainder of the season anybody who used over-the-top language was known as a 'sledge'. (Nov 28, 2004,Sunday Star Times,B9)

noun.

The seed has to be packaged on horses and carried even by men to tracks, where a sledge will take it to the main road, to be bullocked to the different bays for transport by steamer to Lyttelton or Dunedin. (Mar 6, 1890,Otago Witness,9)

noun. (farm vehicle)

Most of the farmers convey their cream to the dairy factory's launch by means of sledges. (May 9, 1928,NZ Free Lance,31)

IRELAND The farm buildings soon collapsed, slips blocked the sledge tracks to the back paddocks, and the harrows and discs rusted away in a tangle of weeds. (1998,Under the Bridge & Over the Moon,14)

We observed day after day in the worst weather the heavily laden dray of one settler proceeding along the road, every journey making the road worse, until the dray being sunk to the axle, a sledge - a more destructive machine by far - was substituted, dragged by the united efforts of ten bullocks carrying a load of less than 200 bricks ... (Aug 16, 1851,Otago Witness,2)

Our son.. calls our place "Sledge - andSliprail Farm." (Feb 26, 1926,NZ Dairy Produce Exporter,38)

BARKER These stacks.. had to be brought down to the flat in rude little sledges drawn by a bullock, who required to be trained to the work. (1873,Station Amusements in NZ,3)

noun.

noun.

FOR SALE, A PAIR OF HARNESS BULLOCKS, equal to any in the settlement for Ploughing and Sledging, with a full set of First-rate Harness, nearly new. (Jul 7, 1860,Otago Witness,4)

I pointed out to the manager of the store that sledging on the County roads and footpaths was an offence under the Council's bye-laws. (Oct 9, 1912,Ohinemuri Gazette,3)

sleep in the Star Hotel¶

phrase. sleep in the open

See: -

[NOTES: cf. sleep with Mrs Green]

... ducks' breakfast,'to float up to,' to blow up to,'to sleep in the Star Hotel' need no explanation. (Apr 2, 1938,Press, The,18) [NOTES: McNab NZ Slang]

sleep with Mrs Green¶

phrase.

BAKER In later years we have records of the phrases to sleep with Mrs Green and to doss in the star hotel, used by tramps to describe sleeping in the open. (1941,NZ Slang,41)

PARTRIDGE To sleep in the open, e.g., in a park: Australian beggars' and tramps': since ca1920. Baker, 1942. I.e., on the grass; cf. the entry at Mrs. Ashtip. (1949,Dictionary of the Underworld,637,1961)

McGILL sleep with Mrs Green open-air slumber in tramp parlance, c.1932. (1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,104)

(1888,NZ Times,Extra) [NOTES: [see go mates]]

noun.

This was really an outdoor room, sometimes at first floor level, where beds were kept in the summer months. (1986,Old New Zealand Houses,200)

noun.

noun.

sleeping-shelf¶

noun. [Rural] a benched area on a hillside to where a sheep will retire at the evening rise.

GUTHRIE-SMITH .. of all surface modifications consequent on the stocking of land, the most curious is the formation of sleeping-shelves, ledges built by sheep themselves for their own convenience. On extensive stretches where there are no available natural camping sites, where hill-tops are distant, or where cliff formation makes their attainment difficult, camps are formed on the slopes. It is in such localities that sleeping-shelves have grown out from the hillsides ... (1921,Tutira,192)

GUTHRIE-SMITH The sleeping-ledge in time becomes perfect, thrusting itself out at right angles to the slope, like a swallow's nest gummed to a wall. [sleeping-ledge.] (1921,Tutira,193)

noun. Slivovitz

sleepout¶

noun. an extra room, often used as a bedroom, attached to or separated from a house

If New Zealand is God's own country, then Golden Bay is his sleep-out, splendidly isolated, slightly different, very laid-back, certainly removed from the rest of the Nelson region. (Jan 29, 2001,Evening Post,17)

4A BOULCOTT-TER. - Modern Flat, furnished; five rooms and sleepout, inspection any day between 10 and 11 morning, or after 4 afternoon. (Aug 4, 1930,Evening Post,3)

Sleepy Hollow¶

noun. Nelson town and city

[Caption] No longer should Nelson be termed "Sleepy Hollow". (Aug 15, 1928,NZ Free Lance,33)

"Sleepy Hollow" can now slumber on peacefully, and with a contented mind for another decade or so. (Mar 23, 1912,NZ Free Lance,26)

Even Nelson - "sleepy hollow," as we call it - boasts of a magnificent water supply. (Jan 21, 1871,Evening Post,2)

The roads about Sleepy Hollow are pretty good too. (Feb 13, 1926,NZ Observer,6)

Nelson is a beautiful place and well-named "Sleepy Hollow". (Dec 18, 1907,Otago Witness,83)

Nelson being sometimes called "sleepy hollow," has been, until now, pretty free of such frolicsome characters, but it seems one or two individuals are begining [sic] buckyism practices; by inserting a few of the absurdities in your valuable paper may, perhaps, prevent the malady extending to others, as even the winners are found to be on the losing side when they appear in the Resident Magistrate's Court. (Aug 22, 1867,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,3)

Our visit ended at Nelson - generally spoken of as "Sleepy Hollow." (Sep 24, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,28)

SUTHERLAND While we were driving along ... Nelson harbour ..., Glennie remarked: They call this placeSleepy Hollow', you know. I've heard it said that you'll sleep a couple of hours longer here than you will anywhere else - it's something to do with the air, they say.' (1956,Green Kiwi,172,1960)

BATHGATE ... Nelson dubbed `Sleepy Hollow' (1874,Colonial Experiences,275)

The `Sleepy Hollow' boys [sc. the Nelson football team] rode rough shod over boisterous Wellington. (1877,Country Journal,1/251)

sleepy sickness/sleeping sickness¶

noun. [Rural] antepartum paralysis in ewes.

What was the incidence of antepartum paralysis (sleeping sickness) compared with that of eversion of the uterus? (Jul 20, 1936,NZ Journal of Agriculture,22)

The more correct name for antepartum paralysis or sleepy sickness is pregnancy toxaemia. (Jun 15, 1939,NZ Journal of Agriculture,467)

The more correct name for antepartum paralysis or sleepy sickness is pregnancy toxaemia (toxaemia meaning poison). It is also known as twin lamb disease, from the fact that in 95 per cent. of cases the ewe is found to be carrying two or more lambs. (Jul 16, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,37)

Antepartum paralysis or 'sleepy sickness' was the major complaint ... (Oct 25, 1951,NZ Farmer,31)

DU FAUR Sleep sickness (pregancy toxaemia.) This disease is sometimes referred to as 'twin-lamb' disease as it is more likely to develop in ewes carrying twins. (1966,Sheep Farming for Profit,163)

sleets¶

noun. marbles

"Huh, sleets again," said Sid but Ginger only flicked his marble even further from the hole. (1949,Hilltop,I.2/19)

SUTTON-SMITH Consider ... the use of the borderline action terms Sleets (Caversham) and Do's (Nth. East Valley) ... meant to overcome a difficulty which sometimes arises in the marble game of Holey. The first player to reach the hole may discover that although he is now entitled to fire at his opponent, the opponent's marble is too far away for him to hit it. He may then attempt to force the opponent to bring his marble nearer to the hole by the use of the action-term `Sleets'. (1953,Unorganized Games,2/770)

SUTTON-SMITH Here are some [marble] terms from Taranaki around 1880-1890: firsts, lay-up, stakes, tips, sticking-taw, nothings, anythings, fade-it, knuckledown stiff, dubs, finking [sic, ?funking], sips, spanning, placing; and from Dunedin School in 1949: knee high, manyies, tracks, screws, nuts, sleets, kills, forces, dig, dubs, cheats. (1981,History of Children's Play,269)

slew¶

noun. [Rural] an angle left or right that sheep take when they are responding to a dog's direction to change course.

Went clean through first flags without trouble and put in a good clean slew, which landed his sheep across the creek. Made a poor slew at the first flags ... (Sep 1, 1925,NZ Farmer,1343)

Slew - the angles - left or right - of a hunt and the new direction sheep take when directed to by a dog. (Dec 15, 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,45)

GORDON By this time, the sheep would be finishing the first set and a right-hand slew had to be applied to line them up for the second set. (1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,151)

verb. [Rural] [shepherding] to direct sheep in a particular direction.

This dog's sheep drifted through first flags, with the dog not interested, but he slewed nicely and he crossed the creek with firm work. (Sep 1, 1925,NZ Farmer,1343)

if the driving was done by a huntaway dog, slewing the sheep would be in order. (May 1933,NZ Farmer,317)

ACLAND .. if you slewed a mob of strong merino wethers too hard against a fence, the fence went flat. (1946,Early Canterbury Runs,40)

HARTLEY The next lesson is devised to teach a dog in advance how to slew sheep. (1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,17)

The 'Lake' country is mainly open shingle and it's mostly 'topside' work - slewing sheep downhill. (Apr 11, 1968,NZ Farmer,45)

MCLEOD Wait would head or hunt or slew with uncanny intelligence. (1970,Many a Glorious Morning,142)

KERR Otairi's huntaways were used to lifting sheep; mine to slewing from above. (2000,High Times in the High Country,173)

verb. to beat, outwit, baffle

[NOTES: SOED labels Aust. & NZ]

PYKE Of their reputation, the miners spoke with bated breath; ... The general impression seemed to be, that Jack Ketch had been `slued' (anglice - robbed of his dues) by the trio. (1873,Wild Will Enderby,1/xi/41,(1889,1974))

In London the peelers down areas will go, / To make love to the cook and the victuals, /But here there're no areas down which to intrude, / So of course the New Zealand bobbies are slewed. (1875,NZ Songster,No.3/89) [NOTES: Thatcher London and the Diggings]

MITCHELL ... or levant from Oamaru/ Without bidding them adieu/ And the merchants we will slew - let them catch us if they can. (1889,Rhymes and Rambles,25)

noun.

"This Scott seems a nice, steady-going sort of a dog. That was a nice slew he made had it been in the right place." (Jun 3, 1897,Otago Witness,34)

NEWTON He [a sheep dog] was so fast that I'd have him away out, past, and beyond any sheep almost before they knew he was coming. In this way I could get in good slews ... Ibid. 169 Slew: To turn or change the direction in which sheep are travelling. To top-side slew is to turn or hunt them downhill. Slewing is done mainly with huntaways and in one of the huntaways events at our trials - Class III - the sheep are hunted on a zig-zag course. This is often called a slew. (1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,26)

verb.

T. Prendergast's Tom hunted his sheep out well about 300yds and slewed to the right, but failed to slew to the left. (Jun 1, 1893,Otago Witness,21)

The dog had to head sheep, slew them, drive them a short distance along a ridge, and then pull to ring. (Apr 15, 1910,Hawera & Normanby Star,7)

In class 3 Mr Reg. Black's Niss worked steadily in the hunt away, slewing well, was under good command, brought back in good style but should have been steadied more. (Jul 23, 1907,Taranaki Herald,8)

ACLAND .. When a dog heads or slews sheep, shepherds speak of his having done a good (etc.) turn. (1933,Sheep Station)

Sheep dog.- Dog to work sheep; collie (q.v.). S.ds. run naturally either to bring sheep towards you or to drive them away; and when a puppy shows his preference he is broken in for that work. The dogs that bring sheep are called heading ds. (q.v.) and most of these can be taught to lead (q.v.) if desired. Dogs which take to driving sheep away are broken in to huntaway and are called htwys (q.v.). Some dogs will both hd. and htwy and are called handy ds. They are not generally high-class heading dogs but very useful about hand and sometimes very useful mustering dogs. Some men have a special slewing d., but a well-trained, hdg. dog or htwy. will usually slew (q.v.). (C.) (Nov 25, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

CRAWFORD If you `slewed' a mob of strong merino wethers ... (1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,40)

HARTLEY Teaching Slewing The next lesson is devised to teach a dog ... to slew sheep. (1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,17)

NEWTON Slew: To slew sheep is to turn them in a different direction to that in which they are going. If sheep are sidling round a face and they have to be turned downhill a dog is run out and above them to `slew' them down. (1966,Boss's Story, The,190)

McLEOD Slew: A huntaway should be able to cast to the side on command and slew in the desired direction. (1970,Glorious Morning,253)

NEWTON A mob of those wethers, slewed out of a high basin, would disappear down a spur in a cloud of dust ... Ibid. 169 Slew: To turn or change the direction in which sheep are travelling. To top-side slew is to turn or hunt them downhill. Slewing is done mainly with huntaways and in one of the huntaways events at our trials - Class III - the sheep are hunted on a zig-zag course. This is often called a slew. (1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,15)

verb. to defeat, overcome, get round (a problem)

BUTLER This [waterfall] stuck us up', as they say here concerning any difficulty. We managed, however, toslew' it, as they, no less elegantly, say concerning the surmounting of an obstacle. (1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,v 67-68)

verb. (of bullocks)

KENNAWAY ... if he [sc a bullock] pulled up hard and `slewed' sharp round on his heels, the stock-horse would come up standing, just as quickly, and be round on his flank in a second. (1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,206)

.. instead of the suggested 25 points for style it would be better to allot them for slewing. (Jan 2, 1941,NZ Farmer,12)

Sheep dog.- Dog to work sheep; collie (q.v.). S.ds. run naturally either to bring sheep towards you or to drive them away; and when a puppy shows his preference he is broken in for that work. The dogs that bring sheep are called heading ds. (q.v.) and most of these can be taught to lead (q.v.) if desired. Dogs which take to driving sheep away are broken in to huntaway and are called htwys (q.v.). Some dogs will both hd. and htwy and are called handy ds. They are not generally high-class heading dogs but very useful about hand and sometimes very useful mustering dogs. sling¶

noun. a payment or bonus; a backhander or bribe

And unless the rule is rewritten it would appear licence holders are forbidden to accept slings or to be paid for newspaper tipping columns... If a driver told an owner, or his friend or partner, how he thought his horse would go (or went the previous week) and that person later slung the driver, on the face of it, the rule was breached. "It must be accepted by HRNZ that for years drivers, trainers and stablehands have accepted by way of a gift a benefit for having provided information." (Jul 27, 2003,Sunday Star Times,B14)

How's this for confidence? An owner of a horse racing at Pukekohe on Saturday told a jockey what his `sling' would be for winning. This is the norm, of course. But this fellow told the jockey two races before his steed was to run. The horse was successful and easily too. (Sep 11, 1982,NZ Truth,2)

slink¶

noun. also called slinkie a) an unborn or stillborn lamb, calf or fawn. b) its skin. a calf or fawn in utero valued for skin markings; a dead lamb (born dead or died soon after birth) which is processed for its skin

N.Z. Slink' In High Demand [heading] ... A coat made from New Zealandslink' is expected to be shown in the Paris autumn-winter fashion shows, which open here next week. For the uninitiated, slink' is made from the skins of stillborn lambs. The material is very light and soft, and is highly-prized in the high fashion world of Europe. Each year, apparently, thousands of ewes die before lambing, in the harsh Southland spring. This provides stillborn lambskin which is processed intoslink.' ... (Jul 22, 1971,Otago Daily Times,3) [NOTES: (Griffiths Collection)]

THOMPSON The tails were salted as was the `slink' (unborn calf) carcass, while the sinews and antlers in velvet were sun-dried. (1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,116)

Calf or fawn in utero valued for skin markings. Ibid. 51 Slink: Dead lamb (i.e., born or died soon after birth) which is processed for its skin. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,22)

slink 2 n. NZ & Austral. still-born lamb or one dead soon after birth, processed for its skin. [orig. = premature calf] (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,721) [NOTES: [cf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict. 1087, sense 4]]

noun.

The slink skin industry in New Zealand had grown in 10 years to a million dollar export business ... It is an industry born out of the statistical fact that even in ideal climatic conditions 10 per cent of all lambs born each season die at birth. (Sep 19, 1980,Dominion,8)

slinky¶

noun. [Rural] a skin of a newly born lamb or other animal.

The number of slinky skins from dead lambs went up from 700 to 20,000. They didn't have a show. (Sep 13, 1973,NZ Farmer,12)

noun. [Rural] an unborn or stillborn lamb.

BROSNAHAN Lambing involves low labour inputs with the shepherds going round the Romneys only once a day to pick up slinkies. (1998,Glenaray 1898-1998,83)

.. pulling out slinkies (unborn lambs) and trying to revive them with mouth-to-mouth, catching trout with their bare hands ... [slinky skin] (Nov 9, 2002,Dominion Post,A12)

noun. unborn deer

MACNICOL I tanned slinky (unborn deer) hides and nanny-goat skins to make mats. (1965,Skippers Road,47)

slinter¶

noun. a fast one; modern usage esp. work a slinter [AND A. n. has this 1864 Thatcher cit.]

See: also slanter

[NOTES: The early NZ uses (ca1870-1900) suggest prons. [ lint , slent , lent ], with main senses crooked',underhand' `dishonestly tricky' etc, both in general use, and as an adj (? sb as attrib). in racing slang. Sc. dial sklent (sclent) sb (OED) a. Sc. variant of slent sb., a slant or slope; ... a side look etc vb Sc and north dial:1. to move, dart, or fall obliquely; to lie aslant; to give a side-look etc b. fig to deviate from a straightforward course, or from the truth. Slent sb' Now dial. [a ON Slent [a mutation of slant ]] 2. on (the) slent aslant. 3. (obs) A sly hit or sarcasm = Slant sb' 5. (1557-1612) vb' Now dial Also 14c. slinte, 15c sclente [a. ON slenta] 1. ... to lie aslant ...]

He says when he meets George Dixon it will be no 'slinter,' but a real honest fight. (Apr 2, 1892,Observer (Auckland),11)

Most people know that a slinter is aconspiracy ... a take-down. (Jun 22, 1950,Southern Cross (Wgton),11)

PASCOE Shearers are still better organized and most sheds have somebody articulate to voice their worries if any `slinters' are feared. (1952,Land Uplifted High,164,1961)

MORRIESON So it's the dirtiest lowest crime ..., but what about the slinter they pulled on Granny? Did they show any mercy? (1974,Predicament,74,1981)

There is a slinter somewhere - but where? (Nov 23, 1938,Auckland Weekly News,96)

Origin only to be guessed at. A false call or call where the driver can't locate the person who ordered the cab. Can be used as a noun - It's a slinter'; adjectivally -The slintered car will get the next job'; or as a verb - `I've been slintered'. (Jul 1983,Metro,no.25 81)

THATCHER A Lyceum Cafe[e-acute] at the top end was started - / It proved a bad place for the restaurant trade,/ 'Twas a `shlinter' for the tenant one morning departed/ Without paying his rent in the Lowther Arcade./ Lowther Arcade!/ This Le-vite said a-dieu to the Lowther Arcade. (1864,Invercargill Minstrel,15) [NOTES: (The Lowther Arcade)]

The controlling officials don't care a dump what the professional stoushers' views may be on the subject; their plain duty will be to protect the public from a recurrence of the `schleinters' which took place in this city in past years. [subject = boxing] (Jul 14, 1906,NZ Truth,56/3/5)

The [Boxing] Association is making a dead set' against the professional talent which has come into such prominence in Wellington of late, and the stoushers' chance of fixing upshleinter goes' is `Buckley's' (Jul 28, 1906,NZ Truth,58/3/3)

Shearers are still better organized and most sheds have somebody articulate to voice their worries if any slinters are feared. (1945,NZ Geographer,24) [NOTES: (Pascoe Canterbury High Country)]

PARTRIDGE A trick, a piece of deceit; esp., work a slinter, to succeed in effecting a trick, a swindle: Australian: C. 20. Baker, 1942 and 1945. cf. Slanter (q.v.), of which it may be a thinned form (1949,Dictionary of the Underworld,638,1961)

STEWART 'Strewth, he's a Bobby Dazzler, that one. Liaison business. That's the biggest slinter in the army.'The biggest which -?' `Slinter. Fiddle. Swan. Look, don't you know?' (1981,Hot & Copper Sky,153)

That the Massey Government, or some big military pooh-bah, tried to work a "slinter" on to the poor limbless returned soldiers by offering them a lump sum annually for upkeep of their artificial limbs, instead of, as at present, keeping them in order at the Government's expense. (Jul 3, 1920,NZ Truth,2)

slintered¶

adjective.

See: slinter n.

Origin only to be guessed at. A false call or call where the driver can't locate the person who ordered the cab. Can be used as a noun - It's a slinter'; adjectivally -The slintered car will get the next job'; or as a verb - `I've been slintered'. (Jul 1983,Metro,no.25 81)

slip¶

noun. [Rural] [stock sales] a young pig.

Livestock sales: big slips 16/- to 17/-. (May 1909,NZ Farmer,408)

The usual practice is to buy the pigs as slips. (Dec 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,559)

Slips and weaners have been in demand. (Aug 16, 1951,NZ Farmer,43)

Weaners and slips have fluctuated somewhat, the trend being downwards during the first week of the fortnight. (Oct 9, 1952,NZ Farmer,40)

A pig underfed in the early stages of growth (particularly as a weaner and a slip) and then 'given the works' with a cheap food is likely to produce an unsatisfactory pork chop. (Sep 10, 1970,NZ Farmer,67)

noun. [Rural] a gouging of a slope or hillside through water erosion.

DARE There had been several slips during the recent heavy rains ... (1956,Rouseabout Jane,20)

SLIP ON RIMUTAKA-ROAD. .. It will take two or three weeks to clear the slip away, and the earth is still coming ... (Jul 6, 1910,Evening Post,8)

The party of men engaged on the Haven Road were digging down a portion of the hill near the Custom House, for the purpose of getting materiel [sic] for the surface of this excellent work, when a slip took place which completely buried Keats, and fell also on two others named Sharman and Mansell. (Mar 11, 1843,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,210)

MCCASKILL .. in the Whangamomona-Ohura inland the deforested hillsides are maimed with scars produced by mass movements of varied morphology: they are, however, known universally in New Zealand as slips. (1973,Hold This Land,40)

MCCASKILL No study of the distribution or mechanics of 'slips' has been undertaken ... (1973,Hold This Land,41)

BRADSHAW & WILLIAMS A number [of farmers] quoted figures such as slips only recover to 80% of production over 20 years and grass on slipped areas go into drought stress three days after slipping. However, many agree that intuitively they know there are costs involved in continuing to farm these areas as well as the loss of grass growth on slips. (1998,Information and Communication Needs,25)

The rapidity of the water undermines the latter, and occasions frequent slips. (Sep 12, 1840,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3)

verb. [Rural] [stock] to lose weight or some aspect of condition; to revert or regress.

STEVENS .. the shepherd who observes after a change of paddocks or a bad break of weather, 'Ewes aren't milking and the lambs have slipped' has at least his eyes on his job. (1958,Sheep. Part 1, Sheep husbandry,62)

verb. [Rural] [ dog trials] to liberate sheep used in a trial.

GORDON .. in the South island, liberating is called slipping, which means they slip sheep on to the mark, using slippers. (1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,196)

But the cunning sheep do not always want to be "slipped" away from their woolly mates. (Apr 19, 2001,Taranaki Daily News,19)

slip bar¶

noun.

See: slip-panel, slip-rail

[NOTES: aka slip-bar]

HINEMOA I forgot to put the slip-bars up (1892,Travels of a NZ Feather, The,7)

Mr. J. W. Baker wrote complaining of slip bars and log fence across Climie road. This was a case of two neighbors disagreeing as to cattle running on adjacent clearings. (Mar 10, 1882,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

The plaintiff, some time since, fenced in section No. 46, and allowed some of the neighbours to put up slip-bars, and use the road through the section, until the other road could be made passable. (Apr 12, 1856,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

slip rail¶

noun. [Rural] the rail of a post-and-rail fence or gate which can be slid back to reveal an opening.

[NOTES: aka slip-rail; also Aust; also figurative]

BARKER ... they all trotted into the stockyard ...and I had nothing to do but put up the slip-rail as fast as I could ... (1868,Station Life in NZ,234,1870)

LADY BARKER He bounded over the slip-rail of the paddock before Karl could get it down. We were too primitive for gates in those parts (1873,Station Amusements in NZ,68)

MORRIS part of a fence so fitted that it can be removed so as to serve as a gate,. Used also for the gateway thus formed. Generally in the plural. Same as Slip-panel. [1870] (1898,Austral English,420)

HENDERSON SLIP RAIL: Slips easily into holes in posts and two or three act as a gate. (1961,Friends in Chains,189) [NOTES: c1900-1920 A Teamster's Glossary in 1961 Henderson Friends In Chains 189]

As for the colonial slip-rail, it is an abomination ... (1902,Brett's Colonists Guide,96)

The old devil father ... took Inias horse, put him outside the boundary, wired up the slip rails and padlocked the gate. (Aug 26, 1903,Chudleigh Diary,419,1950)

BAUCKE From the front door a plain, weedless pathway ... leads down an easy grade to the front gate (slip-rails). (1905,Where the White Man Treads,296)

SATCHELL Lena made no reply, but when the slip-rail was reached she looked quickly at er companion. (1905,Toll of the Bush,31,1985)

They then got through the slip rails close to Himeonas camp and mounted their horses before Himeonas party saw them. (Jul 8, 1912,Chudleigh Diary,457,1950)

LANCASTER The whare, and the young trees, and the slip-rails, where the cows stood lowing, ... (1930,NZ Short Stories,74)

slip-rail: fence with rail which can be slipped out to make gateway. (1947,Reeds' School Dictionary: NZ Suppl.,175)

SCANLAN For an hour Ambrose smoked his pipe as he leant over the slip-rail behind the cow-bails; ... (1948,Dusty Road,81,1949)

Part of a fence, usually two rails so fitted that they can be easily removed to serve as a gate. (1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),372)

slip-rail n. [usually in plural] panels of fence which can be removed to serve as a gate; the gateway itself. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

sliprail n. (usually in plural) panels of fence which can be removed to serve as a gate; gateway itself. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

sliprail n. NZ & Austral. fence-rail forming one of a set which can be slipped out to make an opening. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,722) [NOTES: [cf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict. 1088; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 456]]

RICHARDS Most of the gateways were either `Taranakis' or slip-rails ... (1986,Off the Sheep's Back,103)

KOEBEL Their eyes roam from their horses to the timber of some slip-rails in the wire-fencing. (1905,Return of Joe,228)

In the end we had to grease all the wires and prise him through with a sliprail. (Jul 11, 1910,Triad, The,XVIII(4) : 20)

The long summer morning's muster, beginning before the dark, has finally ended at about 11 a.m. with the big herd of cows and calves safely confined behind the slip rails of the receiving yard. (Mar 23, 1967,NZ Farmer,33)

RICHARDS Most of the gateways were either 'Taranakis' or slip-rails. [slip-rail] (1986,Off the Sheep's Back,103)

She saw him lying down near the slip rails.. The slip rails were down when I got there. (Jul 2, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,20)

Our son.. calls our place "Sledge - andSliprail Farm." (Feb 26, 1926,North & South,38)

"If I lay down a principle and pull down the slip-rails to one worthy object," said the Minister, "they are down to everyone ..." (May 12, 1936,Evening Post,10)

The main point in Smith's story - and he made the rails of the witness-box a convenient substitute for his homestead slip-rails in its telling - was that in March last Wilson was supposed to have insinuated to his (Smith's) son that some couple of dozen head of Wanaka station sheep had been shorn in Smith's shed. (Nov 22, 1928,NZ Truth,5)

You'll meet me at the slip-rails when thecoach comes this evening. (Nov 18, 1899,NZ Times,3)

SCANLON For an hour Ambrose smoked his pipe as he leaned over the slip-rail behind the cow-bails. (1948,Rusty Road,81)

phrase. [humorous; Rural] to go in to town or on holiday from the high country.

LOUGHNAN slip the chain: to get off down the tarmac for a while. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,73)

slip truck¶

noun.

Take a bit of four by two and sprag it through the wheels of the slip truck.... Working as a slip-trucky at the mill. (Nov 12, 1983,Off the Sheep's Back) [NOTES: 1983 Nov 12 2YA Wellington 9.15 am: Spectrum Documentary: G. W. Johnson's working life 1940-46.]

slip trucky¶

noun.

BENNETT Other [timber trade] terms ... are ... slip-trucky, scarfer [etc] (1943,English as it is spoken in NZ,85)

Take a bit of four by two and sprag it through the wheels of the slip truck.... Working as a slip-trucky at the mill (Nov 12, 1983,Radio NZ / National Radio) [NOTES: 1983 Nov 12 2YA Wellington 9.15 am: Spectrum Documentary: G. W. Johnson's working life 1940-46]

slipe¶

noun. farming: wool recovered from pelts in an abattoir or freezing works; wool recovered from pelts in an abbatoir by a wool puller after being chemically loosened with a sodium sulphide and hydrated lime mixture

The chemical action of this solution loosens the wool from the skin, and it is easily plucked off by hand. The wool (called slipe') is then dried and packed in bales for shipment; the skin (now calledpelt') is washed, skivered, and finally pickled ... (1918,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,1/165)

Slipe: Wool recovered from pelts in abbatoir. Body wool typed as woolly lambs, shorn lambs, and sheep. Oddments typed as seconds, thirds, and slipemaster. Ibid. Slipe: Wool recovered by a wool puller, chemically loosened with a sodium sulphide and hydrated lime mixture. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,59)

slipe n. N.Z. 1. wool removed from the pelt of a slaughtered sheep by immersion in a chemical bath. 2. (as modifier): slipe wool. [C14 in England: slype to strip, skin] [? cognate with slip, slippery] (1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1088) [NOTES: [1986 NZPOD 722; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 456]]

Skin and slipe 1s 2 1/2 d to 1s 4d ... (Aug 20, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3) [NOTES: (Extract from the New Zealand Monthly Magazine, 3, 1842-)]

The number of bales of New Zealand wool were 1,968; the prices realized were as follows:- Fleeces, 1s. 1d. to 1s. 10d .. slipe and skin, 1s. to 1s. 4 1/2 d. (May 9, 1855,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

Wool reports of the sales June 28 to 30, received by the San Francisco mail, show the following averages: Kapai clip, 106 bales greasy, average sixpence and seven-tenths .. Tora, 178 bales greasy 6 4-9d, 28 scoured, slipe, and washed 7 3-7d ... (Aug 8, 1898,Poverty Bay Herald,3)

45 bales slipe wool, valued at [GBP]582. (Jul 4, 1889,Hawke's Bay Herald,2)

Medium were from par to 5 per cent. lower, shabby 5 per cent. lower, scoureds and slipes 5 per cent. lower, merinos par to 5 per cent. lower. (Mar 8, 1923,Evening Post,7)

Slipes, medium to coarse crossbred, advanced 5 per cent., and fine wool slipes were 10 per cent. higher. (Jul 6, 1932,Evening Post,12)

adjective. [Rural] [of sheep] with a fleece of 25 to 50 cm length of wool [ that can be sliped off after slaughter.]

Medium slipe ewes $20-$21 .. slipe lambs $27.20 ... (Jul 6, 1995,NZ Farmer,39)

Prime sheep: top slipe ewes $76-$80.20 .. hvy slipe lambs $112-$116. (Aug 14, 2001,Dominion,6)

Stortford Lodge price range .. hvy slipe ewes $73-%76.50; slipe male lambs $112-$117. (Aug 21, 2001,Dominion,8)

Prices paid were: slipe ewes $50-$58 .. Slipe mixed-age wethers made $58.50-$59. (Apr 12, 2001,NZ Farmer,42)

Slipe ewes $68.70 - $73.75. (Mar 19, 2002,Hawke's Bay Today,11)

verb. [Rural] to pull or peel wool from a sheep skin.

PRESTON The pelts [of the frozen sheep] were completely useless: but the wool sliped off was just as good as any other wool. (1978,Woolgatherers,111)

WONZ At the freezing works pelts from slaughtered lambs are treated with a chemical enabling ther wool to be plucked or 'sliped' from the skin. (1980,NZ Sheep and Their Wool,ii)

WONZ After slaughter the skins are chemically treated at the meatworks allowing the wool to be 'sloughed' or 'sliped' off. (1980,NZ Sheep and Their Wool,49)

The agreed opening schedules are based on the average values for sliped wool realised last season. (Nov 2, 1942,Evening Post,4)

noun. a sledge

[The bullock] drew the slipe from the first as quietly as a lamb. [FN] `sledge' (Mar 15, 1851,Journal of Edward Ward,149)

verb. to draw or carry on a sledge N.I.

We attempted to slipe our load across the mud. (Apr 17, 1851,Journal of Edward Ward,170)

slipe wool¶

noun. [Rural] raw wool that has been removed from a sheep skin after it has died or been slaughtered.

Slipe wool has suffered a very serious decline, and low qualities are almost unsaleable. (Nov 22, 1867,Otago Witness,10)

The prices obtained were:- For washed slipe wool, merino, 1s 6d per lb. (Nov 16, 1872,Otago Witness,12)

BREMNER Slipe wool off the skins was cold-water washed by hand and paddock-dried. (1985,Woolscours of NZ,88)

RENNIE Slipe wool is the wool which is removed from the skin after the sheep has been slaughtered. (1988,Agriculture in NZ,25)

Walker's work also led to the practice of inserting steel rods in dumped bales of lower grade slipe wool during dumping, and holding the bales for several weeks. (2000,Wool Grower,Spring 32)

noun.

Sliped wool is the wool obtained from skins which have been washed in water to remove adhering sand and dirt together with a certain amount of the fat. (1908,TrNZI,41) [NOTES: (Wright)]

MACDONALD Slipe Wool - Wool that is taken from the skins of sheep; not shorn wool. (1915,NZ Sheepfarming,88)

The cost of working skins may be set down as 11/2d. per pound of sliped wool ... (1918,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,1/165)

MACDONALD The following wool trade terms are explained:- MUSHY WOOL: Shows no pronounced staple; from badly bred or old sheep. SHAFTINESS: A wool with a pronounced staple. SLIPE WOOL: Taken from the skins of sheep; not shorn wool. (1920,Australian & NZ Sheep Farming,142)

BREMNER Slipewool Wool removed from sheepskins by fellmongers. (1985,Woolscours of NZ,10)

slipemaster¶

noun. a class of wool recovered by a slipemaster

Slipe: Wool recovered from pelts in abbatoir. Body wool typed as woolly lambs, shorn lambs, and sheep. Oddments typed as seconds, thirds, and slipemaster. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,59)

noun. a machine used to recover wool from pelt trimmings in a fellmongery

(New N.Z. Process Replaces `Pie' Wool) This machine, known as the Slipemaster, is now in operation in the majority of New Zealand freezing works, and New Zealand-made machines have been sold to Australia and England. (Jun 13, 1957,NZ Farmer,6)

MORRIESON He had expected to find Entwistle standing at the bend of one of the slipe masters, the machines which had replaced the outcast but fabulously paid gang of men whose job had been to save the precious strands of wool after maggots had devoured the adhering meat. ... He was obliged to watch the steam-gauge of his slipe-master, put up with the roar of the machinery, and sort out and grade the wool which fell on his bench. This wool was thrown into baskets. (1976,Pallet on the Floor,94)

Slipemaster: Machine used to recover wool from pelt trimmings in a fellmongery (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,62)

slip-panel¶

noun.

[Hocken TS] Repaired slip panel of stockyard (Jun 18, 1861,Puketoi Station Diary)

(1867,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,1/136)

His master took the slip-panel down and the dog then rounded the sheep in and yarded them without any orders. (Mar 18, 1867,Richmond-Atkinson Papers,2/236) [NOTES: (C.W. Richmond)]

T.C. KIERNAN Went up the fence as far as the slip panel and found the fence burnt ... (Feb 5, 1879,Diamond Trails of Italy) [NOTES: 1879 Feb 5 T.C. Kiernan Diary in 1921 Guthrie-Smith Tutira 125]

PYKE a whole panel the rails of which can be slipped out and removed `Get off here, Marion,' said Nellie, herself dismounting at the Melrose slip-panel. (1881,White Hood and Blue Cap,121)

CHAMIER One of the bullocks charged furiously against the rails [of the stockyard], bursting out a slip-panel. (1891,Philosopher Dick,11)

slip-panels, slip-rails n. pl. rails or bars in a fence that can be moved to make a gateway. (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,10)

At the suggestion of the ranger it was resolved to erect a two rail fence and slip-panel across the road leading to the Kakaramea pound, the ranger to erect same and charge the board. (Mar 7, 1900,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

Slip panels had been erected on one portion of the road, which was also in parts covered with blackberries. (Nov 28, 1914,Grey River Argus,6)

MORRIS part of a fence so fitted that it can be removed so as to serve as a gate,. Used also for the gateway thus formed. Generally in the plural. Same as Slip-panel. [1870] (1898,Austral English,420)

slipper¶

verb. to beat; to best

NEWBOLD OK then Put your money where you big gob is. Come on. Ten bucks says he slippers you. (1982,Big Huey, The,219)

noun.

HENDERSON SLIPPERS: Worn horses' shoes, often nailed on temporarily. (1961,Friends in Chains,188) [NOTES: c1900-1920 A Teamster's Glossary in 1961 Henderson Friends In Chains 188]

LOVELL-SMITH a used horseshoe as a temporary expedient [I] asked him to let me have an old shoe to put on the mare. ... I said nothing, and taking off my coat, nailed the slipper on, and away we went. (1931,Old Coaching Days,101)

HENDERSON Besides all the other gear, most teamsters [c1900] carried `slippers,' which were tacked on in the event of lost shoes while on the road. (1961,Friends in Chains,109)

ANDERSON I was told that Duke had lost a shoe and ... [Bill] was tacking a slipper on him. `Tacking a slipper' on a horse means nailing on a horse-shoe that has already been used. It is tacked cold to a horse's foot. This is a temporary job to make do until the horse is ready to be shod properly. (1981,Both Sides of the River,162)

noun. at sheepdog-trials, one who releases the sheep

NEWTON ... the slippers had trouble with the sheep and finished up by losing them. (1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,112)

NEWTON ... the slippers had trouble with the sheep and finished up by losing them. Ibid. 169 Slippers: The men who release the sheep and place them in position for the competitor to begin his run. (1971,Ten Thousand Dogs,112)

noun. [Rural] a person who liberates sheep during dog trials [more common in the South Island.]

Liberators (slippers) must ensure that every competitor is given sheep that are sound and in good order. (1991,Constitution of NZ Dog Trial Assoc,32)

GORDON Some of the doings that liberators and slippers have got up to over the years have become legend. (1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,206)

In the South Island these guys are called "slippers" - not the fireside variety. But the cunning sheep do not always want to be "slipped" away from their woolly mates. (Apr 19, 2001,Taranaki Daily News,19)

slippers¶

noun. moccasins

slippery fern¶

noun. [Rural] hard-fern or bracken.

slippery jack¶

noun. the edible mushroom, Suillus luteus

Slippery Jack (Suillus luteus) But if the cepe is a lamentable rarity, its distant cousin, the slippery jack, carpets our pine forests every autumn. Slippery jack is always found near pine trees, so given New Zealand's huge pine population, it may well be our most common edible mushroom. The slipper jack is possibly more accurately known as the pine boletus. (May 2001,Cuisine,110)

Consider the Stinkhorn. The Fairy Club or the the Shaggy Parasol Mushroom. The Slippery Lizard Tuft, King Arthur's Cakes, the brain [sic] Mushroom or the Dead Man's Fingers. (Dec 10, 1988,Dominion,3) [NOTES: (David Hill)]

noun. a card game

slipping¶

noun. [Rural] the gouging of hillsides by water erosion, particularly common in North Island hill country.

BRADSHAW & WILLIAMS A number [of farmers] quoted figures such as slips only recover to 80% of production over 20 years and grass on slipped areas go into drought stress three days after slipping. (1998,Information and Communication Needs,25)

noun. [Rural] the liberating of sheep in a dog trial contest.

GORDON .. in the South Island, liberating is called 'slipping', which means they slip sheep on to the mark, using slippers. (1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,196)

slips¶

noun.

SUTTON-SMITH Action terms which refer to the shooting of the marbles are: Knuckle down Stiff, Knee High, Funks [Flunks sic] or Funnicks, Slips, Firsts and Lasts and Forces. ... The term Knuckle down Stiff' (Taranaki [18]80, Gisborne [18]85, Waitara [18]95) is mentioned by [Lady A.B. Gomme Vo. 1, p.113]. ... The definition I have run to earth reads: <i>Sloven</i>: The torn splintered portion of timber left on a stump or the end of a butt where thekey' finally broke when the tree fell. Syn. spaul, stub-chuck (American) ? also `Barbers'chair', the splintered stump of a newly felled tree. I hope this gives you the information you want. slush lamp¶

noun. [Rural] [used elsewhere but recorded earliest in NZ] a basic light source, being a tin filled with fat in which a wick is placed.

MEREDITH But I mustn't forget the `slush-lamp.' This consists of an old pannikin about three parts filled with clay, and the other part with tallow, in the middle of which is a small piece of rag of some sort (cotton, of course) sticking out of the fat about a quarter of an inch. The rag is lit with a match or a stick from the fire; the wick is fed by the surrounding fat, and the surrounding darkness is made visible. (1875,Adventuring in Maoriland in the Seventies,30,1935) [NOTES: 1872 Oct in c1875 Meredith Adventuring in Maoriland (1935) 30]

If there is one thing more contemptible than another in the way of anonymous criticism, it is, to my mind, the attempts of "Mickey" and "Gordon," who by pot-house wit acquired by long study over the "slush lamp," jeer at the recent information supplied through your columns by Mr Macalister respecting the produce market of New South Wales. SM¶

There arte 36 Small Claims Tribunals in New Zealand and full nationwide coverage is expected by the end of this year. Their basic objective: to provide a low-cost, speedy resolution of disputes involving sums of up to $1000. The means to this end: low filing fees, no strict adherence to the rules of evidence, the use of referees who are not necessarily legally qualified, and restricted grounds for appeal. smallfarmer¶

noun.

What, then, is a smallfarmer? "A vertically challenged agriculturalist," runs the well-worn joke. While names like "smallholder" or the American "homesteader" might be less obvious butts, they are really no more descriptive. "Toy farmer" is obviously derisive, while "hobby farmer" rather unfairly equates small-scale farming with stamp collecting or restoring old cars. Ibid. 42 John Fairweather.. defines smallfarmers (or smallholders, as he categorises them) as people who have a commitment to effective land use, and who earn at least some farm income. They differ from a group he calls "lifestylers" - a term derived from the ubiquitous "life style block" dreamed up by real-estate agents when they began to sell the concept of country living 20 years ago. (Jan 2000,NZ Geographic,No. 45/41)

Small-scaled skinks were first discovered on Motutaiko Island in 1971 and are native to New Zealand. (Jan 2, 2010,Dominion Post,A11)

Colonies of the small-scaled skink (O. microlepis; threat classification: serious decline) arepresent within 10-20 Km of the proposed wind farm. However, O. microlepis [sic] requires looserocks on the ground surface and as a result is restricted to boulder river beds and naturaland artificial screes such as those that form below rocky escarpments and roads ... (Sep 24, 2007,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.meridianenergy.co.nz/Documents/Final%20AEE/Appendix%20F%20Ecology/W07003-3_MEL_CentralWind_LizardsSnailsReport_071015.pdf]

As its name suggests, the elongate body of the small-scaled skink is covered in relatively small, glossy scales. .. The background colour to the upperparts of the body is brownish grey, but a series of stripes extend lengthways from the snout towards the tail. (2008,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.arkive.org/small-scaled-skink/oligosoma-microlepis/]

The area is at about 700m above sea level with extreme winter conditions and is home to the Small-scaled skink (Oligosoma microlepis). (2005,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.nzaee.org.nz/skinks.htm Date is estimate]

The fisheries of the Mohaka and Taharua Rivers are recognized and protected by Conservation Order while the native mistletoe, kaka, falcon, short and long tailed bats and small scaled skinks are among the rare or threatened species found on Poronui. (2008,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.poronui.co.nz/Home/Wilderness.aspx]

smokies¶

noun. opaque brown and grey marbles; also called OYSTERS [OED[S] check

[NOTES: 1945 Baker Aust. Lay. 204 ca1950's Naenae, Wellington (p.c. G. Kennedy)]

SUTTON-SMITH Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as taw' orshooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; dubs',dates', stakes',dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. (1972,Folkgames of Children,174)

KEITH & MAIN Marbles were the currency of childhood and there were an astonishing number of names for them, some referring to the material or colour, others to value or function in the game. There were agates, aggies, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cats-eye, [sic] chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, mollies, peelies, peewees, pisswees, pretties, Scotties, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers and whities. The march of technology added ball bearings - ballies or steelies - which were unbeatable when it came to smashing an opponent's miserable glassie. World War II[roman] brought `clayeys' often imperfectly spherical they were pathetic terracotta substitutes for real marbles. (1984,NZ Yesterdays,288)

smother¶

noun.

[NOTES: 1933 see cit. v1]

[check whether this refers to smother ] (1966,NZ Short Stories,210) [NOTES: 1963 Middleton in 1966 NZ Short Stories 210]

STUDHOLME The third day, as the sheep mobbed up, it was necessary to exercise great care in running a dog, for a rough turn could cause a bolt, or even a smother, if a deep gut came in the way. ... As soon as the whole mob was in hand and had been given a few turns, the danger of a smother lessened. (1940,Te Waimate,123,1954)

noun.

The rider of Nukuhan was in sore straits in the Scurry at Taranaki, as his instructions were to give the chestnut a good smother. Across the bottom bend he was on the outer, but then he came in to the rails, and despite the boy's efforts, he finished second. (Feb 26, 1910,NZ Truth,244/2/7)

noun. [Rural] a suffocation of sheep, usually en masse [ when driven hard downhill or near water, or worried in a paddock by a dog and being forced together into a tight pack. ]

ACLAND They had a bad smother there. (1930,Early Canterbury Runs,128)

BLAKISTON Shepherds dread a 'smother' and when the last creek was crossed, and the sheep safe in a holding paddock we were all very pleased. (1952,My Yesteryears,20)

GASCOIGNE A smother like this is news and you'll be branded a bad shepherd and me a worse owner. A smother is one of the easiest things in the world to happen with sheep if the conditions are there, and we made them, in the first place by running a fence through that hole. (1965,From the Top of a Hill,125)

KERR They [Merinos] roamed far in the days before fences, and mustering was difficult. The new chum found to his cost that 'they'd rush for miles at the sound of a bark, and you would have a pile up and a smother on your hands.' (1976,From the Beginning: chronicles of a county,131)

LOUGHNAN smother: if sheep are bustled into any sort of a defile it only needs one of them to stumble and it will trip others. In next to no time there can be the dreadful and awful sight of a mass of struggling mutton, feet high. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,74)

WATT Bad handling can cause many problems and one of these is smother. (1990,Wild Horses & Me,150)

STACEY Care had to be taken there to prevent a big smother in the bog. (1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,83)

verb. [Rural] [sheep] to suffocate when pushed together too closely.

PHARAZYN Journal Han 15 152 Teddy and W. to lambs to drive them to pen, smothered 10 in a blind gully ... (1848)

CHAMIER There's half a dozen sheep worried and a hundred smothered in the Great Gap ... (1891,Philosopher Dick,248)

MILLS ET AL As shown by their speed and activity lambs are very susceptible to fright and are likely to pile up and smother at the slightest provocation. (1964,Practical Guide to Handling Dogs and Stock,79)

HALL The man on the bottom beat got into trouble. Some sheep had been smothered through a bit of poor shepherding ... (1987,Shepherd's Year, A,84)

verb. see cit. 1933

See: -

There were only ten sheep smothered during the day. (Mar 1, 1885,Wairarapa Daily,2)

FORD Aitken left a mob of sheep run [on] a wrong spur and smothered a large number ... [sic] (Jan 10, 1867,Diary) [NOTES: 1867 Jan 10 Ford Diary in 1981 Crawford Station Years 181]

OGONOWSKA-COATES Smother . If the pens in a woolshed are filled too tight sheep may smother during the night. Sheep are kept in the pens overnight before they are shorn. (1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,97)

Smother.- Run sheep especially merinos, are very easy to s. on broken hill ground. An injudicious turn with a dog in an abrupt gully may stop the lead and cause some sheep to be knocked over. Other sheep make a rush and are brought down too, so that in a second or two there is struggling heap; and before the shepherd can pull them off one another the bottom ones are smothered . They sd. 1200 once on the Stew Point country at Mount Peel, and I believe there was a still worse s . on a station called Roxburgh in Otago. People who fill their woolsheds too tight often smother sheep on a smaller scale: perhaps half a dozen or so in a night. (C.) (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

BURDON Difficulties arose only when they started to go in the wrong direction and had to be stopped, or when a large mob was in hand and a steep, narrow gully had to be crossed; then there was always the danger of a `smother.' Of all breeds the Merino is the easiest to smother, for he moves freer, faster, and more recklessly than any other. If pressed or carelessly handled, some of the leaders may fall or be knocked over and those behind will pile up on top of them until the gully is filled level to the top with struggling sheep. (1938,High Country,108)

PHARAZYN to lambs to drive them to pen, smothered 10 in a blind gully. (Jan 15, 1848,Journal,97) [NOTES: (also 152 chk) Teddy and W. [some of cit missing???]]

In a minute half the mob were in. We pushed our horses in and prevented the others from going in. [36] If they had 3 out of 4 would have been smothered. (May 2, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,35,1950)

POLACK Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called para[as-acute] paraua [a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, mungu nui (black physeter); right whale, tohora (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, mango (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, mpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. (1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202fn)

Snares crested penguin¶

noun. [Environment]

The islands' only endemic seabird is the Snares crested penguin, which stands a little less than knee high and has a jazzy yellow head-crest, a tangerine-coloured bill, pink feet and smart black-and-white plumage. (A small number of birds display a phenomenon called isabellinism, in which the back feathers are pale fawn).Ibid. 66 [Hdg] Like corks in a maelstrom, Snares crested penguins bob about in the churning surf waiting for a wave to lift them onto shore... Snares crested penguins are one of four species of crested penguins - three of them endemic - which breed in New Zealand waters. All possess a pair of distinctive bands called supercilliary stripes, which run from the bill to the back of the head like giant yellow eyebrows... When the feathers are dry, the bands fluff out to create the classic crested-penguin "punk rocker" look... (Mar 2003,NZ Geographic,62/65)

These [birds] include the Snares crested penguins, which raise their young in densely crowded colonies from late August to February each year, competing with millions of other seabirds for food. (Mar 18, 1984,Listener (New Zealand Listener),81)

snark¶

noun. a portable black box which contains a radio receiver, data logger and special computer software package

[NOTES: does not appear to be an acronym]

A radio transmitter recorder ("snark") is placed in the areas where males repeatedly emit their low frequency boom... When kakapo pass a "snark", it detects the radio frequency from each bird's transmitter. (May 8, 2005,Sunday Star Times,A8)

The innovation centres around a portable black box, known as a 'Snark', which contains a radio receiver, data logger and special computer software package. Once placed in the forest, the Snark records the movements of any birds within, say, a 10 metre radius and stores this on its memory. Staff can then come along with a portable mini-computer, plug it into the Snark, and find out what birds have been in the area overnight. (Jan 14, 2006,Dominion Post) [NOTES: http://www.kakaporecovery.org.nz/what/technology.htmlaccessed 14/01/2006Latest website updates: 19 September 2005]

snib¶

noun. the small lever on a lock

Thus snib exists both as noun and as verb. The little lever on the lock is described as the 'snib', and 'snibbed' is used to describe the state of the lock. To 'snib the door' means to set the lever to lock it; to 'snib it open' means to set the lever to make it unlocked. (Oct 1999,NZWords,2(2) 5)

Snib is alive and well in Australia, where it keeps doors closed securely. It can be used as a noun referring to the mechanism which works only from one side of a door in a Yale-type lock and fixes the door closed, or to a latch; and as a verb meaning to engage the mechanism or latch. (Oct 2000,NZWords,4 : 3)

verb.

[NOTES: Re article by Kolstad in NZWords : the word appears in the 1985 edition of "The Tasman Dictionary" published by Macquarie as both verb and noun and also "sniblatch".]

The cry has gone up in protest against Cadbury Schweppes' decision to stop making the green lolly and its two cousins, Tangy Fruits and Sparklers [sic]. Some Web readers smelled a rat in the death of the Snifter, and wondered if Cadbury was using the sweets to drum up publicity. (Sep 20, 2008,Dominion Post,TBC)

The snifter eaters need to arise and unite to bring back the snifter. (Sep 22, 2008,Internet - see Notes,33) [NOTES: http://savethesnifter.co.nz/Default.aspx]

It's a fortnight since Cadbury Schweppes confirmed its company Pascalls was no longer manufacturing Snifters, Sparkles and Tangy Fruits and the backlash has gone global. Slater, 32, said getting rid of the Snifter was about as bad as it got. "Maybe even worse than doing away with pavlova, custard squares, whitebait fritters or roast lamb. We're a country that loves the oval ball: the rugby ball, the league ball, and the lime green ball - the Snifter." (Oct 5, 2008,Sunday Star Times,A4)

RICHARDS Fortunately, there was a timber mill operating nearby. By borrowing horses, they were able to snig the timber home through the bush track. (1986,Off the Sheep's Back,24)

McGILL snig to drag a heavy load with ropes and chains; originally logging word for dragging a log. - snigged home tied up, pulled into place, piled up, as in Frank S. Anthony's Me and Gus ; Barry Crump in Hang on a Minute, Mate refers to a snigging track ; origins obscure, Northern English dialect word. NZA. (1988,Dictionary of Kiwi Slang, A,105)

The County Chairman was present at the meeting, and he ordered me to "snig" two logs about 30ft long and throw them over the gap in the bridge; when I went down I found that there was a gap of 56ft and that I could not get logs suitable for the purpose, as one set of logs had been carried away by the flood, and the other set was not fit to put stringers on. (Oct 26, 1881,West Coast Times,2)

But the men did not stop to do this, for when I went to start the work, expecting the timber all in, I found almost the half of it a mile away from the claim and it had to be snigged in; even the cement and wire cables had to be partly disloaded. (Sep 22, 1894,Tuapeka Times,3)

The engineer asked permission to sue a man named White who was snigging heavy timber for a dredge on one of the county's new roads. (Jun 13, 1900,Grey River Argus,2)

Mr E. J. Low, Kokiri, advertises for sale a light draught horse, broken to harness and suitable for snigging sleepers. (Feb 19, 1906,Grey River Argus,3)

The sawn timber is obtained at Duncan's mill, Coal Creek, thence carted round the bluff to the foot of the creek, then snigged to the top of the spur, and finally sent by aerial tram to its destination on the line of race. (Feb 4, 1902,Grey River Argus,4)

Bardsley We snigged and stumped with gelignite and horses and put up fences. (2000,Land Girls, The,161)

TRIPP Blair. Snigging firewood out of bush. (Jun 1866,Day Book) [NOTES: 1866 June Tripp Day Book in 1967 Harper Kettle on Fuchsia 69]

To drag along the ground by horse or bullocks, especially to drag logs or other timber. The stout chain which goes round the log has a ring at one end, and a hook to which the horses' chains are attached. It is called a snigging chain. (C.) (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

SNIG To haul logs or trees along the ground. syn. SKID v. (1952,NZ Forest Glossary)

(1953,Short Stories (various authors),371) [NOTES: 1947 Vogt in 1953 Short Stories 371]

(Sep 1958,NZ Timber Journal,87/2)

snig vb. (tr.) N.Z. to drag away (a felled log) by a chain or cable. [< E dialect] (1982,Collins Concise English Dictionary,1095) [NOTES: [1986 NZPOD 726; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 459]]

He brought [the bullocks] from Hoe-o-Tainui, where they had been used for snigging logs from the bush. (Oct 1, 1937,Morrinsville Star,4)
