noun. [Rural] [bush-cutting] a load of logs or trees that have to be dragged from their location.

snig-chain¶

noun. [Rural] a heavy metal chain used for dragging or pulling objects.

Wayback felled and sawed his second tree, returned to the river bed, took the nosebag from Jess, hitched the snig-chain over her harnes[s], and led her up the track. (Oct 5, 1904,Otago Witness,82)

Set Shaft Harness, Set Leading Harness, Picks, Shovels, Snigchains, Ropes, &c. (Aug 8, 1896,Timaru Herald,3) [NOTES: Advert]

HAMMOND Therefore this kid had hardly been seen .. when you paid the family a visit to borrow a snig-chain or a separator ring. (1966,This Man's Father had my Father's Farm,47)

HAMMOND .. he was just coming to borrow a snig chain about which he'd phoned us the evening before. (1966,This Man's Father had my Father's Farm,143)

DAHM .. to Phil, who had been born and reared among bullocks and snig chains, it was like taking off to the moon. (2000,People of the Axe, The,70)

Buy a heavy snig chain for less than $200 .. you will also get a tax deduction for the snig chain ... (Jul 26, 2001,Taranaki Daily News,19)

Clearing Sale .. 2x snig chains ... (Dec 8, 2001,Hawke's Bay Today,21)

Clearing sale: new Sunbeam sheep shower, 4 snig chains ... (May 11, 2002,Taranaki Daily News,47)

Clearing sale: .. various snig chains ... [snig-chain; snigchain] (Jun 21, 2002,Hawke's Bay Today,26)

SUTHERLAND He got the blacksmith to make him a really big hook and attach it to a length of snig-chain. (1953,Golden Bush, The,155,1963)

snigger¶

noun.

[Advt] Wanted - Good SNIGGER, must beable to slice. (Apr 20, 1909,Greymouth Evening Star,3)

Ally and his brother Fred had the contract to supply the mill with logs, normally a five man crew would be required to do the work; a winch driver, a faller, a wedger, a snigger and a whistle boy. (2001,Good Bastards: the larrikin's guide to success,24)

WANTED - SNIGGER, BUSHMEN, TRAM LAYERS, and men accustomed to bridge work. (Apr 3, 1901,Grey River Argus,3) [NOTES: Advert]

WANTED for Terawera S.M. Coy Inchonie, one Assistant SNIGGER, two Pick and Shovel MEN (or tram layers), and one assistant BREAKER DOWN. (Aug 11, 1910,Grey River Argus,5) [NOTES: Advert]

MALFROY SNIGGING-TRACKS. ... Good straight tracks make hauling easy. A few pieces of corduroy placed across the track are a great help ... A good snigger will see that a log is not jammed before signalling `Right ahead' to the hauler, and will use his snigging-shoe ... to lift the log out of bad places. Ibid. 27 The snigger has charge of the rope, dogs, and blocks, and must see that his hauling tracks are cut in the best direction ... (1923,Small Sawmills,13)

MARSH Here ... were a winch, a loco-driven circular saw and, close to the ground a steel cable that ran ... into the forest. As we watched it, it quivered. From a hidden and remote distance a human voice gave a ... cry. [102] `That's the snigger,' Sandy said. (1981,Black Beech & Honeydew,101)

Following are the daily rates .. panners-off, motormen, sniggers, bush winchmen, and tractor drivers, 18s ... (Sep 24, 1936,Evening Post,7)

snigging¶

noun. [Rural] the hauling of heavy loads of flax, wood or tree-stumps with a snig-chain and horse, bullock, or, more recently, tractor.

During the last week four men working making sledge track to suspension brdge, snigging material, and shifting poles and transformer from old incline drive and re-erecting at new incline shaft site. (Dec 21, 1933,Evening Post,14)

Sleeper-cutters seem to have practically cut out the whole of this timber within reasonable distance or horse tracks of roads, and in doing so have destroyed millions of young seedling trees in "snigging" or in sqaring ports or sleepers, and then putting a match to the tops and chips. (Sep 5, 1906,Otago Witness,17)

Mr Peattie, the proprietor of the section in which one of them is built, requires compensation for right of access before he allows us to put timber on the ground. In the meantime I have had it stacked on the side of the main road ready for snigging when Mr Peattie is arranged with. (Nov 15, 1879,North Otago Times,2)

From the nature of the work these horses have been occupied in they are especially suitable for logging, snigging and general saw-milling work. (Apr 21, 1899,West Coast Times,3)

"Sawmilling. - Very busy. Men for breaking down, snigging, tram-laying and slabbying are being advertised for ..." (Feb 5, 1916,Grey River Argus,5)

Tenders for snigging or carting 50 tons of rails, close at this office at 6 o'clock this evening. (Jun 11, 1887,West Coast Times,2)

But silver pine, as everyone knows, grows principally on the Pakihis, from which the sleepers can only be got out of by means of "snigging," the ground being soft, almost swampy. (Apr 2, 1901,Grey River Argus,2)

MOWAT In afternoon got 3 snigs of wood ready for snigging. (May 8, 1907,Alexander Mowat Diaries)

JOHNSTON In the early days the flax was pulled to load sites by a single draught-horse, which was called "snigging" .. Snigging: this involved pulling flax out of the gullies to a loading site. (1990,Redan, Valley of Farming and Flaxmilling,164)

They have cost me L1 1s each; snigging between Queenstown and Arthur's Point, has cost me 15s a post, and there has been the 6s 6d for erecting, superintendence being in all cases excluded. (Jul 1, 1864,Otago Daily Times,4)

MALFROY OPERATION COSTS ... (a) Felling (b) ... (c) Snigging or skidding Ibid.39 Snigging .. The pulling of a log endwise along the ground by wire-rope haul, bullock-team, or other power. In America called `skidding.' (1923,Small Sawmills,8)

SARGESON (gloss.) snigging: a method of draggging logs without te use of a sledge. Ibid.279 Snigging: method of dragging posts or logs without a sledge. (1949,I Saw in My Dream,273,1974 ed. Rhodes)

Snigging : Log haulage. (1953,NZ Forest Glossary)

OWEN & PERKINS It was astonishing the tremendous loads they could pull out of the bush along the ground - snigging', that was called. In many places the logs were brought out on what was called acat', which was short for catamaran. A catamaran was a big heavy sledge made of bush timber ... The bushmen would build a special road for them - a corduroy road, or `skidded' road, as we used to call it. (1986,Speaking for Ourselves,160) [NOTES: (Joe Gasparich, Northland kauri country)]

This is done by a low or high lead and is called "snigging". (1944,Korero (AEWS Background Bulletin),2(9) : 25)

I got mine snigging (Jan 10, 1947,Listener (New Zealand Listener),23) [NOTES: Republished in 1953 NZ Short Stories 371]

SNIPE: To round off the end of a log in order to avoid snigging. (Sep 1958,NZ Timber Journal,87)

snig-track¶

noun. [Rural] a path through bush or over land where a log or equipment can be dragged.

At length, after following its course for nearly a mile, they came to a snig track, where somebody had been taking out sleepers, and, going along it some distance, came to the road, and were very glad to get there, and also to find the sun shining brightly, for they both felt miserable and wet. (Jul 10, 1907,Otago Witness,87)

snipe¶

noun. a bird

GUTHRIE-SMITH The species we hoped to make friends with [off Stewart Island] were the Snipe (Gallinaga Aucklandica ), the South Island Crow (Glaucopis cinerea ), and the South Island Thrush (Turnagra crassirostris ). (1936,NZ Naturalist,175)

FALLA et al. Godwits are sometimes referred to as snipe' orcurlew'. Both these names are quite incorrect. (1966,Birds of New Zealand,116)

NATUSCH [Only one of the 18 Northern Hemisphere nesting migratory birds], the snipe (Coenocorypha aucklandica ) is a true New Zealander (1967,Animals of NZ, The,262)

Snipe Coenocorypha aucklandica (GRAY, 1845) ... Snipe found on some of New Zealand's outer islands are named for their resemblance to the migratory Gallinago species of the northern hemisphere. (1985,Reader's Digest Book of NZ Birds,202)

SCOTT At that age he began standing in for his father ... hunting pigs and shooting snipe (godwits) on the dunes. (1987,Seven Lives on Salt River,90)

ANDERSON ... but no other sort of game was seen except a single snipe [ed. fn There is no native New Zealand snipe: this one must have been a migrant from Japan, Gallinago hardwicki.] which was shot and differs but little from that of Europe.] (Feb 1777,Journal) [NOTES: 1777 Feb Anderson's Journal in Cook Journals (1967) 3/807 (Queen Charlotte Sound)]

CRUISE At noon we went on the island to shoot, and killed some red bill and a snipe; the only one that any of us had seen in this country: in its plumage it resembled those found in England, but the bird itself was much smaller. (1823,Journal,150,1957) [NOTES: 1820 Aug 30 in 1823 Cruise Journal (1957) 150]

WILLIAMS ... we have had fresh baked bread, puddings ...ducks, snipe and pigeons; fish of various kinds ... (Mar 28, 1833,Early Journals of Henry Williams, The,302,1961)

SARA MATHEW We saw myriads of snipes [in North Auckland] in the shoal water and shot a dozen of these graceful birds. (Apr 29, 1840,Journal) [NOTES: 1840 Apr 29 Sarah Mathew Journal in 1940 Founding of NZ 132]

Gallinago aucklandica , Gray. Snipe. - Met with in the Chatham Island group. (Nov 1885,NZ Journal of Science,85) [NOTES: (T.H. Potts)]

Gallinago aucklandica . - Snipe. Auckland Islands. (1886,TrNZI,18/113) [NOTES: (Martin)]

Several interesting land birds inhabit the [Snares] island, ... the Auckland Island Snipe >Gallinago Aucklandica ); the grass bird (Sphoeneacus fulvus ), although now rare on the mainland, was frequent on this little island ... (1891,NZ Journal of Science,1/161)

... the most important [Chatham Island] edible sea-birds: AS WRITTEN AS PRONOUNCED ENGLISH hopo ho[macron]p' albatross hakoakoa ha[macron]ko[macron]k' mutton bird taiko tchai[macron]k' pied shear water tupoupou tchu[macron]poup' pied blue billie reoreo ro[macron]ro[macron] Mother Carys chicken turiwati tchu[macron]riwat' dottrel [sic] kuaka ku[macron]k' snipe (1928,BP Bishop Memoirs,Vol. IX No. 5 p.358) [NOTES: 1928 Baucke Manuscript in Skinner and Baucke The Morioris (Bishop Museum Memoirs Vol. IX No. 5 pp. 343-382) 358]

A COMPACT FARM, containing 43 acres of Land, situated at OREWA .. An Oyster bed within three minutes' walk, and plenty of Pigeon, Snipe, and Pheasant shooting. (Dec 2, 1864,Daily Southern Cross,3) [NOTES: Advert]

What takes B C down the Coast so often on Sundays? To shoot snipe I suppose. (Dec 7, 1895,Observer (Auckland),21)

A few plants common to the Auckland Isles, were also found in Fouveaux Strait, and one bird, a snipe, excited our curiosity as being the first of these species seen in New Zealand. (Jul 24, 1852,New Zealand Spectator & Cook's Strait Guardian,3)

THE other evening one of our sportsmen came home with a string of snipe. (Sep 19, 1885,Waikato Times,6)

verb. sawmilling: to trim the end of a log to obviate snagging while snigging; sc a log ?variant of snip

If the weather is favourable, the log is `sniped' or rounded at one end, an iron grip driven into it, and to this the team is fastened. (1902,NZ Illustrated Magazine,5/375)

R. GILBERD A ropey' will learn tosnipe' ... which is a highly-skilled operation. Butt-end of clean-trimmed log is trimmed of angles. Vees are cut at points opposite each other at the butt-end (usually) and are connected by a chopped Dee which runs around in a semi-circle from one to the other. In the Dee is laid a strop', a short length of cable with an eye in each end. The eyes are connected with each other and to a short chain by a shackle; and the chain is attached tothe rope' with a hitch. (1950,Personal Communication)

REED In order to prevent the log from biting' into uneven ground, and enable it to slip over minor obstacles, it wassniped' - that is, somewhat rounded or tapered at the front. (1953,Story of the Kauri, The,179)

(1958,NZ Timber Journal,87/2) [NOTES: [ca -1914]]

After the logs were cut, each was sniped. To snipe a log, the end is chipped all the way round so that it can be handled without catching humps in the ground, stumps and so on; in fact you might say that a log when it is sniped looks rather like the blunt end of a whale. (1951,Radio NZ / National Radio) [NOTES: H.S. McCarroll The Days of the Kauri Bushmen [Radio Talk 2: TS]]

SNIPE To round off the end of a log in order to facilitate snigging. (1952,NZ Forest Glossary)

MOORE The front end of the log was carefully `sniped', that is, its sharp edge was rounded to allow it to skid like a sledge-runner. (1969,From Forest to Farm,42)

OWEN & PERKINS First of all they tapered one end, rounding the log so that it would be able to slide over impediments in its path, because it had to be dragged along the ground. Now these men were called `snipers', and having sniped the log, they then made two cuts, one on each side of the log opposite each other, right into the rounded part - the sniped end. That was for the purpose of holding a heavy chain which attached the log to the yoked bullocks ... (1986,Speaking for Ourselves,159) [NOTES: (Joe Gasparich, Northland kauri country)]

(1966,Short Stories (various authors),190) [NOTES: 1953 Middleton in 1966 Short Stories 190]

snow country¶

noun. [Rural] [sp.use] high country pastoral land that is used for summer grazing only.

PERRY They [Corriedales] are being used on the mountainous snow country of the interior. (1922,Sheep Farming in NZ,1)

NEWTON They were in dangerous snow country, where every sheep left in the fall muster could be written off. (1947,Wayleggo,118)

WHEELER The catchment board and the station have together put in a twenty-mile retirement fence at 3,500 feet to prevent stock from using potentially dangerous snow country. (1971,Historic Sheep Stations SI II,30)

MACGREGOR He was boundary keeping while doing a little fencing, and every day he had to hunt the sheep back out of the snow country. (1980,Dog's Life, A,40)

snow fence¶

noun. [Rural] a fence erected to keep sheep off areas prone to heavy snow in sudden snowfalls.

The wethers can be kept back on the roughest areas, lambs can be weaned on to a clean spelled block, while a snow fence, preventing the sheep from drifting up into the higher basins in the late autumn at the time when snow is due, is a valuable means of preventing mortality and the expense of snow-raking and mustering. (Feb 20, 1937,NZ Journal of Agriculture,101)

MCKENZIE Early in the year 1950 the pilot of the Southern Scenic Airways Trips dropped fencing material on the top of Walter Peak range for repairing snowfences. (1951,Wakatipu Pioneers,122)

SHARPE .. modern high-country owners try to establish a 'snow fence' which runs along the side of a range perhaps 3,000 ft above sea level. (1962,Country Occasions,158)

WHEELER Now with access roads and the snow fence, we only need musterers for two days and do the rest of it ourselves from the homestead. (1971,Historic Sheep Stations SI II,30)

LOUGHNAN snow fence: one which has been built in the full knowledge that it will be damaged by each winter's snow and so will need annual repair. But by then it has done its job for the year of confining sheep within the winter block. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,74)

BARDSLEY We put a snow fence across Mt Karetu before the snow as a snow boundary, because we lost several hundred hoggets one winter. [snow fence] (2000,Loughnan Glossary,41)

snow gate¶

noun. [Rural] a gate that opens vertically rather than horizontally, in use in snowy conditions in high country areas.

ENYS New gate on road (the snow gate that rose in the air instead of opening sideways.) (Mar 2, 1878,Enys Papers)

snow hut¶

noun. [Rural] [sp. use, high country farming] a mustering hut above the snow line.

HARPER The three top snow huts, Waihi Top, Mt Edith Top and the Hat Top were kept provided with rations and blankets, which were stored in tin boxes, safe from rats and mice. Lean to-s were attached to several of the huts, all the top snow ones, for the musterers' dogs. (1967,Kettle on the Fuchsia, The,88)

noun.

Six weeks later A.J. Heine.. made another snow hut. (Jun 1952,NZ Alpine Journal,14(39) : 365)

snow in¶

verb. [Rural] [of shearers] to make [the shed hands] unable to cope with the wool [by working too fast]

See: snowed in

BOWEN With a good run shearers can sometimes snow the pressers in. (1956,Wool Away!,157)

snow ink¶

verb. to snow heavily

Not caring if it `snowed ink' we crawled into our wet sleeping bags. (1936,Hills and Valleys,2/44)

snow leggings¶

noun. [Rural] [mustering and shepherding] fitting oilskin overtrousers to wear in snowy or wet conditions.

SINCLAIR So give me my stick and snow-leggings, It's off to the hills I must go. (1973,Boot in the Stirrup,29)

MACNICOL & TROTTER The snow leggings in the song were used on Mt Aurum station by the older shepherds. The leggings were used to shed the snow. (1987,I, Duncan from Skippers,72)

snow muster¶

noun. [Rural] [high country] an autumn muster.

CRESSWELL The run in those days [1902] was unfenced, and when the snow muster took place every April and the sheep were brought down to safe country, I had to live the winter alone with my dogs at Golden Gully Hut. (1942,Early NZ Families,158)

snow pea¶

noun. a variety of pea whose pods can be eaten along with the peas

[NOTES: Jim writes also sugar pod = sugar pea, mangetout. In NZPOD but not other dictionaries]

snow pen¶

noun. [Rural] a small enclosed snow-bound area, where groups of isolated, snowbound sheep gather.

HALL .. on this particular occasion, at Glencoe, we set out to trample a track through the snow for the sheep to follow once we'd freed them from their snow pen. I stayed at the bottom of the snow pen while Brian, the boss, brought them around to the track we'd made about halfway up the side of the pen. (1987,Shepherd's Year, A,94)

snow pole¶

noun. a pole placed upright to mark out a road or track when it is covered with snow.

The erection of snow poles and wiresacross the Old Man Range is to becommenced on Monday. (Apr 2, 1864,Otago Witness,15)

Persons who have had occasion to come over the Cardrona Saddle and other high roads since the snow fell would have found much help and guidance if snow poles had been erected. (Aug 5, 1903,Otago Witness,31)

The miners ... appreciate the care and thoughtfulness of the Government in erecting snow poles between the Teviot township and Pomahawk Gully, and which, in these snow-covered regions, has been the means of averting much personal inconvenience, ... (Jul 18, 1862,Otago Witness,7)

WOOD ... they got snowed up at Potter's, and tried to make their way out by the snow poles over there. (1875,Waiting for the Mail,36)

DON A bridle track marked by the remains of snowpoles. (1891,Chinese Mission Work,18)

HOCKEN It was sought to make the track over Flagstaff, or the Snowy Mountains as they were then called, safer by erecting snow poles sunk into mounds, and of these there were seventeen to the mile; ... (1898,Contributions to the Early History of New Zealand,172)

PICKERING Out on the tops the old remedy for indicating a route was a pile of stones collected together - the cairn. Anyone can build them, and so once again a more official marking system had to be found. Routes became, as the maps put it, `poled', which [26] meant that metal standards were studded along the tops, These can also be called snow-poles or sometimes waratahs. (1988,Hills, The,24, 26)

Snowpole track to Deep Stn. (1918,NZ Geol. Survey Bulletin,No 19 (N.S.) map opp. p.40) [NOTES: (Tuapeka) Marshall]

BEATTIE It was sought to make the track over Flagstaff ... safer by erecting snow poles sunk into mounds, and of these there were seventeen to the mile ... (1947,Pioneers Explore Otago,76) [NOTES: [Dr. Hocken's History]]

(1959,Tararua,22/49)

McLEOD Coming down Starvation Gully, where the striped `snow-poles' marked the winding road for winter travellers,.... (1870,Glorious Morning,219)

snow river¶

noun. a snow-fed river

Goitre was often caused by fright, but many medical men were of opinion that it was generally caused in Canterbury by the drinking of water brought down by the snow rivers. (Mar 9, 1899,Otago Witness,45)

In the North Island it [the oystercatcher] is never seen away from the coast, but in the South Island one species is widely distributed along the beds of snow rivers and in the barren uplands of Central Otago. (Aug 26, 1939,Evening Post,17)

The wild West Coast, intersected by many bridgeless snow rivers, straight from the Southern Alps, and covered for the most of the part with bush, is probably the roughest bit of country that any New Zealand backblocks parson has to tackle. (Sep 20, 1910,Grey River Argus,1)

THE trout streams of New Zealand may be divided into two classes - Rain Rivers and Snow Rivers. There are only one or two streams in the North Island that come under the later heading, but in the South all the great rivers are fed by melting snows. (Jul 1, 1900,NZ Illustrated Magazine,43)

Within ten years of liberation of a stock of Scottish Burn trout, the waters in which they had been released had possessed all the so-called varieties of trout peculiar to the Old Country, from sea trout at the mouths of the snow rivers to the Scottish species in the small hill creeks. (Aug 28, 1940,Evening Post,8)

But Canterbury is peculiarly favourable, having snow rivers. Salmon always live better in cold than in other water, especially prefering snow fed rivers and very rapid rivers. (Jan 4, 1859,Lyttelton Times,4)

It [Waitaki] is a snow river looks milky before it rises. (May 4, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,36,1950)

BUTLER The Hurunui is not a snow river. (1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,67)

... The Rangitata, one of the great snow rivers, as they are termed. This stream, which derives its source from the glaciers which are embedded in the gloomy and secluded fastnesses of the Southern Alps, is periodically swollen by the melting of the snow and by the heavy rain from the north-west, ... (1871,TrNZI,3/86) [NOTES: Potts]

BATEMAN Very many [in Canterbury] are known as `snow' rivers, owing to the icy coldness of the water. (1881,Colonist, The,26)

In all the snow rivers of Canterbury the fish have been running in considerable numbers for the last few weeks. (Mar 22, 1928,Evening Post,12)

noun. [Rural] [ S. I. high country] a gorged river that drains snow cover.

.. one can see the huge gaps in the mountains - the gorges through which the snow rivers run - as plainly as if they were only rifle shot away. (Mar 1895,NZ Farmer,88)

snow scud¶

noun. [Rural] a brief, cold, stormy shower.

PETER snow scud - brief stormy shower. (2000,Peter Glossary,6)

snow strap¶

noun. [Rural] [mustering] a strap holding oilskin leggings close to one's legs [used in wet weather or snow].

MACNICOL As soon as he could, Archie donned leggings and snow-straps and headed for the spurs where the sheep were. Archie's mustering stick was exchanged for a shepherd's crook, and his packhorses for a tractor; snow-straps were discarded altogether, with his heavy frost-spiked mustering boots. (1965,Beyond the Skippers Road,57)

snow totara¶

noun. [Environment] a dwarf alpine variety of totara, Podocarpus nivalis

We followed deer tracks zigzagging up through snow totara and Dracophyllum, then plugged up through soft snow to Brodrick Pass (5,308ft., taking nearly two hours from camp. (Sep 1958,Tararua,49)

MARK & ADAMS These shrubs, often no higher than the tussocks, vary somewhat from place to place but snow totara (Podocarpus nivalis), mountain toatoa (Phyllocladus alpinus) and some of the mid-sized species of Dracophyllum (D. uniflorum) Hebe (H.odora) and Coprosma (C. pseudocuneata) are widespread. (1973,Plants of NZ,18,1979)

DENNIS Snow totara (Podocarpus nivalis) is found here and there in the west [of Westland]. (1981,Paparoas Guide,164)

DAWSON Snow totara (Podocarpus nivalis) forms low bushes in this community [sc. tussock shrubland]. (1988,Forest Vines to Snow Tussocks,170)

Snow totara, Podocarpus nivalis, also produces red berries, feeding kea and wood pigeons venturing above the bushline. Ibid. 50 [Caption] Seed disperser extraordinaire, a New Zealand pigeon gorges itself on the berries of a thicket of snow totara. Podocarpus nivalis. Unlike the mighty lower-altitude totara, this alpine species never grows to be more than a 3 m-high shrub. (Sep 2001,NZ Geographic,No. 53/47)

snow tussock¶

noun. [Rural] [S.I. high country] a tufty native grass, Danthonia raoulia or D flavescens.

Even down on the lower country, the tussocks grow thickly on the paddock borders. In 1993, Brian gifted an area of snow tussock, fenced off and protected from stock, to the QEII Trust. (Feb 20, 2010,Your Weekend,8)

The genus Chioonochloa (chion = snow;chloa = grass) includes the snow tussocks, or tall tussocks - up to 2 metres high - that make up the grand, golden army that dominates our subalpine grasslands, furring the hills a tawny gold and forming a magnificent backdrop for beer and car commercials. ... [29] Snow tussocks, especially those tolerant of drier conditions, such as the narrow-leaved snow tussock (C. rigida), became widespread at lower altitudes. (Nov 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 66/28)

It was a most uncomfortable situation - not a stick to boil the billy, and nothing but big snow tussocks for the horses to eat. (1910,Tapanui Station,74)

On unploughable country such as this, where snow tussock is, or was, the dominant tussock, the introduction of some leguminous plants may be of some considerable value. (Sep 16, 1940,NZ Journal of Agriculture,183)

ROBERTS & TURNER When high country settlement began in the mid-nineteenth century flax, toi-toi and snow tussock of enormous size grew in profusion, as did spaniard, slippery fern, lawyer bushes and matagouri. (1983,NZ High Country Four Seasons,19)

KERR The fire was roaring up to a patch of silver tussock, which doesn't burn as high as snow tussock. (2000,High Times in the High Country,107)

The curled snow tussock (C. crassiuscula) has the most variable seeding recorded in the world. (Nov 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 66/35)

"Since we've burnt snow tussock and dried it out," says Patrick, "I'm sure we've eliminated many populations of this sort of thing." (Nov 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 66/43)

The hills afford good rough pasture for sheep, being pretty well covered over with white tussock grass, which shows a warmer, drier soil, likely to produce abundantly more native grass that the colder snow tussock country. (Dec 23, 1887,Otago Witness,36)

Now, by actual experiment it was found that the silver tussock, not the snow grass tussock was even superior to the Esparto. (Jan 10, 1872,Bruce Herald,3)

He described the country as snow tussock land, well suited for horned cattle. (Dec 31, 1891,Otago Witness,14)

If the leasee [sic] or licensee of the pastoral lands permits to be burned any snow tussock on his land, except in July, August, and September, he is liable, on summary conviction, to a fine not exceeding fifty pounds. (Oct 10, 1913,Poverty Bay Herald,9)

snow-apple¶

noun.

[NOTES: Kolstad says these are species of Gaultheria and snow-apple in this sense does not appear to occur elsewhere, only in OED2 and US Dictionaries as an apple cultivar. Kerry Carman writes (Sep. 2000): I can supply no other literary reference to snow apples but am sure Neave was referring to the Alpine Snowberry Gaultheria depressa or, more likely, the closely-related G.d. var novae-zelandiae (Mountain Snowberry) with pure white apple-shaped fruits. These, at 1.5 cm, are the largest and juiciest berries in the genus.]

It is certain that snow-apple is a colloquial colonial term for the plant we now refer to as snowberry - possibly the Bush Snowberry Gaultheria antipoda, which is common on Mt Somers. But more likely, from Naeve's description of the fruit, is the Alpine Snowberry Gaultheria depressa, or the closely related G d novaezelandiae, the Mountain Snowberry, distinguished by its pure white, apple-shaped fruits, which, at 1.5 cm, are the largest, juiciest and generally regarded as tastiest in the genus. (Dec 9, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),45)

ANDERSON "We were up at 7.30 o'clock, took some sandwiches and started off to climb Mt Somers. Walked through bush and scrub and over stones, shifting shingle and boulders. Ate any amount of snow-apples, little white berries growing like cranberries and tasting like apples and cream". (1965,Good Logs of Algidus, The,47) [NOTES: Quote from Frank Naeve, written 1864]

snowball¶

noun. ? a kind of raffle

glossary snowball: reward of virtue; Housie organisers' benefit. Main prize at Naafi Sunday teas. (1946,Johnny Enzed in the Middle East)

You remember what you were like after you won that snowball. (1946,Johnny Enzed in Italy,32)

snowball waltz¶

noun. A means of breaking the ice; a pre-selected split up when the music stops and each takes a new partner from others in the hall; this continues until all are on the floor.

[NOTES: Also the name of a book by Renee. Note on conversation with Deidre Macken (60 yrs) about her mother's story (86 yrs). She was in the Wellington Ballet Company in 1926 and on news of Pavlova's tour wrote to her manager enquiring how they could help make her tour and reception more pleasant, her favourite colours, foods, etc. She expressed a great liking for meringue (cakes) so they consulted a chef who produced 3 attempts (e.g. a square cake was rejected in favour of a round one); finally the `soft-centre' variety was chosen. In her honour they named it Pavlova (?cake) and they presented this to Pavlova (? at a gathering) and she liked it a great deal. D. Macken is to research this - ? Ballet company records, etc. Deidre Macken (04) 384-6073 - H.D. Macken, Nairn St.]

At its compulsive best, The Snowball Waltz is an acutely rendered portrayal of human frailty and unexpected fortitude. (Dec 13, 1997,Listener (New Zealand Listener),46)

RENEE The next dance, ladies and gentlemen, is a Snowball Waltz! We knew they did this at real dances because Gertrude played in real dance bands once, which was how our mother met the saxophone player. (1997,Snowball Waltz, The,60)

HALL Balls [in the 1950s] had their own routines : quicksteps, waltzes and foxtrots. Then supper, after which things livened up ; the Snowball Waltz, the Valeta and the Gay Gordons until finally the Last Waltz was announced. (1998,Bums on Seats,57)

With her latest novel, The Snowball Waltz, Renee has reached a new pinnacle of success... The novel takes its title from a dance which begins with two partners who, when the music stops, separate and seek new partners. (Oct 26, 1997,Sunday Star Times,E6)

snowberry¶

noun.

MARK & ADAMS Pernettya macrostigma Col. SNOWBERRY (1973,NZ Alpine Plants,110)

noun.

McLINTOCK Snowberry .. .. mingimingi, tumingi .. .. Cyathodes (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/705-712)

noun.

Enargea parriflora snowberry (1908,AJHR) [NOTES: (And)1908 Cockayne Report on a Botanical Survey of the Tongariro National Park]

Enargea parriflora snowberry (1909,AJHR) [NOTES: (And)Cockayne Report on a Botanical Survey of Stewart Island]

noun.

WILSON Gaultheria antipoda BUSH SNOWBERRY ... Taawiniwini ... False beech ... Shrub up to 1-2 m tall. ... Fruit berry-like, red or reddish pink, formed by swollen calyx around thin capsule. (1982,Stewart Island Plants,64)

(1908,AJHR,C-14) [NOTES: (And)Cockayne Botanical Survey Waipoua Kauri Forest]

noun. a name applied to a number of plants, including mingimingi (prickly heath). See also Taupo snowberry, rock snowberry, weka berry

[NOTES: Kerry Carman writes (Sept. 2000): Gaultheria antipoda is the Bush Snowberry; fruits are 15 mm and may be white, pink, red or purple. Confusing the issue are two other candidates, also commonly called snowberries. (a). Pernettya is also an edible Snowberry, sometimes white, sometimes red. Like Gaultheria it is of the Ericaceae with which it bydrisies freely in the wild. (b). Leucopogon (Epacridaceae) is another edible native Snowberry from the region. It ranges from white through pinks and red to purple.]

CROWE Snowberry Gaultheria antipoda Tawiniwini; bush snowberry Gaultheria depressa Mountain snowberry... Both shrubs are rather similar except that bush snowberry grows up to about 1.5 metres and has leaves 80-16mm long, while mountain snowberry is a low spreading plant seldom more than 10 cm high, with smaller leaves 4-8 mm long. Ibid. 54 In 1864, Barrington.. was grateful at one point for the sustenance these fruits provided: 'I was so weak that I thought I must give in, but I ate plenty of the little snowberries which grow under the snow. They helped us a good deal.' (1997,Field Guide to Native Edible Plants of NZ,53)

Besides grubs, they feed on the berries of various alpine shrubs ... such as the snow berry (Gaultheria) ... (1891,NZ Journal of Science,1/200)

DEMPSEY Eileen Willa ... occasionally brought in dish of mosses and arranged amongst them ... the fragile white bells and the translucent white berries of what in Stewart Island we call the snowberry. It is a lily, she told me. Or she'd bring flowers of the coastal gentian ... (1964,Little World of Stewart island,14)

LAING & BLACKWELL The white fruit of the G. antipoda is known as the snowberry in Otago, and occasionally eaten ... it cannot be recommended to the epicure. (1940,Plants of NZ,344 ff)

BEATTIE Wild berries, fuchsia, snowberry ... (1947,Early Runholding in Otago,153)

HUTCHINSON [Ruahine Mountains] Shrubby Gaultherias (weka-berry and snow-berry). (1947,At Omatua's Fireside,13)

MARK & ADAMS Gaultheria depressa Hook. f. SNOWBERRY (1973,NZ Alpine Plants,108,1979)

MOORE & IRWIN GAULTHERIA DEPRESSA variety NOVAE-ZEALANDIAE. ... White succulent edible fruits' ... are calledsnow-berries', but red and pink ones are almost equally common. (1978,Oxford Book of NZ Plants,110)

BROOKER et al. Gaultheria antipoda Forst.f. Common name: Snowberry Maori name: Papapa ... This little shrub is common throughout New Zealand in scrubland. Possibly it is the plant referred to by James Cowan [in Maori Today] ... although Williams identifies `papapa' as both Pomaderris elliptica (Rhamnaceae) and Gaultheria antipoda. (1981,NZ Medicinal Plants,52)

WILLIAMS Taupuku, n. Gaultheria antipoda, snowberry, a shrub. (1917,Dictionary of the Maori Language,470)

Gaultheria antipoda snowberry (1896,Dunedin Field Club Plant Catalogues) [NOTES: (And)]

McLINTOCK Snowberry .. .. taupuka, taupuku .. .. Gaultheria (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/705-712)

snowberry [s] Gaultheria antipoda Forst.f. (1969,Standard Common Names for Weeds,71)

HALL-JONES ... called the New Zealand strawberry [more commonly called the snowberry or Gaultheria depressa] ... (1971,Mr Surveyor Thomson,61)

All over the spurs and ridges the snowberry (Gaultheria antipoda) was found plentifully, and picked and eaten largely by the party, its delicious coolness being enhanced by the heat of the day. (Feb 17, 1872,Otago Witness,14)

Typical of the sites he surveyed was Macraes Flat, where, in 1986, he noted that porcupine shrubs, snowberry plants and pohuehue vines were stripped of all their ripe fruit where they grew on outcrops inhabited by grand skinks, while plants on nearby outcrops without skinks were untouched. (Jul 2000,NZ Geographic,No. 47/70)

It certainly makes for more interesting walks, when.. you can recognise such delights as ceps, snowberries, or cape gooseberries. (Mar 13, 1993,Otago Daily Times,11)

CAVE & PADDISON Gaultheria. Ericaceae. A genus of 120 species of shrubby plants found mainly in the Americas. There are about 10 New Zealand species, of which all but 1 are endemic. Their common name is snowberry because they bear white to pinkish red fruit. (1999,Gardener's Encyclopedia of New Zealand Plants, The,211)

RILEY The pink, red or white berries of this shrub were gathered in the past by men of the village when larger, more tasty berries were unobtainable. Snowberries are a favourite food of the weka bird, they were also sought by the early sheep musterers and prospectors of Otago in the high country when emergency rations were needed. (1994,Maori Healing & Herbal,322)

WILSON Gaultheria sp. Snowberry... after Gaulthier, French Canadian. (1982,Stewart Island Plants,114)

METCALFE Snowberries are quite edible, although the taste is perhaps somewhat over-rated. In earlier years country people, especially in Otago and Southland, used to gather the fruits and make snowberry pies. (1993,Cultivation of NZ Plants, The,144)

MALCOM, B. & N. Sometimes plants belonging to even different genera can cross - for example, our native Gaultheria, and Pernettya snow-berries cross shamelessly, and only expert field botanists and biochemists can figure out which of the several species in the genus are the parents of the hybrid. (1988,New Zealand's Alpine Plants Inside & Out,105)

SALMON Snowberries belonging to the genera Gaultheria and Pernettyaare found throughout the New Zealand mountains from subalpinbe scrub to the higher herb and fellfields. All species have edible fruits, and records exist of people who have been sustained by eating them. (1992,Alpine Plants of New Zealand (Field Guide),78) [NOTES: 3rd ed. (1st ed. 1968)]

DAWSON Gaultheria depressa var. novae-zelandiae is a prostrate shrub in open places remarkable for its relatively large white, pink or red, berry-like fruits often referred to as 'snow berries'. (1998,Forest Vines to Snow Tussocks,168)

COCKAYNE The Heath Family (Ericaceae) is represented only by the snowberries (Gaultheria and Pernettya). (1967,NZ Plants & Their Story,220) [NOTES: 4th edition]

LAING & BLACKWELL The white fruit of G. antipoda is known as the snowberry in Otago, and is occasionally eaten. Like most of the products of the New Zealand bush, it cannot be recommended to the epicure. (1949,Plants of NZ,344) [NOTES: 5th edition]

THOMSON Masses of flax and speargrass, intermingled with tussac, matagori scrub, snowberry and anise, covered the open ground, and among these grew a profusion of smaller heaths and nerteras, yielding abundant food for birds. Ibid. 212 Kakas were abundant in those days both in the bush and in the open, where they dug at the roots of the speargrass and flax for the larger grubs to be found there, or visited the flax flowers for nectar and the snowberry and ground tutu for their fruit. (1909,NZ Naturalist's Calendar,211)

CROWE Richards describes the fruit of the creeping mountain snowberry as 'edible and rather tasteless.' Earlier travellers, who had perhaps worked up a better appetite, have kinder words for them; J.T. Thomson, while exploring South Otago in 1857, seemed to appreciate the New Zealand strawberry, as he called it, and likens it to the rose apple of India. (1990,Native Edible Plants of NZ,54) [NOTES: 1st ed. 1981]

TAYLOR I was so weak that I thought I must give in, but I ate plenty of the little snow-berries which grow under the snow. They helped us on a good deal, and we reached the top about 2 p.m. [Fn: Gaultheria depressa. (1959,Early Travellers,413)

CROWE I find the flavour of raw snowberries generally sweet and juicy, though later in the season they can be rather dry and tasteless. (1990,Native Edible Plants of NZ,54)

Snowberries (Gaultheria spp) are the most familiar alpine berries, coming in a succulent [47] red, pink or white. Ibid. Snowberry, Gaultheria colensoi, a member of the heath family, is a sprawling, small-leafed shrub found only in the central North Island and Ruahine Ranges. (Sep 2001,NZ Geographic,No. 53/44)

WAITT My great delight was to gather the New Zealand snowberry. This little pure white berry ... the fruit pure as the snow, the leaf and plant like a Scotch blacberry.[sic] (1856,Letter,10) [NOTES: 1856 Waitt Letter to Joseph Thomas 10]

I ate plenty of little snow-berries which grow under the snow. (Jul 2, 1864,Lake Wakatip Mail) [NOTES: 1864 July 2-16 Lake Wakatip Mail (Alphonse Barrington) in Knox Thousand Mountains Shining 202]

snowbird¶

noun.

The white Snow or Icebirds we saw likewise, [[ed. fn] Antarctic Petrel Thalassoica antarctica (Gmelin, 1789).] together with ... the small grey Eggbirds [[ed. fn] Prions, Pachyptila spp.], which some call Sea Snipes (Dec 18, 1772,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/202)

FORSTER We saw Pintadas, Fulmars, Snowbirds & the little grey Eggbird, in great numbers. [ed. fn] Respectively the Cape Pigeon, Antarctic Fulmar, Snow Petrel, and pachyptila spp. (Dec 14, 1772,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/197)

snowbirding¶

noun.

See: cf. snowdropper

MANTELL They kick up a stink if washing's left out overnight. ... There's been a few cases of snowbirding in that area lately. And if the girls lost washing from the lines, the hostel could be culpable. (1980,Murder or Three, A,34)

MANTELL The bottom drawer of the dressing-table was crammed with women's underclothing. ... A few brand new. Others apparently filched from various clothes lines. ... Peacock grimaced. `So what have you got? A repressed old man who's done a bit of snowbirding? ...' (1984,Murder in Vain,84)

snow-board¶

noun.

[NOTES: 1989 Charles Ransom notes: Snow-board - Not found elsewhere, but definition is not very clear -- in any case its application here would be very limited.]

Snow-board- Protective boards fixed on a roof behind a gutter to carry the weight of snow. The snow on melting drips into the gutter through gaps left betwen and under the boards. (1979,SANZ Glossary Building Terminology,105)

snow-cave¶

verb. to use a snow-cave as a base for further mountaineering

In reality of course they were the tracks of another club party who had been `snow caving' near Katie's col. (1948,Canterbury Mountaineer, The,4/18/258)

snow-caver¶

noun. One who excavates a snow cave

We advise future snow-cavers to have the top of the entrance tunnel no higher than the floor of the living space. (Jun 1949,NZ Alpine Journal,13(36) : 93)

snow-caving¶

noun.

The two great advantages of 'snow-caving' are absolute security and adequate comfort. (Jun 1948,NZ Alpine Journal,12(35) : 248)

Although much had been learnt.. in snow caving, the field of the snow house was still open. (Jun 1952,NZ Alpine Journal,14(39) : 363)

[Title] Snow Caving in the La Perouse. (1968,NZ Alpine Journal,00/00)

noun. [Rural] [ high-country ] a steep narrow snow-filled gut between rocks.

HOLDEN In summer the showchute would have been a shingle slide, nothing more than an ugly scar on the mountain face. (1996,Great Hunting Yarns,198)

snowdropper¶

noun. one who steals clothing from a clothesline

See: cf. snowbirding

The constable "spotted" an alleged "snow-dropper" clearing the clothesline at therear of a boarding-house. (Feb 19, 1910,NZ Free Lance,12)

`Snowdroppers' are very active in Auckland at present and the Police today issued a warning to housewives to take in washing at night - or risk finding it gone in the morning. Washing left on lines overnight is being stolen consistently . (Jun 7, 1962,Evening Post,15)

snowed in¶

noun. of the condition when shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table

BOWEN SNOWED IN. Describing the state of affairs when the shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. With a good run shearers can sometimes snow the pressers in. Shearers will be seen at their best when they get ahead of the rest of the shed. They enjoy this snowing in, and usually they make the wool flow faster than ever. (1956,Wool Away!,157) [NOTES: (glossary: Shearing Terms)]

Snowed in: The condition of the sorting table or the shearing board when shearers are working too fast for the shed hands to keep up. (Feb 26, 1965,Listener (New Zealand Listener)) [NOTES: (H.A.L. Laing)]

SNOWED IN: The condition of the table or board when the shearers are working too fast for the shed hands to keep up. (Feb 21, 1968,Straight Furrow,20) [NOTES: [Shearer's language]]

Snowed in: When shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. Also described as woolled-up. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,59)

snowed in: When the shearers get ahead of the men on the wool table and fleeces lie around. (1989,NZ English Newsletter,3/28) [NOTES: (Wallace Shearing Glossary)]

adjective. [Rural] [of a woolshed floor] filled with unrolled fleeces when shearers' work is ahead of shed-hands'.

BOWEN Snowed in. Describing the state of affairs when the shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. (1955,Wool Away!,157)

MAF Snowed-in: when shearers are ahead of the wool table, so that wool is lying around the floor waiting to go on the wool table. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,58)

SQUIRE Snowed in: (woolled up) The condition of the table or the board when shearers are working too fast for shed hands to keep up. [snowed in] (1991,A to Z Glossary of Wool Terms,49)

snowed off, be¶

verb. [Rural] to encounter serious snowy conditions that prevent mustering.

MCMILLAN I went to Glenorchy at the start of the week to muster tall country. When a blizzard blew up we were 'snowed off' the hill. (1981,Tales of the High Country,45)

snow-fence¶

verb.

Newton At one time boundary-keeping after the autumn muster was a major job, but over the years, a big proportion of the block has been snow fenced. (1952,High Country Journey,30)

snowgloo¶

noun.

A.J. Heine's building of a "snowgloo" (a cross between a snow cave and an igloo). (Jun 1952,NZ Alpine Journal,14(39) : 363)

We soon had a comfortable "snowgloo". Inflating my li-lo, I snuggled into my bag. (1958,Tararua,12/66)

snowgrass¶

noun.

There are many less conspicuous snow grasses whose flags don't catch our eye so well. (Aug 27, 1999,Dominion,14)

Pale-green snowgrass and red tussock appear as we pull ourselves up to the peaks of Matanginui and then Maharahara at 1100m. (Dec 20, 2003,Dominion Post,E8)

We followed the saddle towards Balloon over snow grass and most agreeable travel. (Feb 27, 1890,Otago Witness,34)

Stiffer soils.. such as those which produce the large coarse tussock popularly called snow grass, are not good producers of the clovers. (Oct 30, 1890,Otago Witness,17)

There we were, stuck for the night and no more shelter than a snow-grass tussock over us. (Nov 11, 1897,Otago Witness,60)

Snow (sn&omacr.), n. [Add.] Snow grass. (Bot.) (a) A coarse, tall grass of New Zealand (Danthonia Raouli ), persistent through the water. (b) Tussock grass (Poa caespitosa ). (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031)

noun. [Rural] [high country] a tall-growing tussock of Danthonia spp., that can be grazed by sheep when other feed is unavailable.

Cutting snowgrass for thatch. (May 3, 1867,Castle Station Diary) [NOTES: in VANCE (1965) High Endeavour 257]

STUDHOLME The Maori track which led through it to the lake had numerous turns and twists in it to avoid the clumps of snowgrass, manuka and cabbage-trees. (1940,Te Waimate,67)

CONNELL & HADFIELD By a dominant plant is meant that plant in a community which gives the community its characteristic appearance and which may control its structure, e.g. beech in South Island bush, kauri in North Auckland bush, and snow grass in the grassland of the high country in the South Island. (1961,Agriculture,292)

LOUGHNAN snowgrass: big straggly tussocks standing up to four feet high or more and of even greater diameter. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,74)

STACEY With everyone in position we were running through soaking snowgrass trying to muster off as soon as possible. (1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,57)

CURTIS There was a 200 metre band of snowgrass which ran for about two kilometres, in places extending down between scrubby ridges to reach almost the valley floor. (1996,Beneath the Mountain Mist,57)

snowgrass country¶

noun. [Rural] high-country land that grows tussock and can only be grazed in summer.

NEWTON The ridge .. runs to little over 5,000 feet and as it is all open snowgrass country, it is inevitable that the two stations have an annual exchange of stragglers. (1952,High Country Journey,156)

NEWTON Mainly over 3,000 feet, it is primarily red tussock, or snowgrass country, much of it still in its original state. (1969,Big Country of the North Island,139)

MCCASKILL The high-altitude snowgrass country above 4,000 feet occupied about 2,000 acres. (1973,Hold This Land,88)

We came out in the snow-grass country. (Sep 30, 1924,Otago Witness,67)

snowline¶

noun. [Rural] a high country area above which sheep are not grazed in safety except in mid-summer.

ANDERSON In winter the high tops remain permamently snowbound down to a line of about 900 metres; hence the ward `snowline' (1981,Both Sides of the River,8)

ANDERSON A greater number of stations have snowline fences on their winter blocks, ... (1981,Both Sides of the River,8)

CHARLES There's no place I'd rather be,/ Than the top beat/ With a snow-line boundary./ (1981,Black Billy Tea,35)

Snowline.-A correspondent writes: your usage is, of course, different from that of mountaineers, who speak of it as the lower limit of permanent snow in summer.' (Jan 27, 1934,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland]

Mountain peaks and ridges above the snowline. (1915,NZ Geol. Survey Bulletin,No6 (N.S.)/11) [NOTES: (Morgan) The Geology.. of the Buller-Mokihinui Subdivision.Westland]

The grassy downs, the hills from base to snow line clad with various verdure, seem to invite the lowing herds and bleating flocks; ... (Dec 4, 1858,Otago Witness) [NOTES: 1858 Dec 4 Otago Witness in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 9]

BUTLER Here and there at the mouths of the rivers a few flats may exist or rather do exist, but over these rolls upward to the snow line a heaving mass of timber. (Jun 1860,Forest Creek MS,54,1960)

A TRAMP The land ... extends from the snow-line right up to the sleeted peaks (1891,Casual Ramblings,53)

MORRIS Snow-line, n. In pastoralists' language of New Zealand, `above the snow-line' is land covered by snow in winter, but free in summer. (1898,Austral English,425)

PASCOE At one time the Kakapo screamed in the birch country from the sea beach to near the snow line (1957,Mr Explorer Douglas,259) [NOTES: (Birds SW.) c 1899]

The merino occupies and thrives on the wild lands of the colony, from the snow-line to the border of the plains, ... (1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,92)

Snow line.- Roughly the line above which snow lies all the winter and therefore the country above the s.l. is only useful for sheep from October (or even after shearing) until May. (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

The glaciers, in some instances, appear to be considerably lower than the snowline: on the shaded side of Mount Alta, a little below the summit, there is one about five acres in extent, and three feet in thickness. (Jul 26, 1862,Otago Witness,3)

Had it been left to the Motueka public a good track would have been laid out before the snow came to prevent it, and long ere this the track for horses would have been completed up to the snowline, and then finished when the snow cleared off, thus half the work would have been done. (Oct 1, 1870,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,4)

A glacier which has been in descent since first discovered has now nearly reached the timber-line, and we were treated to the singular sight of a large body of ice in midsummer nearly 4000 feet below the snowline. (Mar 4, 1882,Otago Witness,12)

The snowline is very near to the road just here, and the piercing wind of a morning would not give second place even to the "barber" at the Grey. (Jun 23, 1913,Grey River Argus,4)

HENDERSON By the snowline, just above the scrubline, all of a sudden, especially early December, there was a vast sea of mountain flowers ahead. (1984,Tales of the Coast,33)

GORDON Retiring back valleys and land above the snowline (900m or 3,000 ft) is part of a soil conservation scheme to protect mountain lands. (1987,People, Places & Paddocks,179)

~ n.-snow'-line n. in New Zealand, the elevation on the mountains which snow is found in winter but not in the summer. (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,2031)

PYKE The first snow poles were put up on the track from Tuapeka tothe Portuguese' (Captain Macil's) below Miller's Flat; these were only Manuka poles. (1887,History of the Early Gold Discoveries in Otago,106,1962)

Its adaptability was shown by the fact that it grew in sand and dry gravel on the west coast of New Zealand, and at the snowline of the hills near Lake Wanaka. (Jan 24, 1922,Evening Post,6)

Along the snowline between between the Mitre Hut and Mitre Peak, the kit belonging to a missing deerstalker, Mr. H. (Jack) Wilson, was found late yesterday afternoon. (Feb 16, 1945,Evening Post,7)

snowman¶

noun.

MACDONALD All freezing was done for the first ten years [from c1882] by the cold air machines ...[66] The carcases were hung in the chambers, and the cold air was blown through kauri ducts or trunks at a temperature of minus 40[degree sign] Fahrenheit. The carcases, being relatively warmer than the air, always lost moisture to it; this formed snow which blocked the trunks, cutting down the air circulation and giving the `snow-men', who had to crawl through the trunks, a bad time in clearing them. (1957,Canterbury Frozen Meat Company,65)

snow-rake¶

noun.

BURDON an imaginary article The process of extracting sheep [from snow] is known as `snow-raking', and this term gives the old hands an opportunity of playing off an evergreen joke on the new chum. He is advised to get a snow-rake made for himself. (1938,High Country,157)

verb.

verb. [Rural] to clear a track for trapped sheep to move to safety in snowy conditions.

VANCE In 1903 winter dealt a severe blow to the Lilybank flock. During that year Tom Thoms, Peter Pringle, and Godfrey Waters snowraked all of Richmond, then crossed the Macaulay River and snowraked Lilybank. Waters snowraked a mob of twenty double-fleecers out of the high basin at Separation Creek ... (1965,High Endeavour,189)

LOUGHNAN snowrake: to hunt for sheep isolated in deep snow and lead them to safety. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,75)

GORDON In many cases mobs were snow-raked to get them onto the tracks. (1987,People, Places & Paddocks,42)

We aim .. stock on the native hill country .. requiring less time to spot and snowrake. [snowrake] (May 19, 1993,NZ Farmer,15)

Snowrake.- To rescue sheep from snow and bring them to a safer place. Hence s.raker. (C.) (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

snow-raker¶

noun. [Rural] a person involved in tracking down and tramping out sheep buried in snow.

"The hotel, which is situated about three miles from the top of the pass, has for the past week been crowded with travellers who have got so far on their journey into the Mackenzie Country, but at present can go no further: snow-rakers going up in hot haste to some of the back stations, station-owners who have been down-country for the winter anxious to get through and learn the fate of their stock - all waiting for the first opportunity to make a dash over the pass ..." (Jul 22, 1908,Otago Witness,32)

The shepherds, in many instances, go prodding about in the snowdrifts with long poles, after the manner of the kauri gum digger using his spear, and if the pole did not strike the sheep, or the snowraker fall through on top of it, he might very easily walk within a foot of it and be unaware of its presence. (Sep 2, 1908,Otago Witness,24)

The settlers are advertising for snow rakers. (May 14, 1913,Grey River Argus,1)

HOSKEN All of these sheep could have been saved if seen, but drifts of snow covered them and some camps were not found till six weeks later by snowrakers falling into them. (1964,Life on a Five Pound Note,101)

The men asked that musterers should get not less than GBP1 5s a day, as against 12s 6d under the old award; snow-rakers 35s a day, as against GBP1 a day ... (Mar 9, 1920,Ashburton Guardian,6)

Agreement on all points was reached yesterday in the conciliation proceedings connected with musterers, drovers, packers,, [sic] and snow-rakers. (Aug 31, 1939,Evening Post,6)

noun.

See: snow-rake

Little two-seater Robinsons, which some ofthe cockies have, were ferrying snowrakers up to the tops. (Oct 1992,North & South,17)

SHARPE Trudging away from their main track, the snow-rakers packed the snow with their feet into a sort of trail along which sheep could travel. (1962,Country Occasions,177)

snow-raking¶

noun. [Rural] the making of tracks in snow to enable trapped stock to walk out to levels below a snow line.

Musterers to be paid not less than 12s 6d per day if engaged for less than one calendar month, and GBP3 per week if engaged for one month or more, 15s additional for mustering on Sundays; musterers required to do snow-raking to be paid not less than 20s per day ... (Jun 23, 1911,Ashburton Guardian,1)

.. we must admire the fine spirit shown by all engaged in one of the most arduous tasks that sheepmen or novices were engaged in, viz., snow-raking. (Aug 18, 1923,Evening Post,11)

On Morven Hills Station the manager (Mr M'Whirter) is employing numbers of men for snow raking, and has arranged with settlers for temporary paddocking until a thaw comes. (Jul 29, 1903,Otago Witness,30)

A good deal of snow fell in the back country and snow-raking had to be resorted to, but sheep are now safely mustered on to winter country. (Jun 15, 1912,NZ Journal of Agriculture,522)

.. a snow fence, preventing the sheep from drifting up into the higher basins in the late autumn at the time when snow is due, is a valuable means of preventing mortality and the expense of snowraking and mustering. (Feb 20, 1937,NZ Journal of Agriculture,101)

GORDON Snow-raking means slowly tramping, then packing down, a track about a metre deep so that the sheep can be led to safety. (1987,People, Places & Paddocks,42)

BARNES Sheep can get trapped in snow drifts, often buried alive in metres of snow. They have to be rescued. The process is called snow-raking, and it is one of the most soul-destroying, gut-busting jobs in the hugh country. (1987,Country Calendar (TVNZ),116)

KERR Snow raking entails finding mobs, sometimes by spotting steam from the exit hole their breath melts in the highest part of a great cavern of snow, and treading a path out for them. (2000,High Times in the High Country,52)

BARDSLEY We would feed out with hay for them [sheep] there and this meant that we didn't have to do too much snow-raking. (2000,Land Girls, The,43)

Relph He described the difficulties of snow-raking and trying to lead groups of stranded stock down to patches of partially cleared areas on the sunny faces ... (2007,From Tussocks to Tourists,40)

The following winter some shepherds, whilst out snow-raking, found a human skeleton near the site of a prospecting camp on that terrace, and so named it "Dead Man's Flat." (Sep 15, 1894,Star, The,1)

NEWTON Snow-raking: When sheep get held up in heavy snow they often have to be `raked' out onto clear windswept country or down to lower levels. A man has to tramp a track through the snow along which the sheep can follow. This job - snow- raking - is tough, killing work. (1966,Boss's Story, The,189)

`Snow-raking' - that is, taking sheep from high country ... (1907,TrNZI,39/71-89) [NOTES: (Cameron quoted by Benham)]

MOWATT The whole countryside was covered [with snow] to a depth of 18 inches. Snow raking was out of the question as there was no clear ground to which the sheep could be shifted. (Jul 1911,Diary) [NOTES: 1911 July Mowat's Diary in 1969 McCaskill Molesworth 104]

1(b) Any musterer required to do any snow-raking shall be paid not less than 15s. per day while engaged in such work. (1912,Sheepowner's Handbook, The,41) [NOTES: 1912 Canterbury Musterers' and Packers' Award in 1912 The Sheepowners' Handbook 41]

BURDON The process of extracting sheep [from snow] is known as `snow-raking', and this term gives the old hands an opportunity of playing off an evergreen joke on the new chum. He is advised to get a snow-rake made for himself. (1938,High Country,157)

NEWTON I had to spend many hours snow-raking in an attempt to get at least some of the snow-bound sheep down to safety ... (1947,Wayleggo,30)

noun.

The old names for that part of the Southern Alps and foothills which is visible from the plains. The long range of mountains which the inhabitants of Christchurch suppose to be the backbone of the island, and which they call the Snowy Range. All that tract of waste and unappropriated land, formerly in the possession of the New Zealand Company, situated in the Middle Island of New Zealand, being bounded by the Snowy Range of Hills from Double Corner to the River Ashburton, by the River Ashburton from the Snowy Hills to the Sea, and by the Sea from the Mouth of the River Ashburton to Double Corner ... snufflebuster¶

noun. a spoilsport; a fraudulently pious, or overweeningly sanctimonious person. [usually attributed to the Hon. R. Semple, (as snivelling snufflebuster) but earlier used in N.Z. Truth 1905] -->(Perhaps journalistic coinage, or general slang from SNUFFLE + BUSTER (= fellow, `joker') with rhyming and other associations with bluster.

A MEETING of persons interested in forming a 'tea'-total brotherhood, was held last evening at the Ponsonby Hall. There was a large attendance, Mr Snufflebuster being unanimously voted to the chair. (Feb 16, 1889,Observer (Auckland),11)

The word very often used (perhaps invented) by Truth 1905-10 =prohibitionist, wowser' as a derogatory term, and revived in the mid-30's by Hon. R. Semple, Minister of Works, as a picturesque and derogatory term for croaking complainants: -<i>sniffling snufflebusters' became popularly associated with Mr Semple's styles of speech (Aug 19, 1905,NZ Truth,9/1/8)

[A mad parson] thinks ... escorts of angels to attend on the souls of saintly snuffle-busters ... (Aug 19, 1905,NZ Truth,9/1/8)

Prurient Parsonical Parasites. ... A Trinity of Tarnished Tray-trappers ... smug snuffle-busters. (Sep 23, 1905,NZ Truth,14/8/6)

... sanctimonious snuffle-busters. (Jun 1, 1906,NZ Truth,45/4/8)

The object of the Nelson snufflebusters is to stir up strife. (Jul 14, 1906,NZ Truth,56/1/2)

When a cove wanting lodgings advertises himself as a staunch teetotaller, or a Christian young man, it's a sign for the other people in the house he goes to to double lock their belongings. Such snufflebusters arn't [sic] to be trusted worth a crimson anvil. (Aug 4, 1906,NZ Truth,59/1/4)

... our editor does not believe that the snufflebusters will be able to keep him out of Heaven. (Aug 28, 1915,Hutt Valley Independent,5/241/4)

soak¶

noun. [Rural] a sheep dip or bath.

BURDON The soak was a sort of bath .. Soap and sometimes ammonia were added to it. (1938,High Country,83)

CRAWFORD Later the sheep were driven into the 'soak', a sort of bath about 20 feet long by 10 feet wide let into the ground beside a creek. When let out of the soak the sheep were driven on to a platform overhanging the creek. (1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,42)

noun.

See: cf. wash v.

BURDON Washing consisted of two separate operations the first of which was called `soaking' The soak was a sort of bath about twenty feet long by ten wide, let into the ground beside a creek and bricked at the sides to prevent loose earth falling in. It was filled and kept full by water flowing in through a two-inch pipe and a supply of boiling water was kept handy ... Soap and sometimes ammonia were added to it. After the sheep were let out of the soak When soaked and drained the sheep were driven to a creek, tipped in and washed. (1938,High Country) [NOTES: check cite carefully]

CRAWFORD Later [? after washing] the sheep were driven into `the soak', a sort of bath about twenty feet long by ten feet wide let into the ground beside a creek. It was filled and kept full of lukewarm water to which soap and sometimes ammonia were added. (1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,42)

noun. a shower

soaking¶

noun.

BURDON Washing consisted of two separate operations, the first of which was called `soaking'. The soak was a sort of bath ... let into the ground beside a creek ... It was filled and kept full by water flowing in through a two-inch pipe and a supply of boiling water was kept handy ... Soap and sometimes ammonia were added to it. After the sheep were let out of the soak they were driven ... [to] the creek ... tipped in ... and washed clean by men standing in the water. (1938,High Country,83)

soap the geyser¶

[NOTES: includes soft soap, soap, soaping]

SIMPSON An expression in common use Down Under is soap the geyser. A crazy one, surely. It is confined almost exclusively to New Zealand, and its origin is no mystery ... In the Thermal Regions of New Zealand there is a particular geyser that could be made to perform by throwing soap into it, and it was frequently soaped so that it would put up a display for the delight of important visitors. So today, when a New Zealander says, Come on, let's soap the geyser', he meansCome on, let's get going', or `Let's start' (1945,If You'd Care to Know,100)

It would be more appropriate if the laundry whistle was blown when Wairoa geyser was soaped. (Nov 26, 1910,NZ Free Lance,12)

Complaint is made by a correspondent of the Hot Lakes Chronicle against the indiscriminate soaping of the great Wairoa Geyser. The correspondent asserts that, in spite of the well-known fact that the geysers of Yellowstone Park, U.S.A., were almost ruined by too frequently soaping them, the authorities at Rotorua permit the great Wairoa Geyser to be soaped so frequently that from playing from an hour to an hour and a half it has deteriorated into a short action of a few minutes. (May 12, 1903,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

Dr R.W. Raymond read a paper before the late meeting of the Institute of Mechanical Engineers, at Buffalo, on "Soaping Geysers." (Jan 18, 1889,Otago Witness,35)

The problem of bringing about social security has a different background in different countries and is being solved by different methods. It forms a rosette of lanceolate leaves about 6 inches long, with prominent or converging veins, giving the name rib grass' From the rosette rises the slender flower stalk a foot or more in length, with a crowded mass of tiny brown or black flowers at its tip. These names have a bearing on some distinguishing characteristic of the fish. ... The name Soldierfish is derived from the similarities of this fish to the activities of a soldier or picket on sentinel duty. I have often seen Seaperch stand or, rather, rest at attention on its pectoral fins for lengthy periods. When it did move, it moved to the right or to the left with the precision of a well-trained soldier. (1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,344)

there are `social' New Zealand words (solo-parent, ex-nuptial, sole-charge (teacher) and some other educational terms. A few were formerly UK (School Certificate, primer(s), standard(s). solstice¶

noun.

[NOTES: Jim writes: As an attributive, in relation to the winter solstice, this has come into use in NZ recently in compounds such as (winter) solstice carnival, solstice celebration, solstice dinner, solstice party. Any similar usages in the Northern Hemisphere (none are recorded in NSOD or Collins) are likely to relate to the summer solstice, since the winter solstice coincides with Christmas. I havs also seen winter Christmas used in NZ. The development of "solstice" terms might usefully be watched.]

sooling¶

noun.

SUTHERLAND Although inadvertently administered, Angus had been under the influence of sool,' which gave him an unfair advantage over an enemy who was, for the moment, peaceably inclined. Bill had been the victim of an illegal attack. The New Zealand Standards Institute doesn't mention the wordsool' in its code of by-laws. Perhaps it is too simple. Officialdom does things the hard way. It is to be forbidden,' says the Institute,in any public place, to set on, urge, encourage, aid or assist any dog to rush at, attack or worry any person or animal.' This would seem to include baiting, egging, sooling and/or sic-ing, though not specifically mentioned. (1953,Golden Bush, The,122,1963)

sooner¶

noun. [Rural] a lazy dog that would sooner lie in the sun than work [or would sooner have its owner do the work.]

SINCLAIR I went up to Ngamatea Station in the spring with a large team of useless 'sooners' except for one handy dog of great ability, named Wonk. ibid. 95 King was a great dog behind sick or slow sheep on a muster, giving them all the time in the world. In fact, while he waited for a seedy sheep to catch up to the string, he'd look like a proper old sooner. (1973,Boot in the Stirrup,46)

STACEY Because I had no dog I had to use a pot-licking sooner belonging to the boss. (1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,40)

GORDON While we're dealing with the lesser lights of the working dog world, there is also the 'sooner', a slack and useless critter which would sooner lie in the shade. (1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,87)

Dogs of every breed, or any breed, "sooners" and others who have as much pedigree as a chicken raised in an incubator, are permitted to roam on the beaches and swim - the latter when some crank throws a stone or a piece of wood in and tells his puerile pup to "fetchit" - where little children are endeavouring to have the time of their lives. (Sep 9, 1922,NZ Truth,1)

noun. [Rural] (rare) a horse that is reluctant to work.

noun.

Sooner.-Slack, useless dog. So called because he would s. lie in the shade than work. I have also heard Sunday -dog used as an equivalent, because one day's work a week is enough for him. (Jan 27, 1934,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland]

McLEOD Another word for a lazy dog is a `sooner' which is intended to convey that he would sooner you ran than he did. (1951,High Country,43)

noun.

South Island kokako¶

The South Island kokako is said to have been extinct for the past 30 years, although "missing in action" may be a better description as there have been plenty of tantalising clues to suggest that the bird still exists... the South Island kokako is, or was, about the size of a magpie, with steel-grey plumage and distinctive coloured wattles at the base of its beak. It is a distinct subspecies from its North Island neighbour, which has blue wattles and had avoided extinction thanks to a determined effort by the Department of Conservation. Numerous people have reported hearing the southern kokako, with at least one unofficial sighting, in 1996,near the Glenroy River. (Jul 20, 2002,Listener (New Zealand Listener),66)

south-easter¶

noun. used specifically in various places: e.g. Picton, Canterbury

See: cf. southerly buster

ANGAS The position of the harbour of Port Nicholson, at the south-eastern entrance of Cook's Straits, is open to the heavy gales that frequently blow from that quarter in the winter season : between the high lands that rise on each side of the entrance to the harbour, the wind, at such seasons, rushes in, as through a funnel, with unrelenting fury. These `south-easters,' as they are termed [in Picton], generally continue two or three days, the storm being at its [243] height on the second day. (1847,Savage Life,1/242)

This wind is similar to the well-known `south-easter' of New Zealand, which, here, tends up with the land, and so has a south westerly direction (Jul 5, 1851,Lyttelton Times,7) [NOTES: [Canterbury: see notes 2 rev. and 3.]]

ANGAS The position of the harbour of Port Nicholson, at the south-eastern entrance of Cook's Straits, renders it exposed to the heavy gales that at certain times blow from that quarter during the winter season. ... the wind, on such occasions, rushes in, as through a funnel, ... These `south-easters' generally last two or three days, and blow with such terrific violence that no communication can be held [111] with the shipping at anchor in the bay; ... (1866,Polynesia,110) [NOTES: (Wellington)]

southerly buster¶

noun. ? orig Canterbury, but general South Island and Cook Strait. see esp. buster, and see butt=ender; see also south-easter, souther, southern buster, sou'west buster, threeday sou'wester Acland's note and description (1933) applies (also CR. 68): A strong wind with rain, snow or sleet from a southerly direction. The ordinary man in the paddock in Canterbury recognises only three winds: East (from N.E.), sou'wester (from S.E., S. etc, S.W. etc), and nor'wester. As a matter of fact a three-day so'wester usually only lasts two and a half. They are said to be less fierce than in the early days, just as the nor'wester is said to have been softened by the planting on the plains. It may be so in Christchurch ; but I cannot say I notice any difference up-country. The nor' wester may come from any where between due north and due west. In such places as Hororata, where the wind can get at you between two gorges a distinction is made between a Waimakariri and a Rakaia nor' wester; but both are called nor' westers.

[NOTES: Empty but for the note under definition]

noun. [Rural] a cold wind from the south, usually bringing stormy rain, sleet and snow.

[NOTES: also southerly burster, rarely southern burster]

BARR At two o'clock a big southerly busterswished up from the south. (1908,With the British Rugby team,36)

...[The term] is not exclusive to New Zealand. Nor are "southerly busters" - known in Australia as "southerly bursters", please note - or "downbursts", which are nasty downdraughts of wind. (Jun 23, 2002,Sunday Star Times,A6)

southerly buster n. a violent and sudden squall from the south. [corrupt. fr. buster] (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,3)

southerly buster ... An old name for a fierce storm from a southerly direction in both Australia and New Zealand. (1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),55)

buster, southerly n. sudden and violent squall from South particularly in Sydney [orig. burster]. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),5)

Reference had been made to "southerly busters" as being the most dangerous winds as far as navigation in Cook Strait was concerned. (Feb 18, 1921,Evening Post,7)

The order of the day has been for some time past rain; rainbows and southerly bursters, yet there has been nothing but what might have been expected in the midst of winter thus far south, and especially as Port Cooper is the channel for South winds over the Isthmus of Banks Peninsula. (Jul 4, 1851,Australian & NZ Gazette,30/483) [NOTES: (Christchurch)]

BUTLER It is curious to watch the battle between the north-west and south-east wind, as we often see it. ... The southerly `burster', as it is called, gradually creeps up, and at last drives the other off the field. A few chilly puffs, then a great one, and in a minute or two the air becomes cold, even in the height of summer. (1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,8/123)

Southerly burster, - buster.- Three-day Sou'Wester. A strong wind with rain, snow or sleet from a southerly direction. The ordinary man in the paddock in Canterbury recognises only three winds: east (from NE), sou'-wester (from SE, S etc, SW, etc.) and nor'-wester. As a matter of fact a t.d.sw .' usually only lasts two and a half. They are said to be less fierce than in the early days, just as the nw. is said to have been softened by the planting on the plains. It may be so in Christchurch but I cannot say I notice any difference up country. The nw . may come from any where between due north and due west. In such places as Hororata, where the wind can get at you down two gorges, a distinction is made between a Waimakariri and a Rakaia nw; but both are called nws . `Where six-days a week the gale/ Laden thick with rain or [hail] First from sou'-west blows a piercer/ Then veers nor'-west and blows fiercer.' (C.RH., p. 68.) (Dec 2, 1933,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

The fact is that the houses ... are by no means proof against the winds, so when a `Southerly Buster' comes, you cannot keep a candle alight. (1852,Australian & NZ English [TS],72/250,1853) [NOTES: (Christchurch)]

In Cook's Straits, the southerly gales commence with great force about ten o'clock in the morning, increasing in violence until they terminate in gales, accompanied by squalls, raising heavy seas in the channel, which are further augmented as the opposing tide takes place towards sunset, the violence of the gale then subsides, and within an hour after the disappearance of the great luminary a perfect calm prevails, which generally continues during the night, and the following morning until about nine o'clock, when the same warring of the elements is repeated.
