Southern Alps¶

noun. the main range of the South Island

It was for a long time believed that a practicable inland communication between the northern end of this island and the country to the southward did not exist, and that the rugged Kaikoras [sic] formed a barrier from the sea on the east coast, to the great chain of Southern Alps which crown the west coast of the island from its northern to its southernmost end. (Jun 5, 1852,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,58)

The Southern Alps in the Middle Island, form such a prominent feature in the landscape, that even the uncsientific traveller, when he passes along the west coast, cannot but admire their wild and fantastic forms, clad in a garment of snow, and standing boldly against the deep blue sky of New Zealand. (Nov 6, 1861,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,4)

Resuming our journey we came into view of Mount Aspiring, the Matterhorn of the Southern Alps, with its miles of snow and ice-fields glistening in the sunlight, and a little further on lay Pembroke and Lake Wanaka. (Feb 1, 1900,NZ Illustrated Magazine,27)

The foregoing is the title of an exhaustive paper written by Dr Teichelmann, which appears in the New Zealand Graphic Christmas number, with numerous illustrations from photographs taken by the Doctor on his annual mountaineering trips. The author's purpose is chiefly to show that the approach to the Southern Alps from the West Coast side is through more interesting country than from the Eastern side, and that the route is most accessible. (Oct 20, 1904,West Coast Times,2)

At last we landed on a rather muddy and very steep bank, and I almost forgot, in my eagerness to gain a firm footing, that I was indeed on Mount Cook, the monarch of the Southern Alps. (Dec 23, 1890,Otago Witness,37)

THE ARTHUR'S PASS TUNNEL. SOME PARTICULARS.This great work, of which all New Zealanders are justly proud, is to penetrate the Southern Alps under the 'Arthur's Pass Coach Road." [sic] (Jan 20, 1910,Grey River Argus,1)

THE MANAPOURI ALPSCATHEDRAL RANGE ASCENDED..[The Cathedral Peaks are a range on the northern side of Lake Manapouri, and although they are not so lofty as the main chain of the Southern Alps, their exceedingly precipitous character makes them so formidable to the tourist that an ascent has very seldom been attempted ...] (Jan 9, 1915,Ashburton Guardian,2)

IT is not everyone who is privileged to have some portion of the country named after him, but such has been the reward of Arthur Dudley Dobson, civil engineer and pioneer, of Canterbury, after whom Arthur's Pass was named. Mr. Dobson was the first man to traverse the narrow by-pass which gives access from the Canterbury Plains to the narrow productive strip of Westland lying to the west of the Southern Alps. (May 9, 1929,NZ Truth,6)

Southern Alps gecko¶

noun. abundant in inland South Island, mottled grey brown gecko.

[NOTES: Hoplodactylus "Southern Alps"]

The Southern Alps gecko (left) had a more restricted habitat being found predominantly under rocks on scree and inside crevices in rock outcrop and bluff systems. (Apr 5, 2005,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.spbl.co.nz/site/selwyn/files/PDF's/Newsletters/FSC%20Newsletter%20No.%205.pdf]

Two types of gecko are also found in the Mackenzie Basin. The Southern Alps gecko (,i>Hoplodactylus aff. maculatus 'Southern Alps') lives near rocky outcrops, screes, boulder banks and rock tumbles. The jewelled gecko (Naultinus gemmeus) lives in forest and shrubland. (2009,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://doc.org.nz/publications/getting-involved/students-and-teachers/themes/river-life/lizards/]

Most specimens of Southern Alps gecko are readilydistinguished by the combination of small adult size(i.e. 53-60 mm SVL) and a short, tapering distalphalange. In addition, the markings tend to be verydrab, and often include pinkish tones. (Jan 2006,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/otagogeckosa.pdf]

southern Buller's albatross¶

noun. [Environment] Thalassarche bulleri, Buller's albatross

See: Buller's albatross

In keeping with their commanding presence on the wing, on land southern Buller's albatrosses possess an aristocratic mien. Like several other species small albatross (also known as mollymawks) they have dark shadows under their brows, a crescent of dazzling white feathers behind the eyes, subtle shadings of grey over the head and neck and bright slabs of yellow in the bill. The southern Buller's albatross, Thalassarche bulleri, breeds only on the Snares and Solander Island, off the south Fiordland coast, while a closely related species, the northern Buller's albatross, has its breeding headquarters on the Chatham Islands. (Jan 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 61/23)

Henceforward, echoed the <i>Colonial Gazette</i>,the humbug treaty of Waitangi' would be `very properly laid on the shelf'. span-'em¶

SUTTON-SMITH In the nineteenth century the ring game seems to have been the most popular marble game. (In more recent years marble games with holes have had the greater role.) There was Big Ring, in which a circle a yard or more in diameter was drawn on the ground; there was the mullibar variation, in which an outsize taw was catapulted amongst the marbles in this circle. There were Little Ring, Liney, Follows, Follow the Taw, Holey, and then, on a less important scale, Butcher's Board, in which the marbles were bowled through the holes in a board, Eye-Drop, Knock-Backs, Leggings-Out (or Leggin's-Out), Span-'Em, and Backits. The last was more usually a girls' game. (1972,Folkgames of Children,174)

spang-weazling¶

noun.

Perhaps the most intriguing game of this nature [sc. tormenting insects or animals] is Spang Weazling'. This game was played at Denniston in 1930-35. A crawley was placed on the end of a stick the middle section of which lay balanced over a stone. Before the crawley could crawl off the stick a stone had to be thrown onto the other end of the stick so as to catapult the crawley off the stick and over the cliff. A variation of the same game was being played at Denniston when I visited there in 1949. It was called alternativelyHit the Crawley' or `Strike the Crayfish'. In this version the other end of the stick was hit with a batting stick (as in Tip Cat) and when the crawley was catapulted into the air it was hit again with the bat. (1953,Unorganized Games,1/406)

Some years ago there was a game among boys [?in Dunedin] called spangweaselling' - taking kingfishers' nests with the young birds in them and knocking them to bits in the air. <i>(Aug 2, 1965,TV1</i>) [NOTES: 1965 Aug 2 WNTV1Any Questions' (P. Smithell, Dunedin) [spg SPANGWEASELING]]

SUTTON-SMITH There are games recorded in this period for which there is no record before 1900 though they may well have existed under other names. est Coast: Dunk and Davey, Spang Weazling; Wellington: Who Goes Round My Stone Wall, Beg o' My Neighbor, Bellahonie, Run a Mile, On and Off the Bridge, Here Come Two Nuns, Colours, Isaac and Rebecca. Scrag, Diabolo, Bumble Puppy, Homai, Fives; Auckland: My Fair Young Lady, Rushes and Reeds, Surrender the Tower, Walls, Ball Hopscotch, ball games, Solomon Says; Hawkes Bay: Wolf Wolf Go Home, Homai; Canterbury: Poor Old Tom, Rats and Rabbits and Rips, Steps, Skin the Snake, Steal a Peg, Toodle-em-Buck, The Gag; Golden Bay: Who's That Walking Round My House Tonight, I've Come to See Poor Mary Jane, Steps and Stairs, Creeping, Branding, O'Leary; Otago: Sir Roger de Coverley, Who's That Knocking at My Door. (1981,History of Children's Play,231)

Spaniard¶

noun. [Rural] a sharp-spiked native plant of spp. Aciphylla that grows in high tussock country.

See: giant Spaniard, bloody Spaniard, wild Spaniard

[NOTES: also wild Spaniard]

W.H.S. ROBERTS Writing of the Waimea Plain in 1856: - The ground was well grassed, but the speargrass was too plentiful. The pasturage was very good. There was a good deal of scrub in the bends of the Mataura known aswire plant' (Olearia virgata). There were also manuka and koromiko. Maori-heads, a kind of grass tree about three feet high, abounded in the swamps, and in some we saw toitoi grass and raupo. We did not pass any cabbage trees to-day ... we proceeded slowly through tomatakuru scrub, speargrass, Spaniard, snowgrass, and other native grasses ... we camped in a bend with good feed at the Elbow and a swamp on one side. Maori cabbage abounded ...' (1856,Diary) [NOTES: 1856 W.H.S. Roberts Diary in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 18]

PAUL Aciphylla squarrosa spaniard (1857,Letters from Canterbury, NZ) [NOTES: (And)]

THOMSON A new plant appeared here, allied to the cactus, and colonially termed a `Spaniard' It has stout blades with sharp points. (1857,Southern Districts of Otago,311)

BUTLER ... the sluggish creeks and swampy ground thickly overgrown with Irishman, snow grass and Spaniard ... which extend on either side of the river for half a mile or more. ... I will now return to the subject of wild Irishman and wild Spaniard. The former is a thorny tree growing with ungainly unmanageable boughs sometimes as large as our own hawthorn trees ... (Jun 1860,Forest Creek MS,40,1961)

BUTLER [Wild plants] are few, and decidedly ugly. There is one beast of a plant they call spear grass or spaniard, which I will tell you more about another time. (Mar 24, 1860,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,4/49)

BUTLER The Spaniard (spear-grass or bayonet-grass) `piked us intil the bane... (May 1860,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,5/72)

HAAST After crossing a small stream ... we arrived at such an impenetrable thicket of Wild Irishman' andSpaniards', that ... we had at last to give up the attempt with ... hands and faces covered with blood. (1848,Julius Von Haast,210) [NOTES: 1862 Mar 31 Von Haast in 1848 Von Haast Julius Von Haast 210]

VON HAAST ... the gigantic Aciphylla Colensoi, the Spaniard or Bayonet-grass. (1862,Geology of Westland,25) [NOTES: [check against 1879 cit???]]

TAYLOR In the Middle Island ... a great proportion of the land ... is one grand plain of shingle scarcely covered with soil, and only supporting grass ... much inferior to that of the North Island, filled also with spiny bushes of the Tumatakura, and that singular family of plants, the Acifolia Taramea, commonly called Spaniards; . (1868,Past and Present of NZ,202)

KENNAWAY ... we struck up ... towards the [Canterbury] mountains, the country being all level ... with a strong growth of coarse tussocks, pampas-grass, snow-grass (similar to the pampas, but having a deep red tinge in the blade) and spaniard or spear-grass ... (1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,40)

HAAST Our road lay now ... across a grassy flat, mostly overgrown with the same dense vegetation met with on the banks of all our river-flats, namely the spiny Wild-Irishman, and the bayonet-like Spaniard (Aciphylla Lyallii). (1879,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,124)

[Fantastic names of plants] show the imagination running riot; they seem appropriate, though often it is impossible to give any definite reason for the name. ... Spaniard' [likeWild-Irishman' is] another name of unexplained origin. There seems even less connection between the human Spaniard and the vegetable spaniard than between the human wild Irishman and the vegetable wild-irishman; and the conjectured corruption spine-yard', whilst improbable, is no more improbable than the fabledBill's-yard' as the origin of `billiard' (1926,TrNZI,663) [NOTES: Andersen Pop. Names]

Spaniard, speargrass.- Various species of Aciphylla. Plants with stiff sharp leaves like rapiers growing out thickly in all directions from the ground. They were thickest in the hills, but there were plenty on the plains before they were ploughed. Horses avoid them carefully, which makes riding through them unpleasant. There are stories of men falling off and landing on one. Shepherds use the flower stalks for torches when burning. In the 'eighties and 'nineties at Mount Peel they used to all the broader leaved sort Spaniards and the narrower Speargrass; but most people use both names indiscriminately. spawn¶

noun.

WEEKES A very strange appearance presented itself in the water this morning - streaks of a muddy yellow colour extending for miles. Supposing it to be caused by animalculae I had a bucketful drawn on deck. The water was full of them, having a transparent body with a row of yellow spots round the head. They had long tentaculae, and moved briskly through the water backwards, which motion was effected by ejecting water from two openings situated at the base of the tentaculae. These creatures are generally called [32] `spawn' by sailors; being by them considered the spawn of fish and the food of whales. W.H.S. ROBERTS Writing of the Waimea Plain in 1856: - The ground was well grassed, but the speargrass was too plentiful. The pasturage was very good. There was a good deal of scrub in the bends of the Mataura known aswire plant' (Olearia virgata). There were also manuka and koromiko. Maori-heads, a kind of grass tree about three feet high, abounded in the swamps, and in some we saw toitoi grass and raupo. We did not pass any cabbage trees to-day ... we proceeded slowly through tomatakuru scrub, speargrass, Spaniard, snowgrass, and other native grasses ... we camped in a bend with good feed at the Elbow and a swamp on one side. Maori cabbage abounded ...' (1856,Diary) [NOTES: 1856 W.H.S. Roberts Diary in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 18]

BUTLER There were a few scrubby stony flats covered with Irishman and speargrass (Irishman is the unpleasant thorny scrub which I saw going over the hill from Lyttelton to ChristChurch) on either side of the stream; ... [ed fn to 1964 edn ed Brassington and Maling : Matagowry (Discaria Toumatou) and Spaniard (Aciphylla Colensoi). (1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,4/54) [NOTES: 1860 Mar 24 in 1863 Butler First Year iv/54]

LINDSAY The larger species [of Aciphylla] are familiar to the settlers as Spear-grass', orBayonette-grass', Wild' orBloody-Spaniard', [bloody =?] in allusion to their very rigid, strong, poniard-like, sharp-pointed leaves ... Hence a Spear-grass Scrub' on the hill ranges is frequently most formidable ... to men and horses, though it forms one of the favourite hunting grounds of the Wild Pig. In the Matukituki Valley,Bayonette-grass' forms an undergrowth in a dense scrub of prickly thorn ... (1868,Contributions to NZ Botany,49)

MORRIS Speargrass, n. name given to several grasses whose spear-like seeds spoil the wool of sheep, but which are yet excellent forage/plants. They are - (1) all the species of Stipa; (2) Heteropogon contortus, Roem. and Schult., and others (see quotations); (3) and in New Zealand, one or two plants of the umbelliferous genus Aciphylla; also called Spaniard (q.v.). (1898,Austral English,427)

LEE Journey From Nelson to Port Cooper (1851,Journey From Nelson to Port Cooper) [NOTES: 1851 EJ Lee Journey From Nelson to Port Cooper in Paul Letters from Canterbury 108 (in 1940 McIntosh Marlborough 125)]

(Dec 1851,Australian & NZ Gazette,55/393) [NOTES: [see Spaniard]]

The gradual replacement of the spaniard (Aciphylla colensoi, Hook. f.) by self-sown pasturage-plants is most remarkable. ... The common spear-grass (A. squarrosa, Forst.) is often displaced in the same way. (1895,TrNZI,28/19)

VON HAAST ... plants like the alpine spear-grass, Aciphylla Monroi, ... found near the summit of Mount Torlesse, could here be collected. (1948,Julius Von Haast,442) [NOTES: 1865 Von Haast in 1948 Von Haast Julius Von Haast 442]

Spec home builders.. are also beginning to show an interest in sections again. (Sep 1, 1922,Evening Post,13)

noun.

special¶

noun. a special constable in the NZ Wars

MORGAN [The beasts] were taken away for a better purpose, vis.[sic], to feed the `specials' at the Mauku stockade. (Sep 9, 1863,Journal,77,1963)

Jeremiah, it appeared, had put his dirty policemen on full duty that night, and assisted by six specials, they patrolled most part of the night. (Dec 13, 1862,Taranaki Herald,4)

noun. any of the rural recruits sworn in to control urban strikers, especially in the 1913 labour troubles (collectively also called Massey's Cossacks q.v.)

[NOTES: ?dateline -->in the 1932 riots We didn't know what a `Specials' were, but up and down Queen St were groups of men wearing white arm-bands and carrying clubs.]

FRASER Many were under 21, and joined the 'Specials' for the lark and the baton. (1952,Ungrateful People,46) [NOTES: Pagination from 1985 edition.]

BOOTH The Specials! The hatred was still heavy in my father's voice when he talked about them 40 years later... For my father none of that erased Freyberg's part as a Special who volunteered to battle the workers. (1997,Deadline : My Story,28)

BODDY & MATTHEWS Some of the unhappy 'specials', nursing batons completely unloaded, were viewing pictures in the Drill hall, and made no secret of the fact that they found it all very tame. (1991,Disputed Ground,272)

During the day the "specials" sanded the waterfront streets for the benefit of their mounts. (Nov 17, 1938,NZ Observer,10)

HYDE In a theatre, a suave `special' came on at the interval of an amateur first night ... to request the audience not to go out at the moment. (1934,Journalese,60)

HYDE 1913 brought Prime Minister Bill Massey's cockits [sic = cockies?) riding into town - strike-breakers armed with pick-handles ... On the other hand, if one of the `cocky' specials fell among strangers ... he might be wary of the boots that [52] would as soon kick in a strike-breaker's head as not. (1936,Passport to Hell,51)

LAWLOR I found myself mixed up with a violent mob intent on doing harm to the "specials". (1935,Confessions of a Journalist,20)

HYDE not intended `Back in 1913, I did time for crowning a special that cracked my mate in the great strike. (1938,Nor the Years Condemn,171)

FRASER Forty-five people were charged as a result of the riots, including one special constable. He was acting as a special,' </i>said the police in evidence,<i>and had a rifle on his shoulder and a baton in his hand.' (1952,Ungrateful People,48) [NOTES: [In 1932 15 April ?NZ Herald]]

There are those who remember him [Tregear] during the 1913 strike standing with blazing eyes in Cuba Street and shaking his fists at the mounted specials' shouting:Go home! Go home, you - scabs!' (Feb 1953,Here & Now,14)

SINCLAIR .. a rioter running up a back street, screaming hysterically, TheSpecials' are coming!' ... There was rioting and looting in Auckland and Wellington, ugly scenes elsewhere. `Special police' were enrolled. ... The Government passed repressive legislation annulling the traditional safeguards of personal liberty. (1959,History of New Zealand,250)

McLENAGHAN I got mixed up in a stoush up the street with the police, and the specials. (1976,Travelling Man,152)

PUGSLEY ... Massey started enrolling 2000 special constables from the country districts [to counter wharf strikes in 1913]. ... Massey's Specials' were largely Territorial Force. ... They rode in asMassey's Cossacks' (1984,Gallipoli: the New Zealand Story,43)

OWEN & PERKINS (George Davies, Wellington) [caption] Strikers scattering as mounted specials' (Massey's Cossacks') gallop up Featherston Street during the General Strike of 1913. (1986,Speaking for Ourselves,102)

SCOTT Violet Helen ... married Douglas Cromwell Snelling of Maungaturoto, farmer, Boer War veteran and leader of a group of mounted specials who rode to Auckland to break the 1913 waterfront strike. (1987,Seven Lives on Salt River,84)

An unaccompanied special, on foot, was suddenly aware of a man darting out from behind a bridge and hissing "Scab" at him. (Dec 6, 1913,NZ Observer,5)

...the influx of uuntrained special constables was inflaming the strikers and the wider population. The "specials", many of them city businesmen as well as farmhands, signed on for duty at the Town Hall and were issued with wooden batons. (Nov 15, 2003,Dominion Post,E15)

This scheme required less than half the force of mounted "specials". Ibid. 25 There has been such a rush of farmers to act as "specials" that the authorities have had to refuse applications for the present. (Nov 13, 1908,Auckland Weekly News,21)

special claim¶

noun.

Some important legislative proposals are put forward in the Mining Amendment Bill brought down by Governor's Message in the House of Representatives yesterday. .. Where gold is associated with other metals or minerals, a special claim may be granted, and the holders of the claim will be entitled to all metals or minerals within the boundaries of the claim. (Aug 19, 1910,Evening Post,4)

What is a special claim? One would consider it was an extended area, granted as a reward to persevering men who have succeeded in finding probable gold-producing quartz in places in which it was not generally known to exist. (Nov 26, 1869,West Coast Times,3)

A public meeting will be held at the Miners' Institute, Callaghan's, on Monday evening next, "to consider the proposal to cancel the special claim of the United Gold Mining Company, Callaghan's." This claim adjoins the Long Tunnel Claim, and the Company is on the eve of being floated. (Jul 10, 1875,West Coast Times,2)

Sir,- In the up-country mining districts I notice that there are several applications for special claims for working old ground, &c., to consist of 100 acres. If these applications are granted it will mean the locking up and leaving unprospected for many years of vast areas of ground, and will cause incalculable injury to prospectors, miners, and the public generally. (Jan 26, 1895,Thames Star,3)

An application was heard for the cancellation of the Great Western special claim. It was defended by the company, who contended that no provision is made in the Mines Act or regulations thereunder for hearing such application, the regulations applying only to leases. (Oct 3, 1885,Otago Daily Times,2)

Great praise is also due to the "specials" for the prompt manner in which they answered to the call ... (Jan 31, 1849,New Zealand Spectator & Cook's Strait Guardian,3)

The word was out for student volunteers to assist the police as special constables. ..Mulgan was back early the next morning, when the 'specials' were lined up on the tennis courts outside the common room. (2003,Long Journey to the Border,63)

noun. see pink v. 1982 cit.

special for/to you Kiwi¶

phrase. ca1940 on, a catchphrase among NZ soldiers in Egypt, later becoming general . From Egyptain pimps' promises to attract brothel custom `Special to you Kiwi. Very clean. Very hygiene' Used humorously to pass off a personal favour etc

special vote¶

noun. a vote cast at a parliamentary election otherwise than at a polling place in the voter's own electorate on election day, by a voter whose name is on a printed electoral roll.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes : the term was introduced in 1956 (now Electoral Act 1993) and includes votes cast before polling day, overseas votes and votes at polling places outside the home electorate. Similar arrangemnents in other countries appear to have different names. Also special (elliptical)]

So, if the specials split our way, there is the possibility of another list seat. (Dec 6, 1999,Dominion,1)

We have polling places and polling booths, although the term polling booth is often used loosely to encompass also both polling places and what the Electoral Act calls 'inner compartments' where the voter marks the ballot paper. (Jan 1999,NZWords,2)

"Hibs has never been what I would regard as a special-character school and that is relatively simple: it was set up to be an elite school and the Christian bit of it, compared to other integrated schools, is very light." This gold is supposed to have come down the main creek, and not from the Driving creek, from which all the specimen gold has been obtained. (Aug 5, 1862,Colonist (Nelson),2)

Some excellent specimen stone was broken out last night and this morning. (Mar 7, 1872,Evening Post,3)

In Ohinemuri ... where even the best ore carried but a few ounces of gold to the ton, instead of as at the Thames,specimen stone' valued at ounces to the pound. (1912,NZ Geol. Survey Bulletin,No 15 (N.S.)/7) [NOTES: (Waiki-Tairua) Bell and Fraser]

speculator¶

[NOTES: a risky, spur-of-the moment kick with (or at) the ball.]

Evenson had stopped one hot St. Jamesrush by a "speculator" to touch. (Jun 17, 1912,Dominion,6)

Amongst the known kinds of plants are common and rough Bindweed, Nightshade and Nettles, both which grow to the size of small trees; a shruby [sic] Speedwell [fnf Veronica. [ed. [Hebe sp.]]] found near all the Beeches, Sow thistles, Virgins Bower, ... (Feb 1777,Cook's Journals) [NOTES: 1777 Feb Anderson's Journal in Cook Journals (1967) 3/804-805 (Queen Charlotte Sound)]

The Newton backs.. took on a great risk by the number of "speculators" they indulged in. (Jun 4, 1904,NZ Observer,10)

When Hutt attempted to clear with a long speculator Kenny picked up the ball and coolly kicked a field goal. (May 31, 1947,Sports Post,15)

Shortly after Robinson gained ground with a solo speculator attack. (Apr 26, 1947,Sports Post,15)

speculator ... 2. Rugby random forward kick (1985,Collins Compact Dictionary,465) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.; nf. 1986 NZPOD]]

A loose Auckland rush.. threatened the Otago defence, but Dickinson misjudged a speculator. (Aug 24, 1922,Auckland Weekly News,54)

speed¶

noun. class; reputation; way of doing things

NEWBOLD SPEED (n) Class, reputation, way of doings [sic] things. (1982,Big Huey, The,254)

speed cop¶

noun. traffic officer

[NOTES: 1942 see quot. bluey n.]

speed counter¶

noun. the fast checkout counter in a supermarket

Have you noticed how the numbers have increased at speed counters in supermarkets? Ten items of less ... 15 ... Now it's 18... Anyway at the speed counter the other day someone next to me said, "I know you."... By now he was up to item 29, the barcode reader running hot. Speed counter? (Apr 23, 2000,NZ Catholic,8)

speed moll¶

noun. a female drug addict

[NOTES: mole for moll below]

'And there was no shortage of the stuff, given to him.. by a grateful and thankfully nameless biker who had received a handed down girl already attracted to the substance. These girls are known in the trade as 'speed moles' and are flicked around quite casually among the drug fraternity. (Jun 2002,Lucid,No. 9 : 18)

speed wobbles¶

noun. unsteadiness or uncertainty caused by rapid progress or change (especially political or economic change)

[NOTES: first used by Prime Minister Geoffrey Palmer of the Labour government's reforms in the 1980s]

[Hdg] Full-steam ahead on policy but not a speed in sight. Anyone familiar with New Zealand politics in the 1980s will be amused to see that Sir Geoffrey Palmer is dusting off his famous warning about speed wobbles. (Feb 21, 2000,Dominion,2)

Jim Anderton himself used the word "breathtaking" to describe the speed with which Cabinet is overturning the previous policy. "Speed wobbles" - a phrase used by the former Labour Prime Minister Sir Geoffrey Palmer to describe the dizzy pace of the Lange-era reforms - is another term that comes to mind (Dec 23, 1999,Evening Post,4)

There is evidence of a speed wobble in gay literature. (Jan 15, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),43)

There is evidence of a speed wobble in gay literature when a writer as immensely urbane and literate as Alan Hollinghurst loses his grip and produces, in The Spell, a book that fails to combine the manners of high art and the ways of the consumer evolution coming from below. (Jan 15, 2000,Listener (New Zealand Listener),43)

The Clark government is far from falling apart, but its frenetic pace has given it a dose of the speed wobbles too... Her implication that opposition MPs need her approval before talking to members of friendly foreign governments was unworthy of her and seemed a case of opening the mouth before engaging the brain, a sure sign of the speed wobbles. (Apr 2000,North & South,98)

The report was headed that speed wobbles were a worry for the council. (Nov 28, 1996,City Voice,21)

An equally astute Simon Kilroy in the Dominion gave the Bolger administration a serious case of speed wobbles with his analysis of the options. (1995,Paradise Conspiracy, The,267 or 275) [NOTES: Check page number]

If Meikle [sc. a restauranteur] is getting speed wobbles, he is not showing it. (May 24, 1997,Listener (New Zealand Listener),36)

President Michelle Boag, in trying to fit out a turbo charged vehicle to compete with Labour in this year's election race, has a nasty case of the speed wobbles. (May 19, 2002,Sunday Star Times,C9)

They [sc. the Government]had the speed wobbles. (Jun 2, 2000,Radio NZ / National Radio,Al Morrison on Morning Report)

[Lange] brought the economy from closedshop through speed wobbles, to skidmarks. (Feb 26, 1995,Sunday Star Times,C1)

Speedgate¶

noun. [Politics] a minor scandal involving the high speed of a Prime Ministerial motorcade in Canterbury in 2004

See: also Corngate, Dinnergate, Doonegate, Paintergate, Powdergate, Rortagate, Tukugate (after Watergate scandal)

I'm pleased that Helen Clark and Labour are campaigning on trust. So let's see - paintergate, corngate, speedgate, Winstongate, foreshore-and-seabedgate ... (Sep 27, 2008,Dominion Post,B4)

The condust of various skirmishes involving Labour MPs - Paintergate and Speedgate, for instance - raised questions. (Jul 8, 2006,Listener (New Zealand Listener),21)

speedo-flicking¶

noun. rewinding a speedometer reading to show a lower mileage

This [the early 1990s] was the era of "speedo-flicking", when odometers were wound back to a dealer's order. (Oct 18, 2004,Time (NZ edition)) [NOTES: NZ Auto Report, Advertising section: [iii]]

Speedos¶

noun. swimming togs

This was not an easy awareness at a place like Piha, among a breed of men lording the beach in their Speedos. (Jan 2002,NZ Geographic,No. 55/37)

You have to wear speedos when racing. They make you go faster. That's why they're called speedos. (Dec 20, 2000,Capital Times,5)

Speedos celebrate their 75th anniversary this year. We've always thought of them as the great Kiwi togs although, like the pavlova, Australians claim ownership of the "great Aussie cossie". (Nov 22, 2003,Listener (New Zealand Listener),26)

speedwell¶

noun.

speedwell, Australian [s] Veronica plebeja R.Br. (1969,Standard Common Names for Weeds,73)

noun. field veronica

See: also Akaroa speedwell

FORSTER It is remarkable, that though we had seen scarce ten plants in all in flower, among them were three new Speedwells; all of them Shrubby, although there are but few Shrubby ones upon the whole known. [ed. fn] Parahebe catarractae Forst f. and Hebe salicifolia Forst f. (Apr 9, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/251)

POLACK Speedwell, sow, and melon thistles (coetus), virgin's bower, vanilloe, or willow, euphorbia, cudweed, crane's-bill, junchous rushes in all the swamps .. (1838,New Zealand (Polack),1/295)

TAYLOR The chief plants I noticed [on Ruapehu] were a beautiful everlasting, the harebell, 2 kinds of gentian, a pretty speedwell, an epacris ... a wild carrot also abounded. (Jan 30, 1853,Journal,8/70)

COCKAYNE Veronica elliptica speedwell (1910,NZ Plants & Their Story) [NOTES: (And)]

HILGENDORF SPEEDWELL (Veronica [persica]), also called field veronica, is abundant in fields and waste places throughout the islands. It is an annual with trailing stems about 6 inches long,. (1926,Weeds of New Zealand,158,1967)

HUNT It has ... speedwells or veronicas which in England are modest little blue flowers ... but which here in New Zealand are not only an enormous family of numerous species with a range of colours varying from white to dark purple, but, in the form of shrubs and trees (known as Hebes), reach a [137] height of forty feet. (1951,Confessions,136)

TAYLOR SPEEDWELLS (Veronica spp.). ... This weed originated in Southwest Asia and spread through Europe and other parts of the world more than 100 years ago. ... [It] is common throughout New Zealand in field crops and very common in gardens, ... (1981,Weeds of Lawns,104)

noun.

speedwell, water [s] Veronica anagallis-aquatica L. (1969,Standard Common Names for Weeds,73)

noun.

noun.

noun. Veronica diosmaefolia

COCKAYNE (1910,NZ Plants & Their Story) [NOTES: (And)]

noun.

speedwell, turf [s] Veronica serpyllifolia L. (1969,Standard Common Names for Weeds,73)

noun.

COCKAYNE But the germander speedwell, the herb-robert, ... and the foxglove, to mention only a few British plants, are now wild in various places. (1910,NZ Plants,135)

speedy¶

noun.

Saturday nights were the best ... about midnight, when the squares had gone home and the speedies were coming out of their holes. (Oct 10, 1972,NZ Truth,7/1) [NOTES: (`My Life as a Whore')]

speel¶

verb.

But long, long, they waited - the bridegroom came not, at first they all thought the day he'd forgot; and then at last full inquiry revealed that horrid young man from the marriage had 'speeled.' (Sep 18, 1885,Taranaki Herald,2)

"Weel, wife, I ken fu' weel ye speak the truth: / But oh! that I had back the days o' youth, / When I was gay and supple as an eel, / And up the steepest mountains I could speel, / And never, never tired or weary feel." (Apr 17, 1880,Otago Witness,20)

He speeled away on another tour of investigation, and wound up by licking several coats of stage paint off the face of the prostrate Finn, who couldn't resist because he was 'dead.' (Apr 1, 1899,Observer (Auckland),14)

speeler¶

noun.

See: contrast spieler

[NOTES: of race horses; from speel, to go fast]

No tramp ever owned such a speeler! [sc. of a horse] (Aug 20, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,20)

Mr P. Butler's Luna goes to the stud, and will probably visit Albany; the progeny of "Old Sal" should be a speeler. (Aug 11, 1883,Observer (Auckland),6)

Speights¶

noun. brand-name of a long-established South Island beer

"My old man once bought a ton of Speights. It was on special in Dunedin." (Jul 2003,NZ Geographic,No, 64/34)

"Not to sound like I'm doing a Speights ad but ... there was a six degree frost this morning and I was ready to run out in my undies it was so good." (Jul 14, 2002,Sunday Star Times,F7)

...it was completely out of character for a young southern man still developing a taste for Speight's. (Dec 26, 2003,Dominion Post,B1)

Yes, here's to Dunedin, walled in by hills, / allowing odd notions to bubble and gestate / into tasty brews like a spate of Speights... (Jan 2, 2003,Listener (New Zealand Listener),65) [NOTES: David Eggleton]

noun.

Believe me, they know and I know, and perhaps they'll think you know, that, as they say in Speights country: "She's not easy finding the perfect fillet boy!" (Sep 28, 2002,Dominion Post,F6)

Speightsian¶

adjective. associated with the Speights stereotype

Claire did so much middle-distance gazing in thie vast, sprawling two-hour special of the brand new series she was positively Speightsian. (Oct 11, 2002,Dominion Post,B7)

SPELD¶

abbreviation. from Specific Learning Disabilities

One of my pet hobby horses is SPELD teaching - dealing with specific learning disabilities - which some people rather freely refer to as dyslexia, but it's not. It's more than that. (Jun 22, 1985,Listener (New Zealand Listener),27)

spell¶

noun. [Rural] [pasture management] a period of non-grazing of land.

Each paddock had fourteen days' spell before the stock again got round to it ... (Nov 21, 1927,NZ Journal of Agriculture,296)

verb. [Rural] to clear pastures of grazing animals for a period [to allow a crop to develop or ripen, to renew after a period of flood or mud, or to be rid of infection.]

GUTHRIE-SMITH The smaller paddocks were 'spelled,' that is, kept empty of stock for five or six weeks ... (1921,Tutira,226)

If I do burn [tussock] I spell the country afterwards ... (May 3, 1945,NZ Farmer,11)

This [lean feeding of ewes] will also enable some paddocks to be spelled. (Apr 16, 1956,NZ Journal of Agriculture,348)

MCCASKILL Burning was abolished, wing fences were erected high up the slopes to enable the block to be spelled from stock. (1973,Hold This Land,83)

Smaller areas are more prone to infection because they can't be spelled, and smallholders often try to compensate by over-drenching. (2001,Lifestyle Farmer,Aug/Sept 46)

verb. [Rural] to provide stock with a change of feed or location

TAIT Surplus stock are spelled on a property of 50 acres before they are sent into the saleyards. (1956,Farms & Stations of NZ Vol I,57)

STEVENS Even better than this is the regular spelling of the rams. Of the five, three are made good use of for the first few days and two are spelled on good feed. (1958,Sheep. Part 1, Sheep husbandry,37)

verb. [Rural] to rest working animals.

NOLAN The cattle were usually spelled at Okuru for two or three days before moving on eight miles to the Haast River where there was a holding paddock. (1998,Droving Days, The,6)

NOLAN They [dogs] needed to be spelled from time to time. (1998,Droving Days, The,15)

verb. [Rural] to fast [sheep] before shearing, drenching, etc.

Sheep brought in for shearing should be spelled before shedding up, otherwise the pens in the shed get very dirty and much wool is stained. (Oct 15, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,310)

verb. to rest

... leave off and spell a bit (1869,Punch or the Auckland Charivari,172)

MITCHELL It was in 1872, while carting wheat into Timaru from Cave Valley way, I composed the following piece, ... Hold hard, Jock, put the prop-sticks down,/ And let the cattle spell./ O for a gill of Campbellton,/ Or a pint of Tennant's ale,/ (1889,Rhymes and Rambles,25) [NOTES: [1872] in 1889 Mitchell Rhymes and Rambles 25]

NESFIELD We had the tide against us ..., so we stopped at a shanty' on the north shore, andspelled' for a couple of hours. (1881,Chequered Career,60) [NOTES: [check title and punctuation???]]

DUNCAN The word was given to spell a while (1888,Wakatipians,27)

MORRIS Spell, v. to rest [1846] (1898,Austral English,428)

THOMSON He'd scaled the heights of Nevis, `padded hoof' to Albertown,/ Tramped and coached it through Kawarau Gorge and spelled at Arrowtown./ (1909,Ballads about Business,63)

Here and there we heard the distant call of the tui ... and when we `spelled', grey-breasted robins fluttered about us cheekily. (1930,NZ Short Stories,19) [NOTES: 1930 Arthur H. Adams in NZ Short Stories 19]

SCRYMGEOUR One command was to bring back the horse `Brownie' spelling at Ben Coldham's property, and to ride him home, and spell the mount ridden out on this tour. (1960,Memories of Maoriland,181)

verb. to rest (a person or animal) for recuperation

I spelled the horses for an hour and returned to Mt. Peel picking up my tent ... on the way. (May 6, 1864,Chudleigh Diary,131,1950)

FERGUSON Whenever [the bullocks] look fagged I spell them. (1893,Bush Life in Australia & NZ,246)

A Attwood's team are all doing well at Feilding with the exception of Killarney, who is suffering from a swollen joint and is being spelled. (Aug 11, 1906,NZ Truth,60/6/4)

Sheep brought in for shearing should be spelled before shedding up, other wise the pens in the shed get very dirty ... (Oct 16, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,310)

SCRYMGEOUR One command was to bring back the horse `Brownie' spelling at Ben Coldham's property, and to ride him home, and spell the mount ridden out on this tour. (1960,Memories of Maoriland,181)

You can put Mac on with Monty', I told Dawson,and young Jimmy can spell Arthur.' I wasn't going to stand there arguing ... and I wanted a ride fifty miles to the township to get the Limited ... (Mar 3, 1950,Listener (New Zealand Listener),8) [NOTES: (P. Llewellyn)]

The Ulimaroa sailed at 5 p.m. with Gloaming aboard. He will be spelled in New Zealand until Xmas. (Sep 24, 1920,Grey River Argus,4)

Elevonia (Elevation-Merrivonia) has been spelling since she raced at Trentham. (Jun 3, 1914,Evening Post,2)

One at the wheel and another on lookout, with a few to look on and `spell' the rest. (1857,Whaling and Fishing,96)

AUSSIE RA SPELLING .. Aussie Ra has been turned out in the paddock and will not race again this season. (Feb 18, 1936,Evening Post,13)

verb. to rest (land by taking stock off, or by letting it lie fallow)

Spell, to -To take the stock off (a paddock, etc.) (Jan 27, 1934,Press, The,15) [NOTES: Acland]

STUDHOLME The hill lambs were weaned onto a block of country which had been spelled since shearing time. (1940,Te Waimate,97)

LEVY Ridge fencing is essential to control stock and to spell country. (1951,Grasslands of NZ,261,1970)

noun. a break from a job etc.; a holiday (esp. give, take a spell)

See: also spell-oh, breather

ROCHFORT The diggers on coming down to town for a `spell' ... (1863,Adventures of a Surveyor,62)

It's oh, to be a Super/ Along with some western swell,/ Where a man has never a stiver to save,/ But sometimes gets a spell. (Jan 1853,Canterbury Rhymes,17) [NOTES: (The Overseer's Lament)]

Shennan's and Black's drays came with four bales wool. Bullock drivers taking a spell.' (Oct 23, 1859,Puketoi Station Diary) [NOTES: 1859 Oct 23 Puketoi Station Diary in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 102]

[Hocken TS] the latters filly Rareified and taken away. Bullock drivers taking a spell. (Oct 23, 1859,Puketoi Station Diary)

Every now and then he gave us a spell for about 2 min., no more. We had nothing but our shirts so it would not do to stop. (Dec 18, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,70,1950)

Bill can read while he is sitting in the tent ..., and I always have to give the Bull two hours spell in the middle of the day. (Jan 4, 1863,Journal and Letters (Walker))

We gave the horses an hour's spell. (Feb 14, 1863,Chudleigh Diary,77,1950 ed. Richards)

... we were all so breathless that a `spell' (do you know that means rest?) would have been most acceptable. (1867,Station Life in NZ,128,1870)

BAINES The beauty of paddling is that any one of the crew can `take a spell' without throwing the rest much out, ... Ibid. 206 ... I got out of the forest and on the bare fern and tea-tree ranges I sat down to take a spell and think ... (1874,Edward Crewe,104)

KENNAWAY This being so, I got eighteen months' spell ... to clamber back to England again. (1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,129)

NESFIELD I was sitting on a log taking a spell. (1881,Chequered Career,75)

HAY Dandy Jack was restless ... and talked of going to Auckland for a spell. [? sense] (1882,Brighter Britain,1/295)

PYKE The fact that we were liable to berushed' at any time, and our claims limited to 24 feet square did not affect Fox's or West's parties, who worked eight hours a day, with frequent `spells' and Saturday half-holidays. (1887,History of the Early Gold Discoveries in Otago,85,1962)

D'AVIGDOR He and his young wife are now in England for a `spell' (holiday), after three years of hard ... work. (1888,Antipodean Notes,164)

MORRIS In England, a turn at work or duty; in Australasia, always a period of rest from duty. It is quite possible that etymologically Spell is connected with Ger. spielen , in which case the Australasian use is the more correct. See `Skeat's Etymological Dictionary.' (1898,Austral English,428)

BAUCKE My native acquaintance also took advantage of the spell, for ... she inquired if I objected to the smell of torori' (native tobacco); ...My torori; I cured it; take some, try it.' I shuddered. I remembered one day when the tobacco hunger pinched me sore - torori or suffer; ... (1905,Where the White Man Treads,144, 229)

Savoury ran last at Moorefield last Saturday week. He is sore and will require a spell. ... Lingerer was not brought down to the Wellington meeting and the Apremont gelding is to be given a spell. (Jul 14, 1906,NZ Truth,56/2/4)

He has decided to take a spell for six months. (Jul 2, 1891,Wanganui Herald,3)

DAVIN Every time there was a shunt the gang had to have a spell while they waited for the line to clear again. (1973,Not Here, Not Now,273)

The bullocks were tired, and wanted a "spell." (Dec 6, 1879,Auckland Weekly News,5)

20th Jan - I feel a little seedy at the moment due to father too much work ... since session I have had only ten days spell ... [Letter to Fowlds from P.M. Joseph Ward] (Jan 20, 1911,Fowlds Papers, The) [NOTES: 1911 Jan 20 in 1980 Rogers The Fowlds Papers - Politics 1911]

COWAN Grateful were the spells for rest and smoke and the midday billy-boiling half-hour; more grateful still the sundown halt for rest ... (1916,Bush Explorers,10)

WESTON Sometimes we would stop in one of the larger French railway yards ...; at other times ... our spell would be by country lanes. (1918,Three Years with the NZers,72)

While we were waiting for the billy to boil ... taking the mid-day spell after a strenuous morning of post-splitting. (Apr 10, 1920,Quick March,31)

spell n. a turn of period of relief from work; a resting time. (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,1)

BENNETT A spell in New Zealand means a period of rest, rather than of work, and to have a spell' is to take a rest; in this sense it is probably a remnant of the speech of the New Bedford and Nantucket whalers who once frequented New Zealand waters,spell oh!' being recorded (in Moby Dick , for example) as a call to cease work or strenuous exercise. [fn.] 15. It is thus much older than l.C. 19-20,' the date given in Partridge,<i> op. cit.</i>, p. 807, and possibly it is many centuries older; cf. <i>The Owl and the Nightingale,</i> l. 258,lat thine tunge habben spale' where spale is more appropriately translated by rest' than by Skeat'sturn of work.' (1943,English as it is spoken in NZ,91 [and fn.])

BLAKISTON There was one very hot February in which the Australians, accustomed as they were to dry heat, had to knock off for a spell while the New Zealanders were able to keep going. [sc. shearing] (1952,My Yesteryears,20) [NOTES: [f. c1869]]

THOMSON We had very few spells in the three-hour trip and were about all-in by the time we reached the fly-camp. (1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,33)

JOSEPH `What about a flick or something next Friday? We'll both need a spell by then.' (1962,Pound of Saffron, A,34)

(Nov 22, 1957,Listener (New Zealand Listener),4/3)

BACON The workmen were having a spell ... The foreman nodded as we came near, squinting up at us from where he sat nursing a mug of black tea. Goodday, mates. Like a mug of brew?' ...Yeah, there's plenty in the billy.' (1963,In the Sticks,84)

SARGESON spell: break from work or routine. (1964,Collected Stories,303)

spell n. Australia, a period of rest from work, whence spell-oh. v.int. spell, to rest, especially in phrase have a spell. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

spell n. in Australia, period of rest from work, whence spell-oh; v.i. rest, especially in have a spell. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

spell ... NZ & Austral . period of rest from work. ...2 v. ... NZ & Austral. rest, allow (person, horse) to rest. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,738) [NOTES: [cf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict. 1114; 1985 Collins NZ Compact Dict. 465]]

DAVIN (1970,Not Here, Not Now,273)

Spell (sp&ebreve.l), n. (Relief in work.) [Add.] 1. (b) Hence, a period of rest from work; a vacation. Zealand ... Spell, v. i. [imp. & p. p. SPELLED (sp&ebreve.ld); p. pr. & vb. n. SPELLING.] [See SPELL, n., 1. (b) above.] To rest from work for a time. Baldwin Spencer. ... Spell, v. t. to allow an interval of rest to (one). (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031)

At each township south of Hastings food and refreshment depots were open all day, forms and chairs were sent out to give a spell from travelling, and everything was free. (Feb 7, 1931,Evening Post,12)

noun. a division of time in a rugby football game; a half; a period of play in sport

Usually in the second spell ... play is getting more exciting. (1900,NZ Illustrated Magazine,3/237)

MULGAN A try in each spell ... (1934,Spur of Morning,23)

spell A length of time, as `I think we are in for a spell of bad weather' (1958,Whitcombe's Modern Junior Dictionary (8th edn),379) [NOTES: [Is this appropriate here???]]

Nothing was scored in the spell... / (1923,College Rhymes,22) [NOTES: (1888) 1923 College Rhymes 22 [Otago Univ. Review]]

On account of the high wind, the sides played in four spells of twenty minutes. (Sep 19, 1910,Evening Post,4)

Jas O'Dwyer scored during the second spell and W. O'Dwyer converted. (Sep 10, 1894,Marlborough Express,3)

The game was played in four spells of 20 minutes. In the first and second spells neither side succeeded in scoring, but in the third spell the Zingari by grand play, especially in the scrummages, secured a touchdown, but the try for a goal was a failure. (Apr 22, 1882,Otago Witness,21)

noun. pumping spell, water leak

Making but little water. [Mar 1] ... Carpenter caulking on the larboard side, Ship making about One Spell in 3 hours. (Feb 29, 1836,Piraki Log,29,ed. Anson 1911)

spell day¶

noun. [Rural] [droving and mustering] a day of rest for horses, dogs and travelling stock.

NOLAN The goodwill of the farmers along the way was also essential as the cattle had to be paddocked and grazed for the night. Occasionally a 'spell day' was necessary as they became footsore with the continual travel on rough tracks and stony river crossings. (1998,Droving Days, The,5)

spell ride¶

verb. [Rural] to take two saddle horses on a muster or trip so that one can be rested.

ANDERSON We will be able to spell ride with two hacks each. (1962,Life's Roundabout, A,73)

spelled¶

adjective. of land etc

spelled paddock¶

noun. [Rural] a fenced area that has been closed to grazing to restore pasture health or to avoid disease.

By mid-June the spelled paddocks should be densely covered with leafy, high-quality pasture .. it is possible to start grazing off the spelled paddocks and carry the whole herd through the rest of the winter on grass alone. (Jan 16, 1956,NZ Journal of Agriculture,61)

GASCOIGNE The sound ewes were put out to graze on a spelled paddock which should by now be clean as it had been unused by stock for some weeks. (1965,From the Top of a Hill,69)

DU FAUR The hill paddock can be used as a holding area, and the ewes can then be grazed in the spelled paddock, preferably break-fed, for one to two hours daily. (1966,Sheep Farming for Profit,58)

spell-ho¶

noun.

See: spell-oh

CHARLES Smoko! Spell ho! Billy on the boil!/ Light a fag and take a drag,/ And rest your bones from toil./ 2. v (1981,Black Billy Tea,91)

spelling¶

noun. pausing for rest

SUTHERLAND After the short horizons of the clearing this panorama was always welcome and the spot became a regular `spelling' place on the way in or out. (1953,Golden Bush, The,121,1963)

noun. [Rural] the resting of pasture or paddocks from constant grazing.

STEVENS Alternate grazing and spelling of pastures is simple enough under some systems of farming. (1958,Sheep. Part 1, Sheep husbandry,64)

There is no run-scale example yet of the improvement possible on depleted winter country by the system of spelling outlined ... (Sep 1961,NZ Journal of Agriculture,261)

noun.

BOOTH Like 'spelling', where work gangs had at least one man too many at all times and thus one member 'spelled', did nothing, for set periods but for full pay (1997,Deadline : My Story,36)

(Jan 5, 1916,Poverty Bay Herald,7)

noun.

spinner¶

noun. a fast racehorse

WILLIAMS & REEVES Or suppose you're on a spinner',/ He can never prove a winner/ .../ When he should have been amoral' [cert]. (1891,Double Harness,3)

noun. a two-up operator

LAWSON Percy Gray was spinner, and Alf Burke, the boxer - you know, the man who takes the bets ... Well, everything was going well till [?] spun two coins very high - trying to float' them - that means land them without spinning them more than twice ... Someone else picked up [the penny], looked at it, and shoutedBoys, it's a grey - two tails on it!' (1957,Gold in their Hearts,90) [NOTES: [reference 1870s?]]

WILSON It was like a bazaar [on the troopship]. In the centre was a boxing ring and the two-up spinners were operating inside it. (1956,Sweet White Wine,137)

spinner ... n. (Sl.) man who tosses coin in two-up school. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

n. (slang). man who tosses the coin in a two-up school. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

HILLIARD In the centre stood the spinner with his kip and two pennies. (1976,Send Somebody Nice,75)

spinner ... NZ & Austral. person who tosses coin in the game of two-up. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

(1966,Short Stories (various authors)) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

noun. the carbon skid on the end of tram-poles which makes the connection with the overhead electrified wire (Perhaps used earlier for the wheels which were replaced by carbon skids.)

[NOTES: ca1953 Wellington (F.M. O'Brien)]

noun. a device for unrolling rolls of wire along a fence line; =(spinning) jenny -

Jenny: Device for unrolling rolls of wire along a fence line. May be called a spinning jenny or a wire spinner. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,28)

noun. a humorous euphemism for a .303 bullet fired (illegally) at trout

THOMSON Having small interest in different types of lures, flies and whatnots, I asked the field officer what kind of bait he caught it on, the reply being a nickel spinner'! ... Cliff told me that thenickel spinner' was a .303 rifle bullet. Ibid. 169 The remainder of the day seemed to drag slowly, and we took a stroll up the river to try our luck with a spot of fishing with a nickel spinner. (1952,Deer Hunter: The Experiences of a NZ Stalker,101)

LELAND nickel spinner: Another horror story for the devoted fisherman. A BULLET (not necessarily nickel plated) fired at a trout (or any other fish). This almost always misses but it stuns the fish which then float to the surface to be gathered in. (1980,Personal Kiwi-Yankee Dictionary, A,70)

spinning¶

noun. [Rural] the action of a huntaway sheepdog, by retreating and turning right around when confronted head on by sheep.

See: turning tail

If a youngster is let away with it, 'turning tail' will just become a habit. Huntaway's [sic] do a similar trick - often called 'spinning' - rather like a pirouette. (1984,NZ Journal of Agriculture,Jan/Feb 13)

spinning jenny¶

noun. [Rural] a device for feeding out fencing wire.

WESTMACOTT At first I did only the boy's jobs such as tending the spinning jenny off which ran the wire which they threaded through the iron standards .. (1977,After-Breakfast Cigar, The,3)

Ross placed it over a spinning Jenny, an ingenious device which simply unwound as the wire was pulled. (Mar 21, 1981,Listener (New Zealand Listener),67)

Clearing sale: .. 4 snig chains, spinning jenny, docking scrim ... (May 11, 2002,Taranaki Daily News,47)

noun. a device for paying out wire along a fenceline; a wire spinner; a device for unrolling rolls of wire along a fenceline; jenny; wire spinner

He then asked me to get another coil of wire....The coil, 650 metres long, was heavy stuff. Ross placed it over a spinning Jenny, an ingenious device which simply unwound as the wire was pulled. He then set off down the fencing lane. [? line] I watched Jenny do her stuff without fault until 200 metres of wire had unwound. (Mar 21, 1981,Listener (New Zealand Listener),67)

Jenny Device for unrolling rolls of wire along a fence line. May be called a spinning jenny or a wire spinner. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,28)

[I learned how to] use a spinning jenny for running out new wire;... . How to erect a flood gate across a river. All the skills of the fencer were shown to me. (Jan 5, 1984,Dominion,5)

Spiral¶

noun.

[NOTES: See also Raurimu Spiral]

EXPRESS ASCENDING THE SPIRAL. (Jun 26, 1912,Evening Post,13) [NOTES: Photo Caption]

Six cars of the Auckland express which left Wellington at 3 p.m. yesterday were derailed and dropped 14 feet four miles north of the Raurimu Spiral at 1.30 a.m. today. (Jan 6, 1945,Evening Post,8)

spit tacks¶

phrase. be angry

spit the dummy¶

phrase. to give way to a fit of anger, to have a temper tantrum

[NOTES: Orsman says originally Australian [1987]]

It wasn't the chef who spat the dummy. It was another customer who was irritated by what was filling his or her schnozz. (Dec 19, 2001,Capital Times,17)

I would spit the dummy and refuse right then and there to ever again accompany Gav to the stockcars. Sheesh, that's a bit heavy, he says. (Sep 27, 2001,Evening Post,8)

So while Warwick, a sort of male version of the Ingham twins, spat the dummy to play the field, and William courted legal agonies, enter Tyler and Kate, who prepared for the birth of their son Cyrone. (Oct 3, 2001,Evening Post,16)

As negotiations continued, the proposed rise in the lake level was reduced to 8.4m. But then New Zealanders spat the dummy. (Jun 15, 2002,Listener (New Zealand Listener),36)

He shouldn't spit the dummy; it doesn't do him credit. (Dec 19, 2000,Independent Herald (Wellington),1)

Jiang Zemin spat the dummy because - unlike his country - we have free speech, or so I thought. (Sep 19, 1999,Sunday Star Times,A10)

He has had enough setbacks in his time to have spat the dummy many times over. (Nov 14, 1999,Sunday Star Times,B20)

Coupled with a dazzling array of obscure antipodean slang expressions - marking the wood? spitting the dummy? - the effect is X-rated Kylie Mole. (Sep 24, 1990,Listener (New Zealand Listener),5)

spit weed¶

noun.

MOORE & IRWIN CARDAMINE. Certain Northern Hemisphere bitter cresses of this genus are the despair of New Zealand gardeners. The long flat pod splits explosively from below, flinging seeds afar, hence the name `spit weeds'. (1978,Oxford Book of NZ Plants,40)

noun.

spittlebug¶

noun.

[Mrs Annette Wale of Johnsonville writes:] `For the last two or three years in spring I have had a new garden pest, ... I call it the Spittle Bug because it lives in a white foam on the underside of leaves, and the foam looks like spittle. It is a small lime-green bug with a pointed end. ... Spittle Bug is commonly known by this name and it is also called Cuckoo Spit. It is more apparent this year because of the very wet season, but it is by no means a new pest. (Dec 5, 1986,Evening Post,20)

spotted skink¶

noun. a skink distinguished by white or green black-edged flecks on its back and tail.

[NOTES: Oligosoma lineoocellatum aka Mackenzie skink. There is a subspecies known as Spotted skink "Mackenzie Basin" Oligosoma aff. lineoocellatum "Mackenzie Basin"]

"We hope that we will soon find Spotted Skinks(Oligosoma Lineocellatum) which are also thought to be present on the Cape Kidnappers peninsula." (Dec 2008,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.oceanbeachnz.co.nz/files/pdf/Dec08_LR.pdf]

In the greater Christchurch City area (including the Port Hills) there are, or have been inrecent times, at least four (possibly five) species of lizard; two species of gecko,Hoplodactylus maculatus (common gecko) and Naultinus gemmeus (jewelled gecko), andtwo species of skink,Oligosoma lineoocellatum (spotted skink) and Oligosoma spp.("common" species) ... (1996,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://researcharchive.lincoln.ac.nz/dspace/bitstream/10182/676/1/wmr_9.pdf]

Tony Jewell Recently published genetic data suggests that the spotted skink (as here defined) involves three distinct species ... However, despite being separated by very deep levels of genetic divergence, the species remain externally indistinguishable and further work is needed before they can be separated. (2008,Reptiles and Amphibians of New Zealand)

Almost half of New Zealand's reptiles are threatened or endangered. It is now illegal to handle or keep in captivity any native lizard without a permit from the Department of Conservation. Some, such as the spotted skink (Oligosoma lineoocellatum), are still widespread, although their numbers are probably dwindling. (2009,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.wildaboutnz.co.nz/index.php?option=com_content&view=article&id=85:lizards&catid=27:land-animals&Itemid=78]

The Landcare Research team has sought answers through an intensive study of two species: the speckled skink Oligosoma infrapunctatum and the green spotted skink Oligosoma lineocellatum. (Dec 1997,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://nzsm.webcentre.co.nz/article888.htm New Zealand Science Monthly Online]

Spotted skinks also have a scattered distribution indicating that they may once havebeen widespread in lowland areas of the southern North Island south of HawkeBay. Spotted skinks are known from about 10 sites on the mainland North Islandfrom Napier, the Wairarapa and Wellington areas ... The species is also foundon islands in Wellington Harbour .. on islands in the MarlboroughSounds and is widespread in the eastern South Island ... In the North Island, spotted skinks coexist with brown, speckled and common skinks. (2002,Internet - see Notes) [NOTES: http://www.doc.govt.nz/upload/documents/science-and-technical/TSRP48.pdf Department of Conservation Te Papa Atawhai]

Spotted skink: Oligosoma lineoocellatum, 111mm in length from snout to vent (minus tail). It is much bigger than the common skink which is 73mm. The king of the lizards in Ponatahi Lizard Sanctuary on Tim Hewitt's farm, he says he first saw them in the 1960s in their hundreds, but now they're rare. (Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2)

It will take us between five and ten years to get the populations up. The spotted skink, for example, only breeds after aged [sic] three." (Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2)

"Without more help, saving the spotted skink and other lizards would be an uphill battle," he says. "We needed something to keep the predators out of the area, so we decided to build a predator-proof fence." (Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2)

" .. this is the only site away from the coastal margin where spotted skink remains part of the fauna and is a reminder of the value that these small patches of remnant vegetation provide." (Aug 5, 2009,Wairarapa News,2)

spottie¶
