[NOTES: ca1940 Havelock (but I suspect much earlier: HWO)]

SUNDERLAND & TAYLOR ... Mr Knox as he came down [to the mustering camp] for a pannikin of tea and a helping of spottie. (1981,Sunrise,44)

noun. young deer (usually fallow) up to 3 months of age

SLATTER I could get right back into the bush and live in deer cullers' huts. ... I know a lovely little valley where I've shot some spikers and some nice spotties when the fawns are about. (1959,Gun in My Hand, A,169)

Spottie: Young deer (usually fallow) up to 3 months of age. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,22)

spotties¶

noun. measles

[NOTES: 1953 14 M A6 Thames DHS 31 SPOTTIES -->1953 14 M A15 Thames DHS 31 SPOTTIES -->1953 15 M A27 Thames DHS 31 SPOTTIES -->1984 17 F E59 Pakuranga Coll. 4 SPOTTING THE TACENT ?n or aj -->1984 17 M E97 Pakuranga Coll. 31 SPOTTY [sickness: ?=measles]]

spotting¶

noun. drinking liquor

See: cf. spot v.

[NOTES: cf. spot v. ca1930 Havelock (W.H.B. Orsman)]

[Hdg] The "Spotting" Habit. Youngpeople of 16 and over.. thought it brightand clever to appear "three sheets in thewind" at country dances and made apractice of running out after everydance to motor cars to "have a spot." (Jul 11, 1930,Northern Advocate,7)

GASKELL It was a pity Taumarunui was dry. She could do with a few spots herself to take away the taste of these last two weeks. 1978 editorial note 189 spots'. Any alcoholic drinks, but usually spirits. The verbal formsto spot' and spotting' were common. <i>(1947,All Part of the Game,84</i>) [NOTES:School Picnic [check title - not `Big Game'???]]

CHERRILL Pa wouldn't have got into the way of spotting the way he has ... . (1950,Story of a NZ Sheepfarm,73)

HARTLEY Mother believed dancing was worldly if not sinful, and she was frightened that we might start spotting'. Mother's twin fears were carnal sin and having aspot'. (1987,Swagger on Our Doorstep,180)

noun.

See: cf. spot v., spoiling; gridironing

OLIVER The runholder was protected against intruders: cottages, fences and homesteads gave him a pre-emptive right over a set number of contiguous acres. Fences and cottages could be so disposed as to give the runholder rights over the best of the land - sources of water and wood, strips surrounding isolated and thus inaccessible pockets. Grid-ironing' andspotting', as these selective practices were called, were certainly used by many runholders to tie up large areas, but probably not to the extent alleged by horrified land tenure radicals in later years. (1968,Story of New Zealand, The,108)

CRAWFORD Gridironing' was the practice of buying twenty acre sections fronting on a road, so spaced as to leave sections of nineteen acres between them, and as these had to be auctioned the small farmer stood litttle chance of outbidding the run-holder who usually retained them without having to purchase them.Spotting' was buying up key positions, fertile land, and leaving the barren, water courses, entrances to valleys, road lines, ... . (1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,94)

SCOTTER When investigating the change from pastoral lease to freehold in any locality, the student, brought up on Pember Reeves (see e.g. S.E.I. [State Experiments 1902] 234) searches immediately for evidences of the methods by which the runholder retained his grasp of the land. These practices called gridironing and spotting can be defended: there is no need to do so here. If spotting is practiced - the purchase of selected areas with water and shelter for the control this gave over the surrounding country - a study of the Crown grant index maps and of the dates of the original titles supplies no evidence of it. (1948,Run, Estate and Farm,13)

CARR The practice of which I speak is called in New Zealand spotting'</i> or <i>spoiling' country. [???a verbal not nominal use] (1856,Waste Lands of Wellington, The,30)

Green, one of the settlers, is endeavouring to purchase land in various places spotting ... . (1865,McLean Papers,25/132 [1866 xxv/139]) [NOTES: (Harris, Tauranga)]

CRAWFORD McLean brought to light some of the pitfalls of spot freeholding when he wrote in September 1970: The promiscuous `spotting' of this run with small blocks of freehold ... [sic] may have in a measure attained the primary object of excluding extensive purchase ... (1981,Station Years,47) [NOTES: 1870 Sep in 1981 Crawford Station Years 47]

MORRIS Spotting, n. New Zealand equivalent for the Australian picking the eyes out,' andpeacocking.' Under Free-selection (q.v.), the squatter spotted his run, purchasing choice spots. (1898,Austral English,431)

spotting n. selecting the best parts of an area; peacocking.-spot v.t. (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11)

BURDON The other and yet more harmful method was to buy isolated sections all over a run to prevent or hinder large purchases by anyone else; to pick out the fertile and leave the barren; to take the grain and leave the husk. This was called `spotting.' (1938,High Country,123)

BAKER Spotting was applied to provinces other than Canterbury ... It was probably formed on the basis of the Australian terms pick the eyes out of the country and peacocking. (1941,NZ Slang,26)

SINCLAIR `Spotting' was the purchase of strategic points, such as the mouth of a gorge, river-banks and other watering-places, so as to exclude rivals from large areas of adjacent land. (1959,History of New Zealand,156)

spotting N. in New Zealand selecting the choicest parts of an area, picking the eyes out and leaving the poorer parts. See gridironing. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

spotting ... n. in N.Z., selecting the choicest parts of an area, picking the eyes out, and leaving the poorer parts. See gridironing. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

noun. [Rural] a purchase of scattered strategic and productive areas of land to dissuade other purchasers.

FULLER For the capitalist, by what is colonially termed 'spotting a Run', that is, picking out parts of it only to buy, may command the pasturage of the whole of the remaining portion ... (1859,Five Years' Residence in New Zealand,72)

MORRIS spotting. New Zealand equivalent for the Australian 'picking the eyes out' and 'peacocking.' (1898,Austral English,431)

STEWART The squatters contended that they had to adopt all these expedients of spotting and gridironing in self-protection. (1940,William Rolleston: a New Zealand statesman,61)

BAKER With the opening up of new land in this country .. a host of new expressions came into being, among them the Canterbury Pilgrims, shagroons, prophets, pre-Adamites, v-hut, gridironing, and spotting. (1941,NZ Slang,24)

The method of either gridironing, that is buying up the freehold of strategic parts around, or spotting, buying the strategic and fertile patches of an area that was customary with hill country settlers of the early days, was adapted by Mr Hugh Duff when taking up Whakarara ... (Nov 15, 1952,Weekly News,33)

noun. [Rural] [aerial mustering] the sighting of stragglers and stray stock.

A Cattle Muster on Molesworth. With the spotting we've missed seventeen. (May 4, 2000,Country Calendar (TVNZ))

DOMINY Now on occasion, when spotting or straggling, some run-holders save time by using a helicopter to drop them in the back country. (2001,Calling the Station Home,169)

spotty¶

noun. a small sea-fish

MALCOLM He and Ted would spend hours.. fishing for 'spotties', other names are butterfish or kelpie or.. Pakirikiri. (1982,Where it all Began,105)

...there were quite deep holes formed in the sand at the bow and stern where we would swim or catch small six inch long fish, known as 'spottys', on a line with a small hook. (Jun 2003,NZ Memories,No. 42/33)

Regarding the fishes themselves, the following were the number of days on which the principal varieties were in the market during the year .. Spotty, 128 ... (Aug 18, 1877,Otago Witness,7)

There are various other kinds of fish which afford good sport, such as elephant fish, horse mackerel, gurnard, and spotty, &c. (Dec 17, 1886,Otago Witness,27)

Pseudolabrus bothryocosmus , Richardson. Locally known as butter-fish' orspotty'; very common. (1906,TrNZI,38/551) [NOTES: (Thomson, Otago)]

PSEUDOLABRUS COCCINEUS (=PSEUDOLABRUS MILES). Spotty. Caught during all months of the year, but seldom seen in the Auckland market. (May 1922,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,5/93) [NOTES: Phillipps and Hodgkinson Further Notes on Edible Fishes]

They were `spotties,' those voracious little sea-fish so well known round the wharves and harbours of our coast. (1901,TrNZI,33/219)

McGILL spotty a fish. (1989,Dinkum Kiwi Dictionary, The,96)

Spotties were soon on the job and within a couple of minutes we had landed half a dozen. (Nov 16, 2002,Dominion Post,F12)

He has a twopenny line and a bit of borrowed meat, and in all this rolling ball of time the only patch that interests him is traversed by a "spotty." (Feb 4, 1913,Evening Post,2)

noun. sea perch

[NOTES: ?Helicolenus percoides [John Dory] (Australian poddly) [check the below against later authorities, for scientific name, sea-perch/spotty tangle] (cf.1957); pohuiakaroa =spotty [Helicolenus percoides john dory, Maori chief]

WILLIAMS Pohuiakaroa n. ... Helicolenus percoides ) 1. (?usu.) Pseudolabrus celidotus pakirikiri a small wrasse. (1971,Dictionary of the Maori Language,287,1971)

WILLIAMS Pohuiakaroa n. ... Helicolenus percoides ) 1. (?usu.) Pseudolabrus celidotus pakirikiri a small wrasse. (1971,Dictionary of the Maori Language,287,1971)

They were `spotties', those voracious little sea-fish so well known round the wharves and harbours of our coast. (1901,TrNZI,33/219)

Pseudolabrus Celidotus ... Spotty. (1911,Records of the Canterbury Museum,1/224) [NOTES: Waite]

Pseudolabrus celidotus Forster. According to Waite ... this is the correct name of the spotty referred to in my previous list as P. botryocosmus Richardson. (1913,TrNZI,45/231) [NOTES: (Thomson, Otago)]

PSEUDOLABRUS CELIDOTUS (Forster). Spotty . Common in all shallow water in rocky localities. Large examples are sold as `butterfish' in Dunedin. (1921,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,4/117) [NOTES: Phillipps Notes on the Edible Fishes]

At the Portobello Marine Fish - hatchery the swimming form has been taken from the stomachs of the following fishes: Smooth-hound (Mustelus antarcticus ), Spined dogfish (Squalus fernandinus ), Warehou (Seriolella brama ), Red cod (Physiculus bacchus ), Hapuka (Polyprion prognathus ), Tarakihi (Dactylosparus macropterus ), Maori chief (Nolhothenia macrocephala ), Kelp-fish (Coridodax pullus ), Blue cod (Parapercis colias ), Spotty (Pseudolabrus celidotus ), parrot-fish (Pseudolabrus miles ). ling (Genypterus blacodes ), and Leather jacket (Pseudomonacanthus scaber ). (1923,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,6/111) [NOTES: (Thomson and Thomson)]

PHILLIPPS Pseudolabrus celidotus (Forster). SPOTTY; PAEKIRIKIRI. (1927,Bibliography of NZ Fishes,41,1971)

Pseudolabrus celidotus (Forster). Spotty. (1938,TrRSNZ,68/412) [NOTES: Graham Fishes of Otago Harbour]

GRAHAM Spotty Pseudolabrus (Lunolabrus) celidotus (Bloch and Schn.) (Syn. Labrus poecilopleura Cuv. and Val., Julis notatus Richardson, Labroides asellinus Richardson, Sparus stellatus Richardson, and Labrichthys fucicolor Hutton) (1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,408) [NOTES: 1955 Whitley Namelist in 1956 Graham NZ Fishes 408]

GRAHAM SPOTTY (PAEKIRIKIRI) Pseudolabrus (Lunolabrus) celidotus (Bloch and Schneider) ... [Ibid. 275] The name Spotty is derived from the presence of spots on each side of the fish. The name Butterfish used in the North Island for them is from the yellow or buttery colouring on the undersurface. In Canterbury they are called Guffy, but for what reason I have yet to learn. It is a very pretty fish, more especially when seen in the water. (1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,272, 275)

PARROTT THE SPOTTY Pseudolabrus celidotus (Richardson) ... Maori name: PAEKIRIKIRI ... This was one of the first species of fish collected in New Zealand by Europeans, and was described and named in 1801. The Spotty belongs to the Parrotfish family (Labridae ) and is also related to the Butterfish and Kelpfish. Ibid. 170 Spotty Pseudolabrus celidotus Butterfish; Guffy (1957,Sea Anglers' Fishes of NZ,131)

WILLIAMS Pakirikiri, ... 4. Pseudolabrus celidotus, spotty; a fish. [Ngapuhi] (1957,Dictionary of the Maori Language,254)

McLINTOCK Spotty.. .. paketi, pakirikiri, tangahangaha .. .. Pseudolabrus celidotus (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/705-712)

NATUSCH Parochialism runs strong in most of us, and many will note indignantly the absence of a familiar local name. The difficulty is that Stewart Island butterfish = Wellington spotty, while Wellington butterfish=Stewart Island greenbone. Ibid. 224 Family LABRIDAE (wrasses) ... are known by various local names: spotties, soldiers, kelp fish, parrot fish, etc. Pseudolabrus celidotus , a sandy black-marked fish common about wharves, is well known to small boys with bent pins, and to older fishermen whose bait it nibbles. (1967,Animals of NZ, The,207)

DOOGUE & MORELAND SPOTTY ... Other names: Pseudolabrus celidotus ; butterfish, kelpie, guffy. None is widely used. Paketi, pakirikiri (Maori). (1966,Sea Anglers' Guide,257)

MORELAND SPOTTY [Pseudolabrus celidotus ] ... Other names include paketi, kelpie, guffy, butterfish and pakirikiri. (1967,Marine Fishes,22)

WILSON SPOTTY The common little Spotty is known to every boy or girl who has even gone fishing along the tide line. ... Other names are kelpie, guffy, butterfish, pakirikiri and paketi (Maori). Gets its most common name from a large, black spot on its upper side. (1981,Fisherman's Bible,207)

AYLING SPOTTY (Paketi) Pseudolabrus celidotus ... The spotty is a moderate sized wrasse that reaches a maximum length as an adult male of about 26cm ... (1982,Collins Guide,254,1984)

spotty ... 2 n. NZ small variety of wrasse. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,742) [NOTES: [nf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict.]]

[species name] spotty 2 .. [scientific name]Pseudolabrus celidotus .. [other name(s)] guffy (Jul 23, 1986,Codes for Species in NZ Waters)

PAUL Spotty Pseudolabrus celidotus Alternative names include paketi, kelpie, and butterfish (the last two being misleading). Restricted to New Zealand ...The girdled wrasse, P. cinctus, is rather similar to the spotty but grows larger ... It occurs around the South Island but is not common. (1986,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,107)

PAUL et al. [index to common names 283-293] spotty [TS] 1683, 1717-27, 1745 (1987,Fishes: A Bibliography)

HUTTON & HECTOR The pohuia-karoa is the proper sea-perch of these waters, that name having been applied in mistake to a small wrasse which is generally called the spotty or poddly. (1872,Fishes,108)

HECTOR SEA PERCH ... The Pohuiakaroa (Sebastes percoides ), though not figured deserves mention, as it is a small fish representing in these seas the genus to which the Norway Haddock belongs. ... It is the proper Sea Perch of these waters, that name having been by mistake applied in the Catalogue to a small Wrasse (No.67), which is generally called the Spotty or Poddly. [No.67 is Labrichthys celidota ) (1872,Edible Fishes,108)

MORRIS S. percoides spotty/poddly 3. [?same as above] Labrichthys bothryocosmus Ibid. 431 Spotty, n. a New Zealand fish, a Wrasse, Labrichthys bothryocosmus , Richards.; also called Poddly (q.v.), and Kelp-fish (q.v.). (1898,Austral English)

Spotties, Marare .. [Scientific Name] Labrichthys bothryocosmus (1878,TrNZI,10/326) [NOTES: [Maori or Settlers' Name] (P. Thomson, Otago)]

SHERRIN SPOTTY (Labrichthys bothryocosmus ). ... [92] According to Mr. Thompson's observations, the spotty is also known in Dunedin as the butter-fish, as when writing in 1877, he said: The spotty, or butter-fish of our local fishermen, has been very plentiful this year, and had been brought to town in large numbers at times; was in the market 128 days, as against thirty-four days for last year.' ... adding in the most tantalizing manner possible,There are two sorts of spotty - a big and a little.' And then, after saying the fishermen called them kelp-fish, writes: `Spotties in market 154 days' (1886,Handbook Fishes of NZ,91)

2. Mokohinou Islands . - Hapuku (or groper), hiwihiwi, barracouta, maomao, spotty, parrot-fish, leather jacket, korokoro-pounamou. Ibid. 204 12. The Brothers (Cook Strait). - Rock-cod, spotty, butter-fish, red-cod. Ibid. 211 Wrasse, or Spotty (Labrichtys bothryocosmus ). NUMBER OF FISH RECORDED - 36. LOCALITIES - Mokohinou, the Brothers, Bligh Sound, Milford Sound. (1892,TrNZI,24/203) [NOTES: (Thomson)]

Both the scientist and a well-known deep-sea angler who was consulted did not consider that "spotties would be likely to form the bulk of the food of swordfish. (Feb 7, 1939,Evening Post,15)

noun. fish type incl. brown trout

HISLOP The net was only a short one, but ... the going was good, and noon saw us back [from the Pleasant River mouth] ... with half a sack of nice flounders - a great catch which also included a few spotties; but of course these were put back into the river. (1943,Pure Gold,28)

Well out into the [Auckland] harbour was the paketi pond', where children could easily catchpaketi', as we called the fish usually called spotties' or, by the Maori, pa[macron]kirikiri. <i>(Aug 8, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),61</i>) [NOTES: SinclairAt the Point']

Each of these spots can produce spotties and herrings for the smaller kids and bigger fish like kahawai, snapper and kingfish for bigger kids and adults. (Nov 16, 2005,Western News,00)

noun. a spotlight

McGILL spotty a spotlight, often used when fishing for flounder. (1989,Dinkum Kiwi Dictionary, The,96)

noun. [Marine] occas. and locally for rig (=spotty shark)

[species name] spotty 1 .. [scientific name] -- [other name(s)] Could refer to spotty [Pseudolabrus celidotus] or rig [Mustelus lenticulatus], Hastings and New Plymouth region commonly used for rig (Jul 23, 1986,Codes for Species in NZ Waters)

[caption] "New Zealanders adore fish whether it's a spotty off the wharf or a scallop from the harbour." (Sep 3, 2006,Sunday Star Times,ESCAPE 3)

Wrasse, Parrot-fish, and Spotties were often in the market. (1878,TrNZI,11/384)

Wrasse, parrot-fish, and spotties are often in the market. There are two kinds of spotties, big and little. The Wrasse and Parrotfish are mostly caught outside among the kelp, and with the Spotty are indiscriminately named Kelp-fish by the fishermen, though the term Butterfish is also given to the smaller sorts. Notes (P. Thomson, Otago) (1879,TrNZI,11/384)

spotty shark¶

noun.

[NOTES: not clear that this is NZ term; one citation]

They prefer rig, elephant fish or spotty shark. (Nov 8, 1997,Dominion,1)

spousal maintenance¶

noun.

Proposed amendments to the Family Proceedings Act will also give a judge the power.. to order the husband (or a de facto partner) to pay the wife (or his/her de facto partner) maintenance money out of his income from the date of their separation till possibly the date of their deaths. Such a payment is called spousal maintenance. (Jun 1, 2000,Dominion,8)

spout wind¶

noun.

First the nor'-wester, chased the flames for a mile or two; then when the people began to breathe a little freely, the wind chopped round to sou'-west, and blew as only a "spout-wind" can, and drove the fire back again. (Jan 28, 1908,Nelson Evening Mail,2)

When the first big fire occurred in Nelson in August, 1866, that town was in as helpless a state as Havelock is now. A "spout" wind was blowing, and eighteen houses were destroyed. (Jun 24, 1885,Marlborough Express,2)

Clothes fire-dried, and off next morning through miles of the Hope Saddle porridge, tons of rain, and overgrown cycles of keen spout wind. (Sep 16, 1897,Otago Witness,23)

HODDER [The Waimea] is visited by a strong local wind, which blows with considerable violence, especially during the summer months. It is called the `spout wind', and is attributable to the peculiar configuration of the mountain ranges. (1862,Memories of NZ Life,46)

G.M. WILSON (Nelson) There was a pretty strong wind blowing, what they call a `spout wind' from the fact of its coming down the valley on the town. (Feb 14, 1873,Diary) [NOTES: 1873 Feb 14 G.M.Wilson Diary in 1973 Wierzbicka Wilson Family 177]

HOOD Nelson, though it has its `spout wind' possesses generally a happy freedom from destructive gales. (1875,Chowbokiana,77)

spouter¶

noun. a whaling ship

MANSON Port Underwood itself, puncturing the northern end of Cloudy Bay, was a hub of activity in 1842, with sometimes large numbers of whaling ships - or `spouters' - of many nations lying at anchor for the season. (1981,Widow of Thorndon Quay,2) [NOTES: [c1842]]

noun. [Rural] a person involved in spout-washing sheep in the late 1800s.

The wet-chuckers-in, from their pulpit-like pen above, can see when either pair of spouters has finished a sheep, and their duty is to keep the supply up to the demand. Each spouter is professedly [sic] provided with a complete waterproof suit - sou'wester, gum-boots, and oilskin coat .. When the spouters have placed a sheep in position under the spout ... (1888,Textile Educator I,278)

BREMNER Each well had two spouts of cold water and four hands called 'spouters' who tilted the sheep, parting the wool to rinse out all the grass seed, sand, sticks, bark and thistles. (1985,Woolscours of NZ,15)

spout-wash¶

verb. [Rural] to wash sheep prior to shearing, using a concentrated spray of water in a large bath.

WILSON & FRASER At first the sheep were spout-washed before being shorn. (1936,Book of the Pioneers, The,6)

spout-washer¶

noun. [Rural] a person who washes sheeps using a channel or spout from above.

The spout-washers admitted losses of one per cent, the river-washing lost half per cent. During the operation of washing sheep, some of them sicken, as washers term it, and a few faint ... (Aug 20, 1864,Weekly News,8)

spout-washing¶

noun. [Rural] the washing of sheep with water directed through a spout or channel from above.

Spout washings have their advocate. The spout-washers admitted losses of one per cent, the river-washing lost half per cent. During the operation of washing sheep, some of them sicken, as washers term it, and a few faint ... (Aug 1864,Weekly News,20)

WILSON & FRASER To enable washed sheep to get to the shed clean, the land in that part was held back until the last sale, and with that sale, spout-washing ceased. (1936,Book of the Pioneers, The,6)

CRAWFORD Another method was 'spout washing.' Each sheep after swimming about and soaking for five minutes was brought under a shoot of water falling from a height of about 2 feet. (1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,42)

sprag¶

noun. a spike inserted in a spoke to lock the wheel

Witness did not think the accident would have occurred if a sprag were used, but sprags were never used, although timber was always available. (Sep 10, 1896,Otago Witness,10)

FAILING TO SPRAG. Before Mr W.G. Kenrick S.M. at the Magistrate's Court on Monday the Inspector of Mines (Mr R. Tennent) charged Steve Fenette and John Duggan (Blackball miners) with a breach of the Coal Mining Act, wherein they failed to put one sprag in "holeing" for the first 10ft and one sprag for each additional 5ft in accordance with Rule 36. (Oct 25, 1905,Grey River Argus,4)

A sprag was put in to ensure safety. The neglect of putting sprags in was a danger to life. (Jan 24, 1911,Grey River Argus,1)

I was round the whole of the working faces yesterday (Thursday), and I had occasion to caution many of the men about not setting "sprags," and I believe the deceased was one of them. (Apr 1, 1882,Grey River Argus,2)

MAHONEY Four brake systems were in common use : sprags which were bars jammed in the spokes of the wheels, wooden brake shoes applied to the tread of the wheels, wooden board brakes applied to the face of the wheels, and centre rail brakes. (1998,Era of the Bush Trams in NZ, The,17)

LAWRY Will backed the dray up carefully, the sprag was checked in position, and Bill and Lynn started unloading the rocks. (1850,Good Luck & Lavender,46)

sprag n. in mining, etc., a piece of wood inserted between a rope and its pulley to prevent movement. (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11)

MORRIS Sprag, n. In gold-mining. See quotation. The word is used in England, applied to coal-mining. (1898,Austral English,431)

PEARSON Fred with an eye torn out when a badly-aimed sprag flew back from the spoke of a downhill truck. 1963 Ibid. 421 [gloss] sprag: A piece of metal or wood inserted between the spokes of the wheel of a moving truck in order to brake it. (1963,Coal Flat,205)

If a race has to be halted, the simplest way to hold it is to lock the wheels on one of the boxes. This is done by inserting a short sword-like piece of steel into the wheel-spokes. Once again, the north-of-England dialect comes into play and the piece of steel is known as a sprag . Its smaller brother, the sprig (though it has acquired a new meaning on the football field), was originally a short headless nail, a sprig being essentially a smaller sprag. (May 2, 1981,Listener (New Zealand Listener),43) [NOTES: [I.A.Gordon: West Coast Strongman Mine]]

A check was made by the officer in charge before any action was taken and the list of refuse put out at night includes stuff that is patently trade refuse, sawdust, cardboard boxes, leather clippings, and sprags, shop sweepings, and flower discards, but paper was the biggest item by far. (Nov 29, 1939,Evening Post,11)

"The problem," said Mr. McKeen, "has become more and more one for State enterprise, and if the Opposition would co-operate instead of attempting to put a sprag in the wheel of further progress we would be getting somewhere." (Aug 31, 1944,Evening Post,6)

verb. to catch, spike, snag the flesh or clothing on a protruding spike of wire, metal, etc.

[NOTES: (The NZ sense of sprag n and v would seem to derived from a dialect variant of sprig : cf. EDD sb4, and vb 8. and OED sprig sb 2. The NZ sense possibly also associated with SNAG, SNIG, STAG (q.v.), and stake , of similar meaning. EDD sprag sb2 citation looks suspiciously close to the NZ sense, though the Yks sense given suggests otherwise.) ca1900 at least Havelock (W.H.B. Orsman)]

THOMSON All he did was sprag the wheels, he put a bit of timber through and locked the back wheels. (1986,Haliburtons of Glenfarg,36)

The man [pulling the end of the wire rope out of the `eye'] has to stand on the logs as they float and risk getting spragged on the wire rope. (1954,NZ Forest Services Report) [NOTES: 1954 NZ Forest Service Report (TS)]

While hauling out a winch-rope [sc. a wire rope], I spragged my fore-finger through the glove I was wearing.' <i>Comment </i>. [by the authority]The wire spragg [sic] became embedded in [X's] finger.' (Nov 23, 1957,NZ Forest Services Report) [NOTES: 1957 Nov 23 NZ Forest Service Accident Report (Nelson)]

verb.

So it is with the present Upper House. You are apt to froget [sic] there is such a thing, till you find the chariot of progress has both wheels spragged! (Nov 11, 1920,Grey River Argus,5)

Several wheels were "spragged" and a start made. (May 27, 1869,Daily Southern Cross,4)

The trial was one ton weight, in a waggon with all the wheels spragged. (Dec 14, 1878,Otago Witness,4)

NEWTON ... I am told that in descending into the Stanley, they spragged the [waggon's] wheels and simply dragged it straight down through the shingle. (1952,High Country Journey,184)

DEWAR The most advanced innovation on this line was the dobbin, a wheeled truck that would hold about a yard of material. It was run on wooden rails extending from the cutting face to the adjacent gully or filling and added to as the work advanced, ... [114] ... On reaching the end of its run the dobbin was either spragged or tipped by means of a cradle. (1953,Chaslands,113)

The trial [of horses] was one tonne [sic] weight in a wagon with all the wheels spragged. (1914,History of North Otago,182,1978) [NOTES: 1878 Nov 28 in 1914 History of North Otago (1978) 182]

G. W. Johnson's working life 1940-46. Take a bit of four by two and sprag it through the wheels of the slip truck. (Nov 12, 1983,Radio NZ / National Radio) [NOTES: 1983 Nov 12 2YA Wellington 9.15 am: Spectrum Docmentary:]

noun. usually a sharp strand protruding from a wire rope, or the sharp end of a piece of wire or jagged metal, which can enter and so catch or `snag', or spike one's flesh, clothing, etc.

While hauling out a winch-rope [sc. a wire rope], I spragged my fore-finger through the glove I was wearing.' <i>Comment </i>. [by the authority]The wire spragg [sic] became embedded in [X's] finger.' (Nov 23, 1957,NZ Forest Services Report) [NOTES: 1957 Nov 23 NZ Forest Service Accident Report (Nelson)]

sprag-hand¶

noun. a septic condition (mainly wire-rope handlers) caused by spragging on wire-ropes

[a gear-store is an equipment store from which stevedores draw the slings, nets, etc for their work] For all these long years I've been lumbered/ With Gear-Store related complaints./ From `spragg-hand' through handling bum wires,/ To throwing-up, wobblies and faints./ (May 1985,Ship 'n Shore,7)

sprat¶

noun. also called kupae a small, edible, marine fish, related to the herring

A sort of basket work is now a great deal seen as a head-dress, and in these cases it is stewed over with a little silver fish, something like a common sprat, which gives it a light and graceful character. (Jul 9, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3)

The first specimen was brought to me on the 6th of September last, and in every respect appeared to me to resemble the clupea sprattus, or common sprat. (Nov 15, 1843,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2)

SHERRIN SPRAT (Clupea sprattus ). ... [94] Sprats are called kupai by the Natives at the Thames, and are found in great abundance - in tons, Mr. Masefield says - in the early months of the year in the Kaipara waters. Ibid. 306 Clupea sprattus L. Sprat, or Kupai (1886,Handbook Fishes of NZ,92, 94)

  1. Moeraki . - Rock-cod, gurnard, parrot-fish, butter-fish, sprats, conger-eel (1892,TrNZI,24/204) [NOTES: (Thomson)]

The following is a list of the fishes which are chiefly met with in the market: hapuku, kahawai, red-snapper, snapper, tarakihi, moki, trumpeter, frostfish ... gurnard, mullet, sea-mullet, ... flounder or patiki, ... grayling, smelt, kokopu, sardine, sprat, eel (tuna), black-eel, conger-eel [168], and silver-eel. (1892,NZ Official Handbook,167)

DRUMMOND & HUTTON ...the sprats, which come into shallow water in the winter. (1902,Nature in NZ)

Harengula Antipoda ... Sprat. (1911,Records of the Canterbury Museum,1/160) [NOTES: Waite]

Amblygaster antipodus Hector. The sprat, which is very common on the east coast ... is frequently mistaken for the [Clupea neopilchardus ] species. (1913,TrNZI,45/234) [NOTES: (Thomson, Otago)]

There appear to be three species of fish belonging to the family Clupeidae in New Zealand waters, viz., Engraulis antipodum , or anchovy; Sardinia neopilchardus , or pilchard, and Harengula antipoda , or sprat. Ibid. 316 The sprat is the smaller of the two, but in the numerous notices of these fish, the name `sprat' probably includes in many cases immature pilchards. Ibid. 319 In the case of fish-stomachs examined at the station, sprats have been found in red cod, blue cod, southern king-fish, barracouta, and spined dog-fish; and pilchards in barracouta. (1926,TrNZI,56/314) [NOTES: (Young and Thomson)]

WILLIAMS Kupae , n. Clupea sprattus, sprat . [1957/157 Clupea antipoda ; 180 C. antipodum ] (1917,Dictionary of the Maori Language,183)

The sprat (Amblygaster antipodus ) is always abundant on the coast. (1918,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,1/137) [NOTES: (Thomson)]

CLUPEA ANTIPODA Hector. Sprat; Kupae . (Jun 1921,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,4/118) [NOTES: Phillipps Notes on the Edible Fishes]

SPEIGHT The Southern Pilchard (Sardinia neopilchardus ,...) and the New Zealand Sprat (Clupea antipodum ) are known from Canterbury,... (1927,Natural History of Canterbury,195)

PHILLIPPS Clupea antipodum (Hector). SPRAT; KUPAE. (1927,Bibliography of NZ Fishes,12,1971)

Clupea antipodum (Hector). Sprat. Kupae . (1938,TrRSNZ,68/402) [NOTES: Graham Fishes of Otago Harbour]

BEATTIE I recollect the Maoris going after sprats at Matannic ... They dried the sprats on mats and ate them dried. (1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,22)

PHILLIPPS SPRAT OR KUPAE Clupea antipodum (Hector) (1940,Fishes NZ,11)

GRAHAM Sprat Maugeclupea antipodum (Hector) (Syn. Clupea mulleri Klunzinger and C. holodon Regan) (1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,399) [NOTES: 1955 Whitley Namelist in 1956 Graham NZ Fishes 399]

GRAHAM SPRAT (KUPAE) Maugeclupea antipodum (Hector) (1956,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,102)

The tip of Point Chevalier was a park known as the Reserve', ringed with pine trees and macrocarpa which led to the Piper Rocks, where boys and men ... caught sprats and piper, which were excellent eating. <i>(Aug 8, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),61</i>) [NOTES: SinclairAt the Point']

PARROTT THE SPRAT Maugeclupea antipodum (Hector) ... Maori name: KUPAE. (1957,Sea Anglers' Fishes of NZ,26)

NATUSCH The sprat (maugeclupea ...), ... about three inches long, is smaller than the pilchard, but otherwise very much like it. (1967,Animals of NZ, The,207)

AYLING SPRAT Sprattus antipodum ... They are a deeper-bodied fish than the pilchard and are more laterally compressed, with a prominent row of scutes along the midline of the belly. (1982,Collins Guide,104,1984)

[species name] sprat .. [scientific name] Sprattus antipodum .. [other name(s)] sardine, herring (Jul 23, 1986,Codes for Species in NZ Waters)

PAUL Sprats Sprattus antipodum, S. muelleri Also called New Zealand herring, sometimes sardine. ... quite similar to Northern Hemisphere sprats. (1986,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,41)

PAUL et al. [index to common names 283-293] sprat 1638 ... [index to common names 283-293] sprat 503, 542 (1987,Fishes: A Bibliography)

noun. herring, yellow-eyed mullet, aua

SORENSON MULLET, YELLOW-EYED (a) Scientific name: Aldrichetta forsteri. (b) Suggested commercial name[s]: Sea Mullet; New Zealand Kipper (smoked); Rollmops (pickled). (c) Other common names: Herring (in error and best dropped); Common Mullet; Sprat (in error). (d) Principal localities where taken: Tauranga, kaipara, lake Ellesmere. ... The name `Herring' has been applied widely and for a long time to the New Zealand Yelloweyed Mullet which is not a Clupeid and therefore only very distantly related to the true Herring of European waters. (1970,Nomenclature of NZ Fish,39)

WILSON HERRING More often than not a Yelloweye Mullet, but the fish that is widely known as the herring' in our coastal waters. Also known assprat', though this term also covers the young of several species including anchovy, yelloweye mullet and several other small fish. There are only two, true' herrings in our waters. <i>Ibid.</i>164 The Yellow-Eye has a much narrower head than the Grey and is the ubiquitous, but misnamedsprat' or `herring' of our wharves. Ibid.243 SPRAT: see Yellow Mullet (1981,Fisherman's Bible,120)

English Name Native Name ... ... Sprat or Sardine Aua ... (1849,NZ Journal,9/125) [NOTES: 1849 NZ Journal (Vol. IX) 125 (quoting Anglo Maori Warder Oct 5)]

DOOGUE & MORELAND YELLOWEYE MULLET ... Other names: Aldrichetta forsteri ; herring, common mullet, sprat; sea mullet, river mullet (Australia); aua (Maori). (1966,Sea Anglers' Guide,220)

McLINTOCK Sprat .. .. kupae .. .. Clupea antipodum (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/705-712)

MORELAND YELLOWEYE MULLET [Aldrichetta forsteri ] ... Other names are herring, common mullet, and sprat. (1967,Marine Fishes,48)

PAUL Yellow-eyed mullet Aldrichetta forsteris ... Often incorrectly called herring or sprat in New Zealand. (1986,NZ Fishes: An Identification Guide,113)

SORENSON ANCHOVY (a) Scientific name: Engraulis australis. (b) Suggested commercial name[s]: Anchovy. (c) Other common names: the following names of related Clupeids and Engraulid fish are sometimes applied to anchovy - Herring, Sprat, Sardine, Pilchard, although the true Herring of European waters (Clupea harengus ), does not occur in New Zealand. (d) Principal localities where taken: Hauraki Gulf, Gisborne, Tasman Bay, Marlborough Sounds. (1970,Nomenclature of NZ Fish,10)

noun.

[NOTES: pilchard and general, one citation]

SORENSON PILCHARD (a) Scientific name: Sardinops neopilchardus . (b) Suggested commercial name[s]: Pilchard; Sardine. (c) Other common names: Sardine; Sprat; Anchovy; Herring. (d) Principal localities where taken: Auckland, Gisborne, Tasman Bay, Marlborough Sounds. (1970,Nomenclature of NZ Fish,40)

spray¶

noun. a reprimand, a telling-off

[Hdg] MG gives spray. Mark Geyer never minds giving anyone a serve. (Apr 25, 2004,Sunday Times (NZ),B7)

"Lauiti'ti got a spray at halftime, and I didn't think he did anything in the second half." (Aug 3, 2003,Sunday Star Times,B1)

Key forward Ali Lauiti'iti said the "spray" he got last weekend was deserved... After the match, coach Daniel Anderson took the unusual step of publicly reprimanding Lauiti'iti, describing the normally block-busting second rower as "a non-entity tonight". (Aug 9, 2003,Dominion Post,D4)

A public spray can quite often have a reverse effect on the individual whereas a good one-to-one, honest and constructive discussion can be far more effective and allows the player to retain his pride. (Aug 10, 2003,Sunday Star Times,B6)

spray dip¶

noun.

Warekauhau has a spray dip so the sheep are not actually dunked. (1987,Country Calendar (TVNZ),124)

spray-dip¶

noun. [Rural] a system of cleansing sheep of keds, lice and other parasites using an overhead spray.

See: sheep shower

GASCOIGNE The introduction of spray-dips a few years ago, whereby sheep arerun through on the level or held in a tank while the spray jets function, made an easy task of dipping. (1965,From the Top of a Hill,33)

GASCOIGNE But spray-dips, for better or worse, were still in the future in this last year of Manu's stewardship with me. (1965,From the Top of a Hill,34)

verb. [Rural] to spray animals with insecticide.

COOP The ideal solution to the dipping problem would be to spray-dip off shears ... (1959,Shearing Ewes before Lambing,26)

spray-dipping¶

noun. [Rural] the spraying of sheep with an anti-insecticide.

[NOTES: anti?-insecticide]

COOP With spray-dipping the situation is slightly different as the length of wool makes penetration of the dip to the skin very difficult. (1950,Shearing Ewes before Lambing,26)

The term 'dip' is a hangover from when plunge dipping was the only option - it has latterly been joined first by spray-dipping and now by the pour-ons. [spray-dipping] (Aug 1987,NZ Journal of Agriculture,36)

noun.

Spray Dipping proved to be not only quicker and better, ut the cost of dipping per sheep was substantially lower than other methods. (Jan 1960,NZ Dairy Exporter,20)

spraydrift¶

noun. airborne industrial or agricultural chemical spray

Spraydrift from 2,4-D butyl ester, our most widely used weedkiller, has been blamed for health problems ranging from cancer to headaches... Before his death, Foley had put forward a paper that reflected the industry's view of 2,4-D - that is, that volatile spraydrift was causing no problems and there was no need to get rid of it. (Sep 7, 1996,Listener (New Zealand Listener),21)

spray-on¶

noun. [Rural] a systemic stock insecticide that is sprayed on to an animal's back.

For prevention [of fly strike] it is often more practical for the lifestyle farmer to use long-acting pour on or spray-on treatments. (2002,Lifestyle Farmer,Oct/Nov 62)

spread one's blanket¶

phrase. to make a (?makeshift) bed

See: spreader

CHAMIER The men ... asked permission to `spread their blankets' in the wool-shed. (1891,Philosopher Dick,415)

We are informed by a gentleman who recently visited the Thames that, notwithstanding the great number of hotels and boarding houses, the towns of Shortland and Grahamstown are at present so overfull of population that arrivals by late steamers experience the utmost difficulty in obtaining room even to spread their blankets on the bare floor. (Oct 27, 1869,Daily Southern Cross,7)

The two men spread their blankets on their vehicle's spacious interior. (Jan 23, 1941,Evening Post,7)

spreader¶

noun.

WAKEFIELD ... `spreaders' are blankets. Ibid. 1/319 Thus pigs and potatoes were respectively represented by "grunters" and "spuds"; guns, powder, blankets, pipes and tobacco, by "shooting sticks, dust, spreaders, steamers," and "weed". (1845,Adventure in NZ,1/318)

PARTRIDGE Spreader . 2. A blanket: whalers': C. 19. E.J. Wakefield' Adventure in New Zealand, 1845 (recorded by B., 1941). (1949,Dictionary of Slang Addenda,1181)

spreader n . whalers slang for a blanket. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

noun.

SLATTER Some of his best days had been spent working as a postal assistant ... He had been a spreader in the mailroom and a dragger on the landing. (1968,Pagan Game, The,85)

noun.

HENDERSON SPREADER: Three-foot stout stick fitted to rear of horses' trace chains to keep chains apart. (1961,Friends in Chains,189) [NOTES: c1900-1920 A Teamster's Glossary in 1961 Henderson Friends In Chains 189]

noun. see cit.

GORDON Spreaders : the hooks and bar for spreading back legs. (May 27, 1951,Personal Communication) [NOTES: ca1951 May 17 Feilding Freezing Works terms p.c. Colin Gordon]

noun. [Rural] a metal device used in dressing a mutton carcass.

LOUGHNAN spreader: a metal device to hold the forelegs of a mutton carcass apart to facilitate some of the dressing, particularly the Y-cut. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,77)

spreader board¶

noun. [Rural] a board fitted at the rear of a konaki, sledge or trailer, for the even spreading of animal manure on to paddocks.

The types of spreader boards in use are many and varied, some being more efficient than others. ..In this case the spreader board is 18in. to 24in. wide and 6 ft.long. The manure falls into this box and thus finds it way out through the opening between the front of the box and the spreader board ... (May 15, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,513)

spread-man¶

noun. one who inserts spreaders between the back legs of carcases

GORDON Spread-men: those who put in spreaders. (May 17, 1951,Personal Communication) [NOTES: ca1951 May 17 Feilding Freezing Works terms p.c. Colin Gordon]

spree¶

noun. in NZ from c1840 used for happy drinking bouts, as well as for shearers' and sailors' drunken orgies:

BEST [On Lieutenant Shortland's show of official force to Wellington colonists, 18--] `You may easily imagine how disappointed I was that the [Wellington] Council did not shew [sic] fight. It would have been such a spree to have blown up their magazine and besides that I should have been entitled to ?10 and 9d. per diem tentage and forage money for actual service and should also have had the pleasure of licking them, instead of which no sooner did we appear than they all sneaked off.' (1843,Letter) [NOTES: a1843 (1837-1843) Best's letters in Mitchell Library undated newspaper article in Journal (1966) 410]

CAMPBELL Sailors having ... a harsh captain, or a desire for a spree. (1840,Present State of NZ,24)

... he is altogether an adept at Colonial life. Instance, when he commences a drunken sprey (as he calls it) he invariably puts all his money into the soles of his shoes or boots, excepting that portion he intends spending .... (Jan 24, 1852,Journal) [NOTES: 1852 Jan 24 Monson's Prison Journal in 1978 Locke The Gaoler 54]

RICHARDS ... and after, perhaps three years of fearful hardship, so much of the [sealers'] money as might be uncondemned would be dissipated in Sydney in a few days' spree'. <i>(1852,Whaling and Sealing,5</i>) [NOTES: 1843 May 2 in 1863 C.HeaphyA Chapter on Sealing' Southern Monthly Magazine June I/No 4 pp173-176 in 1982 Richards Whaling and Sealing 5]

ANTHONY Mark, do you know this, I believe I'll have to break out in a good old woolly spree, pretty soon. (1936,Follow the Call,102)

PHILLIPPS J.P. who has been on the spree at W.W. is laid up with a bad head in consequence (Apr 28, 1867,Journal Kept at Rockwood and the Point,101)

WOOD Rain came at last, and with it money, and Jim settled down to a regular spree. (1875,Waiting for the Mail,106)

English people are given to associating the idea of a `spree' with that of a bacchanal orgy. Not so We. With us the word is simply colonial for a festivity of any kind, public or private. And whatever may be the primary object of a spree, it is pretty certain to end with a dance. (1882,Brighter Britain,1/272)

BEATTIE A remittance man who was in receipt of at least [pounds]400 a year from Home would go on a spree and drink [pounds]5 away every day ... (1939,First White Boy Born in Otago,55)

SLATTER I had made the money as they told me I would. So then I spent it. Not in a sudden spree like shearers come to town, but in a deliberate determination to go under and stay under. (1959,Gun in My Hand, A,13)

MANTELL Lucky we found it [an abandoned car] first ... Before some larrikins commandeered it for a joy riding spree.' (1980,Murder or Three, A,78)

ROCHFORT [We] were shortly lulled to sleep by the heavy breathing of several sailors, who had evidently just come home from a `spree'. (1853,Adventures of a Surveyor,19)

THATCHER (The Caledonian Gathering) What a jolly spree the other day,/ Don't think that I am blathering,/ I'll give you just a short account/ Of the Caledonian gathering./ (1864,Invercargill Minstrel,5)

We hope his conscience pricks him, andthat he will spend all profits made on a"spree" for the boys. (Mar 14, 1917,Chronicles NZEF,II/14 : 33)

spree-up¶

noun.

SYDER & HODGETTS A convivial gathering. .in 4;`Come round on Saturday night. We're having a bit of a spree-up because it's Tommy's last night before he goes. The beer's fixed up, bring your sax though, of course.' (1962,Australian & NZ English [TS],979,1974) [NOTES: (1962-63)1974 Syder and Hodgetts Aust. and NZ English [TS] 979]

sprig¶

noun.

[NOTES: Jim Blakeley (508 College St, Palmerston North, 5301; blakeley@ihug.co.nz) remembers pre-WWII usage of "sprigs" as opposed to "studs" in Scotland re soccor boots, also used with regard to golf shoes. "Am almost certain that the word was also used to describe the small nails that cobblers used in repairing leather shoes. Possibly derived from sprig of heather??" Alan Burnett (aged 75) writes from 21 Hector St, Herne Bay, (2/10/1999) that when he was a child in Scotland aged about 10 "we nailed SPRIGS on our soccer boots - obtained from the local cobbler.]

MOURIE & PALENSKI An air of panic descended on the room asplayers scrambled about looking for new,legal sprigs. (1982,Graham Mourie Captain,109)

McMENAMIN Hooper.. made his way to Denton Park,clutching a new pair of boots, into whichhe had not had time to insert sprigsbecause he was running late. (1986,Glory Days,28)

Men studied their sprigs intently. (Aug 4, 1984,Listener (New Zealand Listener),23)

I suspect the major difference between the two teams is that the dye on the Canadian jerseys doesn't come out in the wash and the sprigs on their boots don't bend when they run on them. (Sep 30, 1991,Listener (New Zealand Listener),20)

LISTEN! We have Men's Boots from 8s 6d, with heel tips and sprigs. (Sep 6, 1899,Tuapeka Times,4) [NOTES: Advert]

72 pairs Chrome Balmorals, heel and toe-plates, sprigs; sizes 1 to 3. (Jul 6, 1904,Otago Witness,27) [NOTES: Advert]

12 [pairs] Gents.' Shoes, Sprigs ... (Aug 16, 1853,Daily Southern Cross,1) [NOTES: Advert]

CONEY The English malthoid... almost trips me,dragging at my sprigs... Ibid. 124Like flies around an Australian, the sideclusters to borrow sprigs for a widerange of boots, and sprig tighteners formetric and AF dimensions. (1986,Playing Mantis,112)

ON SALE, at the Stores of the undersigned - Black and green teas .. an assortment of leather, hobnails, sprigs, &c. (Mar 19, 1842,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,1) [NOTES: Advert]

It's all right... You don't feel the sprigs when you're fit. (Aug 18, 1979,Listener (New Zealand Listener),13)

sprig ... NZ & Austral. (usu. pl.) stud on sole of Rugby (or soccer etc.) boot; (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,743) [NOTES: sprig ... NZ & Austral. (usu. pl.) stud on sole of Rugby (or soccer etc.) boot;]

ORBELL To overcome this difficulty.. the writer buys a pair of football boots, the sprigs are removed and a thin extra sole is fitted the full length of the boot. (1952,Comfort & Commonsense in the Bush,29)

HENDERSON The boots are very heavy, with sprigs all over the soles, and the heels have three sharp spikes to prevent slipping. (1967,Return to Open Country,70)

There are eight coots in Waikato jerseys.. with the sun gleamin' on the sprigs, which are still slightly bloody from the last game. (1976,Loosehead Len's Bumper Thump Book,7)

McLEAN At a stoppage, the natural reaction of players was to hoist one foot up, wipe the mud from the sprigs of the boot and then perform the same act for the other foot. (1977,Winter of Discontent,108)

noun. the result of sprigging in rugby union

The smell of liniment, the cry of "It'smine" and sprig marks are no longerlimited to men, with Rugby a fast-growingsport among women. (Jul 9, 1993,Evening Post,34)

Take us back to the days when ideal men were real men, hard but fair, who could carry six fence posts under each arm or do their own dentistry with a pair of pliers. In those time, sprig marks down the back and a bit of blood here or there were considered hard-won character buildings of honour. (Jan 5, 2003,Sunday Star Times,A6)

Take us back to the days when ideal men were real men, hard but fair, who could carry six fence posts under each arm or do their own dentistry with a pair of pliers. adjective.

noun.

verb. to escape from prison

spring burn¶

noun. [Rural] [S.I. high country] an annual spring burning of tussock.

Spring burns cause the destruction of all the accumulated dead material of the tussocks that are acting as a soil mulch ... (Jun 15, 1910,BLANK ENTRY,9)

The spring burns lessen the general vitality of the pasture ... (Jun 15, 1910,BLANK ENTRY,10)

spring burning¶

noun. [Rural] an annual burning of noxious pasture growth or tussock in spring.

spring calving¶

noun. calving in July and August

Most farmers plan calving for July and August (euphemistically called spring calving) to take advantage of spring grass growth, which starts in September and usually peaks in late October or November. (Mar 2003,NZ Geographic,62/26)

noun. [Rural] a stream fed by an underground spring.

PORTER As he trotted through the shallow spring creek, he stumbled on a loose boulder. (1970,Under the Nor'West Arch,30)

spring eczema¶

noun. [Rural] a photosensitive skin- and liver-damaging condition in cows and calves.

.. it doesn't explain why some calves get spring eczema while still in the rearing shed and not been out in pasture. (2001,Fencepost.com,Tony Gumboot)

spring heat¶

noun. [Rural] a period of oestrus in mares that lasts as long as four weeks.

noun. [Rural] a lamb born in early spring and fattened for the Christmas market.

noun. [Rural] a drafting or tally muster before stock are put on to summer grazing blocks.

noun.

noun.

[NOTES: ca1940 Waikato (R.C. Nelson)]

sprog: offspring, child (1980,Lynfield College, Auckland) [NOTES: (Goldie Brown Collection)]

spruce¶

noun. also as attrib spruce(-)tree se also spruce fir 1. probably =RIMU

Also began to Brew Beer with the leaves and branches of a tree which resembles the Americo black Spruce Inspissated Juce of Wort and Melasses. [fn] cf. Cooper: ` ... began to make Beer from a Tree of a Rosinish quality intermixt with the Tea Plant. [fn] Rimu Dacrydium cupressinus : Tea plant Manuka L. scoparium. (Apr 1, 1773,Cook's Journals,2/114,1961)

... the most considerable [timber] here [in Dusky Sound] ... is the spruce tree as we call'd it from the similarity of its leaves to the America black spruce, but the wood is more ponderous and of a reddish colour ... . (May 11, 1773,Cook's Journals,2/135,1961)

BAYLY The largest [NZ trees] are the spruce tree (from the tops of the branches of which we made Spruce Beer which was very good which are 12 or 14 feet round and 50 or 60 feet high and exceeding strait ...). (Apr 12, 1773,Journal) [NOTES: 1773 April 12 Bayly's Journal in 1908 McNab Historical Records 2/206]

FORS The next morning we drank Tea made of spruce which had afine [sic] taste ...[ed. fn] Dacrydium cupressinum Lamb; the Rimu or Red Pine. (Mar 29, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/243)

LEDYARD We had also made a considerable quantity of beer from the spruce of that country, which is good and in unbounded plenty. (Feb 1777,Journal,21,1963)

FORSTER ... the resemblance it bore to the fir tribe ... soon convinced us that it was fitter to serve the purposes of [130] the American spruce-tree, and that a palatable and wholesome liquor might be brewed from it, as a kind of substitute for spruce-beer. ... The spruce of New-Zeeland is a very beautiful tree, and conspicuous on account of its pendant branches ... (1777,Voyage Round the World,1/129)

BELL Many of the Trees were large enough for the Masts of Ships, - and the grain of the Spruce Tree is very close and durable. (Nov 1791,Journal of Voyage in HMS 'Chatham',50)

FORSTER The Sprucetree is not so copious [at Queen Charlotte Sound] as at Dusky Bay . The Teatree is more common than there, but for the greater part more shrubby, though there are likewise some very tall ones in this place. (Jun 8, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/296)

noun.

MENZIES We found large trees [at Dusky Bay] of what has been called New Zealand Spruce (1791,Journal) [NOTES: 1791 Menzies's Journal (Vancouver Expedition) in [?d] McNab Historical Records 2/484]

spruce beer¶

noun.

[NOTES: Cook's Journals do not appear to use the collocation spruce beer, but speak of a beer brewed from SPRUCE, among other plants.]

BELL - the Cooper was sent on shore [at Dusky Bay] to sett up the Casks - and a Party was sent Brewing Spruce Beer. Some were employed Wooding & Watering. (Nov 1791,Journal of Voyage in HMS 'Chatham',45) [NOTES: 1791 Nov Nov E.Bell Journal of Voyage in H.M.S. `Chatham' (Vancouver expedition) (MS ATB) 45]

TAY I feel assured a pleasant beverage like spruce beer might be manufactured from its [kauri] sap. (Nov 14, 1839,Journal,2/171)

WILKES They also make a pleasant beverage, resembling spruce beer, which they call wai-maori. (1852,U.S. Exploring Expedition,1/302)

SHORTLAND The leave[s] of the manuka' (<i>leptospermum scoparium </i>) furnished Captain Cook with a substitute for tea ...; and ... he used the small branches of this shrub and of the treerimu', (dacrydium cupressinum ,) in equal proportions, to make a decoction from which he brewed spruce beer, frequently referred to by him as a valuable anti-scorbatic. (1851,Southern Districts of NZ,128)

From the leaves of the rimu Cook brewed `spruce beer' (1926,TrNZI,?/662) [NOTES: Andersen Popular Names]

The captain was kept busy in other quaters - one of which was procuring a brew he called 'spruce beer' out of rimu and manuka leaves flavoured with juice of wort and mollasses for the crew. (Oct 2005,NZ Memories,No 56, p61)

It is this tree which the sawyers call the red pine; and if the tree is young, may be easily known by its branches gracefully bending downwards. Capt. Cook prepared a spruce beer out of the younger branches of this tree, of which a drawing is given in his voyage. (Sep 12, 1840,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,3)

.. its tariff is limited to the brief and ill-assorted trio of spruce beer, musical instruments, and vinegar. (Jun 17, 1859,Daily Southern Cross,3)

.. the license authorises him to sell "at the sign of the Duke of Malborough various liquors, including a ginger beer and spruce beer." (Mar 18, 1908,Grey River Argus,3)

TO THE PUBLICANS AND STOREKEEPERS ON THE DIGGINGS .. always on Sale - .. ginger beer, spruce beer, lemonade ... (Dec 30, 1857,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

FORSTER reference to American beer ... the resemblance it bore to the fir tribe ... soon convinced us that it was fitter to serve the purposes of [130] the American spruce-tree, and that a palatable and wholesome liquor might be brewed from it, as a kind of substitute for spruce-beer. ... The spruce of New-Zeeland is a very beautiful tree, and conspicuous on account of its pendant branches ... Ibid. I/143 But the constant supply of fresh fish ... together with the spruce-beer and the myrtle-tea, contributed to keep us healthy ... even in this damp climate. (1777,Voyage Round the World,1/129)

BAYLY The largest [NZ trees] are the spruce tree (from the tops of the branches of which we made Spruce Beer which was very good which are 12 or 14 feet round and 50 or 60 feet high and exceeding strait ...). (Apr 12, 1773,Journal) [NOTES: 1773 April 12 Bayly's Journal in 1908 McNab Historical Records 2/206]

FORSTER The fresh water river was another animated Scene of Business: a brewery provided a salutary & palatable potion from [266]the decoction of spruce & New-Zeeland Tea mixed with the Essence of malt & Melasses for our Ships-Company. (Apr 24, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/265)

FORSTER A little brandy & water commonly called grog [by the seamen] or Spruce beer with a little brandy & sugar commonly called kalibogas is the liquor drank on these [`Marooning'] Expeditions. (May 7, 1773,Resolution Journal of J.R. Forster, The,2/271)

EDGAR Since our arrival a great number of the new [sic] Zealanders have come from different parts of the Sound and taken up their abode in Ship Cove - we were now busily employ'd in cutting Wood compleating our Water - brewing Spruce Beer - boiling down the Blubber we got at the Island of Desolation, making Hay, repairing our rigging Sails &c. (Feb 12, 1777,Log) [NOTES: 1777 Feb 12 Thomas Edgar's Log in 1908 McNab Historical Records 2/227]

H. SHUTTLEWORTH, MANUFACTURER OF CORDIALS AND MINERAL WATERS, DEVON AND QUEEN STREETS, NEW PLYMOUTH. SODA WATER .. Spruce beer ... (Aug 29, 1863,Taranaki Herald,4)

spruce fir¶

noun. rimu

This species of Dacrydium [cupressinium] is the one mentioned by Captain Cook as the Spruce Fir of New Zealand. (Oct 6, 1841,New Zealand Gazette & Wellington Spectator,2)

SEEDS on SALE, ex John Philips .. 1 [lb.] Spruce Fir ... (Jun 12, 1852,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,61) [NOTES: Advert]

1 CASE CHOICE ORNAMENTAL SHRUBS, &c., from the Nursery of J. HENRY AND CO., Taranaki, comprising .. Rhododendrons, Variegated Flax, Crinums, Spruce Fir ... (Jul 24, 1869,Daily Southern Cross,2) [NOTES: Advert]

A number of American plants were pointed out, all doing well, and there is a spruce fir in a most healthy state. (Mar 19, 1870,Otago Witness,6)

CAPTAIN RAVEN [? rimu] She [a ship built in Dusky Bay] is planked, decked, and ceiled with the spruce fir, which in the opinion of the carpenter is very little inferior to English oak. There are various kinds of timber in Dusky Bay, but that which is principally fit for shipbuilding is the spruce fir, which may be cut along the shore in any quantity or size for the construction of vessels from a first-rate to a small wherry. ...[179] Tea they made from the spruce and tea-trees. (Nov 2, 1793,Letter) [NOTES: 1793 Nov 2 CAPTAIN RAVEN to Lieutenant-Governor King in 1908 McNab Historical Records I/178, 179]

NICHOLAS Of the other trees noticed by Capt. Cook ... is one resembling the American spruce fir, and from the leaves of which a very wholesome liquor was brewed. This was called the New Zealand spruce fir, from its similarity to the former tree, ... growing to a great height, with long pendant branches, covered with articulated leaves in a flourishing state of verdure. (1817,New Zealand (various authors/titles),2/247)

noun.

To do my job properly, I had to pick up the meaning of spruik along with such things as the subtle differences between a galah, a ning nong and a nong. Mostly, it came up as the noun spruiker, a loud talker advertising snake oil or aggressively pushing some line at a meeting. Australians use spruiker as Americans use spieler and huckster, as a sort of alternative to spin doctor. It is also occasionally heard in New Zealand. (Jul 28, 2004,Dominion Post,B5)

Spud Monday¶

noun. [Rural] the first Monday in August when Nelsonians traditionally plant early potatoes.

A Nelsonian became quite excited theother week and informed us all Nelsonwould be holding holiday that day. Shesaid they called it "Spud Monday" in thegarden province because it was the firstday of spring and the new potatoes wereto be planted that week. (Sep 14, 1927,NZ Tablet,58)

Nelson has always observed the first Monday in August as a holiday, for no other apparent reason than that it is a great holiday in the Old Country. In Nelson they call it "Spud Monday," because advantage is generally taken of it to plant early potatoes. (Aug 17, 1910,Poverty Bay Herald,3)

Do you come from Sunny Nelson, and, if so, did you, as a staunch Nelsonite, plant "spuds" on Spud Monday - the first Monday in August? (Sep 26, 1942,Evening Post,6)

Until comparatively recently Nelson observed the first Monday in August as a provincial holiday, after the English custom of its observance as bank holiday. Locally styled as "Spud Monday," this day has become the accepted time for the general planting of early home garden potatoes. (Aug 15, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,154)

It was Spud Monday in Nelson this week so it's a reminder for us to buy seed potatoes to get them greened up for planting ... (Jul 29, 2004,Hawera Star,32)

When supplies came, the half-starving community declared a holiday and a feast- of potatoes. This day which coincided with England's August Bank Holiday was thereafter held asSpud Monday' (Oct 1978,PSA Journal,14)

spur¶

noun. a branch or offshoot of a reef; ??=leader

VICTORIAN MINER Any reefs that may be found in this part of the country will not prove reefs in the true sense of the word but mere spurs' orleaders', and these much broken and full of `faults' (1862,Rambles through Goldfields) [NOTES: (Otago Times)]

noun. a ridge or side hill; in NZ one would probably `go up a spur to get on to a (main) ridge'

SHAW The mountains of New Zealand have a peculiarity of shape which I have never seen in any other part of the world. This singular feature consists in part from numerous spurs which branch off in every possible direction. (1858,Gallop to the Antipodes, A,156)

The Waipa is believed to rise in the high snowy mountains behind Tui, which are part of a range, being a spur from the great range or backbone of this island. (1838,Journal of Royal Geog. Society,8/418)

PFAFF He and three mates were encamped on a leading spur running down to the river. (1914,Diggers' Story, The,122)

HARPER The rough spurs were where the rabbits were. (1967,Kettle on the Fuchsia, The,91) [NOTES: Quote from Tripp 1889]

LANCASTER I was thinking t' build on the mic-a-mic spur. (1904,Sons o' Men,292)

His house is at the foot of a high spur. (Mar 22, 1873,Auckland Weekly News,20)

SY MONDS The Waipa is believed to rise in the high snowy mountains behind Tui, which are part of a range, being a spur from the great range or back-bone of the island. (1838,Cloudy Bay,?26,1979)

MATHEW The Hills [76] are lofty ... rising rapidly ... and forming an endless variety of `spurs', which are partially clothed in Timber, but chiefly with fern alone. (Mar 11, 1840,Journal) [NOTES: 1840 Mar 11 F.Mathew Journal in 1940 Founding of NZ 75-76]

WAKEFIELD ...steep spurs from the high mountains ... come down into the sea. (1848,Handbook for New Zealand, The,235)

After keeping the ridge for about two miles, the path turns down a spur, which is about two miles in length, ... (Jan 25, 1851,Lyttelton Times,6)

SHORTLAND The descent we found more steep and rugged; the northern slope of the hill having no friendly spur near us, such as that along which we had ascended, did not offer the same facility for making a road. (1851,Southern Districts of NZ,173)

W.H.S. ROBERTS We often went a long way down the wrong spur, and had to return, as we could never cross any swamps between the low ridges. (Aug 3, 1856,Diary) [NOTES: 1856 July 3 W.H.S. Roberts Diary in 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 23]

looked for lambs but could find no tracks. ... he has been told ... that a small mob of weaners are just to the right of the dray spur on the rough ridge. (May 2, 1861,Puketoi Station Diary)

Went on the hills burning and Greenly lit a fire on a spur that had grass and flax six feet high on it. (Oct 3, 1865,Chudleigh Diary,201,1950)

BARKER ... shut in gradually from our view by spurs of hills running down to the shore, sometimes in bold steep cliffs, and again in gentle declivities, with little strips of bush or scrub growing in the steep gullies between them. (1867,Station Life in NZ,116,1870)

The scene opens on a rolling plain, flanked by rocky spurs' of the ever-present mountains; a plain of unequal surface, broken byterraces', and watercourses, and of varying width - irregular. (1873,Wild Will Enderby,3/iii/81,(1889,1974))

KENNAWAY ... the hill-spurs get steeper, and the gorges get deeper, ... (1874,Crusts: a settler's fare due south,184)

TOMLINSON Long tussock-covered spurs about a mile long, reached to the top on both sides. (1968,Remembered Trails,40)

In 1868 my orders were to ... see that ... no hill or spur had more sheep on it than it could well carry. (1907,TrNZI,39/73)

Spurs are good travelling to lead to thegrassland up above. (1939,Canterbury Mountaineer, The,VIII/93)

FROBISHER [He] proceeded to scale the steep ferny face of the spur. (1893,Sketches of Gossipton,42)

noun. [Rural] [hill country mustering] a ridge or side hill.

MCKEE WRIGHT New fences climb the warm brown spurs to guard the scrubber ewes. (1898,Station Ballads,46)

GUTHRIE-SMITH .. sledged posts from Tylee's spur and cut some Kohi posts for the horse paddock. (1926,Tutira,122)

MARTIN If the 'face' was not large, only a top beat and bottom beat would be necessary, but usually the 'spurs' had to be sidled or traversed across by several men. (1990,Forgotten Worker, The,64)

DOMINY .. sheer rock above me and a grassy basin defined by steep shingly spurs ... (2001,Calling the Station Home,175)

Square Dinks¶

noun.

[NOTES: WW1]

AITKEN Next came the New Zealand Rifle Brigade from Mersa Matruh, first the 2nd Battalion, nicknamed the Square Dinks' (asquare dinkum bloke' being idiomatic Australian for a genuine fellow) from the distinctive black patch on the upper sleeve; later the `Diamond Dinks', who wore a diamond patch and had been in action with British and Sikhs in the defeat of the Senussi on Christmas Day. The alternative name of the Rifle Brigade, the E.L.O. (the Earl of Liverpool's Own) had been quietly allowed to lapse. (1963,Gallipoli to the Somme,46)

noun.

noun. often renting from the Crown vast tracts of land for pasturage at an almost nominal sum. The term is still frequently, but incorrectly, used for a man rearing and running stock on freehold land.Pastoralist is now the more favoured term.

squatter ... NZ & Austral. hist. settler having no formal or legal title to land occupied by him, or later one occupying pastoral land as tenant of the Crown; Australian sheep-farmer, esp. on a large scale. Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term forrunholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., flock owners,'flock masters,' pastoralists,'run holders,' run owners,'sheep owners,' sheep holders,'sheep masters,' squatters,'station holders,' station owners,'stock holders,[sic] and stock owners.' The wordsheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... [12] Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `runholder' was the most used, and it is the word that I think should be substituted. (1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11)

Squat́.ter (-t&etilde.r), n. [Add.] 3 . The owner or occupant of a sheep run; a sheep farmer. In Australia the word had at first the sense of a settler without title; but its use was gradually extended to persons who occupied crown land for sheep raising under a lease or a license, and afterwards to those also who held their sheep runs as freehold. Finally the word became the common name for a sheep farmer, whether occupying leasehold or freehold property. It is, however, giving way to the newer term pastoralist . (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031)

stabknife¶

noun. stagknife

SUTTON-SMITH Stagknife (K-31), a universal game of nineteenth-century childhood, was important because it was played with the most treasured play object of all boys, the pocket knife. Although known in nearly all parts of New Zealand by the name of Stagknife, the game was also known as Bites, Jackknife, Stabknife, Knifey, Momley Peg, and Throwing the Knife. ... There were generally two players ... who each sought to deflect the point of the pocket knife from certain parts of the body by a flick of the hand in such a way that the blade would stick firmly into the ground. ... Every movement had to be done three times. SUTTON-SMITH Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as taw' orshooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; dubs',dates', stakes',dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. stal¶

noun. cavers' elliptical for stalagmite and stalactite

These tubes eventually disappear under a growth of crystals and become stalactites. The water dripping from their tips releases still more calcium carbon as it hits the floor directly below, forming stalagmites, sometimes mirror images of the stalactites above. This process, repeated in its infinite variations, can produce an exquisite cave decor, a tanbtalising display of beauty comparable perhaps only with the artwork of hoar frost. But the "stals," as they are commonly known, are not just aesthetic; stored within them is a wealth of geological and climatic information. "The cross section of a stal shows annual growth rings [25] just like those of a tree trunk,"... (Apr 1997,NZ Geographic,No. 34/34)

stalling¶

noun.

noun.

New Zealand's 100,000 Polynesian natives have long been Labor's pets, benefit especially from family payments of ten shillings a week per child, which they call `stallion money' [check details???] (1950,Time (NZ edition))

stamp¶

noun.

McARA Stamps: The stamps pulverised the ore after it had passed through the crushers and been reduced to minus-two-and-a-half-inch size. They crushed it to a pulp, with water, until it passed through the 10-mesh (to the linear inch) screens on the mortar-box. There were five stamps (each weighing 1250 lb) to a mortar-box and they operated at 110 drops a minute from a height of 8 ins, crushing approximately 7 tons per 24-hour-day. They were driven by a camshaft, tappets attached to the long stamp stems being lifted in a particular sequence and then the whole weight of the stamp allowed to fall on the ore. Wear of iron was approximately half a pound per ton of ore crushed; the shoes and dies were cast in the Waikino foundry. (1978,Gold Mining at Waihi (Glossary),333)

NOLAN Stamp: a heavy weight, operated by machinery, used to crush ore in a stamping battery. (1983,Gold Fossicker's Handbook,113)

The battery consisted of ten head of stamps, of a very old type, driven by a traction engine. (1935,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,16/111)

noun.

HOCKEN A bare-faced attempt was made to enrol the Maoris, who ... were considered to be householders ... within the meaning of the Act. To secure their votes the `flour and sugar' policy was resorted to. It was known that the names of many persons of the right colour - or stamp as it was then called - but ineligible would be forwarded for enrolment, ... (1898,Contributions to the Early History of New Zealand,144)

stamp mill¶

noun.

stamper¶

noun.

COLIN GORDON The carcases are washed and wiped by a wiper, then a stringer, generally a boy, puts strings on the front legs and necks, and they go over to the clock which counts them. The carcases then go to the pusher-up who pushes them along to the scales to be weighed and graded. A stamper stamps the carcases and a ticket-boy puts a grade ticket on them out at the scales after the grader has graded them for weight and size. (May 17, 1951,Personal Communication) [NOTES: ca1951 May 17 Feilding Freezing Works terms p.c. Colin Gordon]

noun.

Kurunui Battery ... of six stampers, and one stamper specimen battery with Berdans at the end of tables to grind the tailings. ... The battery has three stampers in each box, double cams, quickslver placed in battery boxes, grating perpendicular, with round holes. The copper-plate tables are about 12ft. long by 5ft. wide, and raised about 14in. above the blanket boards; ... [The blankets] appear to be ordinary grey blankets of a very inferior description. (1868,Thames Miner's Guide, The,93)

BAINES Seth never worked the machine when the wind would have carried the thump of the stamper in the direction of the mill, ... (1874,Edward Crewe,261)

HAY The next objects of interest are the quartz-crushing batteries. ... The smallest has four stampers, and the largest sixty-two. (1882,Brighter Britain,2/279)

'H' (1898,Grain of Gold, The,5) [NOTES: [see cit. crushing room]]

HENDERSON STAMPER: Heavy weight used to crush quartz. (1961,Friends in Chains,189)

There are 200 stampers in these [Waihi] works. We saw the whole process from rock to gold. (May 15, 1987,Chudleigh Diary,441,1950)

The mill on the Hauraki claim consists of a fifteen-stamper battery, Wilfley, vanner, berdans, and accessories. (1907,NZ Geol. Survey Bulletin,No.4 (NS) 112) [NOTES: [Coromandel]]

The crushing machinery in all these batteries consisted of four to ten heads of light stamps, and the gold-saving plant of amalgamated copper plates, with or without the addition of a small berdan. (1908,NZ Geol. Survey Bulletin,No.6 (NS) 26) [NOTES: [Mikonui]]

stamper, stamphead n.apparatus for reducing quartz to fine sand. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

stamper, stamphead n. apparatus for reducing quartz to fine sand. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

Stampers : Part of the machinery used to crush the ore at the battery. (Sep 1999,Ohinemuri Regional History Journal,43 : 14)

Over the next few decades, Prices produced hundreds of stamper batteries for crushing rock,...berdans (devices for separating gold dust from crushed rock), steam engines [79] and boilers for the goldfields at Thames and later those at Te Aroha and Waihi. (Apr 1997,NZ Geographic,No. 34/78)

noun. the space occupied by a shearer on the shearing-board; position occupied by a shearer on the BOARD; espec GET A STAND, to be taken on as a shearer, to get a job shearing; the area immediately surrounding an individual shearing machine in a shearing shed [AND 1888]

Leptoscopus , stargazer; b. Geniagnus, catfish; c. Kathetostoma , flathead or Chinaman). (1967,Animals of NZ, The,222)

WILSON Most gurnards are brownish-red but larger specimens are often bright red on top and white below. The Stargazer is sometimes known as the Mud Gurnad, River Gurnard or Mud-Grubber Gurnard but is in fact no relation. This was called the start, and the bullocks were coupled together by a chain with a hook on each end and approximately 9 foot long (that was the coupling chain). It was hooked into the back link of the start on one pair and the front link of the start of the pair immediately behind them, and so on with the next pair. State farm¶

noun. [obsolete]

[NOTES: farm owned and run by the state (possibly to provide employment) Check MacGibbon's State Farm Bill of approx 1896]

STATE FARMS. ... The Hon. Mr. J. Mckenzie, Minister of Lands, has successfully initiated a system of paying parties of working-men to fell bush on Crown lands, giving to these men the option of choice of lands so felled and cleared. ... A State Farm proper of about 1,000 acres has been commenced at Levin ... Fifty-two men, eight women, and twenty-five children are on the ground, the men doing the preparatory work, cutting roads ... , felling bush ... getting ready for starting the permanent homestead. ... [244] It is the intention of the Government, when, after some years, the farm has been cleared of bush and brought under cultivation, to make its working purely co-operative. ... There is every probability that the State Farm will become a paying investment on the capital expended, as well as an outlet for ... labour - viz., that of elderly men - which cannot find occupation elsewhere in times of pressure ... (1894,NZ Official Yearbook,243)

STATE FARMS. The Minister of Lands has successfully initiated a system of paying parties of working-men to fell bush on Crown lands, giving to these men the option of choice of lands so felled and cleared. Ibid. H6/3 A State Farm proper of about 1,000 acres has been commenced at Levin... Fifty-two men, eight women, and twenty-five children are on the ground, the men doing the preparatory work, cutting roads through the forest, felling bush for burning, planting orchards, &c.. getting ready for the permanent homestead to be laid out... The State Farm is directed by an able agriculturalist as Manager, who is appointed by the Government... There is every probability that the State farm will become a paying investment on the capital expended, as well as an outlet for a description of labour - viz., that of elderly men - which cannot find occupation elsewhere in times of pressure, but which has deserved well of the colony by previous long and hard service. (1894,AJHR,H6/2)
