MORRIS originally the house with the necessary buildings and home-premises of a sheep-run, and still used in that sense; but now more generally signifying the run and all that goes with it, Stations are distinguished as Sheep-stations and Cattle-stations. (1898,Austral English,436)

Station, n. Sometimes sheep s., cattle- s., or dairy-s., (PAUL, p. 68); originally the hut, yards, and buildings where a squatter stationed himself to work his run; but now usually the whole property, including the stock and leasehold country. It has been used in both these senses in Australia (whence the word came) since the 'thirties. ([1898 Morris Austral-English]) (1) The original sense is still preserved up country, where the men always speak of in at the s., when they are out on the run; also in the word out-s. (q.v.), which has no other meaning than the house, yards etc. (2) The secondary sense of a property with freehold, leasehold, buildings, and stock. (3) Any fairly large property, carrying over 2000 or 3000 sheep. (4) Adjective as in s.horse, belonging to the owner, not to one of the man, whose horses are private; s. sheep, not one belonging to a neighbour; s.-bred, not a bought sheep. (5) Since the 1890s, auctioneers in their advertisements have taken to speaking of s. lines of sheep, though 70 per cent. of those so designated at the autumn ewe fairs come from farms or grazing runs. ([1898 Morris Austral-English]) (Dec 16, 1933,Press, The,21) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

BEATTIE The custom in the old days was to call the buildings on a run the station,' and the land that went with it wasthe run.' On a big property you could find several stations,' and the principal one was calledthe home station,' while the others were out-stations.' This was the old Australian usage which was carried over to New Zealand at first, but gradually the signification was altered by loosely calling the whole run a station, and then the real station became a homestead and the out-stations became shepherds' huts. In this present book it will be noticed that generally the writer has preserved the olden custom of calling the main buildings the station and the land the run. The runs over in Australia being, as a rule, much larger than those in New Zealand, thestation' and out-station' phraseology was preserved much longer than over here, where even in advertisements in the latefifties we see the English word homestead' ousting the colonial wordstation.' (1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11)

It is usually understood that in the early days the word station' denoted the owner's house and its immediate buildings, whilerun' meant the whole property. Strange to say, I only noted the word station' twice, and each time with a diverse meaning. On July 21, 1865, the diary says:Sold 17 head of cattle - remaining on station 15 head.' Then on September 11, 1865, we read: `Wilkinson returned to the Home Station.' The first of these entries means the whole run - the second the homestead or main buildings. (Jul 21, 1856,Puketoi Station Diary) [NOTES: 1947 Beattie Early Runholding 115 quoting 1856 July 21 Puketoi Station Diary]

BEATTIE When I first read this inscription [in the Memorial Church, Cave], the word sheep-men' made me involuntarily flinch. Years later, when I had forgotten it, I suddenly met it again, and again I recoiled. So aghast was I that I spent weeks collecting every old term forrunholders' I could, and I found thirteen, viz., flock owners,'flock masters,' pastoralists,'run holders,' run owners,'sheep owners,' sheep holders,'sheep masters,' squatters,'station holders,' station owners,'stock holders,[sic] and stock owners.' The wordsheepmen' is a modern Americanism, and using this anachronism mars a splendid memorial. ... [12] Of all the thirteen terms found in old documents, the word `runholder' was the most used, and it is the word that I think should be substituted. (1947,Early Runholding in Otago,11)

Statute of Westminster¶

noun.

SINCLAIR The New Zealand Government was trying to resist the inevitable. It deplored the Balfour report, which defined Great Britian and the Dominions as `autonomous communities. . .equal in status' ... It sniffed at the Statute of Westminister, which brought the legal position of the Dominions into conformity with their practical status. Ibid. 291 In 1947 the Statute of Westminister was at last adopted, giving legal fulfilment to the fact of sovereignty. (1959,History of New Zealand,239)

stay¶

verb. to lodge or reside permanently or regularly

PARTRIDGE Stay. To lodge or reside regularly or permanently: standard Scots (C. 18-20) >, in late C. 19, Colonial, esp. South African, Australian, and New Zealand. (O.E.D.). (1937,Dictionary of Slang,826)

noun. [Rural] a brace or prop for fenceposts [especially angle posts and strainers.]

"Stays", which hold the strainers inposition, number the same way. (May 9, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),51)

MOWAT Putting stays on wire across river. (Nov 29, 1905,Alexander Mowat Diaries)

The cheapest and most expensive Dropper in the market. A perfect stay and post saver. (Mar 9, 1907,Farmers' Union Advocate,15)

RIDDOLLS At all corners and gateways, and at specings of not more than 12 ch. in an unboken length of fence, heavy strainer posts, braced by a stay, are needed to resist the pull of the fencing wire. (1958,Farm Engineering,408)

RIDDOLLS Stays should never be less than 9 ft. long , and are usually 10 ft. If the resultant pull is slightly below the centre of the stay, and so does not tend to tilt the strainer over at the top. (1958,Farm Engineering,410)

A stainless steel fencing stay such as is used on Hunter fences could be inserted through and keyed on the bottom. (Apr 11, 1968,NZ Farmer,17)

MAF Stay: Support for a strainer or angle post. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,29)

FISK Once the post is in it needs to be stayed. The stay is usually 1.8-2.4 m long. (1996,Practical Smallfarming,11)

The next step in the fencing process and a most important one is building a sound and strong stay. It is also desirable to match the stay in proportion to the strainer for size - eg a No 1 strainer with a thin stay looks ridiculous, as would a No 3 strainer with a big thick stay. (2001,Lifestyle Farmer,Feb/March 42)

verb. [Rural] [ fencing] to brace a post with a stay or prop.

RIDDOLLS Bracing and staying strainers .. on hilly country the next step is to place a breast block across the front of the strainer facing the strain. (1958,Farm Engineering,414)

I strung a couple of extra snarly 3in barbs atop the new 8-wire boundary line and stayed the barbs up fairly liberally with totara battens. (Aug 10, 1972,NZ Farmer,39)

FISK Once the post is in it needs to be stayed. (1996,Practical Smallfarming,11)

noun. breastplate, stay foot; a piece of timber placed in the ground to support the stay at a strainer, angle, or corner post; sometimes called STAY FOOT,

stays¶

Those related to ways of shooting marbles were cribbing, firsts, fudging, funks, funnicks, funnigans, flunks, forces, knee-high, knuckle-down-stiff, knuckles, and lasts. Terms connected with the movement of the marbles were: cannons, clears, dead-stick, double-hits, fires, funs, gees, haystacks, in smug, keeps, kills, kisses, lay-ups, manyes, ones, pink, ringer, rolls, scat, screws, skinned, skun, spiders, sported-off, stays, stops, tracks, throughs. noun. ?mainly pl ball-bearings used as marbles ca1918-20 Auckland (man 66 yrs) .br quite common p.c. G. Kennedy 1979

McGILL Steelies were banned. (1989,Kiwi Baby Boomers,45)

KEITH & MAIN Marbles were the currency of childhood and there were an astonishing number of names for them, some referring to the material or colour, others to value or function in the game. There were agates, aggies, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cats-eye, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, mollies, peelies, peewees, pisswees, pretties, Scotties, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers and whities. The march of technology added ball bearings - ballies or steelies - which were unbeatable when it came to smashing an opponent's miserable glassie. World War II brought `clayeys' often imperfectly spherical they were pathetic terracotta substitutes for real marbles. (1984,NZ Yesterdays,288)

The bigger or more skilful boys won mostof my marbles off me, their glassies orsteelies (ball-bearings) blasting my claydakers ruthlessly out of the ring. (Aug 8, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),64)

  1. Xenicus lyalli (Rothschild, 1894) Stephen Island Wren (1970,Annotated Checklist of Birds of NZ,64,1980)

[Hdg]The tale of the lighthouse-keeper's cat: Discovery and extinction of the Stephens Island wren (Traversia lyalli)... The Stephens Island wren Traversia lyalli is widely quoted as having been discovered and promptly exterminated from its only locality, Stephens Island, New Zealand, by a single lighthouse-keeper's cat. Examination of archival and museum records indicates that this account is oversimplified... (2004,Notornis,51(4): 193) [NOTES: Galbreath & Brown]

The following birds are now extinct, or very nearly so, some only to be found in un-get-at-able places to the human, but not to the stoat and its relatives, or luckily on the sanctuaries: The saddleback .. the Stephens Island wren .. and stitch bird. (Feb 29, 1916,Evening Post,3)

verb. to book up on credit; to put on the slate; to chalk up

And his tumbler with brandy half filling, He'll drink and commence then to skite; And replies when he's asked for the shilling, `Stick it up, you know me, it's all right.' (1875,NZ Songster,No.3/69)

noun.

The Ashburton Club travelled in an express with four horses, and one of the incidents of the journey was a "stick up" in the river. (May 26, 1896,Ashburton Guardian,3)

verb. in phr. stuck up with porpoises: of a whale, to be slowed by playful porpoises

GRADY Stuck-up with porpoises - Porpoises that have slowed a swimming whale down by playing with it. This assisted the whalers. (1982,Perano Whalers)

verb. to bring (a vehicle, thing, a person, a job) to a standstill (often in passive form: be, get stuck up)

[NOTES: (1) The regular word for the action of bush-rangers stopping passers-by on the highway and robbing them.(2) In the case of a bank or a station, simply to rob. [1846] (3) Humorously applied to a collector or a beggar. In Twenty - five Years of St. Andrews' (vol. ii. p. 87), A. K. H. B. tells a story of a church dignitary, who was always collecting money for church building. When a ghost appeared at Glamis Castle, addressing the ghost, the clergyman began - thathe was most anxious to raise money for a church he was erecting; that he had a bad cold and could not well get out of bed; but that his collecting-book was on the dressing-table, and he would be extremely obliged' for a subscription.' An Australian would have said hestuck up' the ghost for a subscription. [1890]]

  • if you get stuck up by any creeks you'll very likely see cattle marks ... (a creek is a stream) but there is nothing that ought to stick you up at all if you keep out of the big swamp at the bottom of the valley. (Jun 1860,Forest Flora,37,1960)

The cow and steers stuck us up at the yards so we left them in the paddock. (Jul 9, 1862,Chudleigh Diary,47,1950)

An old cow stuck me up about a mile from the stockyard ... Millett and I worked our whips well on her. When she rushed one, the other stock-whipped her. (Feb 21, 1863,Chudleigh Diary,78,1950)

BUTLER At last we came to a waterfall. This `stuck us up', as they say here concerning any difficulty. (1863,First Year in Canterbury Settlement,64)

MEREDITH We started all right [on our journey], but had not got beyond the city boundary when the horses stuck us up. (1875,Adventuring in Maoriland in the Seventies,80,1935)

WHITWORTH ... when we told him ... we'd been stuck up by the water, he ... said ... `Ah, stuck up, were you?' (1879,Spangles and Sawdust,26)

REID Push on or you will be stuck up. Not by bushrangers, ... but by time and tide which wait for no man. At the first opportunity he `stuck up the mail' ... merely to secure a passage to town (1884,Rambles on the Golden Coast,73)

WILSON Far more often have the rivers to be forded, as is the case with the Otira ... where ... it is so wild that the coaches are sometimes `stuck up' for days, lest in trying to cross they should be washed away. (Jun 3, 1894,In the Land of the Tui,88)

HARPER At present, owing to the unbridged state of the rivers and frequent rain, there is great risk of loss of time by being `stuck up' by floods. (1896,Pioneer Work in the Alps of NZ,32)

MACDONALD These places taken together with frequently flooded rivers ..., often `sticking us up' for hours or days at a time. (1910,Reminiscences,19)

BEATTIE The back blocks of Southland are not inaccessible places. Until you are stuck up by the great West Coast mountains ... you can get round ... (1913,Trade Hunting,[12])

DAVIDSON The only drawback to these trips was the likelihood of being stuck up now and then by flooded rivers. (1930,Sketch of His Life,75)

Stick up.- Bring to a standstill. (A bushranger was said to s.u. his victims.) `If you get stuck up by any creeks ... you'll very likely see cattle marks by following the creek up and down.' (Butler A First Year in Canterbury Settlement], p. 143; [1898 Morris Austral-English]). (Dec 16, 1933,Press, The) [NOTES: Acland Glossary]

MASTERS When they got stuck up in trying to get over the saddle, as they invariably did, they naturally made back to get him to help them over with his horses. (1959,Tales of the Mails,25)

You see there was a judgement summons up against me and I stuck up Dr. McArthur, as I thought, in the street and explained to him if my name went in the papers and ward saw it, he might stick up my promotion. (Dec 13, 1902,New Zealand Free Lance,14)

verb. to hold up (a job, etc.)

Commenced shearing. Meikana and Piripi Nehu as press men stuck me up. I gave them five minutes and sacked them. ... I put on young Wood as pressman as he was near at hand ... and put on my two station boys as fleece boys. The shed did not stop one minute. (Nov 4, 1889,Chudleigh Diary,368,1950)

DAVIN You might want it to coax Pompey [a ferret] out if he sticks you up. (1949,Roads from Home,161)

verb. to refuse to sail (a vessel)

PUGH WIL.LIAMS stick her up: used among seamen when they refuse to sail a vessel. (1951,Letter)

verb. to stop dead; to be hindered from proceeding

The river was very high ..., having got over that you had to walk some way and then get into a bullock dray and cross a branch that people at home [sc. England] would look at a long time ..., the bullocks sticking up in the middle each time. (Nov 4, 1865,Chudleigh Diary,203,1950)

TUCKER We passed only two vehicles on the road - one being an old coach `stuck up' two years ago and left. (1884,Letter from Abroad,83)

CHAMIER ... one cursed lot [of sheep] stuck up in the middle of the stream. Ibid. 429 (1891,Philosopher Dick,247)

Two drays belonging to the Messrs. Baird of Waikouaiti, were the first to be "stuck up" in this manner, and though a stout resistance was made, the drivers were compelled to yield, and the flour was sold at the price dictated by the diggers, viz., 1s. 6d. per lb. (Sep 9, 1862,Otago Daily Times,5)

verb. to run up; knock up

Having noticed in the papers that you want a few sheds stuck up, pulled down, or some other old thing, I thought as I've nothing else to fall back on just now I'd take it on. (May 6, 1911,NZ Truth,306/4/6)

.. but sticking up boards everywhere to meet the eye of the weary traveller - "No accomodation at the shepherd's hut," or in other words, "No road through Glentilt." (Aug 31, 1861,Otago Witness,5)

They have stuck up a post in the middle of the Waitetuna river, and have defied William Naylor to come any further with the road. (Jun 10, 1862,Daily Southern Cross,3)

verb. to bail up (pigs)

MEREDITH It sometimes takes up to half an hour to scramble through the rough gullies to where the dogs have the pig stuck up. If the bulldog were released before reaching the quarry, he would `go in' at once, and would probably be exhausted with holding the pig before we could get there, and possibly get killed. A bailed-up pig makes periodical rushes at the baiting dogs, ... Ibid. 97 In the morning our dogs stuck up a mob of pigs on a small, clear-topped rise. (1875,Adventuring in Maoriland in the Seventies,64,1935)

verb. to accost (a person for a favour)

[NOTES: ca1951 Wellington He stuck us up for a donation]

BODELL ... one day he passed my store and I stuck him up and asked for my money, ... (1890,Soldier's View of Empire, A,211,1982)

THOMPSON ... he ... shtuck me oop in street ... und borrowed the rhino to file. (1909,Ballads about Business,11)

HARPER Suppose we stick him up tomorrow [sc. about a job]. (1934,Windy Island,236)

SARGESON stuck: stuck him up (on the street), accosted him; stuck up (by the police), questioned. (1964,Collected Stories,303)

BURGESS ... had he attempted to stick him up Mr Fox would have shot him dead. (1866,Confessions,107,1983)

FARJEON `We can stick up the escort in the Black Forest', he ses ... (1866,Grif: a Story of Colonial Life,7)

CLAYDON I was `stuck up' - to use a favourite colonial expression - by a newly arrived immigrant from England, in a New Zealand city not long ago, and asked ... (1886,Popular Handbook to NZ,10)

You see there was a judgement summons out against me and I stuck up Dr. McArthur, as I thought, in the street and explained to him if my name went in the papers and Ward saw it, he might stick up my promotion. (Dec 13, 1902,NZ Free Lance,14)

verb. to hold up (a person or vehicle) and rob on the highway; thence, to rob (a bank)

WEKEY The consequence [of many leaving ill-equipped] was, that some of those who carried up provisions with them were `stuck up' on the road, and the principles of communism were practically realised on the way to the Dunstan El Dorado. The first detachment of gold-seekers gradually arrived ... (1862,Otago As It Is,51)

Two of them enter[ed] the bank after the hour of closing ... `sticking them up' (1855,Maungatapu Murders,11)

NESFIELD Burgess ... insisted on `sticking' the old fellow up. (1881,Chequered Career,79)

Stick (st&ibreve.k), v. t. [Add.] To stick up. (a) To detain, especially on the highway, for the purpose of robbing; as, to stick up a traveler or a mail coach. (b) To rob on the highway; also, to rob, in general. (c) To apply to, for money, for one's signature for a petition, or the like. [Colloq.] (d) to accost in the street. [Colloq.] (e) To pose; to puzzle. [Colloq.] (1898,Merriam-Webster Third International,2031)

stick ... stickup v.t. to hold up and rob; (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11)

v.tr. of bushrangers, to hold up and rob: whence sticker-up a bushranger: by extension any such hold-up, as of a bank. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

stick-up v.t. of bushrangers, to hold up and rob; whence sticker-up, bushranger; by extension any such hold-up, as of a bank. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

A local business man states that on Monday night he was stuck up by a local man with two revolvers, who apparently was not clear as to what he was doing. (Apr 13, 1910,Hawera & Normanby Star,5)

The escort is not considered safe by the diggers, who decline sending gold in bulk with an insufficient guard, to be almost certainly "stuck up" on its way to Dunedin. (Sep 20, 1861,Daily Southern Cross,3)

A sensation has been caused in this district by a Maori being struck up by an armed man at Waihua Hill, Napier road, and relieved of his horse, saddle and bridle. (Oct 30, 1906,Hawera & Normanby Star,5)

On their way they called at the smithy, stuck up the blacksmith, and took from his chest some articles of clothing and provisions, besides a double-barrelled gun, powder and shot; one rummaging the cottage, while the other stood sentry at the door. (Nov 18, 1857,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,3)

A[b]out nine miles from the Armed Constabulary station, the coach was stuck up by twenty or thirty natives, who rescued the prisoner from the Armed Constabulary escort. (Sep 12, 1877,Evening Post,2)

FILLET, used as a noun only. (1952,NZ Forest Glossary)

noun.

noun. a notice of a traffic offence (usually gummed onto the vehicle or `stuck' under a windscreen wiper); a bluey

Inspectors were posted on all the main motor roads, and every motorist was pulled up and asked to produce his license. Some did, quite a few did not, and names and addresses were taken in those uncomfortable black notebooks which inspectors and others carry. Each car was marked by a small sticker by the inspector in order that it should not be stopped again by another inspector, but there was one driver who objected strongly to stickers, small, large, and of any colour, and before his afternoon's drive was ended he had been pulled up four times, duly noted in the black book, and presented with a sticker at each stop. Those who hold that the existing car parking regulations would work quite satisfactorily if only they were enforced can have no complaint over the activities of traffic inspectors in the central business area yesterday afternoon, for "stickers" were applied to windshields in right generous fashion. noun. [Rural] a slaughterer of stock.

noun. [Rural] a device that holds one beast at a time for slaughtering.

sticking pen¶

noun. [Rural] a small enclosure to hold stock for slaughter.

SLATTER The sticking-pen far below me down the tunnelled slope from the top of the ramp. From there comes the pained lowing of goaded cattle and the sharp crack of the lethal hammer wielded by the nonchalant bloke leaning over his platform above the trapped beast. Ibid. 67 I'd like to see them ... racing the chain, that remorseless heartless chain. And when the last is scrubbed and the chain is switched off, going down for a shower ... I'd like to see them on the chain. Even the learners' chain. In that narrow cell of concrete with the lambs swinging in quick time up the ramp from the sticking-pen ... Lambs hooked on to the chain and progressing slowly along while the row of men standing alongside slash and tear and nick with knives while others punch briskets or pull the skins from the swinging carcases. More men rip out the guts and throw the heart and liver on to the small-goods table ... and the skins and innards and hooves and ears all go by chutes to the departments below. Ibid. 227 The tourists ... never see the dogs running over the backs of the sheep jammed in the saleyards or the pet sheep leading them slyly up the ramp into the sticking pen at the works ... (1958,Gun in My Hand, A,12)

LOUGHNAN sticking pen: that one which feeds the sheep into the sticking box. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,78)

KERR Freezing works yarders reward an individual sheep, called the Judas sheep, to lead others to the sticking pen. (2000,High Times in the High Country,82)

sticky weed¶

noun. catchfly

HILGENDORF CATCHFLY (silene [gallica]). Varieties of this species have been named S.anglica and S.quinque vulnera. [1967 quinquevulnera] Common names are spotted catchfly, flycatcher, sticky weed, and five wounds. It is common in cultivated land and waste places such as gravelly river-beds throughout both islands. ... The flowers are white or often dark red, or sometimes white with a blood red blotch on each petal so that this variety is called quinque vulnera, `five wounds' (1926,Weeds of New Zealand,74)

stickybeak¶

verb. to pry

stickybeak n. prying inquistive person;. v.int. to pry be inquisitive. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

sticky-beak n. prying inquistive person; v.i. pry, be inquisitive. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

stickybeak NZ & Austral. sl. 1 n. inquisitive person. 2 v.i. pry (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,754) [NOTES: [cf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict. 1142]]

"Pushed it open, and sticky-beaked in," interrupted Rodney with the candour of an elder brother. (Oct 18, 1924,Evening Post,15)

Each group will have a tour guide and we provide gatekeepers for security - no one can stickybeak through the homes but us. (Oct 30, 2002,Capital Times,6)

noun. one who is always sticking his beak into others' business; an inquisitive or interfering person, one who sticks a nose into others' business; inquisitive interfering

[NOTES: ca1920 W.H.B. Orsman often corrupted to stinky beak ca1982 L.Bauer: not used in Britain]

BURTON [He] shuffles off with an audible ... exhortation to a young policeman to keep his distance and not be a stickybeak. (1945,In Prison,19)

But Mr Terris has called on Mr Mallard to get his "sticky beak" out of council business. (May 6, 2003,Dominion Post,A8)

BALLANTYNE You wouldn't marry a stickybeak like Joy, for instance. (1948,Cunninghams, The,122) [NOTES: 1976 edition]

stickybeak n. prying inquistive person;. v.int. to pry be inquisitive (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),625)

sticky-beak n. prying inquistive person; v.i. pry, be inquisitive. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),18)

(Dec 8, 1986,Radio NZ / National Radio) [NOTES: Morning Report interview: Maggie Barry and Australian producer of Crocodile Hunter [Dundee] discussing terms that had to be changed for a North American audience]

stickybeak NZ & Austral. sl. 1 n. inquisitive person. (1986,NZ Pocket Oxford Dictionary,754) [NOTES: [cf. 1982 Collins Concise Eng. Dict. 1142]]

Because every grown-up was at church ... we didn't have to worry about nosey-parkers or sticky-beaks. (Aug 1986,Islands,37/45)

(1979,Heinemann NZ Dictionary,1080)

Mr. Stickybeak or Mrs. Nosey Parker may have something against the couple, and they may go along to the office of the Registrar and, by payment of half a crown, obtain a copy of the birth certificate of the youngest child, or ask for particulars of the marriage. (May 17, 1924,NZ Truth,5)

stiff¶

noun. an unlucky person (gambler here)

If they are silvery' they will walk out again; ifstiff' they will work a week or two to get a few shillings to take them on the road again,.. (Sep 15, 1906,NZ Truth,65/3/6)

adjective. penniless; unlucky

PARTRIDGE I'll admit I was stiff when I lost that fifty francs, but my cobber produced another ten; and when the ring-keeper said `Up and do 'em', I collected 200 francs. ...How did yo get down here, Joe? Joe. Well, I was so stiff I nearly turkeyed off from the line, but I decided to wait. Ibid. 288 ... it's time we all took a tumble to ourselves and discussed something pleasant, say a little party. A. I'm stiff. C. How are you holding, D? D. All right. (1935,Slang Today,287) [NOTES: 1935 A.E. Strong WW1 scene in Partridge Slang Today 287]

SARGESON But Terry said he was stiff because the one he would have picked had been taken. (1946,That Summer,73)

[Caption to a cartoon of a dead body, labelled "that mortgage investment"] STIFF. (Aug 5, 1940,Evening Post,9)

Brown' can be a stiff unless he's grubby or boozed. If he were a stiff it would be Arthur M. Brown' orA. Morris Brown or A.M. Brown, Esq.,' Jordan joked. Ibid. 94 You are a chronic stiff, a bum, a deadbeat, a soak, an optimist. (1965,Rhetoric at the Red Dawn,89)

POLACK Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called para[as-acute] paraua[a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, mungu nui (black physeter); right whale, tohora (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, mango (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. TheGrab your dumps' was the roar, as we all rushed in for our own, and anybody else's one could get. (1943,Pure Gold,22)

SUTTON-SMITH Marbles had a language of its own. There were names for the marbles, the games, and all the various aspects of the play. There were terms for marbles such as taw' orshooter', referring to the marbles used to fire with; dubs',dates', stakes',dukes', or `changers', referring to the marbles put down to be fired at. Then there were the terms referring to particular kinds of marbles: for example, agates, aggies, aggotties, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cat's eyes, chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, molly-bars, mulley-bars [mullibars: large marbles], peelies, peewees, piss-wees, pretties, Scotties, Scottish alleys, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers, white alleys, and in more recent years ball-bearings, chippies, plastics, and woodies. (1972,Folkgames of Children,174)

KEITH & MAIN Marbles were the currency of childhood and there were an astonishing number of names for them, some referring to the material or colour, others to value or function in the game. There were agates, aggies, American alleys, blood alleys, bomb-squashers, bonies, bonsers, bottlies, bull's eyes, bum-squashers, cats-eye, [sic] chinkies, connies, duckies, eggies, glassies, Greeks, milkies, mollies, peelies, peewees, pisswees, pretties, Scotties, smokies, stinkies, stonies, stripies, tom-bobblers and whities. The march of technology added ball bearings - ballies or steelies - which were unbeatable when it came to smashing an opponent's miserable glassie. World War II[roman] brought `clayeys' often imperfectly spherical they were pathetic terracotta substitutes for real marbles. (1984,Yesterdays in Maoriland,288)

Stinkies - these were marbles made from clay, they did not work very well. (1987,Alfredton,75) [NOTES: Quote from c1935]

PARK One steelie to twenty-four ordinary clay stinkers was what I charged, and a fair price it was. (1992,Fence Around the Cuckoo,62)

stock unit¶

noun. [Rural] a measure of land's carrying-capacity [ the annual feed requirements of an animal, e.g. 1 ewe = 1.0 SU, 1 Jersey cow = 6.0 SU. One stock unit requires approx 520 kg of good quality pasture dry matter per year.]

MAF Stock unit .. also referred to as ewe equivalent. It is the feed requirement used as the basis of comparison for different classes and species of stock. It expresses the annual feed requirements equivalent to one 55 kg ewe rearing a single lamb. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,7)

Stock units are based on the conversion ratios first recommended by Professor Coop from Linclon College in 1965. These ratios are ewes per head 1.0, hoggest [sic] 0.6, others per head 0.8, cows per head 6.0.. (Aug 1984,NZ Journal of Agriculture,28)

Steers are equivalent to about six stock units ... (Sep 1986,NZ Journal of Agriculture,8)

They run 8000 SU of sheep, beef and deer with the majority, 6000 SU, in sheep. [sU] (2002,Wool Grower,Spring 25)

noun.

Hdg] Wharfies v Seagulls : Scene setfor big stoush on the Aucklandwaterfront. (Mar 24, 1995,Independent (Auckland),6)

[Caption] You won't be forgetting Faenzain a hurry - Or the Stouch across theSenio, Santerno and Sillaro. (Dec 24, 1945,NZEF Times,IV/235 : 3)

Act's troops, less electable by the day, sit solemn, with the exception of Richard Prebble, who re-animates in any stoush. (Mar 6, 1999,Listener (New Zealand Listener),15)

The danger is that they [sc. talkbackhosts] begin to see themselves less asprofessional interviewers and more aspublic performers - and what is moreentertaining than a good old stoush. (Jan 25, 1993,Dominion,8)

A small group of Hannon supporters then allegedly waded into the stoush with bottles. (Aug 18, 2003,Dominion Post,A2)

We met opponents' boastsWith boots and stoush. (Aug 8, 1919,Hawke's Bay Herald,7)

verb. to fight, bash

See: stoush n.

[NOTES: stoush n. also stouch (1891 cit.) Also passive: to be fought, bashed.]

He began badly and got stoushed the whole way, eventually finishing well back. (Aug 13, 1910,NZ Truth,2)

Py gorry, I go up Queen Street and stoush the first black man I see. (Sep 22, 1926,NZ Observer,3)

He is always wanting to "stouch" someone, and last of all when he received an eye opener, - or, to put it more literally, an eye closer - in this respect, satisfaction reigned supreme. (Nov 30, 1891,Wanganui Herald,2)

Harry had put his feet up on the opposite seat and the conductor remonstrated, whereupon Harry promptly stoushed him. He dealt out the same sort of kindness to two passengers who came to the conductor's assistance and cleaned them up, too. (Aug 10, 1918,NZ Truth,6)

And if any people want to try an' stoush your Royal pa, / We'll come an' 'elp 'im scrap 'em, every time! (Jul 17, 1901,West Coast Times,4)

He began badly and got stoushed the whole way, eventually finishing well back. (Aug 13, 1910,NZ Truth,2)

adjective.

It requires no great clairvoyant power to know that he knew in his heart that he was getting licked. It was apparent to the veriest novice in Pieman Mclntosh's stoush Stadium. (Nov 7, 1911,NZ Truth,3)

A second medal was the special gift of two sports who were strong supporters of the Irish-Australian stoush artist. (Aug 2, 1913,NZ Truth,3)

Maori is a most effective "stoush' [sic] language, and Mr. Kaihau used it with the skill of a pastmaster. (Oct 22, 1904,Evening Post,9)

Musson's boxing school in Christchurch had the distinction of turning out every winner at the big stoush fixture in Christchurch the other day. (Apr 29, 1922,NZ Truth,8)

WHEN Lou was selected to make the trip to Australia, he had the right credentials, he having met and beaten a number of boys who, to-day, are figuring high in stoush society. (Jun 26, 1930,NZ Truth,12)

Magistrate Hunt heard the story on Monday, granted the request, and order [sic] the stoush artist to relieve himself of 30s every week towards the support of his wife. (Dec 23, 1922,NZ Truth,2)

stousher¶

noun.

[NOTES: aka stoucher, incl. fig.]

One night, hard upon Christmas of last year, Bill Buggins went, in company with his bosom pal 'Arry Stousher, to have a ''bob's worth at the Opera House.'" (Dec 12, 1899,Observer (Auckland),22)

The cry was up for 'stoushers' - and they [sc. the football team] one and all obeyed. (1898,Lay of Bantry Bay,27)

He inflicted a fine of GBP2 and costs. [sic] and ordered the damage to the cab to be paid. This should teach the beery stousher a lesson. (Feb 8, 1908,NZ Truth,6)

The few men available in Australia just now have fought and re-fought each other until the public has grown tired of their styles and their reversals of form, and the game is no longer a prolifically financial one, either for the promoters or the stoushers themselves. (Feb 9, 1918,NZ Truth,8)

The controlling officials don't care a dump what the professional stoushers' views may be on the subject ... (Jul 14, 1906,NZ Truth,3)

stoushing¶

noun.

A witness in an alleged assault case at Palmerston N. during the week said that the complainant told the accused, alleged to have done the stoushing, that he was too pretty to fight. (Jun 29, 1912,NZ Truth,1)

Murphy is the more scientific fighter, but Triffen's wild and woolly stoushing quite disconverted him, and he was completely outed in the early stages of No.3 when in a dazed state, and no longer able to take a collected view of the political situation. (Nov 3, 1906,Star, The,1)

A perusal of the Melbourne Cup records shows that good three-year-olds are invariably a source of annoyance to the older horses and as Phar Lap looks one right out of the box there is every reason to believe that if he goes to the post fit and well he will take a power of stoushing. (Oct 31, 1929,NZ Truth,13)

﻿Pity the poor voters. The election isstill six months away, but alreadypolitical stoushing is reaching fullcampaign pitch. (Apr 5, 1993,Dominion,2)

straddle¶

noun. a straddle carrier

At ground level, the straddles are bigger than I thought. Three stories high - surrounded by gigantism I have taken to measuring just about everything against buildings - and weighing 60 tonnes apiece, they have an appealing way of getting about... Straddles are run with the efficiency of worker bees. (Sep 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 65/62)

straddle carrier¶

noun.

The container is then raised clear, the lifting mechanism rolled back in, and the container lowered to the wharf, where it is picked up by a straddle carrier - a transporter on wheeled stilts - and bundled away to storage. (Sep 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 65/62)

straggle¶

noun. [Rural] a small group of sheep evading muster.

These musterers who climbed several hundred metres around dawn to drive straggles of sheep down to the valley floor might work their way in time to be head musterer, foreman or manager, amd ultimately perhaps attain their own lease. (Aug 2002,Forest & Bird,27)

verb. [Rural] to find straggler sheep [and often to blade-shear bellies and under-necks so that they can walk out in a muster.]

MOWAT McWhirter and self straggled the Trig. (Dec 28, 1916,Alexander Mowat Diaries)

STRONACH So after three days of mustering about the paddocks, with a dagging thrown in, we were glad to get away up Yoe Creek again to straggle the ewe country. To straggle a block of country means of course to muster in the stragglers. (1953,Musterer on Molesworth,31)

WESTMACOTT In bush country they have to straggle the new burns after a first muster. (1977,After-Breakfast Cigar, The,145)

PETER We straggle a block and trace the roughies as they usually have a double fleece. i.e. we muster for the stragglers and blade-shear bellies and under neck so they can walk out. (2000,Peter Glossary)

DOMINY Now on occasion, when spotting or straggling, some run-holders save time by using a helicopter to drop them in the back country. (2001,Calling the Station Home,169)

verb. [Rural] [stragglers and wild sheep] to wander without direction.

GUTHRIE-SMITH In one way or another hundreds of sheep thus straggled from the run. (1921,Tutira,140)

WESTMACOTT The sheep straggled up the valley and we followed ... (1977,After-Breakfast Cigar, The,115)

OGONOWSKA-COATES .. sheep sometimes went wild, wandering the back country and straggling up the river flats. (1987,Boards, Blades & Barebellies,11)

straggle hunting¶

noun. [Rural] searching for straggler sheep

NEWTON His partner is a well-known flying man and is one of the originators of the practice of straggle hunting by air. (1952,High Country Journey,13)

straggle muster¶

noun. [Rural] sheep that have missed an initial muster, and are gathered in the straggle muster.

RICHARDS Before leaving Otupae, Roger Pearce and I had been asked if we would return in three weeks to shear the 'straggle muster.' (1989,Pioneer's Life, A,47)

noun. [Rural] a secondary muster to collect stock missed in initial muster.

The local knowledge of each committee is and has been invaluable, particularly in ensuring proper mustering ands where necessary, subsequent 'straggle musters' before shearing and dipping operations. (Feb 1966,NZ Journal of Agriculture,25)

verb. [Rural] to have a second muster to gather stragglers that have missed a first or main muster.

STRONACH For the rest of us, fifteen long days, if the weather kept fine, and then fifteen more days to straggle muster the same block. (1953,Musterer on Molesworth,25)

NEWTON .. we finished up by straggle mustering the whole of the summer country again. (1964,Straggle Muster,107)

MACGREGOR On one occasion we were out straggle mustering for sheep missed in the main muster. (1980,Dog's Life, A,12)

NEWTON There was a good gang up the Ant.. at which the gang could camp during the fortnight the sheep were held there, and from which they could straggle-muster the rest of the country. (1966,Boss's Story, The,38)

verb. [Rural] to clear the bar at closing time.

Straggle muster - gathering sheep missed during the main muster. Also pertains to the [Dog Trial] Club Secretary on his third attempt at clearing the bar! [straggle] (Dec 15, 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,46)

straggle tally¶

noun. [Rural] a total number of sheep missed in an initial muster, but mustered in later.

NEWTON .. the Lake Coleridge station itself at that time shore 22,000 sheep and that season the straggle tally (sheep missed) was under 400. (1947,Wayleggo,37)

NEWTON The other day the talk got round to 'straggle' tallies ( sheep missed in a muster.) I reckon that place must hold a world record for a straggle tally. (1964,Straggle Muster,106)

straggle-mustering¶

noun. [Rural] a second gathering to collect stock missed in an initial muster.

Straggle mustering. (Feb 11, 1868,Castle Station Diary,260) [NOTES: in Vance (1965) High Endeavour]

NEWTON This straggle-mustering after the autumn muster had never been practised at Mount White. (1966,Boss's Story, The,38)

straggler¶

noun. [Rural] 1.a sheep or cattle beast missed by a mustering team or a sheep or cattle beast that has strayed on to a neighbouring property, more common when natural boundaries preceded fences. 2. a ewe that is late to lamb; a late-lamber. 3. a slow-moving sheep at the back of a mob.

See: hermit; double-decker; double-fleecer; stray

The bulk of the wools offered was made up largely of stragglers and other late shorn sheep, and its character therefore was not up to the usual average, and it could not therefore be expected to establish a high range of values ... (Apr 5, 1894,Otago Witness,13)

The lamb was found by defendant in a paddock adjoining one of his camping paddocks, and taking it to be a straggler he had it killed under a custom which he said was long prevailed of accommodation paddock owners killing stragglers and accounting for them if called upon to do so. (Jun 3, 1904,Wanganui Herald,6)

ORMOND A good shearing day - got through 1431 sheep - all greasy ewes with exception of stragglers from the wether block. Jan 19. David out all day clearing off stragglers. (Jan 18, 1865,JD Ormond Stockbook 1864-1866)

MURISON Sent Wilkinson to Drysdales to head weaners whilst Read searches for stragglers. (Sep 13, 1865,Puketoi Station Diary)

MURISON Shearing stragglers. (Mar 29, 1867,Puketoi Station Diary)

CHS, TS, Kite and Jim went mustering the reserve for stragglers. (Mar 1, 1879,Tutira Station Diary)

BRABAZON Went around big section. Saw no stragglers. (Nov 24, 1892,Brabazon Diaries)

One or two stragglers omitted in the dipping may infect the whole flock and the inspectors have lynx eyes for sheep showing vermin. (Apr 1896,NZ Farmer)

An Inspector of Stock may require a stock owner to muster his flock on a given date for the purpose of returning stragglers to their owner. (1919,Livestock in New Zealand,48)

NEWTON The ridge..runs to little over 5,000 feet and as it is all open snowgrass country it is inevitable that the two stations have an annual exchange of stragglers. (1952,High Country Journey,156)

HALL Bob Metherell looking for stragglers in the Sly Burn, a tributary of the Greenstone River. (1987,Shepherd's Year, A,77)

KERR A nor'wester swayed the slack bridge and there were stragglers, perhaps 200 or 300 of them, peppered throughout the mob. 2. (2000,High Times in the High Country,117)

There are several ways of dealing with the stragglers. If there is a small paddock at liberty, the ewes to lamb can be taken from the docking yard and put in it. 3. (Oct 1926,NZ Farmer,01)

WESTMACOTT So we only had to keep the stragglers moving for a mile or so to the next crossing where they had bunched again when we came up to them. (1977,After-Breakfast Cigar, The,157)

HALL I'm holding the front of the mob so the winter-weakened stragglers can catch up. (1987,Shepherd's Year, A,9)

BARNES Skilfully Fly weaves her way back and forth behind the mob, nudging the occasional straggler. (1987,Country Calendar (TVNZ),123)

RICHARDS A sharp whistle and he will hold the lead until the stragglers catch up. (1989,Pioneer's Life, A,85)

straggler shearing¶

noun. [Rural] the shearing of sheep missed in an initial muster.

To-morrow begins the straggler shearing, a mild after-glow of the big event in December. (Dec 25, 1901,Otago Witness,13)

Finished straggler shearing. (Mar 2, 1869,Castle Station Diary,261) [NOTES: in Vance (1965) High Endavour]

straggler wool¶

noun. [Rural] long fleecewool shorn from sheep that have missed shearing.

MCLEOD Crutchings, eye clippings and late-shorn straggler wool make up a number of small lines which are a nuisance during the main shearing. (1954,On the Hill,8)

straggler's fleece¶

noun.

Wool. - Crutchings; 3 1/2d to 4 1/2d; straggler's fleece, up to 6d; dead wool up to 5 1/2d. (Aug 24, 1897,Marlborough Express,2)

straggler's wool¶

noun.

The wool catalogue consisted of the usual assortment arriving at this season of the year, viz - straggler's wool, crutchings and seedy lots. (May 18, 1898,West Coast Times,2)

About 500 bales are being submitted, mostly stragglers' wool, pieces, and locks. (Apr 13, 1915,Evening Post,8)

straggling¶

noun. [Rural] a second mustering for missed stock.

NEWTON The boys also did a bit of straggling and collected quite a useful tally of woollies. (1966,Boss's Story, The,81)

NEWTON Straggling: Mustering country a second time to get any sheep that have been missed. i.e. straggle-mustering. (1966,Boss's Story, The,189)

LOUGHNAN scratch or scratch-mustering: as distinct from straggling or straggle-mustering, which is a full-scale operation to gather in stock previously missed, scratching - often just a one-man operation - is the task of seeking out pockets of stock known to have been missed. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,69)

straight¶

noun. a 'neat' beer?

"Four straights and a dash?" she said, gathering up the empty handles skilfully in her fingers. (1949,Book, a Miscellany,9/30)

straight dinkum¶

noun.

See: fair dinkum

[NOTES: cf OED straight wire, also NZ fair dinkum.]

"As about the ranger," he added, "well a bloke told me straight dinkum, that he had seen him in the township this afternoon." (Aug 25, 1905,Bush Advocate,2)

"Ah, now you're serious, I'll tell you straight dinkum," replied Jack, "My surname is really a French name of very ancient lineage. ..." (Sep 4, 1915,NZ Truth,10)

*Guaranteed straight dinkum at Northland. (Dec 16, 1931,Evening Post,10)

straight hunt¶

noun. [Rural] [dog trials] an uphill course that tests the skills of huntaway dogs and their owners.

In Gisborne district nearly every club puts on a class for a straight hunt. (Mar 1931,NZ Farmer,231)

Straight Hunt - Class 4 in dog trialing and precisely what the name infers, to complete a 20 metres wide course that runs 400 metres up the hill. 52 points for hunt, 27 for style and 21 for noise. (Dec 15, 1983,NZ Journal of Agriculture,46)

GORDON One of those runs won the New Zealand Straight Hunt in 1983, despite the fact that, when the trio were nearing the top of the hill, they seemed to be considering a swing to their right. (1998,Three Sheep and a Dog,140)

KERR Sheep - it is in their nature to be inconvenient - are invariably over or down or up there, and shepherds want them somewhere else. They must be hunted to that place, in dog trials off the flat and up the hill in the Straight Hunt. (2000,High Times in the High Country,136)

Whitehead then went on to win the straight hunt by a point, with Graeme Northcott (Uriti) and Ned finishing second. (Mar 6, 2000,Taranaki Daily News,18)

straight off the turnips¶

phrase. (also hot off...) exceedingly countrified, raw

Country Jack does not appear to be straight off the turnips, taking his Motukarara running as a guide. (Oct 30, 1932,Ellesmere Guardian,3)

PARTRIDGE Turnips, straight off the. Applied to one who is a country bumpkin or very green: New Zealanders' (- 1932). (1937,Dictionary of Slang,918)

N.T. MOAR (Jan 1952,Personal Communication) [NOTES: ca1952 Jan p.c. N.T. Moar (fide R. Mason). Always been in use in his family]

HENDERSON My first steamrollered week at Riwaka School, hot off the turnips, included: [an electric shock trick]. (1938,Down from Marble Mountain,83)

Straight up on Oi¶

phrase.

A member may swear on their gang, for example, using the words, Straight up on Oi, or Straight up on the Mob. This implies an absolute word of honour, 'like swearing on your mother's grave'. (Oct 1999,NZWords,2(2) : 2)

straight/right off the heather¶

phrase. [Rural] of shepherds who immigrated in the nineteenth century directly from Scottish farmland.

STUDHOLME ..they were both great sheep men, coming straight off the heather. (1940,Te Waimate,92)

STUDHOLME In the early days most of these [shepherds] were Scots, many of them right off the heather. (1940,Te Waimate,119)

CRAWFORD The shepherds, mostly Highland Scots right off the heather were indispensable. [right off the heather] (1949,Sheep and Sheepmen of Canterbury,125)

straight-arsed¶

adjective. dull, boring

"We wouldn't be sitting in front of the TV becoming straight-arsed people that live boring uneventful lives like all you people trying to stop us having fun." (Aug 25, 2005,Wellingtonian,27)

straight-billed kiwi¶

noun. [Environment] any of the three species of flightless nocturnal birds of the New Zealand genus Apteryx (fam. Apterygidae)

58. Apteryx oweni, Gould. Kiwi, Straight-billed Kiwi, Grey Kiwi, Blue hen of the diggers. - The breeding season extends through several months, eggs having been obtained on the West Coast during a considerable portion of the [506] year. (Sep 1885,NZ Journal of Science,505) [NOTES: (T.H. Potts)]

strain¶

verb.

[NOTES: Also strain up. To stretch and tighten fence wire.]

The wire to be strained is placed in the gripper, which holds it firm and secure, and the chain attached to the gripper is then drawn through a ring in a bracket attached to the straining-post. (Aug 7, 1884,Waikato Times,2)

Can you, or any of your correspondents, inform me as to the advantages or disadvantages of having wire fences put up with small rollers left on for the purpose of straining up the fences? (Aug 27, 1879,Poverty Bay Herald,2)

The "automatic wire tightener" is not used either for straining up fences or mending fences, neither was it invented for either of those purposes. (Aug 8, 1895,Otago Witness,16)

The second job he obtained was fencing on a farm outside Gore on the main road, and he earned 11s for about 4 1/4 hours' work in straining up fences. (Jun 8, 1934,Evening Post,9)

strainer¶

noun. a sunken tree

The raft was repeatedly stranded on shoals and snagged by sunken trees, called "strainers" in whitewater parlance. (Sep 2003,NZ Geographic,No. 65/32)

noun. [Rural] a large post used for fence corners and at the end of each strain or stretch of wire.

WOODHOUSE Tenders for a fence... Iron standards, 6 wire, 15 strainers to the mile. (1982,Blue Cliffs,8) [NOTES: Quoted from 1865 Timaru Herald]

BRABAZON Dragged strainers and carted posts and some rails &c. (Jul 21, 1893,Brabazon Diaries)

BRABAZON Put in 2 strainers. (Jul 22, 1893,Brabazon Diaries)

Reinforced concrete strainers and intermediate posts are preferable to wood. (Apr 15, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,347)

LOUGHNAN strainer: the end post of a fence, or a section of it, which takes the end-strain of the wires. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,80)

It was now time to put in the posts between the strainers. (Mar 21, 1981,Listener (New Zealand Listener),67)

FISK Once the end strainers and angle posts are all in you are ready to run out a wire to get a line. (1996,Practical Smallfarming,13)

NEWBOLD Hey Mister, you reckon this strainer needs a tie-back? (1982,Big Huey, The,170)

The biggest corner and gate posts arestrainers - the biggest size is No 1 andthey get smaller with No 2 and No 3. (May 9, 1987,Listener (New Zealand Listener),51)

"If you just had a glimpse of the strainer, with the axe marks where it's been trimmed.." (Aug 1959,NZ Dairy Exporter,116)

[Advt] The only method of keeping the short strains tight is to use a Hayes Paramount Strainer on each wire. (Jul 1959,NZ Dairy Exporter,59)

CRUMP He led the way down to the skids where they'd been splitting the short ends of logs into posts and strainers on the days when it was too wet or windy to work in the bush. Ibid.159 Sam and Jack split posts, battens and strainers. (1961,Hang on a Minute, Mate,143) [NOTES: 1970 edition]

HENDERSON Right. We've put our strainers and our posts in. (1965,Open Country,55)

noun. [Rural] a tool to tighten the wires in a fence.

This strainer can be used to obtain an exceptionally high strain. (Oct 27, 1938,NZ Farmer,37)

LOUGHNAN strainer: a tool for straining wire. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,81)

Two wire strainers held the existing wires in place. (Mar 21, 1981,Listener (New Zealand Listener),67)

MAF strainer: Tool used to tighten the wires in a fence. [wire-strainer] (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,30)

HOLCROFT 1984 This meant work with a strainer, animplement I was still learning to use. (Jun 1992,North & South,65)

noun.

strainer post¶

noun. [Rural] a large fence-post used to stretch or strain wires.

See: straining post

We'd heave four strainer post into those 80cm holes and ram the earth, for unless they were buried that deep, that tight, the cattle would rub them sideways. (Dec 10, 2000,Sunday Star Times,C3)

HENDERSON Mr Rangi laid where he'd fallen at the foot of the strainer post. (1971,Our Open Country,40)

Mother was out to express regret at the deep marks cut in the grass by the wheels, but to rejoice at sight of a fine lot of firewood, and to seat Bubbles on the flat-topped strainer-post that thence she might croon at the horses and at Teddy, who with wide-open mouth and lolling tongue held on by the jolting sticks. (Oct 5, 1904,Otago Witness,82)

On long strains, attach one strainer to each wire midway between strainer posts. (Jul 1959,NZ Dairy Exporter,59)

Generations of farmers have bent fencing staples trying to attach their fencing wire to puriri strainer posts. (Jan 1992,NZ Geographic,112)

GUTHRIE-SMITH A kerosene case nailed to the top of a strainer-post. (1921,Tutira,148)

At the ends of each fence should be a good strainer post stayed in position in the normal way. (Apr 15, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,347)

KERR Once he dented the brand-new three-tonner's mudguard on a strainer post. (2000,High Times in the High Country,28)

straining post¶

noun. = strainer (post)

See: strainer post

[NOTES: incl fig]

HENDERSON The foundation of a good seven-wire fence is to have good sound straining posts placed down in the ground to about four feet depth, and securely braced or stayed against the strain of the wire. (1965,Open Country,54)

LYTTELTON, from Wairau - 4 barrels rum, N. Edwards and Co.; 1 box, Beatson; 1 box, Snow; 1 pkge, Jones; 7 straining-posts, Braithwaite. (Aug 2, 1864,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

Przemysl helped to hold the gap between the rivers, and acted as a straining-post which could take much of the tension exerted by the enemy on the Russian fronts. (Jun 5, 1915,Evening Post,5)

A great variety of iron fencing standards, straining posts, and tools for straining wire fencing are show by the New Zealand Implement Company and J. Mackay of Nelson... This is the kind of standard that would be most suitable for fencing off breaks of turnips or for any temporary purpose, as no staples of fastenings of any kind are required. (1886,AJHR,H-5/4)

A notch should be cut in each straining post about three feet from the ground. (1883,Brett's Colonists Guide,77)

stranger¶

noun. [Rural] a neighbour's sheep that has slipped the boundary-fence or the notice of a boundary-keeper.

See: stray

ORMOND Straggling sheep left on the run - 50 stranger sheep also. (1864,JD Ormond Stockbook 1864-1866,1)

ORMOND Found 6 rams (strangers) in flock. (Mar 31, 1866,JD Ormond Stockbook 1864-1866)

Drafted sheep from back country. G Goodall got 100 of Waikari sheep, no other strangers. (Jan 21, 1879,Tutira Station Diary)

STUDHOLME We took turns in sending the strangers back; one year we would drive back the sheep belonging to Blue Cliffs, Otaio, or other neighbouring stations, and collect our own from them. (1940,Te Waimate,124)

MOWAT Drafted the sheep that John brought down from Walkers yesterday, only got a few ewes and some strangers. (Mar 2, 1943,Alexander Mowat Diaries)

MILLS ET AL There may be 'strangers' in the mob. These he will pick up by their various earmarks and run off into a separate pen if available ... (1964,Practical Guide to Handling Dogs and Stock,72)

strangers: neighbour's sheep amongst your own - his stragglers. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,81)

SALISBURY Collecting strangers, that is sheep belonging to neighbours which was also a job that was looked forward to as it usually meant a cup of tea or a feed and meeting other people. (1994,I Was So Lucky,106)

SALISBURY About this time I was also sent down to Waipaoa Station to collect strangers. (1994,I Was So Lucky,107)

strangle teats¶

verb. [Rural] to milk cows.

GORDON The introduction to Out of Town said it was a celebration of those who 'cut scrub, drained swamps, sowed swedes and strangled teats.' (2001,Fresh Fields,16)

strap-toothed whale¶

noun.

[NOTES: strap-toothed whale]

"The animal is one of the so-called beaked whales, and is known as the strap-toothed whale, on account of the two peculiar teeth which grow from the lower jaw and curve over the upper jaw, so that the mouth is almost prevented from opening. .." (Mar 29, 1912,Colonist (Nelson),6)

Believed from a description to be of the strap-toothed variety, a whale of about 35ft in length and over 6ft high has been washed up at Ocean Beach, Whatipu, about a mile from Huia, states the "New Zealand Herald." (Feb 14, 1940,Evening Post,8)

The strap-toothed whale ( Mesoplodon layardi ) is, at least when adult, at once recognized by the two long strap-shaped teeth which, originating from the mandible in front of the hinder end of the symphysis, grow upwards and backwards, eventually curving round the upper jaw and preventing the mouth from being opened beyond a certain distance. (1922,NZ Journal of Science & Technology,5/136) [NOTES: (Oliver)]

Strathmore weed¶

noun. a shrubby native weed of spp Pimelea, poisonous to stock.

CROWE Pimelea prostrata Pinatoro; Strathmore weed... Part eaten : The berries. No other part of the plants should be eaten as Strathmore weed has been known to poison livestock. (1997,Field Guide to Native Edible Plants of NZ,43)

LEVY Strathmore weed, a low-growing shrubby plant found on poor, friable soils, if eaten when stock are forced on it in a holding paddock, may cause staggers and death, particularly if the stock are afterwards driven. (1970,Grasslands of NZ,305)

A waggon broke down at Miki Miki, Wairarapa; the horses were turned out, and partook of "Strathmore weed," which the local horses will not touch. (Sep 6, 1910,Poverty Bay Herald,3)

I am forwarding you specimens of the Strathmore weed. I interviewed Mr Hewer, coach-proprietor, Strathmore and Stratford, re the matter. He informs me that the weed is very injurious to strange horses..This Strathmore weed proved to be two species of native plants, Pimelea lyalli and P prostrata. (1900,Leaflets for Farmers,55 2)

The first case of Strathmore weed poisoning known in the Wairarapa occurred some days ago ... (Sep 21, 1908,Dominion Post,5)

Strathmore weed (Pimelea prostrata) this plant is fairly widespread throughout New Zealand. (Feb 24, 1966,NZ Farmer,29)

I am forwarding you specimens of the Strathmore weed. I interviewed Mr. Hewer, coach-proprietor, Strathmore and Stratford, re the matter. He informs me that the weed is very injurious to strange horses... This Strathmore weed proved to be two species of native plants, Pimelea lyalli and P. prostrata. (1900,Leaflets for Farmers,No. 55/2)

Mr. Gooch, Stratford cab proprietor, has had the misfortune to lose a horse, the animal having been poisoned by the "Strathmore weed," about which there was some talk a little while ago. (Jul 14, 1899,Hawera & Normanby Star,2)

The first case of Strathmore weed poisoning known in the Wairarapa occurred some days ago, when out of a number of draught horses stricken two died... He noticed.. little clumps of a weed very like the garden daphne growing in the paddock where the horses had been feeding... The weed in question is native, and known by the names Mataikairanga and Strathmore. The name Strathmore was given after the name of the locality near Hawera, where the first reported case of animal sickness through eating the weed was made known some eight years ago... The first symptoms of Strathmore poisoning are loss of appetite, and then dullness. followed by tremors, staggering, distressed breathing, and convulsions, which in the severe cases are followed by death. (Sep 21, 1908,Dominion,5)

Strathmore Weed (Pimelea prostrata. The first outbreak.. was due to the plant Pimelea prostrata commonly known in the North island as "Strathmore weed". (1926,NZ Journal of Agriculture,XXXIII/102)

There are several species of Pimelea in New Zealand... It is known in New Zealand generally as Strathmore weed, from the name of a Taranaki town where posoning of horses was first recorded. (1934,NZ Journal of Agriculture,XLIX/152)

DSIR Strip cropping: rolling land is sometimes cropped in contour strips separated by strips of pasture. (1947,Report,170) [NOTES: Soils & Related Agricultural Aspects of Mid-Hawke's Bay]

RIDDOLLS The electric fence gives control of stock with a minimum of fencing material, and is ideal for movable fencing, eg, for break or strip grazing of pasture and forage crops. (1958,Farm Engineering,428)

CONNELL & HADFIELD Also called strip grazing, break feeding, and close folding, rationed grazing is a still more intensive method of achieving controlled grazing. (1961,Agriculture,304)

David is highly pleased with the strip grazing as he is using 25% less hay and the hoggets are in better order. (Nov 13, 1975,NZ Farmer,19)

Mr Parks runs an all-grass system with winter ewe management a mixture of strip and block grazing. (Jun 15, 1994,NZ Farmer,31)

WHITE & HODGSON Strip grazing is where a temporary electric fence is used to offer a strip of pasture in a paddock each day to the herd/flock, normally without a back fence to keep animals off previously grazed pasture. Block grazing differs from strip grazing to the extent that the herd/flock is offered pasture on a daily basis with both a front and back temporaray electric fence, and daily blocks are rectangular in shape. (1999,NZ Pasture and Crop Science,156)

The rare striped skink is a good case in point. Of medium size - up to 76 mm SVL - this species is attractively marked with a copper-brown stripe flecked with fawn down its back and a broad pale-brown stripe along each side. (Jul 2000,NZ Geographic,78)

There were 100 men working at and in connection with the stripper mill, and when the new machines were installed there would be not fewer than 150. (May 2, 1941,Evening Post,9)

It is the stripper which makes that peculiar wild beast-like, snarling noise, which can be heard for miles. (Feb 13, 1890,Otago Witness,9)

R.M. Crosbie, Nelson, submitted a [flax] stripper with a revolving beater-bar, strong and easily cleaned and take to pieces. (1895,Ann. Rep. Dept of Agriculture,III/53)

HUNT In 1867 an Auckland engineer invented a machine which extracted fibre from the flax plant by beating the leaves between two metallic surfaces - a revolving metal drum (equipped with beaters) and a fixed metal bar... This machine (which became known as a 'stripper') heralded the beginning of large-scale production of flax fibre. (1987,Foxton 1888-1988,111)

HUNT A second stripper.. was erected alongside the mill in 1889. (1987,Foxton 1888-1988,13)

Each stripping machine affords employment to a couple of boys; one of them feeds and the other takes the fibre away; but the company intend having the process so much altered that the flax will be delivered by means of a revolving-table. .. Each stripper will put through about one ton of green flax, producing about 4 cwt. of finished fibre per diem. (Mar 17, 1869,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,4) [NOTES: Reprinted from the Lyttelton Times 16 February.]

noun. (grass-seed stripper)

Grass-seed strippers were exhibited by Messrs. Duncan and Both and MacDonald. (1886,AJHR,H-5/7)

stripper-keeper¶

noun. [Rural] a worker involved in the processing of hemp from flax.

WANTED by a thoroughly Competent Man, a situation as Engine-driver and Stripper-keeper. (Aug 16, 1889,Manawatu Herald,3)

Many stripper-keepers allow their strippers to run too long before tuning them up again ... (Feb 15, 1912,NZ Journal of Agriculture,135)

stripper-slip¶

noun. [Rural] [flax harvesting] a worker or machine that strips flax fibre.

On the 17th July the Commissioners were given a practical demonstation of the patent stripper-slips machine. This machine undoubtedly does its work well, but the Commissioners are of the opinion that stripper-slips are really a form of waste which should be eliminated from the industry. The combined machine improves the colour of the stripper-slips, and afterwards turns them into marketable tow. (Oct 20, 1914,NZ Journal of Agriculture,263)

stripping¶

noun. [Rural] the removing of the first and last milk from a cow's udder.

By double stripping you make sure that all the cows are thoroughly milked. (Aug 1, 1919,NZ Farmer,1064)

There has been no stripping for four years. (May 1, 1945,NZ Dairy Exporter,14)

No stripping has been done at milkings for the last 15 years. (1956,Farms & Stations of NZ Vol I,123)

noun. [Rural] the continuous cultivating and cropping of land in the same ground, usually with the same crop.

noun.

To prevent contamination of the milk after it has been drawn, some precautions unusual in New Zealand are taken. The main one is the use of a covered stripping-bucket. (Oct 1938,NZ Journal of Agriculture,348)

He put the stripping weight on, took the cups off the next cow, swung the gate open with one hand and flipped the back rope on the hook with the other. (Mar 10, 1960,NZ Dairy Exporter,96)

strippings¶

noun.

See: stripping

Wherever [the milking machines] were used the cows soon went dry, owing to the machines not having attained the knack of drawing the "strippings" of the last of the milk. When cows are not "stripped" properly. as every dairyman knows, they soon go dry. (Jun 19, 1890,Otago Witness,7)

Silently and swiftly there steals up "She who drinks skim milk or steals the strippings," and into that bucket goes her nose. (Dec 18, 1926,NZ Dairy Produce Exporter,36)

strong-eye/strong-eyed¶

adjective. [Rural] [of heading dogs] that control sheep with a hypnotic stare.

The naturally careless or, to use the shepherd's term, "slack" dog can never be taught to perform like this, though he may up to a certain stage be infinitely less trouble than the strong-eyed, keen one, but, then, no matter what amount of trouble is taken with him, he always requires to be kept at high pressure in training to keep him up to the mark, whereas with the other, once perfect always so. (Nov 9, 1899,Otago Witness,39)

LILICO ... how to prevent the several faults that the strong-eyed young dog will assuredly acquire if not taken in time. (1934,Sheep Dog Memoirs,4)

HARTLEY If the pup is from a 'strong-eye' strain he will begin to stalk the rubber and the trainer can begin to employ the whistle of command intended to bring him on to sheep. (1949,Shepherd's Dogs, The,5)

LOUGHNAN strong-eye: intensive and powerful use of eye by a dog. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,81)

adjective. [Rural] [of sheep] primed without being overfat.

Strong-wool growers united yesterday to form a farmer co-operative that will market 20 per cent of the national clip. (Oct 9, 2002,Dominion Post,C3)

adjective. [Rural] [of sheep] flyblown.

Once an animal has been struck, the infestation area spreads rapidly. (2002,Lifestyle Farmer,Oct/Nov 62)

stubbies¶

noun. skimpy men's shorts

[NOTES: usually in pluraL]

Knox, nearing 50, still takes to the road several timnes a year and performs - the man in jandals and stubbies - mixing songs with drinks, making us mad, or making us laugh... (Aug 20, 2002,Dominion Post,B9)

[Advt] Sporty stubbies. Available now in sizes 78cm - 104 cm. Cool, comfortable polyester cotton mix makes these great wearing... Basic stubbies. These are also available in the colours as the sporty stubbies... Sizes are 78 cm - 104 cm and feature front and hip pocket. (Oct 22, 1980,Evening Post,20)

Almost 30 years ago Aussie businessman Philip Levy saw a gap in the market for an inexpensive, all-purpose men's short. What else could you get for less than $2 other than a handkerchief or a crass tie in a bargain bin? They were launched in July 1972 and within two days inhabitants of Brisbane, always a place of limited cullture and unlimited heat, had snapped up 50,000 pairs.... The pollution of New Zealand male wardrobes with stubbies began with the first exports in 1977... "The stubby was a cheap short, revolting. They reminded me of rugby shorts only ruigby shorts were more comfortable. They're still out there in country towns... They were revolting, everything exposed. You couldn't afford to sit down in them." (Jan 9, 2002,Evening Post,10)

[Hdg] And they call it Stubbie love... Writer Dianna Dekker called them zipless. Wrong. The sporty Stubbies in your picture had a zip. A very fine zip... What Stubbies did have was class, plenty of ass and a little pocket perfect for keeping change and stones without disturbing your stride - walk, skip or run. (Jan 16, 2002,Evening Post,6)

I refuse to wear jandals anywhere, and will not entertain picnic pals who wear stubbies, but an esky is the only way to go for picnic packaging. (Feb 2, 2002,Dominion Weekend Magazine,4)

The tennis gear is a tribute to those 1970 icons of mate attire, stubbies. "Pixie and I had both been to different op shops and without knowing it had bought the same stubbies. To do something with them, we went for a run - just a fitness run - both wearing our stubbies. People were laughing so much we thought we would do it again... Because our stubbies were awfully short we'd stop at intersections and do lunges and stuff. (Nov 3, 2004,Capital Times,5)

Now at one point there were 42,000 people in the Post Office, every person was in there in seniority order, with your name, your grading, your rank, your salary. When you applied for a job, 30 others might apply for it with similar status, so the Promotion Board would refer back to the stud book - which everyone had access to - and it would show you that 'he gets that because he's the most senior person, not the most suitable, the most senior person. stuff¶

verb. [Rural] [dummying] to apply for a land ballot for a family member.

Under the heading of 'Stuffing the Ballot' the Canterbury Times shows how the above can be done. The Canterbury Commissioner furnishes even more striking illustrations of the method in which the ballot is 'stuffed' by eager applicants. 'Out of three hundred and three applicants at our last ballot,' Mr Humphries says, 'there were no fewer than forty-two single women, besides a great number of married women, and there was not one of either condition that did not bear the same name as some one of the male applicants.' Mr John Hay, the Southland Commissioner says that he can see no way by which the system provided by the Act of 1892 could be improved upon, but he strongly urges that only one mode of ballot for all tenures and all classes of land should be adopted, and that this should prevent more than one member of a family applying for the same section. (Nov 5, 1903,Hawera Star,2)

New Zealand straddles the southern arm of the so-called Subtropical Gyre, the massive counter-clockwise flow of water around the South Pacific. From South America, water moves westward to Australia, turns south and strengthens as the East Australian Current; then off New South Wales it turns east as the Tasman Front, passing around Northland to spawn the weak West Auckland current (extending to Auckland) and the strong East Auckland Current (extending to East Cape). (Nov 2002,Forest & Bird,306/15)

sultana bird¶

noun. pukeko, Porphyrio melanotus

noun.
