summer¶

verb.

See: also winter verb

NEWTON Apart from summering the ewes from weaning time until the rams go out the actual Rainbow country is now carrying only the 400-odd breeding cows. (1973,Big Country,29,(1977))

WHEELER Our 45,000 halfbreds summer high on the Nevis block,' says Frank,and winter far below on sunny spurs.' (1982,Historic Sheep Stations of NZ,7)

verb. [Rural] [high country] to carry stock through the summer season on land that is unproductive, dangerous and snow-covered during winter.

The two-tooths are summered on the high country. (Sep 27, 1951,NZ Farmer,9)

NEWTON It is bushbound country, and although it is a real death trap in the winter could summer a tremendous number of sheep. (1952,High Country Journey,140)

NEWTON In the good old days, a fence ran from Lake Tennyson through to the Wairau and the country beyond the fence, the Rainbow block, summered the two-tooth ewes and the entire wether flock - anything up to 20,000 sheep. (1952,High Country Journey,188)

NEWTON St James, in those days, summered the entire wether flock on the Clarence country.. (1964,Straggle Muster,6)

NEWTON Mt White summer their whole flock up the Esk.. ibid. 10 The bulk of the flock is summered at the head of the Esk. (1964,Straggle Muster,9)

NEWTON ... it is real shingle country but, for all its harsh appearance, it summered the bulk of the wether flock ... (1973,Big Country of the South Island,193)

ASPINALL Mr Harry Barker summered cattle in both Aspiring and Shovel Flats. (1993,Farming Under Aspiring,40)

summer block¶

noun. [Rural] [high country] an area in where sheep can only safely graze without risk of snowfalls in summer.

ANDERSON I was caught up immediately in the routine of drafting, of the cheerful bedlam in the yards before the flocks are shorn and transferred to their summer blocks. (1966,Over the River,132)

HALL On a miserable wet day after the spring shearing, Jim Metherell is driving these sheep back out to their summer block. (1987,Shepherd's Year, A,19)

HALL This beautiful stretch of water is Lake Luna, on Mt Creighton Station, and we're driving a mob of wethers past on the way in from their summer block. (1987,Shepherd's Year, A,76)

summer burn¶

noun. [Rural] [S.I. high country] an annual summer burning of coarse tussock.

Summer burns. These are by far the most destructive of all. The summer burns actually kill out the tussock. (Jun 15, 1910,NZ Journal of Agriculture,10)

CUMBERLAND In the heavy rains which almost inevitably follow summer burns .. sheet wash is rampant. (1944,Soil Erosion in New Zealand,19)

summer country¶

noun. [Rural] [high country] land that can be grazed only in the summer when free of snow.

MORRIS Summer country n., in New Zealand (South Island) country which can be used in summer only; mountain land in Otago and Canterbury, above a certain level. (1898,Austral English,444)

Of all those stations possessing country above 3,000 ft, the grazing-ground is more or less sharply divided off into what is called 'summer country' and 'winter country.' (Jun 15, 1910,NZ Journal of Agriculture,7)

.. the merino is mustered from the summer country at levels between 7,000 ft. and 8,000 ft., and within the shadow of the glaciers. (Feb 20, 1937,NZ Journal of Agriculture,98)

COOP During the mid-summer and autumn the sheep are pushed up on to the 'summer country' - the highest part of the run. (1949,Animal Nutrition,94)

This is all high altitude log country - grand summer country, but subject to snow in winter. (1969,Big Country of the North Island,245)

Beyond Queenstown there is absolutely nothing but pastoral country, most of it summer country at that, which I affirm from personal knowledge cannot be profitably worked except in very extensive tracts. (May 14, 1881,Otago Witness,13)

To what Mr Duncan had said it might be answered that a flock-owner there would, for his own protection, and for stock farming an pasturing purposes, buy winter country as well as summer country. (May 30, 1868,Otago Witness,7)

This is all good summer country, and also includes some first-class land on the flat known as the Upper Taieri Flat, and adjoining what was, until last year, Patearoa Station, but which is now all cut up. (Feb 8, 1905,Otago Witness,35)

noun. [Rural] land that does not dry out in summer.

Good summer country with excellent stock handling facilities. (May 5, 2001,Hawke's Bay Today,21)

noun. a high-country farming term for an area that is usable in summer as pasture, but not in winter.

See: winter country

"In those cases where there is no natural boundary between winter and summer country it would on many runs be practicable to fence off the unsafe country, with a view to ensuring that sheep mustered down on to the winter country in the autumn could not drift back between storms on to unsafe country and be lost, were it not for the heavy expense involved in fencing ..." (Aug 13, 1938,Evening Post,13)

MORRIS Summer Country, n. In New Zealand (South Island), country which can be used in summer only; mountain land in Otago and Canterbury, above a certain level. (1898,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),444)

PERRY The higher country, and that having a southerly aspect, which is likely to hold snow to some depth in the winter months, is termed `summer country', for it is unsafe for sheep in the winter, and is used only for summer grazing. (1922,NZ Sheepfarming,88)

NEWTON In high country a lot of the country, i.e., the hinterland and higher areas, carries too much snow to carry any sheep in the winter. Accordingly, it is only stocked in the summer and is known as summer country.' Conversely, safe country which is saved for the winter iswinter country.' (1949,High Country Days,197) [NOTES: (1950), (Gloss.)]

STRONACH This block is good summer country and splendid mustering. (1953,Musterer on Molesworth,9)

SHARPE ... sheep which act like that stay out on the summer country until they are either found in a `straggler muster' or buried by snow. (1962,Country Occasions,123)

summer country n. in South Island of New Zealand country which can be used for grazing only in summer. (1966,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Whitcombe's),626)

NEWTON Summer country: high-country run comprises summer and winter country. The former is the higher or shady country which carries a lot of snow during the winter and is then uunsafe for stock. Winter country is the lower and sunnier country on which sheep can safely be carried during the winter. (1966,Boss's Story, The,189) [NOTES: (Gloss.)]

Summer country n. in S. Is. of N.Z., country which can be used for grazing in summer only. (1968,NZ Contemp. Dict. Suppl. (Collins),19)

MCCASKILL The Molesworth cows have to travel up to 120 miles moving from summer to winter country and back. (1969,Molesworth,182)

WHEELER In the South Island the terms summer' andwinter' country have a very real meaning for the station owner. (1973,Historic Sheep Stations NI,92)

NEWTON A large proportion of the country - the shady and hindermost areas - is suitable for summer grazing only ... Such country is known as `summer country' (1947,Wayleggo,14)

summ'er country n. land that can only be used in the summer. (1929,Whitcombe's Etym. Dict. Aust-NZ Suppl.,11) [NOTES: actual dates: c1929-1936]

GRAY I rode up the Orari run ... to put a mob of sheep back on to the Blue Mountain, which is the farthest of their summer country. (Feb 27, 1876,Quiet with the Hills,42) [NOTES: 1876 Feb 27 Peache Jnl in 1970 Gray Quiet with the Hills 42]

In the lower subalpine belt tall tussock grassland is common in both Islands, but its major development is in South Island. ... Largely used by the station-owner as his `summer country' it has not escaped the modifying influences of stock and fire, ... (1936,Handbook for New Zealand (ANZAAS),95) [NOTES: (Allan)]

noun.

The river once reached becomes the natural highway, being navigable for light-draught steamers and boats to almost the southern extremity of the district; and the land being practically level along the proper right bank, there is also, with few and trifling impediments, chiefly creeks, a good summer road all the way, either at the river side or at a little distance from it. (Aug 1, 1868,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,4)

summer sickness¶

noun. a form of food poisoning, a usually brief but prostrating illness characterised by vomiting and diarrhoea and associated with hot weather.

[NOTES: Jim writes : Not in DNZE or overseas dictionaries available to me. the British equivalent may be summer flu, a term I have seen in English fiction but itself not in dictionaries. Summer sickness has perhaps become less common with the ubiquity of refrigeration.I recall press references to it in the 50s and 60s. It is also more medically diagnosed these days - e.g. it is attributed to salmonella or campylobacter or even giardia. It has been associated with the collection of rainwater from house roofs - that can be contaminated by bird droppings.]

.. our usually filled to overflowing Chemistry 1 lecture had only about 20 students present. On enquiring why, my New Zealand friend said in a hushed, embarrassed voice that it was "summer sickness". adding that the citizens of Auckland were laid low every year with this. I asked her what summer sickness was, and she quietly told me it was vomiting and "the runs". (Sep 13, 2008,Listener (New Zealand Listener),5)

Barbara Anderson And some Spanish cream, which she had read somewhere was an excellent culture medium for the summer-sickness bug if left unrefrigerated. (1992,Portrait of the Artist's Wife,42)

Phyllis Davis in letter to husband Geoff We are still putting up with Pupuke [Lake] water in the taps in spite of all the agitation some months ago and there is still the business of fetching fresh water from the tanks. Which reminds me there has been a tremendous amount of summer sickness in Auckland and most families have suffered ... (Apr 11, 1941,Personal Communication)

"If we got the summer sickness, instead of drinking lemonade, we always had L&P." (Feb 24, 2007,Press, The,D2)

.. Professor L.H. Briggs, associate professor of chemistry at Auckland University College, has spent 30 years studying the properties of these plants .. Koromiko, for instance, has been used to cure summer sickness ... (Oct 12, 1955,NZ Herald,2)

Phyllis Davis in letter to husband Geoff I believe I had a slight attack of summer sickness as it is politely called here. I see in the paper that it is very widespread in Auckland. (Mar 30, 1941,Personal Communication)

Summer sickness is very prevalent and many business firms have a high proportion of absentees amongst staff. (Mar 29, 1941,NZ Herald,3)

summer spinach¶

noun. Tetragonia expansa , = NZ SPINACH

See: spinach

CRAIK Discovered in Cook's first voyage by Sir Joseph Banks, and was boiled and eaten as greens by the crew.' CTN, p. 183 <i>Tetragonia expansa </i> summer spinach -->[?is this Andersen] Among the useful plants to which we are indebted to New Zealand, we must not forget their summer spinach (T. expansa), which was discovered in Cook's first voyage by Sir Joseph Banks, andwas boiled and eaten as greens' by the crew. It was afterwards seen by Forster at Tangataboo, though it was not used by the natives; but Thunberg found the Japanese aquainted with its value as a pot-herb. It was introduced into Kew Gardens in 1772; but the first account of it as a vegetable worthy of cultivation was published ... in the Annales d'Agriculture for 1809. [Craik is often quoted on this matter: e.g. in 1841 Ward Information Relative to NZ 49.] (1830,New Zealanders, The,183) [NOTES: (And)]

MORRIS Spinach, New Zealand, n. Tetragonia expansa , Murr., N.O. Ficoideae ; called also Iceplant in Tasmania ... discovered in New Zealand by Captain Cook, though it is also found in Japan and South America. Its top leaves are eaten as spinach, and Cook introduced it to England, where it is also known as Summer Spinach. (1898,Austral English,429)

sun helmet¶

noun.

[NOTES: Jim writes : NSOD defines this as a cork etc helmet formerly worn by whites in the tropics. Macquarie 1981 is similar., (Not in Collins). But I recall it from the 30s (and later?) as the name for a child's cloth sunhat made with an extension at the back to protect the neck. I have found no citations, however. DEH adds: I remember these. I think they disappeared when troops returned from the Middle East and the cult of protection from the sun gave way to the cult of the sun. They may now have returned, judging by photos of primary school children wearing similar headwear.]

TURNER A sun hat or sun helmet, a cloth hat of the same shape as a sou'wester, was frequently worn by children a generation ago. (1966,English Language in Aust. & NZ, The,173)

[Drosera spathulata] (1870,TrNZI,2) [NOTES: (AND)]

FEATON DROSERA. (Linn.) The Sundew ... one can scarcely examine a plant without finding the wings and legs of insects, on one or more of the leaves. ... This extremely interesting genus is represented in New Zealand by six species, all of which are said to digest meats, and are known to [142] the settlers as `Fly-catchers'. (1889,Art Album NZ Flora,141-142)

Drosera spathulata Sun dew (1870,TrNZI,2/124) [NOTES: (ARMSTRONG BOTANY CANTERBURY)]

[caption] Sub-alpine and lowland swamps may provide a habitat for sundew (Drosera spathulata). (1983,Land of the Mist,66)

DAWSON Several species of the insect catching sundews (Drosera) with their glistening leaf glands are frequently present [in mountain bogs]. (1988,Forest Vines to Snow Tussocks,183)

[Caption] Sundews (Drosera,..) are tiny carnivorous plants found in boggy ground. Sticky droplets on the hairy red leaves ensnare small insects, which the plant consumes using its enzymes... One often sees the carcasses of small insects caught in their leaves - a grim clue as to how these plants get their nitrogen and phosphorus. (Sep 2001,NZ Geographic,No. 53/47)

sun-dog¶

noun. known to mountaineers as `the maid of the mist'

39 About Sun Dogs'.</i> And mention of [Charles] Douglas ... recalls a curious theory he propounded ... when we were discussing meteorological phenomena of the high Alps, and in particular thesun dog', that luminous coloured halo produced by the sun's rays shining through a damp and vaporous atmosphere. (Mar 20, 1920,Quick March)

sundown¶

verb.

PASCOE I have plenty of Tucker here certainly, but I haven't a cent in my pocket - I am literally without a pocket -and would have to sundown my way amongst strangers ... (1957,Mr Explorer Douglas,153) [NOTES: 1891 Jan 29 Douglas in 1957 Mr Explorer Douglas 153]

sundowner¶

noun. formerly, a swagger who arrived at a place at sunset so that he could claim traditional food and shelter without the need to work for it.

noun. [Rural] a swagger or itinerant who arrives at a property in the evening when work is finished, hoping for a bed.

They are delighted to see the "sundowner" again; to see the "swagger" on the roads. (1909,NZ Parliamentary Debates,146/102)

Only let him occupy one of the many roadside farms to which he alludes for a few months, and be subjected to the daily and hourly pesterings to which we are subjected by hundreds of swagmen, sundowners, and other loafers - the majority of whom cannot do a day's work when they get the chance - and it strikes me very forcibly that his goodly Samaritan learnings [sic] would receive such a shock that he would experience no difficulty in understanding the reception he met with. (Feb 22, 1871,Bruce Herald,6)

WILSON .. they were odd members of the idle class known as the swaggers and sundowners. (1894,In the Land of the Tui,248)

LOUGHNAN sundowner: (ii): a swagger who times his arrival just at the right time for the evening meal. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,81)

The moon was shining brightly as the three "sundowners" approached. (Feb 12, 1887,Auckland Weekly News,8)

BRADSHAW The [peripatetic labourers] in the colony are known by the name of Swaggers' orSundowners' Swaggers, because they carry a swag or bundle on their backs ... Sundowners, because they never approach a habitable place before sundown lest they should be requested to take a further stroll. (1883,New Zealand As It Is,26)

Old sun-downers told ... yarns of ferocious mastiffs ... It was quite certain that the most persistent swagger had never obtained the inevitable feed and shake down there. (1889,Zealandia,1/31)

DAVIDSON Kelly [a detective] had on more than one ocasion swagged it for weary miles after his prey as an orthodox sundowner, or in taking his turn in the harvest field, or at a threshing mill. (1889,Stories of NZ Life,2)

WILSON About these wayfarers Mr. Cameron had something to tell me, for they were odd members of the idle class known as swaggers and sundowners ... [249] So far as I could discriminate, swaggers (those who, snail-like, carry their worldly possessions on their backs) are men occasionally willing to do a day's work for a night's lodging and a couple of meals. Sundowners (those who have no possessions to carry) walk from station to station during the day, and, sleeping under a haystack until sunset, make their appearance at that hour before the `whares' or huts provided for them, and demand from the owners supper and shelter, which are generally granted. (1894,In the Land of the Tui,248, 249) [NOTES: 1891 Dec 21 in 1894 Land of the Tui]

MORRIS a tramp who takes care to arrive at a station at sundown, so that he shall be provided with tucker',/I>(q.v.) at the squatter's cost: one of those who go about the country seeking work and devoutly hoping they may not find it. (1898,Austral English,444)

Possibly before next harvest we shall hear a cry raised by the squatter.. that those who are about do not want work; that they are sundowners. (Mar 20, 1890,Otago Witness,15)

BRADSHAW fn The term swagger' is applied to a man who tramps from place to place in quest of work, carrying all his worldly goods in a swag, or bundle, thrown across his back. Thesun-downer' is one who tramps from place to place pretending to seek employment, but, as a matter of fact living upon the supper and breakfast with which he is supplied at most up-country stations. He fears to arrive too early in the day, lest he should be requested to seek a bed elsewhere, and hence the name with which he has been endowed. (1888,New Zealand Of Today,181)

PYKE Now, a sundowner' ortussocker' for the terms are synonymous - is a pastoral loafer; one who loiters about till dusk, and then makes for the nearest station or hut, to beg for shelter and food. (1873,Wild Will Enderby,Bk III ch x 105) [NOTES: (1889)]

D'AVIGDOR Those who join it [the professional unemployed] are distinguished from sundowners' ... by working chiefly in towns instead of in the open country, and in swarms instead of alone. It has, therefore, several advantages oversundowning'. The professional unemployed need not tramp ten, twelve, or twenty miles a day, and he always has congenial company. (1888,Antipodean Notes,154)

D'AVIGDOR The language of the Australian Colonies is not in the least like the last mentioned [`Daily telagraphese']. (1888,Antipodean Notes,165) [NOTES: [check spg???]]

noun. [Rural] a dog reluctant to work in hot sunny conditions [ preferring to lie in the shade or in a water-trough. ]

See: sooner

STRONACH My dogs I tied to the iron fence outside the hotel. They were...; Maud, a bob-tailed bitch, one of the borrowed ones and already under suspicion as a 'sundowner.' (1953,Musterer on Molesworth,2)

MACNICOL The playful pup grew to a large .. dog. He proved too easy-going and too much of a 'sundowner' for hill work. (1967,Skippers' Canyon,129)

SINCLAIR He looked a true sundowner, and this job he was, but get him on lambs breaking at a gate at shearing time and he'd toil until his feet were raw. (1973,Boot in the Stirrup,95)

LOUGHNAN sundowner: (i) a lazy dog. (1981,Loughnan Glossary,81)

MAF Sundowner: Dog that leaves its work, especially when hot and noisy. A lazy dog. (1982,MAF Agricultural Glossary,25)

SCURR Sundowner:- A dog that won't work in the sun. [sun-downer] (2000,Rabbiters' Glossary,2)

sunfish¶

noun.

In May last the wanganui Museum was fortunate to secure an unusually large specimen of the sun-fish (Orthagoriscus mola). (1897,TrNZI,29/286)

Closer inspection revealed a more unusual beast; one very large sunfish (Mola mola), dead after stranding on the fast outgoing tide. (Jun 9, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),32)

But landing the big one is rare, and curses are heard loud and clear when a heavy line gets gaffs in hand and hearts beating, only for a huge but worthless sunfish to be hauled to the surface... Sunfish are almost invariably alive, despite being hooked for hours on end, and are cut free. "They've got a big, floppy fin and look you right in the eye and while they get our hopes up and are a real hassle, I still love them," Mr Kerr said. (May 15, 2004,Dominion Post,C1)

noun. a piece of cloth at the back of a hat to protect the neck from the sun

GEE Then he picked up a cloth cap from the edge of the stand and set it on his head. The sun-flap covered his neck. (1992,Going West,267)

noun.

Seldom in modern times has a natural manifestation in the physical world attracted such universal attention or excited so much admiration and wonder as the recent so-called sun-glows. (1884,TrNZI,17/357) [NOTES: (MEESON)]

sunnies¶

noun. sunglasses

In the essential category [of extra equipment] are helmet, sunnies (to ward off flying insects as well as UV),.. a chainbreaker to fix bent links.. and a banana or two. (Feb 1997,North & South,98)

A staunch-looking Maori swaggers up the front steps of the Reserve Bank Building in downtown Christchurch. Leathers, wrap-around sunnies - he acts as if he owns the place. (Feb 10, 2001,Dominion,28)

Hold the sunnies. (Apr 2004,TV1) [NOTES: Fair Go]

The sunnies make him look mean, though. (Mar 24, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),33)

He keeps searching for something - Gucci sunnies, cellphone, his soul? - in the pockets of his engineered-denim ensemble and slumping down. (Jul 7, 2001,Listener (New Zealand Listener),65)

I had found my sunnies and had them on and thought, 'I'll die with my sunglasses on so I won't look bad when they find me'. (Jan 11, 2003,Dominion Post,A11)

[Advt] Hot Summer Prices on Summer Sunnies (Dec 12, 2001,Dominion,4)

sunny face¶

noun. [Rural] a north-facing slope on hill country.

See: shady face

Sheep seem all right as all on steep sunny faces which have been partly cleared. (Jul 11, 1957,St Leonard's Station Diary,126) [NOTES: in MacFarlane (1946) Amuri]

It [spiked blue-grass] appears to be able to establish itself on dry sunny faces which have become denuded of vegetation. (Aug 15, 1911,NZ Journal of Agriculture,6)

CUMBERLAND After less than a century's occupance, the very appearance and shape of sunny and shady faces stand in marked contrast. (1944,Soil Erosion in New Zealand,76)

The unimproved pastures consist of silver tussock, sweet vernal, and browntop, and they tend to revert to matagouri on the sunny faces and to fern on the shady faces. (Feb 15, 1956,NZ Journal of Agriculture,121)

From a Departmental trial of inoculated clover seed sown with and without fertiliser on a sunny face and a dark face it has been found that fertiliser is necessary to enable a quick establishment of clover plants, particularly on the sunny face, though a reasonable strike on the unfertilised dark face was obtained. (Jul 1959,NZ Journal of Agriculture,19)

New fencing has been done mainly to divide the broken areas from the flat, and to separate the shady from the sunny faces. (Sep 27, 1962,NZ Farmer,2)

.. in the main if possible, the northerly or sunny faces of the farm should be separated from the southerly aspects. (Nov 1963,NZ Journal of Agriculture,381)

The hogget block on Tara Hills consists of four faces, two sunny and two dark. (Nov 21, 1963,NZ Farmer,54)

Banks Peninsular [sic] farms divide into main areas, the sunny and the shady faces whose needs are totally different. (Sep 1985,NZ Journal of Agriculture,16)

STACEY I was told to take 600 weaned lambs out over the Robinson Saddle to the Elliott country and spread them over the sunny faces for the winter. (1996,Tales of a Tussock Jumper,61)

sunporch¶

noun.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes: Not in English or NZ dictionaries (including OED) but recorded in Macquarie 1981. Still current.]

DUCKWORTH The sunporch is okay for occasional dirty stop-outs like yourself, but I don't want it cluttered with boy's junk. (1989,Message from Harpo, A,263) [NOTES: check quote]

In the 1960s.. further additions were made - an enclosed sun-porch on the front and an irregularly shaped bathroom at the rear. (May 1994,NZ Historic Places,47/35)

sunstrike¶

noun. the sun striking through a car window and dazzling the driver

[NOTES: Jim writes : Used in the latest NZ Road Code. I have not seen it elsewhere and there is no dictionary reference. It seems unlikely to be a distinctive NZ word. Check with British equivalent of Road Code.]

...possibly a bit of sunstrike in the Ngauranga Gorge. (Oct 14, 2003,TV1) [NOTES: Jim Hickey, weather forecast]

Crash analyst Senior Constable Trevor Buchanan of Dunedin police said in his statement that weather conditions, sunstrike and dust were not considered contributing factors to the crash. (Dec 17, 2003,Dominion Post,A5)

People crossing Moorefield Road near the Johnsonville Medical Centre on a sunny day should not rely on the pedestrian crossing for safety after sunstrike was blamed for two accidents recently. (Jul 16, 2003,Norwester,4)

Sunstrike can occur at sunrise or sunset, when the sun's rays hit your windscreen at a low angle. This can make it difficult, or even impossible to see... Be prepared for possible sunstrike when driving at sunrise or sunset, particularly when turning or driving towards the sun. (Apr 1999,Official New Zealand Road Code, The,78)

"The sun comes through on the windscreen." "Sunstrike.""No, dirtstrike." (May 31, 2001,Radio NZ / National Radio,Kim Hill/ Bennett)

[Hdg] Court rejects elderly driver's sunstrike plea. An octogenarian driver who tried to get the Court of Appeal to overturn his conviction for hitting two women because of sunstrike has had his appeal dismissed. (Nov 11, 2003,Dominion Post,A6)

[Hdg] Sunstrike made bus invisible say witnesses. Witnesses at the trial of a Wellington man whose car crashed into the back of a trolley bus, fatally injuring its driver, said yesterday that "blinding sunstrike" rendered the bus invisible just before the accident... Despite regular trips to the airport, she said she had never seen sunstrike as bad, describing the phenomenon as "an accident waiting to happen." (Nov 14, 2001,Dominion,3)

super¶

noun. [abbreviation; informal] short for superphosphate

...it was found that with regular and heavy application of cobaltized super, pastures improved and livestock did well. (Aug 2004,NZ Memories,No. 49/39)

The seed was mixed with is own weight of serpentine super. (Feb 1960,NZ Dairy Exporter,8)

Mr Cockayne stated that.. "it had been definitely proved that Lime and Sulphur was the best fertiliser to use." (Jul 31, 1926,NZ Dairy Exporter,47)

A dressing of DDT to get rid of the myriad grass grubs and some super and potash to kick the pasture along would turn the trick. (Sep 1959,NZ Dairy Exporter,33)

BROWN "You know how you insist on your 13 cwt. Mangold manure, also on lime and super, etc., for topdressing exhausted pastures?" (1939,Farmer's Wife, The,49)

I think that it's much wiser to use the crushed rock phosphate than super. (May 29, 1959,Listener (New Zealand Listener),26)

Farmers in other areas may be better advised to spend some money on super and potash. (Jan 1972,NZ Dairy Exporter,00) [NOTES: Check page]

Putting on a dressing of lime in the autumn, followed by super in the spring, is good practice. (Nov 1922,NZ Journal of Agriculture,315)

Mr Cockayne stated that.. "it had been definitely proved that lime and super was the best fertiliser to use." (Jan 31, 1926,NZ Dairy Produce Exporter,47)

Farmers in other areas may be better advised to spend some time on super and potash. (Jan 1972,NZ Dairy Exporter,10)

noun.

[NOTES: beekeeping]

The "supers".. are the name given to a hollow, four-walled shell which is placed above the original hive when it is full, and so gives the bees added incentive to build more honey. (Oct 29, 1947,NZ Observer,21)

noun. high octane petrol

The Mobil station in town sells super for about 98 cents a litre. (Nov 1993,Geological Society of NZ Newsletter,102/69)

verb. [Rural] to add superphosphate fertiliser to pasture [ to increase fertility and carrying capacity.]

GUTHRIE-SMITH The 'lure of improvements' is still to me as great as ever - the particular form of vice now being indulged in is 'supering' light land! (1929,BLANK ENTRY,194) [NOTES: in Woodhouse (1959) Guthrie-Smith of Tutira]

noun. a southern hemisphere rugby union competition, superseded by Super 14 in 2006 and by Super 15 in 2011

Maybe they should hold the next Super 12 match in the daytime, or still at night but without floodlights and give the players glow in the dark jumpers... (May 10, 2003,Listener (New Zealand Listener),6)

Each year the Super 12, the showbiz end of 115-man rugby, bursts out like an impatient cork from a bottle of Daniel le Brun. (Mar 3, 2000,Evening Post,22)

[Hdg] From squadie [sic] to the man: Steinmetz steps up ... For the first two [years] he had more need of a pair of tweezers than rugby boots, for not once was he required for Super 12 action despite being part of the Hurricanes squad. (Apr 22, 2000,Sunday Star Times,B3)

(1907,NZ Statutes,7 Edw. VII 63/286)

supervision¶

noun. a sentence introduced by the Criminal Justice Act 1985 to replace release on probation.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes : It subjects the offender to the oversight and control of a probation officer. Supervision in England is primarily a welfare order placing a child under local authority or probation officer supervision, although it may also be an adjunct to a suspended sentence. Note that the term probation order is no longer used in NZ, but probation officer is, and that pre-sentence report corresponds to the English social inquiry report.]

When surf patrols effected a mass rescueof 26 people from heavy seas atScarborough, Western Australia,.. theysaved a New Zealander who had done asmuch for surf life-saving as anyone has. (Apr 21, 1954,NZ Truth,12)

surf province¶

noun.

This control has been widened and strengthened until today there are 10 district [life-saving] associations, often wrongly called `surf provinces'. (1966,Encyclopaedia of New Zealand, An,3/328)

surf racer¶

noun.

Surf racers don't wait for summer to get back in the water. (Apr 11, 2001,Capital Times,2)

surf racing¶

noun.

Lyall Bay surf racing team Craig Jones, Nic Mulcahy and Ryan Johnson overcame boisterous seas to win gold in the Premier single rescue event on in front of their home clubrooms on the weekend. (Apr 11, 2001,Capital Times,2)

surface creep¶

noun. [Rural] wind and water erosion where soil is moved downhill en masse.

WHITE & HODGSON The process by which wind moves soil are suspension, saltation and surface creep. (1999,Pasture Plants & Pastures of NZ,300)

WHITE & HODGSON surface creep: the slow mass movement of soil down slopes, primarily under the influence of gravity but facilitated by saturation with water. (1999,Pasture Plants & Pastures of NZ,310)

surface stuff¶

noun.

Lowrie and party are carting surface stuff to the battery for treatment. (Oct 17, 1910,Thames Star,2)

Of the three who remained, one was a young man of evident experience as a digger, who kindly shewed us the various holes in the vicinity that they had sunk, and the various parts of the creek and its branches in which they, as well as their predecessors, had been engaged in washing what may be termed [t]he surface stuff. (Mar 21, 1856,Daily Southern Cross,3)

A recent flood had slightly damaged the protective works; but this had been rectified and the ground was getting richer and shallower, so that they had less surface stuff to move for the amount of gold obtained. (Nov 29, 1894,Otago Witness,17)

The surface stuff of the Tapu Company is improving, and five tons yesterday from a surface leader realised more than any other crushing has done at Tapu. (May 20, 1870,Daily Southern Cross,3)

Mr. Hall yesterday took off 50oz. of amalgam off the top plates, after passing through about 5 tons of the surface stuff from the top of the leaders; the crushing is continuing. (Oct 19, 1868,Daily Southern Cross,4)

This week the dredge obtained 18oz, and was only working surface stuff. (May 14, 1901,Grey River Argus,2)

CHUDLEIGH I commenced making shafts to test for gold. The water stoped me but I shall try the surface stuff. (Jul 21, 1887,Diary,356)

surface work¶

noun.

The second mode [of tin mining], or streaming, is much more primitive and easy. This may be termed `surface work', as it is generally carried on in moorland plains and valleys, in shallow pits of only a few feet in depth, and at but a small distance below the surface of the ground. (1900,TrNZI,32/311) [NOTES: (Colenso Cornish Tin Mines)]

surfaceman¶

noun. a workman who keeps road surfaces in repair, and verges and gutters clear.

The County clerk, Piako County, wrote asking what rate of pay the County is giving surfacemen, foremen and ordinary labourers. (Dec 7, 1917,Ohinemuri Gazette,3)

Salaries .. Surface man [GBP]117 0 0. (Dec 1, 1862,Otago Daily Times,6)

The council decided to instruct surfacemen to clear the roadsides where there were long stretches of unoccupied land. (Jan 27, 1939,Evening Post,8)

We understand surface men will be employed on the Great South Road during the winter. (May 30, 1863,Daily Southern Cross,10)

I want to know how it is that one surfaceman can monopolise work by employing his sons, whilst other surfacemen get orders to dismiss their relations at once? (Aug 30, 1882,Tuapeka Times,6)

Attention was drawn, amongst other matters, to the near termination of the engagements of surfacemen, nightman, and lamplighter. (Jun 9, 1899,Timaru Herald,3)

After hearing Mr Ross, the Board decided to instruct one of the surfacemen to attend to the necessary repairs. (Feb 13, 1905,Wanganui Herald,6)

GUTHRIE-SMITH ... the only bipeds who upon their feet utilize the King's Highway are surfacemen and swaggers, ... the surfacemen preoccupied with the more material problems of metal and mud. (1927,Bird Life on Island & Shore,/15)

Studholme ... as we were putting 120 head [of cattle] across the Waitaki Bridge, something frightened them, they set off at top speed, ... nearly killing two surfacemen, who had foolishly come on to the bridge at the far end. (1940,Te Waimate,141,1954) [NOTES: -]

Within a few miles of Lawrence, I noticed two surfacemen just emerging from their homes - about half-past nine - apparently traversing the locality in search of something to do, while the condition of the roads was such that they need not have gone ten yards without finding an abundance of scope for their energies. A lttle further on two other surfacers were at work, with overcoats comfortably buttoned up to the chin, pretending to rake gravel into the wheel-ruts on a new-made piece of road. (Jun 6, 1877,Tapanui Courier) [NOTES: Tapanui Courier in 1977 Marks Hammer and Tap 371]

surfacer¶

noun. OED 2. one who mines near the surface

HAAST As soon as a storm has subsided, the beachers' orsurfacers,' as they are called, examine the coast-line near their houses. When they come upon one of the rich spots, the fine particles of gold being often visible to the naked eye, they at once remove the black layer of sand out of the reach of the tide, and wash it when convenient. (1882,Geology of the Provinces of Canterbury & Westland,/159) [NOTES: [AND 1852, 1863] -->1879]

MAY SURFACER: on the West Coast, applied to a digger working a sea-beach claim. (1967,West Coast Gold Rushes,/528) [NOTES: (1962)]

ELDER (1930,Goldseekers and Bushrangers in NZ,155) [NOTES: [see BEACHER]]

noun. a surfaceman (q.v. 1877 cit.)

A little further on two other surfacers were at work, with overcoats comfortably buttoned up to the chin, pretending to rake gravel into the wheel ruts on a new made piece of road. (Jun 6, 1877,Tuapeka Times,3)

surface-sow¶

verb. [Rural] to sow seed on the surface of soil so that it germinates there, rather than being tilled.

It is thought that this harrow will act as a substitute for the plough on cleared fern land, where it is intended to surface sow. (Sep 13, 1881,Bay of Plenty Times,2)

An extension of the leases would encourage the tenants to surface sow thier land, and, in the event of further severe weather, they could then save their sheep by hay feeding. (Sep 7, 1904,Otago Witness,8)

.. a large portion of which a fire has run; having been surface-sown with grass. (1902,Settler's Handbook of NZ, The,2)

You do not state whether you require grass land for sheep or cattle, whether the seed is to be surface-sown or after the plough. (Mar 1907,NZ Farmer,207)

It is intended to surface-sow with grass-seed (principally Chewing's fescue, clovers, cocksfoot and crested dogstail) a block of mountainous country ... (Sep 15, 1913,NZ Journal of Agriculture,343)

Several courses were open to us:- (1.) to burn the existing growth, and surface-sow with a mixture of grass-seeds. (May 20, 1921,NZ Journal of Agriculture,260)

STUDHOLME Grass was surface-sown on the burnt patches ... (1940,Te Waimate,101)

Following the initial drainage work, the earlier farmers, after cutting down the remaining bush and scrub, burned off and surface sowed the land. (Jan 15, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,11)

ELLISON Allison had broken in part of his and also had burnt and surface-sown some hills ... [surface sow] (1956,Whirinaki Valley, The,38)

surface-sowing¶

noun. [Rural] the sowing of pasture grass seeds on the surface of the soil, without tilling.

By far too little attention is paid to surface-sowing of grass seed by those who have stretches of land in the native state. (Mar 5, 1896,Otago Witness,5)

His main improvement has been cutting down tea-tree on the better land, burning off, and surface-sowing: and he now has 120 acres down in turnips. (Jan 30, 1913,Evening Post,11)

JOHNSTON Rode out to run and looked at surface sowing. (Apr 1, 1874,Johnston Diary)

Its [cocksfoot's] chief value lies in it being a strong, hardy grower, and specially adapted for surface sowing upon bushland, hillsides and other places ... (May 1909,NZ Farmer,338)

A little surface sowing with European grasses sometimes takes place after the spring burn. (Jun 15, 1910,NZ Journal of Agriculture,8)

.. districts which were either firstly infested with blackberry or Californian thistle; or secondly, bush-districts where the surface-sowing of grass-seed was the customary method of laying down grass. (May 22, 1914,Hawke's Bay Herald,3)

What grasses are best adapted for surface-sowing on this class of country, bearing in mind the dryness of the summer months? (May 20, 1921,NZ Journal of Agriculture,313)

Pastures were slowly established by felling the bush in winter and spring, burning the fallen timber and underscrub in the summer, and surface sowing English grasses and clovers on the ash of the burns. (Apr 16, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,346)

TAIT By underscrubbing, burning off and surface sowing of seed, a beginning was made in the grim struggle of developing the land into a farm. (1958,Farms & Stations of NZ Vol III,123)

On the other side similar country is being developed by surface sowing, fertiliser and stocking. [surface sowing] (Aug 13, 1970,NZ Farmer,51)

surface-sown¶

adjective. [Rural] [of land] sown in seed without tillage.

This finely undulating ground is exhausted by hundreds of years growth of fern and ti-tree, which returns nothing to the soil, so that surface-sown grass is found to be a failure. (Mar 25, 1876,Daily Southern Cross,1)

There were 137 acres under crop and 150 acres of rough feed surface-sown. (Oct 13, 1866,Weekly News,5)

The uncultivated land was surface sown, and the grass has grown for over twenty years .. high fern, flax and tutu covered the ground. (May 12, 1888,Egmont Star,6)

I have seen turnips surface sown in a bush clearing the first opportunity after burning off the felled bush, and the yield has been exceptionally good. (Sep 1888,Egmont Star,22)

450 acres burnt fern (surface-sown.) (Jun 3, 1909,Weekly News,4)

This is usually surface-sown country, and may be limestone hills in cocksfoot and ratstail, or sandstone hills in danthonia and browntop. (Jan 15, 1945,Journal of the Polynesian Society,13)

The improvement of the surface-sown hill-country grazing land will be very important in the post-war economy of the Dominion. (Jul 16, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,13)

The more fertile surface-sown hill country of the North Island. [surface sown] (Feb 20, 1950,NZ Journal of Agriculture,121)

surface-sown country¶

noun. [Rural] land upon which seed has been sown without tillage [usually hill country or land difficult to plough.]

This is usually surface-sown country, and may be limestone hills in cocksfoot and ratstail, or sandstone hills in danthonia and browntop. (Jan 15, 1945,NZ Journal of Agriculture,13)

surfacing¶

noun.

There is plenty of water close to this patch of surfacing. (Jan 28, 1855,Nelson Examiner,2)

MORRIS Surfacing, n. (1) Wash-dirt lying on the surface of the ground. (2) verbal. Gold-digging on the surface of the ground. [1861] (1898,Austral English,446)

HARPER [South Westland] An old hatter' living just above the beach, and looking out for patches of beach gold, orsurfacing' which was thrown up by the surf. (1946,Memories of Mountains,?)

HARPER [gold-bearing black sand] A few diggers live here [Gillespies Beach, West Coast], working for gold on the beach ... This beach combing' is sometimes profitable, as a great deal ofsurfacing', or black gold-bearing sand, is now and then deposited after a storm, ... (1896,Pioneer Work in the Alps of NZ,83)

surfer¶

noun. a surfacer q.v.

VON HAAST Generally the greater portion of the sand is removed, but in favourable spots, sheltered either by a slight indentation in the coast-line, or by some large pieces of drifted timber, its heavier particles remain; these consist [529] of black iron-sand (both magnetic and titaniferous oxide of iron) associated with small garnets and with gold. These black layers are often one or two inches thick, and repose upon coarse quartzose sands. As soon as a storm has subsided, the beachers' orsurfers' as they are called, examine the coastline near their houses. When they come upon one of the rich spots, the fine particles of gold being often visible to the naked eye, they at once remove the black layer of sand out of the reach of the tide, and wash it when convenient. (1948,Life & Times of Sir Julius von Haast,528-529) [NOTES: 1868 Von Haast in 1948 Von Haast Julius Von Haast]

surf-hurdling¶

noun.

[NOTES: cf. surfing]

BAKER Surf-hurdling seems to be ... New Zealand ... though there is reason to suspect it is used extensively in the Pacific. It describes the practice of landing goods from a ship to shore in an open boat on an exposed coastlne. The taking of goods, especially wool, from shore to ship in an open boat is also termed surf-hurdling. (1941,NZ Slang,/57)

SOLJAK New Zealanders have coined or adapted many expressions to meet local requirements, as illustrated by the following: ... surf hurdling: landing goods from ship to shore, or vice versa, in an open boat (1946,New Zealand: Pacific Pioneer,118)

surfie¶

noun. a surfaceman

noun.

Surfie, lover of Auckland's west coast,.. Harvey's flair and unpredictability provide refreshing relief from the pedestrian and the everyday. (Jan 2000,North & South,63)

I spent a year and a half after that bumming around Taranaki beaches as a surfie. (Dec 1998,Mana,37)

"There are plenty of great whites out here. "I've caught half a dozen or so, sometimes with surfies just a few hundred metres inside. White pointers like to hunt in murky water and they hunt Hector's dolphins." (Mar 30, 2002,Listener (New Zealand Listener),27)

Bruce is a reconstructed surfie. (Dec 27, 1986,Listener (New Zealand Listener),26)

BARNETT & WOLFE By the end of the decade [1960s] therewas a sizeable subculture of surfers, or'surfies' as they were known. (1993,At The Beach,42)

The ocean side of Raglan is where the surfies are found. (2000,Directions,Summer 2000 No. 46 : 22)

It's a fair haul around the coast, but worth the trip even if it's just to see the Great Whites chasing the surfies. (Dec 12, 2001,Evening Post Drive,3)

surfie chick¶

noun. a surfer's girlfriend or follower

An Australian magazine.. allotted two pages among over 1000 to an interview with a "surfie chick" which itemised the number of men she had known and the amount she had spent on bikinis. (Dec 27, 1986,Listener (New Zealand Listener),27)

surfing¶

noun. the bringing ashore of goods and supplies by means of surfboats launched from a ship

He added a rider that regulations were necessary requiring surf boats and oil launches used for surfing to be licensed. (Aug 7, 1913,Evening Post,4)

What I would strongly urge upon the Government is that two thoroughly competent and reliable surfmen be carried in addition to the officers, to always take charge of the boats whilst surfing; they should of course be paid more than the ordinary A.B. (Jun 13, 1899,Evening Post,2)

Inner Harbour and Gisborne Reach - / Tallow and wool away; / Barrels and bales, with a curse for each, / Surfing 'em out from a sounding beach, / Wet to the back with spray. (Dec 23, 1905,Evening Post,12)

To all old experienced hands on the West Coast, and looking back to the Hokitika disasters in the old days, emphatically it will not suit at all surfing on this Coast. (May 31, 1880,Grey River Argus,2)

MASTERS Owing to lack of harbours, mail, supplies and produce had to be what was termed, surfed. On arrival, the coastal boat would anchor in the most convenient position offshore. A connecting link between shore and ship would then be made by bullock or horse wagons going out as far into the surf as possible, and being met by surf boats from the ship. Surfing was a tricky job ... (1959,Tales of the Mails,134)

MASTERS We then headed for Wangaehu, where, in his young days, as a bullock driver for Mr. Saint-Hill Alex had taken part in the surfing of wool. (1959,Tales of the Mails,138)

surl¶

noun. surliness

There have been occasions when we have been overcome with a sense of surl on the part of serving sorts. (Dec 14, 2003,Sunday (Sunday Star Times Magazine),18)

survey camp¶

noun.

If you have lived in a survey camp.. you are in a receptive mood for this article. (Nov 24, 1938,NZ Observer,11)

survey district¶

noun.

[NOTES: Jim Cameron writes : This is not specifically recorded in DNZE but is referred to under the entry block. A block is a primary division of a survey district; a section (among many other meanings) is the usual secondary division. Eg "section 12, Block IV, Tiffin Survey District". See also deposited plan.]

surveyor's station¶

noun.

GODLEY ... Harewood forest where there is a surveyor's station (shed). (Nov 1850,Letters,147,1950)

The Brilliant went up the channel of the Waimea, some distance beyond the surveyors' station, to land her cargo, where she now lies in three fathom at low water. (Jul 16, 1842,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,74)

suspension¶

noun.

Also worrying, last year there were almost 22,000 stand-downs (students removed for up to five days) and suspensions (student's future decided by board of trustees) from schools. (Dec 22, 2002,Sunday Star Times,C6)

A suspension is more serious [sc. than a stand-down]. It can lead to expulsion. It's initially imposed by the principal but students and parents are entitled to make arguments at a board of trustees meeting about the suspension before the board decides on further action. sustainable logging¶

phrase.

Despite testing his caucus colleagues' patience with his advocacy of "sustainable logging", he is not immune from the flak that the party is now attracting (Sep 21, 1999,Dominion,9)

Suter's skink¶

noun. [Environment] a skink unique in New Zealand for laying eggs rather than live young, and for its habit of foraging under water.

See: egg-laying skink

[NOTES: Egg-laying skink Oligosoma suteri aka Diving skink]

[Oligosoma species... are generally found in fairly open areas, and are active during the day (except for Suter's skink which is atypical of the genus in various respects).Ibid. 78 Unique among Oligosoma species, Suter's skink is nocturnal. (Jul 2000,NZ Geographic,No. 47/67)

swag¶

noun. a load, often as a bundle

According to promise, I hasten to inform you that on the 16th ult. we started for these mines on foot, each carrying his "swag" - mine weighed 50 lbs. (Oct 16, 1852,Otago Witness,2)

The swags included 5 lb boiled beef, 3 lb ham, 5 lb ship-biscuits.. and a tent. (1910,TrNZI,42/14)

He did not see a swag open in the loft of the stables on the morning of the 29th, nor did he hear the police removed one from the loft. (Jul 1, 1899,Marlborough Express,4)

He did not see a swag open in the loft of the stables on the morning of the 29th, nor did he hear the police had removed one from the loft. (Jul 1, 1899,Marlborough Express,4)

They don't know where their "swags" are. (Dec 31, 1863,Lyttelton Times,4)

I here experienced the utility of tying my baggage to the side of the canoe, had I not adopted this method, I should possibly have lost the whole of my swag . (Sep 9, 1842,NZ Colonist,4)

BLAIR He left the Wiapori [sic] with only his swag / The cradle he left to his debtors. (1889,Lay of the Old Identities, The,48)

verb. to carry as or in a swag

The pigs were ''swagged ''' into Dunedin and thence taken to the heads where they were sold to the whalers for flour, sugar, &c. (Jan 2, 1890,Otago Daily Times,9)

As you have just been through this district, you can realise the position of some of the settlers here, being forced to do their improvements, swagging their tucker through standing bush, and some of them will have to swag their grass-seed on to their burns, not having even a pack track. (May 27, 1904,Taranaki Herald,7)

A few of the Waikato diggers have left for the Anatoki, owing to the difficulties they had to encounter in "swagging" their provisions over "Kill Devil Hill." (Feb 15, 1860,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,2)

The route we found to be over a spur, on the north side, covered with low brush (higher than the saddle), thence descending into a small creek, following which you again enter the Taramakau, and have to follow it for three miles, through a gorge, scrambling over the rocks and wading through the water with much difficulty, greatly increased by our supplies, which then weighed over 1,200 lbs., and had to be swagged. (Aug 24, 1859,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,5)

verb. [Rural] to travel on foot, carrying a swag.

See: also swag it

It is the intention of Henderson to get about four hundredweight of stone as quickly as possible, which will be swagged down to Knowles' camp, and then packed to Palmerston. (Sep 10, 1880,Taranaki Herald,3)

The following day preparations were made for attacking Mount Cook, and provisions were swagged up to a height of 7500ft, where Green bivouacked. (Jan 29, 1890,Poverty Bay Herald,3) [NOTES: (Reprinted from the Christchurch Press)]

OWEN & PERKINS I took to the track, I came up north and swagged with a character that was well known on the track at that time. (1986,Speaking for Ourselves,68)

PASCOE He left his camp standing on 9 March, swagged down the river, launched the canoe and floated down the stream to reach the coast after dark. (1959,Great Days in NZ Exploration,140)

CHINN After a while two of my working companions suggested that we "swag" our way through the country. (1963,Packtrack to Highway,43)

swag it¶

verb.

2 Accounts from the Twelve-Mile continue very good, although a considerable number have taken the fever, and swagged it off. (Mar 30, 1865,North Otago Times)

True, during the past few weeks, men if really desirous of obtaining work might have swagged it into the Piako and Waikato districts, but it would have been in the face of some little real and a large amount of imaginary difficulty had they done so, and in such case the latter is quite as great a deterrent as the former. (Apr 4, 1876,Waikato Times,2)

Next day swagged it to the Manapouri station. (Mar 6, 1890,Otago Witness,35)

I once 'swagged it' from Toko to beyond Strathmore in mid-winter, and can truthfully state that no man has any business to take his wife and children to such an out-of-the-way portion of 'God's Own Forsaken Country.' (Apr 10, 1908,Hawera Star,5)

VANCE To and from stations, shearers 'swagged it,' travelling in groups of about half a dozen for companionship and for safety in crossing rivers. (1965,High Endeavour,51)

VANCE The fast transport which we take for granted today makes us forget that in earlier times, the station hand who wanted to go to another station, or downcountry, had to 'swag it.' (1965,High Endeavour,67)

LOUGHNAN swag: a musterer will complain if he has to swag it, as this means that he has to carry his bedroll out to the camp instead of tying it to a packsaddle. [swag it] (1981,Loughnan Glossary,81)

swag strap¶

noun. a strap on which to attach a bundle which is often carried on the bag like a pack.

[NOTES: 2. fig. LOOK (OUT) FOR ONE'S SWAG STRAPS -->1937 Partridge Dictionary Slang 1190 Swag-straps, look for one's. `To consider leaving one's job in search of another', B., 1941: New Zealand (mostly rural): late C. 19-20. In Australia, shearers' s.: C. 20: B., 1942. -->1941 Baker NZ Slang 41 We may recall the country use of the phrase to look for one's swagstraps, to consider leaving one's job in search of another. -->1951 Acland Early Canterbury Runs Glossary 374 Look out for one's swag straps.- Thinking of leaving his billet. -->express: look out for one's swag straps -->1934 January 20 The Press 15 *Looking out for his swag straps.-Thinking of leaving his billet. -->1966 Phillipps Maori Life and Custom 172 In some localities a kawe, or swag strap, made from the bark of the lacebark tree ... encircled the baby's body so that it could not fall to the ground [from its mother's back].]

The western river descent is good travelling for a mile, but then, from the precipitous falls over which the water cascades, it is impracticable: in proof of which, one of the men, who by accident went down, had to be hauled back again by the swag straps, or else would have had to remain as food for the rats. (Aug 24, 1859,Nelson Examiner and New Zealand Chronicle,5)

Tents, Box cords, Swag Straps ... (Oct 11, 1861,Daily Southern Cross,2)

In rolling the blankets around this waif that had been human, and fastening them together, scarce a word was spoken, and then only in a low tone; and taking our swag straps to lower the body carefully to the bottom of the grave, we laid him in his last resting place, and so, without the rites of his church, a mourner's tear, or his friends' knowledge, he was covered up, and passed away from earth, its joys and troubles. (Mar 5, 1872,North Otago Times,4)

About 300 sets of swag straps were sent out this morning per coach to Pungarehu for the use of detachments that may be ordered to traverse the bush. (Oct 28, 1881,Taranaki Herald,2)

swagger/swaggie¶

noun. [Rural] swagman [ an itinerant who wanders from one rural property to the next, often for work but always for food.]

Along the Kiwitea district nowadays (and nights) no swaggers are to be seen. (Feb 20, 1909,Evening Post,9)

When the swaggie called at Tarkalion's farm the fire was out, and there were only ten matches in the house. (Oct 12, 1895,Taranaki Herald,2)

ROBERTS I had passed three swaggers on foot today, I think the first I have seen since leaving top house. (May 16, 1856,Roberts Diary,63) [NOTES: in Hawkins (1957) Beyond the Waimakiriri]

WILLIAMS Yet work he never seemed to get, The disappointed swagger. (1889,Colonial Couplets,28)

C W RICHMOND .. they travel the country as 'swaggers' and 'sundowners' - claiming everywhere at the stations food and free quarters. (Mar 29, 1894,Letter,598) [NOTES: in Scholefield (1960) Richmond-Atkinson Papers II]

WILSON .. they were odd members of the idle class known as the swaggers or swaggies and sundowners ... (1894,In the Land of the Tui,248)

noun.

Sept 23, 1884... Swagger came here tonight. (1959,Women of Westland,37) [NOTES: 2nd edition]

They are delighted to see the "sundowner" again, to see the "swagger" on the roads. (1909,NZ Parliamentary Debates,146/102)

Elva Sonntag tells with gentless and compassion how Russian Jack, last of the swaggers, visited her Wairarapa home. (Jul 10, 1982,Listener (New Zealand Listener),87)

He [Russian Jack - Barrett Krumer] set out to walk to Wellington to find another ship and spent the next 53 years on the road as a kindly and highly regarded gentleman swagger who would not accept hospitality without first working for it. (Jul 19, 2000,Dominion,13)

According to the local press a Swaggers' Club has been formed in the neighbourhood of Carterton. (Jul 9, 1904,NZ Observer,16)

A small child observed a "swaggy" approaching and ran in terror to his mother, telling her there was "a funny thing just like Father coming up the track." (Jun 14, 1913,NZ Observer,17)

OWEN & PERKINS I was down to what swaggies call a 'heatwave knot' - down to a very light bedroll. (1986,Speaking for Ourselves,70)

It was comparatively easy to induce an old swaggie to spend a night in the hut. ... The shack was surrounded, the poor old swaggie arrested and later sentenced to imprisonment for being found in possession of an illicit still. (Mar 17, 1923,NZ Truth,6)

He has the swagger's stoop. (Nov 11, 1897,Otago Witness,49)

A swaggie, and two or three lime-kilnworkers, were sitting in the bar. (Sep 13, 1919,Hawke's Bay Herald,7)

OWEN & PERKINS Now these blokes like Riverina Dick, the established swagmen, they didn't seek company - the fair dinkum swagger, he liked to be on his own - but they're prepared to take on an apprentice. (1986,Speaking for Ourselves,68)

The swaggers of my childhood were silent men. (Nov 29, 1986,Listener (New Zealand Listener),69)

swaggers' hut¶

noun. [Rural] a sheep station shelter for swaggers and other itinerants.

swaggers' whare¶

noun. [Rural] a station shelter for swaggers and other itinerants.

swagging¶

noun.

With the advance of civilization, game of all kinds has retreated into the wilds, and once where the swamp turkey abounded and the wild duck loved to feed is now devoid of all game except perhaps in the early morning as the birds are moving to some favoured feeding ground or to the sanctuaries, which are great institutions in their way, as they not only provide the birds with a shelter out of range of their natural enemy and his fowling piece, as well as a breeding ground, but they are responsible for keeping the birds at certain periods in those localities from which ere this they would have migrated, had it not been for the sanctuaries which at the present moment are packed with game seeking security from the sportsman's gun. swill¶

The word "dregs" refers to the drippings from the taps in a bar and to the overflow from the glasses as they are filled. These dregs are sometimes called "swill".. or "slops". When they are mixed with beer for sale the resultant liquid is colloquially known as "Wompo". The term has been in use among barmen for as long as one experienced licensee could recollect - from twenty to thirty years.., and it is known to the man in the street. SWNZ¶

noun. [acronym; Environment] Sustainable Winegrowing New Zealand

Growers are required to self-assess using a SWNZ scorecard and are audited each year for compliance. (2006,Internet - see Notes,1) [NOTES: http://www.huia.net.nz/about/winegrowing.asp]

SWNZ is a voluntary programme, which has nevertheless been widely adopted by the industry and now covers about 65 per cent of the country's vineyard area and 70 per cent of total production. But to get everyone toeing the green line, from the 2010 vintage, wineries must participate in an audited sutainability scheme - SWNZ or an alternative - to be included in New Zealand Winegrowers' global marketing programme. (Aug 8, 2007,Viva,16)

Are you interested in joining 'SWNZ for wineries' when it goes live in 2004? (2003,Internet - see Notes,1) [NOTES: http://nzwine.com/assets/SWNZ_for_wineries_requirements.pdf]

POLACK Among the piscivorous tribes, are those well known in Europe under the appellations of snapper, tench, haddocks, pollock, salmon, gurnets, john dory, hakes, bream, sword-fish, elephant-fish, diodons, pipe-fish, cod, parrot-fish, flounders, skate, cat and dog-fish, sting-rays, eels. - Among the larger tribes that sport in shoals in the vicinity of the shore, are, sperm-whales, called para[as-acute] paraua[a3-acute] (physeter macrocephalus); black whale, mungu nui (black physeter); right whale, tohora (balaena mysticetus); finback, (balaena physalis); sun-fish (diodon mola); large-lipped whale (balaena mysticetus); large-lipped whale (balaena musculus); hump-back (balaena gibbosa); shark, mango (squalus); hammer-head (zygaena); pilots, (scomber); flying-fish (exocaetus volitans); and an infinity of others, besides a great variety of testaceous and crustaceous fishes that almost cover the rocks under water, such as clams, muscles, oysters, crays, cuttles, limpets, wilks, gigantic muscles, a foot in length, cockles, sea-ears, sea-eggs, star-fish, mutton-fish, &c.; from the latter the pearl is procured which they insert in the eyes of their carved images and boxes. (1840,Manners & Customs of the NZers,1/202 fn)
